ミラー指数.desc: Sets of integers that describe planes and directions in a crystal. For a plane, the reciprocals of its intercepts on the axes are reduced to the smallest integer ratio and written (hkl); a direction is written [uvw].

about.h: Finding the indices of a plane
about.p: The Miller indices of a plane are found by the following steps. First, read the points where the plane meets the crystal axes x, y and z (the intercepts) in units of the lattice parameters a, b and c. Next, take the reciprocal of each, clear fractions to get the smallest integer ratio, and write the result in parentheses as (hkl). For example, if the intercepts are 1, 2 and ∞, the reciprocals are 1, 1/2 and 0, giving (210). A plane parallel to an axis has an infinite intercept on it, so that index is 0. Negative intercepts are shown with a bar over the number. If the plane passes through the origin, move the origin to a neighboring lattice point before reading the intercepts.

about.h: Direction indices and families of equivalent planes
about.p: Direction indices are the coordinates of a point reached by moving from the origin in that direction, reduced to the smallest integer ratio and written in square brackets as [uvw]. In cubic crystals many planes are equivalent by symmetry; (100), (010), (001) and so on are written together in braces as {100}, and equivalent directions together in angle brackets as <100>. Cubic crystals have the convenient property that the [hkl] direction is exactly perpendicular to the (hkl) plane, so angles between planes can also be found from dot products of directions. Note that this property does not hold in general for tetragonal or hexagonal crystals.

The interplanar spacing of a cubic crystal is calculated as d = a/√(h² + k² + l²). Planes with larger indices have smaller spacings, and their XRD peaks appear at higher angles. Depending on the arrangement of atoms in the unit cell, however, diffraction from some planes cancels out and does not appear. In BCC only planes with h + k + l even diffract, and in FCC only planes with h, k and l all even or all odd (the extinction rules). Correctly indexing the peaks is the starting point for determining lattice parameters and identifying phases.

For hexagonal crystals such as HCP, Miller–Bravais indices (hkil) are widely used, with three axes a₁, a₂ and a₃ at 120° to each other in the basal plane plus the c axis. The relation i = −(h + k) holds, and the advantage is that equivalent planes have the same pattern of numbers. For example, the basal plane is (0001) and prism planes take the form {10-10}. These indices appear constantly in materials and device specifications, for wafer orientations, the orientation of epitaxial films and the notation of slip systems, so it pays to be able to picture a plane's orientation from its indices.

faq.q: What do the different kinds of brackets mean in Miller indices?
faq.a: (hkl) denotes a single plane, {hkl} a family of planes equivalent by symmetry, [uvw] a single direction, and <uvw> a family of equivalent directions. The slip system of FCC, for example, is written {111}<110>.

faq.q: How do I write a negative intercept?
faq.a: A negative index obtained after taking the reciprocal is shown with a bar over the number. In plain text a minus sign is sometimes used instead, as in (1-10).

faq.q: Are the (200) and (100) planes the same plane?
faq.a: They have the same orientation, but (200) denotes a set of planes with half the spacing of (100). In XRD, the second-order reflection from (100) is treated as a first-order reflection from the (200) planes with half the spacing.

面心立方格子.desc: A crystal structure (FCC) with atoms at the corners of the cube and at the center of each face. The unit cell contains 4 atoms; the coordination number is 12 and the packing factor about 0.74. Examples include Cu, Al and Ni.

about.p: FCC is the structure obtained by stacking the most densely packed {111} planes in the sequence ABCABC…, and it is also called cubic close-packed. The atoms touch along the face diagonals, so the nearest-neighbor distance is a/√2; for copper (a = 0.3615 nm) it is about 0.256 nm. Besides Cu, Al, Ni, Au, Ag and Pb, γ-iron and austenitic stainless steels also have this structure. A major reason to study it is that most FCC metals are soft, highly ductile and easy to form.

about.h: Many slip systems, and no embrittlement at low temperature
about.p: FCC has 12 slip systems of the {111}<110> type, 4 planes × 3 directions, which easily satisfy the five independent slip systems a polycrystal needs to change shape freely. In addition, the stress needed to move dislocations (the Peierls stress) is small and depends little on temperature. FCC metals therefore stay ductile even at liquid-nitrogen temperature and show no distinct ductile-to-brittle transition like BCC metals. This is why aluminum alloys and austenitic stainless steels are chosen for LNG tanks and cryogenic vessels.

about.h: Size and number of interstitial sites
about.p: An FCC unit cell contains a net 4 octahedral sites, at the body center and the midpoints of the 12 edges, and 8 tetrahedral sites, at the centers of the eight small cubes into which the cell can be divided. In the hard-sphere model, the largest sphere that fits has a radius about 0.414 times (octahedral) or 0.225 times (tetrahedral) that of the host atom. Carbon in γ-iron sits in octahedral sites. The NaCl structure can be understood as an FCC array of anions with all octahedral sites filled by cations, and zinc blende as one with half the tetrahedral sites filled.

about.h: Stacking faults and the ease of work hardening
about.p: A perfect FCC dislocation (a/2)<110> splits into two Shockley partial dislocations (a/6)<112>, with a stacking fault between them where the stacking sequence departs from ABC. The lower the stacking fault energy of a metal, the wider the separation of the partials and the harder cross-slip becomes, so the metal work-hardens more readily and forms twins more easily on annealing. In general, aluminum is a typical example of high stacking fault energy, while silver and austenitic stainless steels have low values; this helps explain differences in their work hardening and recrystallization behavior.

faq.q: FCC and HCP both have a packing factor of about 0.74, so why do their properties differ?
faq.a: The close-packed planes are stacked ABC in FCC and AB in HCP, so the number of slip systems differs. FCC deforms easily even as a polycrystal with its 12 slip systems, while HCP has few basal slip systems and tends to have lower ductility at room temperature.

faq.q: Are face-centered cubic and cubic close-packed the same thing?
faq.a: Yes, they are the same structure. The {111} planes perpendicular to the body diagonal of the unit cell are the close-packed planes, and the structure made by stacking them in ABC order is face-centered cubic when described with a cubic unit cell.

faq.q: How is the nearest-neighbor distance in FCC found?
faq.a: The atoms touch along the face diagonal, so the nearest-neighbor distance is half the face diagonal, a/√2, equal to twice the atomic radius. For aluminum with a lattice parameter of 0.405 nm, it is about 0.286 nm.

体心立方格子.desc: A crystal structure (BCC) with atoms at the corners and the center of the cube. The unit cell contains 2 atoms; the coordination number is 8 and the packing factor about 0.68. Examples include α-iron, Cr and W.

about.h: How the atoms touch, and typical metals
about.p: In BCC the corner atoms and the body-center atom touch along the body diagonal, so the nearest-neighbor distance is √3a/2; for α-iron (a = 0.2866 nm) it is about 0.248 nm. Besides the 8 nearest neighbors, there are 6 second-nearest neighbors at distance a, only about 1.15 times farther away. α-iron, Cr, Mo, W, V, Nb, Ta and high-temperature β-titanium are BCC, and a notable feature is that many high-melting metals such as W, Mo, Nb and Ta are included.

BCC has no truly close-packed plane. The slip direction is fixed as the close-packed <111> direction, but besides {110}, the {112} and {123} planes also act as slip planes. On the other hand, the core of a screw dislocation spreads out three-dimensionally, so the stress needed to move dislocations (the Peierls stress) is large and rises sharply as temperature falls. BCC metals therefore show a large increase in yield stress at low temperature and become prone to brittle cleavage fracture. This is why ferritic steels show a distinct ductile-to-brittle transition.

about.h: Many interstitial sites, each of them small
about.p: BCC has a packing factor of about 0.68, lower than FCC, and a larger total volume of interstitial space, but that space is divided among many small sites. In the hard-sphere model, the sphere that fits has a radius about 0.29 times (tetrahedral site) or 0.15 times (octahedral site) that of the host atom. This is why the maximum solubility of carbon in α-iron is as small as about 0.022 wt%. Carbon and nitrogen distort the lattice asymmetrically, so they strengthen it strongly, and they gather at dislocations, causing yield-point phenomena and strain aging.

about.h: Allotropy of iron and identification by XRD
about.p: Pure iron is BCC α-iron below 912 °C, FCC γ-iron from 912 to 1394 °C, and BCC δ-iron again from 1394 °C up to its melting point of 1538 °C. In the BCC-to-FCC transformation the volume per atom decreases by about 1%, so the transformation point can be found by dilatometry. In XRD, only planes with h + k + l even diffract in BCC, so peaks appear in the order (110), (200), (211)…. This sequence differs from FCC's (111), (200), (220)…, so the crystal structure can be identified from the indices of the peaks.

faq.q: What are the close-packed plane and direction in BCC?
faq.a: The close-packed direction is the body diagonal <111>, and the most densely packed plane is {110}. However, the planar packing fraction of {110} is about 0.83, lower than that of the FCC {111} plane (about 0.91), so it is not a truly close-packed plane.

faq.q: Why do BCC metals become brittle at low temperature?
faq.a: The stress needed to move screw dislocations rises sharply at low temperature, so the stress reaches the cleavage fracture stress before the metal yields. This appears in the Charpy impact test as a temperature range where the absorbed energy drops sharply.

faq.q: Is the CsCl structure BCC?
faq.a: No. The ions at the corners and the body center are different species, so a translation to the body center does not bring the structure into coincidence, and the Bravais lattice is simple cubic. A structure is BCC only when the corner and body-center sites hold the same atoms.

六方最密構造.desc: A crystal structure (HCP) formed by stacking close-packed planes in an ABAB… sequence. The coordination number is 12 and the ideal c/a is about 1.633. Examples include Mg, Ti and Zn.

about.p: HCP is the structure obtained by stacking close-packed planes in the sequence ABAB…. The hexagonal prism usually drawn contains a net 6 atoms: 12 × 1/6 at the corners, 2 × 1/2 at the centers of the top and bottom faces and 3 inside. The unit cell of the lattice (a prism with a rhombic base) contains 2 atoms. When hard spheres touch ideally, c/a is √(8/3) ≈ 1.633, with a coordination number of 12 and a packing factor of about 0.74, the same close packing as FCC. Mg, Ti, Zr, Zn, Co and Be have this structure at room temperature.

about.h: Actual c/a ratios and how slip occurs
about.p: The c/a ratios of real HCP metals deviate from the ideal value: they are large for Zn (about 1.86) and Cd (about 1.89), nearly ideal for Mg (about 1.62), and small for Ti and Zr (about 1.59) and Be (about 1.57). In metals with large c/a, the basal planes are widely spaced and basal slip dominates. In Ti and Zr, whose c/a is below the ideal value, prismatic slip occurs readily. Even within HCP, which slip systems operate changes the ease of deformation and the textures that develop, so c/a is an important guide.

about.h: Why ductility tends to be low
about.p: For a polycrystal to change shape freely, five independent slip systems are needed. Basal slip in HCP, {0001}<11-20>, has only three systems, only two of them independent, and it cannot accommodate deformation along the c axis. Unless pyramidal slip with a c-axis component or deformation twinning operates, deformation becomes incompatible at grain boundaries and cracks form easily. This is why magnesium alloy sheet is hard to press at room temperature and is often formed warm, and why titanium is not as easy to cold work as FCC metals.

Because HCP crystals have low symmetry, the Young's modulus, thermal expansion coefficient and ease of slip differ between the c-axis direction and directions perpendicular to it. Rolled sheet readily develops a texture with the basal planes aligned with the sheet surface, so strength and formability vary with direction in the sheet. In the zirconium alloys used for nuclear fuel cladding tubes, texture is controlled so that precipitated hydrides are aligned in an orientation that resists cracking. For HCP metal parts, properties must be considered together with how the crystal orientations are aligned.

faq.q: Why is the ideal c/a 1.633?
faq.a: Three spheres in the lower layer and one above them touch to form a regular tetrahedron, whose height is √(2/3) times the interatomic distance a. Since c is twice this height, c/a = 2√(2/3) = √(8/3) ≈ 1.633.

faq.q: How many atoms are in the HCP unit cell?
faq.a: The primitive unit cell with a rhombic base contains 2. Counted in the hexagonal prism, there are 12 × 1/6 at the corners + 2 × 1/2 at the face centers + 3 inside = 6, equivalent to three primitive cells.

faq.q: What is the difference between HCP and FCC?
faq.a: Both are made by stacking close-packed planes, but the stacking is ABAB… in HCP and ABCABC… in FCC. A single stacking error creates an HCP-like sequence inside FCC, so some metals, such as cobalt, switch between HCP and FCC, at about 420 °C in its case.

原子充填率.desc: The fraction of the unit-cell volume occupied by atoms, treating atoms as hard spheres. About 0.52 for SC, about 0.68 for BCC and about 0.74 for FCC and HCP.

about.p: The atomic packing factor is found as n × (4/3)πr³/V from the number of atoms n in the unit cell, the atomic radius r and the unit cell volume V. There are three steps: (1) count the atoms in the unit cell, allowing for sharing; (2) fix the relation between the lattice parameter a and r from the direction in which atoms touch; (3) calculate the volume ratio. The result is π/6 ≈ 0.52 for SC (a = 2r), √3π/8 ≈ 0.68 for BCC (√3a = 4r) and π/(3√2) ≈ 0.74 for FCC (√2a = 4r). The result does not depend on r and is determined by the structure alone.

about.h: Relation to coordination number and density
about.p: In general, structures with larger coordination numbers have higher packing factors, increasing in the order SC (coordination number 6), BCC (8), and FCC and HCP (12). The packing factor, however, only expresses a geometric fraction; density is determined from the atomic mass and unit cell size as ρ = nM/(N_A a³). For the same element, a difference in packing factor shows up as a volume change, as when iron changes from BCC α-iron to FCC γ-iron and the volume per atom decreases by about 1%. Note that it cannot be used to compare the densities of different elements.

about.h: Some strong materials have low packing factors
about.p: The covalently bonded diamond structure has a coordination number of 4 and a packing factor of only √3π/16 ≈ 0.34, yet diamond is one of the hardest substances. The packing factor is a geometric value for packed hard spheres and says nothing about bond strength or directionality. Also, the real size of an atom changes slightly with coordination number, and the apparent radius becomes somewhat smaller as the coordination number decreases. Furthermore, a higher packing factor does not mean that each interstitial site is smaller; relative to the host atom radius, the FCC octahedral site is larger than any interstitial site in BCC.

about.h: Application to ionic crystals and planes
about.p: For ionic crystals, the calculation uses the radii of both cations and anions. For sodium chloride with the NaCl structure (Na⁺ 0.102 nm, Cl⁻ 0.181 nm, a = 0.564 nm), it is about 0.65. The planar packing fraction, which describes how densely atoms are packed on a plane, is found in the same way: π/(2√3) ≈ 0.91 for the FCC {111} plane and about 0.83 for the BCC {110} plane. Planar packing helps explain which planes become slip planes, surface energies, and how etching and crystal growth rates depend on plane orientation.

faq.q: What is the difference between atomic packing factor and density?
faq.a: The packing factor is the fraction of the unit cell volume occupied by atoms and is dimensionless. Density is mass per unit volume; even with the same FCC packing factor, aluminum (about 2.70 g/cm³) and copper (about 8.96 g/cm³) differ greatly.

faq.q: What is the packing factor of the diamond structure?
faq.a: The unit cell holds 8 atoms, which touch along the body diagonal at a distance of a√3/4, giving a packing factor of √3π/16 ≈ 0.34. Silicon and germanium have the same structure, which contains a lot of empty space.

faq.q: Why does the atomic packing factor not depend on the atomic radius?
faq.a: The touching condition fixes a as a constant multiple of r, so both the atomic volume and the unit cell volume scale with r³, and r cancels in the ratio. For the same structure, every element gives the same value.

転位.desc: A defect in which the arrangement of atoms in a crystal is disturbed along a line. Metals deform plastically as dislocations move on slip planes. There are edge, screw and mixed dislocations.

about.p: The theoretical shear strength needed to shift an entire plane of atoms at once is estimated at about one tenth of the shear modulus, yet real metals yield at stresses a thousandth of that or less. Dislocations explain this large gap. With a dislocation present, there is no need to break atomic bonds all at once; the crystal slips by rearranging bonds a few at a time near the dislocation line, much as moving a ruck in a carpet shifts the whole carpet. How easily a metal deforms plastically is therefore determined by how easily its dislocations move.

The type of dislocation is determined by the relation between the Burgers vector b, which gives the magnitude and direction of slip, and the direction of the dislocation line. An edge dislocation has the form of an inserted extra half-plane of atoms, with b perpendicular to the line. In a screw dislocation the atomic planes connect like a spiral staircase, with b parallel to the line. Most dislocations are mixed dislocations combining the two. An edge dislocation has a unique slip plane and, at high temperature, can climb up or down by absorbing or emitting vacancies. A screw dislocation can cross-slip onto another slip plane.

Most strengthening methods for metals work by obstructing dislocation motion. Solid-solution strengthening stops dislocations with the strain fields of solute atoms, precipitation hardening with fine precipitates, grain refinement with grain boundaries, and work hardening with entanglement of dislocations among themselves. Cold working raises the dislocation density from about 10¹⁰ m⁻² to about 10¹⁵ m⁻², increasing strength while lowering ductility. Conversely, when recovery and recrystallization occur during annealing, the dislocation density falls and softness and ductility return.

Dislocations can be observed directly by TEM as lines of diffraction contrast caused by strain. At a surface, etching forms etch pits where dislocations meet the surface, and counting their density gives the dislocation density. Silicon wafers are made essentially dislocation-free, but if dislocations are introduced during processing, for example by thermal stress, they increase leakage current and become sites for precipitation of metal impurities. When a film with a different lattice parameter is grown, misfit dislocations form at the interface to relax the strain, and threading dislocations may remain in the film.

faq.q: How do dislocations multiply?
faq.a: During plastic deformation they multiply by mechanisms such as the Frank–Read source, in which a dislocation pinned at both ends bows out and generates loop after loop. The dislocation density therefore increases as working proceeds, causing work hardening.

faq.q: How are dislocations and the Burgers vector related?
faq.a: If you make a closed circuit around a dislocation, a closure failure remains compared with a perfect crystal. This is the Burgers vector, which gives the amount and direction by which the crystal is displaced when the dislocation passes.

faq.q: Why do dislocations move with difficulty in ceramics?
faq.a: In ionic bonding, slip must avoid bringing ions of the same sign together, and in covalent bonding the bonds are strongly directional, so slip systems are limited and the Peierls stress is large. At room temperature ceramics therefore fracture in a brittle manner before deforming plastically.

バーガースベクトル.desc: The vector giving the closure failure of a circuit taken around a dislocation. For a perfect dislocation in FCC it is (a/2)<110>. It determines the type and energy of the dislocation.

about.h: Finding it with a Burgers circuit
about.p: Make a closed circuit around a dislocation, stepping the same number of atoms in each direction, and then follow the same steps in a perfect crystal without the dislocation: the circuit fails to close and a gap remains. The vector representing this gap is the Burgers vector b. Its sign depends on the conventions for the direction of the circuit and whether the vector runs from start to finish or finish to start (such as the FS/RH rule), so calculations must stick to one convention. The vector b corresponds to the amount and direction of slip when the dislocation passes, and many dislocation properties are determined by it.

about.h: Values for each structure and Frank's rule
about.p: The energy of a dislocation per unit length is about Gb²/2, proportional to |b|², so b is chosen as the shortest lattice translation vector. Typical choices are (a/2)<110> in FCC (magnitude a/√2), (a/2)<111> in BCC (√3a/2) and (a/3)<11-20> in HCP (magnitude a). This gives about 0.256 nm for copper and about 0.248 nm for α-iron. The guideline that a dislocation lowers its energy by splitting into two whose Burgers vectors satisfy b₁² > b₂² + b₃² is Frank's rule, and it also explains the dissociation into partial dislocations in FCC.

about.h: A vector that does not change along the line
about.p: Even where the dislocation line curves, the Burgers vector of a single dislocation is the same everywhere. Where b is perpendicular to the line the dislocation is edge, where parallel it is screw, and in between it has mixed character. A dislocation therefore cannot end inside a crystal; it must exit at a surface, form a loop or join other dislocations at a node. The sum of Burgers vectors flowing into a node equals the sum flowing out. Note also that an edge dislocation moves in the direction of b, whereas a screw dislocation moves perpendicular to b.

about.h: Determination by TEM, and plastic strain
about.p: In TEM, dislocation contrast almost vanishes under the condition g·b = 0, where g is the diffraction vector. Finding this invisibility condition for two different g vectors fixes the direction of b. In addition, the rate of plastic shear strain produced by moving dislocations is γ̇ = ρ_m b v (ρ_m is the density of mobile dislocations and v their average velocity), so b is the quantity linking dislocation motion to macroscopic deformation. The force on a dislocation is also estimated as τb per unit length, the product of the shear stress τ and b.

faq.q: How do you calculate the magnitude of a Burgers vector?
faq.a: For a vector of the form (a/n)<uvw>, the magnitude is (a/n)√(u² + v² + w²). For example, (a/2)<110> in FCC copper (a = 0.3615 nm) is 0.3615/√2 ≈ 0.256 nm, equal to the nearest-neighbor distance.

faq.q: What is the Burgers vector of a partial dislocation?
faq.a: A partial dislocation has a short vector that is not a lattice translation vector. The Shockley partial in FCC is (a/6)<112>; because it leaves a stacking fault behind it, partials exist not singly but as pairs with a stacking fault between them.

faq.q: What happens to the Burgers vector if the line direction is reversed?
faq.a: Its sign is reversed. Even for the same dislocation, the sign of b is set by the choice of line direction and the circuit convention, so when adding dislocations or considering reactions, the same convention must be used throughout.

拡散係数.desc: The coefficient D expressing how readily atoms diffuse, in units of m²/s. It depends on temperature in the Arrhenius form D = D₀exp(−Q/RT).

about.p: The diffusion coefficient D is the proportionality constant in Fick's first law, J = −D(dC/dx), that links the concentration gradient to the flow of atoms (the flux). Its unit is m²/s (cm²/s is also common), and the larger it is, the faster atoms spread. A rough distance over which atoms spread in time t is √(Dt). For example, with D = 10⁻¹¹ m²/s, atoms spread about 0.2 mm in one hour (3600 s). It is the basic quantity for estimating carburized case depths, dopant diffusion depths and the growth of reaction layers in solder joints.

about.h: Temperature dependence and the Arrhenius plot
about.p: The diffusion coefficient depends exponentially on temperature, D = D₀exp(−Q/RT). Q is the activation energy needed for an atom to jump to a neighboring site, and D₀ is a constant that includes the vibration frequency and jump distance. Plotting ln D against 1/T (an Arrhenius plot) gives a straight line, and Q is obtained from its slope −Q/R. The larger Q, the stronger the effect of temperature, and a difference of a few tens of degrees can change the diffusion rate several times over. In calculations, it is essential to convert temperatures to absolute temperature.

about.h: The mechanism changes the order of magnitude
about.p: Small atoms such as carbon, nitrogen and hydrogen in iron move by interstitial diffusion, jumping between interstitial sites, so their diffusion coefficients are large. Substitutional atoms diffuse by the vacancy mechanism, moving only when a vacancy arrives next to them; the activation energy also includes the vacancy formation energy, so diffusion is far slower. In addition, diffusion along grain boundaries, surfaces and dislocations, where the atomic arrangement is disordered, has a lower activation energy and can dominate over lattice diffusion at low temperatures. This is why grain boundary diffusion stands out in polycrystalline thin films.

When different atoms diffuse into each other, as when two metals are bonded, the diffusion coefficient of each kind of atom (the intrinsic diffusion coefficient) must be distinguished from the interdiffusion coefficient that describes the overall change in concentration. The difference between them shows up as marker movement and void formation through the Kirkendall effect. In practice, the diffusion coefficient at the treatment temperature is calculated from literature values of D₀ and Q, and the concentration profile is predicted with the error-function solution. Values differ between data sources, so it is safer to compare several before use.

faq.q: Why is the unit of the diffusion coefficient m²/s?
faq.a: In J = −D(dC/dx), the flux J has units of (amount)/(m²·s) and the concentration gradient (amount)/m⁴, so D has units of m²/s. This is also consistent with √(Dt) being a length.

faq.q: How many degrees must the temperature be raised to double the diffusion coefficient?
faq.a: It depends on the activation energy and the temperature. Solve ln 2 = (Q/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂); for example, with Q = 150 kJ/mol and T₁ = 1200 K, raising the temperature by about 58 K roughly doubles the diffusion coefficient.

faq.q: How are the diffusion coefficient and the diffusion length related?
faq.a: A rough diffusion distance in time t is √(Dt) (or 2√(Dt), depending on the definition). The distance is proportional to the square root of time, so doubling the depth takes four times as long.

フィックの法則.desc: The basic laws of diffusion. The first law states that the flux is proportional to the concentration gradient, J = −D(dC/dx); the second gives the change of concentration with time, ∂C/∂t = D(∂²C/∂x²).

about.h: The first law and the steady state
about.p: Fick's first law, J = −D(dC/dx), states that the flux of atoms J is proportional to the concentration gradient and flows from higher to lower concentration; the minus sign indicates this direction. In a steady state where the concentration profile does not change with time, this equation alone gives the flow rate. Permeation through a plate whose two faces are held at constant concentrations is an example, used in hydrogen permeation tests, hydrogen purification with palladium membranes and the evaluation of gas-barrier films. If the membrane is made thicker, the flux decreases in inverse proportion to the thickness.

about.h: The second law and the error-function solution
about.p: When the concentration changes with time, you solve the second law, ∂C/∂t = D(∂²C/∂x²), derived from the first law and conservation of mass. For diffusion into a sufficiently thick material (initial concentration C₀) with a constant surface concentration Cs, the solution is (C − C₀)/(Cs − C₀) = 1 − erf(x/(2√(Dt))). For example, with D = 1.0×10⁻¹¹ m²/s and a 10-hour treatment, √(Dt) is about 0.6 mm, and the depth at which the concentration lies exactly halfway between the surface and interior values is about 0.57 mm. This is the basis for estimating carburizing and nitriding depths.

about.h: The true driving force is the chemical potential
about.p: Fick's laws treat the concentration gradient as the driving force, but strictly it is the gradient of chemical potential that moves atoms. Usually the two point the same way, so this causes no trouble, but when other elements make the chemical potential gradient point the opposite way, atoms move from lower to higher concentration in uphill diffusion. Darken's experiment is well known: when steels with and without Si are joined and heated, carbon escapes from the Si-containing side. Spinodal decomposition is another example, in which the apparent diffusion coefficient is negative.

In impurity diffusion in semiconductors, predeposition with a constant surface concentration gives an error-function profile, while drive-in with a fixed amount of dopant gives a Gaussian profile, C = Q/√(πDt)·exp(−x²/(4Dt)). In both cases the diffusion depth is proportional to √(Dt), so doubling the depth needs four times the time, or a temperature rise that quadruples D. In practice D may depend on concentration, and the Boltzmann–Matano method is used to obtain D from a measured concentration profile.

faq.q: How should Fick's first and second laws be used?
faq.a: The flow rate in a steady state, where the concentration profile does not change with time, is found with the first law. For non-steady problems in which the profile changes with time, such as carburizing or doping, the second law is solved under the boundary conditions.

faq.q: Under what conditions can the error-function solution be used?
faq.a: When the surface concentration is constant, the material is thick enough compared with the diffusion depth to be treated as semi-infinite, and the diffusion coefficient can be treated as constant regardless of concentration. Thin plates or treatments in which the surface concentration changes need other solutions.

faq.q: What does the minus sign in J = −D(dC/dx) mean?
faq.a: It means the flow goes from the higher-concentration side to the lower. When concentration decreases with x (dC/dx < 0), J is positive and the flow is in the +x direction.

空孔.desc: A point defect in which an atom is missing from a lattice site. Its equilibrium concentration rises with temperature as exp(−Q/kT), and vacancies carry the diffusion of substitutional atoms.

about.h: A defect that always exists, even in equilibrium
about.p: Forming a vacancy breaks bonds and raises the energy, but it also increases the configurational entropy because the number of ways to arrange the vacancies grows. The Gibbs energy is therefore not at a minimum with zero vacancies, and the equilibrium vacancy concentration is given by n/N ≈ exp(−Qv/kT). With Qv = 1.0 eV, the fraction of vacant lattice sites is about 1.6×10⁻¹⁷ at 300 K and about 9×10⁻⁶ at 1000 K, a change of more than 10 orders of magnitude with temperature. The vacancy formation energy tends to be larger for metals with higher melting points.

If the change in length ΔL/L of a heated specimen and the change in lattice parameter Δa/a measured by XRD are recorded together, their difference gives the vacancy concentration as Δn/N ≈ 3(ΔL/L − Δa/a) (the method of Simmons and Balluffi). This works because atoms move to the surface when vacancies form, so the whole specimen expands more than the lattice parameter alone. Other methods measure the increase in electrical resistance from vacancies retained by quenching from high temperature, or use positron annihilation, in which positrons trapped at vacancies have longer lifetimes.

about.h: Vacancies in ionic crystals, and how they differ from interstitials
about.p: Ionic crystals must stay electrically neutral, so vacancies form as pairs of cation and anion vacancies (Schottky defects) or as pairs of a vacancy and an interstitial ion (Frenkel defects). When impurities of different valence are added, charge-compensating vacancies form in amounts fixed by the composition, the oxygen vacancies in stabilized zirconia being an example. Self-interstitials in metals have formation energies several times larger than vacancies, so they are far fewer in thermal equilibrium, and most of them are created by irradiation or plastic working. In reactor materials, for example, such vacancy–interstitial pairs are produced in large numbers.

about.h: Roles in diffusion, aging and irradiation
about.p: Substitutional atoms diffuse by exchanging places with vacancies, so the diffusion rate is set by the concentration and mobility of vacancies. When an aluminum alloy is quenched from the solution-treatment temperature, excess high-temperature vacancies are retained and speed up solute diffusion even at room temperature, advancing natural aging. When the vacancy flow is biased in one direction, Kirkendall voids form. In nuclear reactor materials, vacancies created by irradiation cluster into voids, causing swelling, an increase in volume. Part of high-temperature creep is also carried by vacancy diffusion.

faq.q: Why is a crystal with zero vacancies not in equilibrium?
faq.a: Creating vacancies raises the energy, but the number of ways to place them is enormous, so the configurational entropy rises and the Gibbs energy is lower with a small number of vacancies present. Vacancies always exist at any temperature above 0 K.

faq.q: Which are more numerous, vacancies or interstitials?
faq.a: In metals, equilibrium vacancies are far more numerous. A self-interstitial distorts its surroundings strongly, so its formation energy is several times that of a vacancy, and its equilibrium concentration is negligibly small.

faq.q: How much does vacancy concentration change with temperature?
faq.a: It follows exp(−Qv/kT), so it changes enormously. In many metals, about one lattice site in ten thousand (10⁻⁴) is vacant just below the melting point, while the equilibrium concentration at room temperature is many orders of magnitude smaller. Quenching retains some of the high-temperature vacancies at room temperature.

破壊靭性.desc: The ability of a cracked material to resist fracture. It is expressed as the critical value of the stress intensity factor, K_IC (in MPa·√m), and fracture is judged by comparing it with K = Yσ√(πa).

about.h: The stress intensity factor and the fracture condition
about.p: The intensity of stress at a crack tip is expressed by the stress intensity factor K = Yσ√(πa). σ is the remote stress, a is the crack length (the depth for a surface crack, half the length for an internal crack), and Y is a factor determined by the shapes of the crack and component. When K reaches a critical value for the material, the crack propagates suddenly and fracture occurs; this critical value is called the fracture toughness. Its unit is MPa·√m, notable for containing both stress and crack length. It lets you compare numerically not just strength but resistance to cracks.

Fracture toughness values change with plate thickness. Thin plates are close to plane stress with a large plastic zone at the crack tip, so the apparent value is high; thick plates are in plane strain, and the value drops and levels off at a constant minimum. This value is the plane-strain fracture toughness K_IC, where the subscript I denotes loading that opens the crack (mode I). K_IC can be treated as a material constant and is a conservative value for design. Typical values are about 50–150 MPa·√m for structural steels (lower for higher-strength grades), about 20–45 for aluminum alloys, about 3–5 for alumina and below 1 (about 0.7–0.8) for soda-lime glass.

In general, raising strength by heat treatment or other means tends to lower fracture toughness. The higher the strength, the smaller the crack that can be tolerated, and since the critical crack length is proportional to (K_IC/σ)², the effect is large even when the working stress is the same fraction of the strength. Aircraft and pressure vessels therefore select materials for toughness as well as strength. In ceramics, toughness is raised by measures such as transformation toughening in zirconia and crack bridging by fibers or particles. In metals, grain refinement and reducing inclusions improve toughness.

In damage-tolerant design, you assume the largest crack that nondestructive inspection might miss and check that K at the working stress stays below K_IC. Combining this with the Paris law for fatigue crack growth rate, you estimate the number of cycles for the crack to reach its critical length and set the inspection interval. For highly ductile materials with large plastic zones, K is hard to apply, so elastic–plastic fracture mechanics parameters such as the J-integral and the crack-tip opening displacement (CTOD) are used. Which parameter to use is judged from the ductility of the material and the dimensions of the component.

faq.q: How does fracture toughness differ from impact energy (Charpy absorbed energy)?
faq.a: Charpy impact energy is the energy needed to break a notched specimen; it is convenient for comparing materials and evaluating the ductile-to-brittle transition, but it is not a value that can be used directly in design. Fracture toughness is a material constant that lets you predict fracture quantitatively from crack size and stress.

faq.q: Where does the unit of K_IC, MPa·√m, come from?
faq.a: In K = Yσ√(πa), σ is in MPa and a in m, giving MPa·√m. Y and π are dimensionless.

faq.q: What is the fracture toughness of ceramics?
faq.a: About 3–5 MPa·√m for alumina, about 5–8 for silicon nitride and about 6–10 for partially stabilized zirconia, from a few tens of times to a few times lower than metals. Ceramics therefore fracture easily even from small flaws, and their strength scatters widely.

0.2%耐力.desc: For materials without a distinct yield point, the stress that leaves a permanent strain of 0.2% after unloading. It is found where a line parallel to the elastic line, offset by 0.2% strain, meets the stress–strain curve.

about.h: A yield measure for materials without a yield point
about.p: A tensile test of mild steel shows a yield point where the stress drops suddenly, but aluminum alloys, copper alloys, austenitic stainless steels, high-strength steels and others pass smoothly from the elastic to the plastic range. The 0.2% offset yield strength is the stress that leaves a permanent strain of 0.2% (a strain of 0.002) on unloading, adopted by convention as the yield strength. The JIS and ISO tensile test standards denote it R_p0.2, and in English it is called the 0.2% offset yield strength or proof stress.

about.h: Points to watch when reading it by the offset method
about.p: Shift the straight elastic line of the stress–strain curve by 0.2% along the strain axis and read the stress where it intersects the curve. For example, for an aluminum alloy with a Young's modulus of 70 GPa and a proof stress of 280 MPa, the elastic strain at that point is 0.4%, so the total strain is about 0.6%. If strain is calculated from crosshead displacement, deformation of the grips and the machine itself is added and the elastic slope appears too low, so to read the proof stress correctly, strain is measured with an extensometer attached to the specimen.

about.h: Difference from the elastic limit and tensile strength
about.p: The 0.2% offset yield strength is not the limit below which no plastic deformation occurs (the elastic limit) but a conventional value that already includes a small plastic deformation. In fact, minute plastic strains occur even at lower stresses. Some applications use a 0.1% or 0.01% offset, and the smaller the offset, the lower the value. Tensile strength is the maximum load divided by the original cross-sectional area, a different quantity. The ratio of proof stress to tensile strength (the yield ratio) expresses the margin between yielding and fracture.

about.h: Use in design and in comparing materials
about.p: In the static strength design of machine parts, the allowable stress is often set by dividing the 0.2% offset yield strength by a safety factor, as a criterion for avoiding permanent deformation in service. It is also convenient for comparing steels that have a yield point with alloys that do not on the same basis. However, higher-strength materials tend to have higher yield ratios and can approach fracture soon after exceeding the proof stress, so elongation and toughness are also checked. The proof stress in compression or at high temperature can differ from that in room-temperature tension, so data matching the service conditions are needed.

faq.q: What is the difference between 0.2% offset yield strength and the yield point?
faq.a: The yield point is read from an actual sudden drop or plateau in stress on the stress–strain curve, and there are upper and lower yield points. The 0.2% offset yield strength is a value defined by the convention of 0.2% permanent strain for materials that show no yield point.

faq.q: Why is the value 0.2% used?
faq.a: It was chosen by convention as a permanent strain small enough to hardly affect a part's function yet reliably measurable with an extensometer. Depending on the application, such as precision springs, offsets of 0.1% or 0.01% are also used.

faq.q: What symbol is used for the 0.2% offset yield strength?
faq.a: In the tensile tests of JIS Z 2241 and ISO 6892-1 it is written R_p0.2. Textbooks and design data may also write it as σ0.2 or σ_y, and the unit is MPa (N/mm²).

ヤング率.desc: The ratio of stress to strain in the elastic region, E = σ/ε. It is set by interatomic bonding: about 200 GPa for steel and about 70 GPa for aluminum, and it hardly changes with heat treatment.

about.h: A measure of the stiffness of interatomic bonds
about.p: Young's modulus is determined by the curvature of the interatomic bonding potential (the stiffness of the bonds). It therefore tends to be larger for substances with strong bonds and high melting points: about 1000 GPa for diamond, about 410 GPa for tungsten, about 200 GPa for steel, about 120 GPa for copper, and about 70 GPa for aluminum and glass. Polymers are a few GPa or less and rubber is a few MPa, a range of about six orders of magnitude across material types. It is a basic design quantity that sets the stiffness, deflection and natural frequencies of parts.

It can be found from the slope of the elastic range in a tensile test, but the elastic strain is small, about 0.1%, and deflection of the machine is included, so the accuracy is not high. Accurate values are measured by the resonance method, which uses the resonant frequency of a specimen, or the ultrasonic pulse method, which uses the speed of ultrasound. The speed of longitudinal waves in a thin rod is √(E/ρ), about 5000 m/s for steel with a Young's modulus of 200 GPa and a density of 7850 kg/m³. For thin films and small regions, nanoindentation, which analyzes the unloading curve of an indenter, is used.

about.h: Confusion with strength, and dependence on crystal direction
about.p: Young's modulus expresses resistance to deformation and is separate from resistance to failure (strength). Even when quenching increases the strength of steel several times, its Young's modulus hardly changes. If you want less deflection in a part, switching to a high-strength steel does nothing; you must change the cross-sectional shape or choose a material with a higher modulus. In a single crystal the value also varies with direction; for iron it is about 125 GPa in the <100> direction and about 273 GPa in the <111> direction. The value for a polycrystal is an average of these.

about.h: Use in design and specific stiffness
about.p: Deflections in tension and bending are inversely proportional to Young's modulus; for beams they are set by its product EI with the second moment of area I (the flexural rigidity). When lightness also matters, materials are compared by specific stiffness E/ρ, but steel (about 200 GPa, 7.85 g/cm³), aluminum alloys (about 70 GPa, 2.70 g/cm³) and titanium alloys (about 110 GPa, 4.5 g/cm³) all come to nearly the same value, about 25 GPa/(g/cm³). Among metals, therefore, designing the shape of plates and beams is what pays off, and a large increase in specific stiffness requires composites such as CFRP.

faq.q: How are Young's modulus and the shear modulus related?
faq.a: For isotropic materials, G = E/(2(1 + ν)), where ν is Poisson's ratio. For steel (E = 200 GPa, ν = 0.3), G ≈ 77 GPa. Young's modulus expresses resistance to tensile deformation and the shear modulus resistance to shear.

faq.q: What is the unit of Young's modulus?
faq.a: The same as stress, Pa, and GPa is common for metals. Strain is dimensionless, so Young's modulus has the same unit as stress. Steel's roughly 200 GPa can also be written 2.0×10⁵ N/mm² (MPa).

faq.q: Do harder materials have higher Young's moduli?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Hardness is resistance to plastic deformation and changes greatly with microstructure, such as how easily dislocations move, whereas Young's modulus is set by bond strength. Quenched and annealed steels differ greatly in hardness but have almost the same Young's modulus.

疲労限度.desc: The stress amplitude below which a material effectively no longer fails under cyclic loading. It often appears at around 10⁶–10⁷ cycles in carbon steels but is not distinct in aluminum alloys.

about.h: The horizontal part of the S–N curve
about.p: The S–N curve is a log–log plot of the number of cycles to failure under repeated loading at various stress amplitudes. For carbon and low-alloy steels, the curve becomes nearly horizontal from around 10⁶ to 10⁷ cycles, and below that stress amplitude the material effectively does not fail. The stress amplitude of this horizontal part is the fatigue limit, often given as the fully reversed value from a rotating-bending test. Aluminum and copper alloys show no clear horizontal part, so they are evaluated instead by the fatigue strength at a set number of cycles, such as 10⁷.

There is an empirical guideline that the rotating-bending fatigue limit of steel, for smooth polished specimens, is roughly half the tensile strength. For high-strength steels above about 1400 MPa in tensile strength, however, internal defects such as inclusions become crack origins, so raising strength no longer raises the fatigue limit much. Proportionality to hardness is also used as a guideline, but all of these are statistical trends that also vary with material lot and microstructure. In actual part design, test data or standard values are used and corrected for the size and surface effects described next.

about.h: Factors that lower the fatigue limit
about.p: Even for the same material, the fatigue limit is lowered by surface roughness, part size, notches, tensile mean stress and corrosive environments. For notches, the correction uses not the stress concentration factor itself but the fatigue notch factor, which includes the material's notch sensitivity. In corrosive environments, pits keep forming on the surface, so no fatigue limit appears. In the very-high-cycle range beyond 10⁸ cycles, failure can start from internal inclusions and leave a pattern called a fish-eye on the fracture surface, so the fatigue limit is not an absolute limit.

about.h: Design and ways to improve it
about.p: In infinite-life design, the fatigue limit of specimens is multiplied by factors for surface, size, reliability and so on to estimate the value for the part, and mean stress is corrected with a Goodman diagram or similar. Most fatigue cracks start at the surface, so treatments that introduce compressive residual stress at the surface are effective. Examples include shot peening, carburizing, nitriding and induction hardening; polishing the surface to reduce scratches and reducing inclusions in steel also raise the fatigue limit. Welded joints have much lower fatigue strength than the base metal because of the weld toe shape and residual stress, so they are handled by separate design standards.

faq.q: What is the difference between fatigue limit and fatigue strength?
faq.a: Fatigue strength is the stress amplitude that causes failure at a set number of cycles (such as 10⁷), also called the fatigue strength at N cycles. The fatigue limit is the stress amplitude below which failure effectively does not occur, used for materials such as steel whose S–N curve has a horizontal part.

faq.q: How is the fatigue limit determined?
faq.a: Many specimens are tested in rotating-bending or axial fatigue tests at various stress amplitudes, their cycles to failure are measured, and the limit is found from the horizontal part of the S–N curve. Statistical methods such as the staircase method, which raises or lowers the stress one step at a time, may be used to estimate the mean and scatter.

faq.q: How do you design with a material that has no fatigue limit?
faq.a: For materials such as aluminum alloys that have no horizontal part, use the fatigue strength at the number of cycles the product will experience during its life. If the stress amplitude varies, damage is summed with Miner's rule to estimate life.

クリープ.desc: Deformation that progresses over time under a constant load. It becomes significant above roughly 0.4 times the melting point (in absolute temperature) and passes through primary, secondary (steady-state) and tertiary stages before rupture.

about.h: Three stages, and the quantities used in design
about.p: A strain–time curve under constant load passes through primary creep, in which the strain rate gradually falls; secondary (steady-state) creep, in which work hardening and recovery balance and the strain rate is nearly constant; and tertiary creep, in which void formation or necking accelerates the rate, ending in rupture. In design, the minimum strain rate, the steady-state creep rate, and the time to rupture (the creep rupture time) are important. The empirical Monkman–Grant relation, in which the product of the two is nearly constant, is also used to estimate life.

The steady-state creep rate is often expressed in the form ε̇ = Aσⁿexp(−Q/RT). In dislocation creep, by dislocation climb and glide, the stress exponent n is about 3 to 8; at low stress and high temperature, diffusion creep (n ≈ 1), in which grains elongate by atomic diffusion, dominates. Diffusion creep includes Nabarro–Herring creep, with diffusion through the grains, and Coble creep, with diffusion along grain boundaries, whose rates are inversely proportional to the square or cube of the grain size. The activation energy Q is often close to that for self-diffusion.

Creep becomes significant at roughly 0.3 to 0.5 times the melting point (in kelvin), so in low-melting materials it occurs even at room temperature. For tin-based solders with melting points of about 490 K, room temperature is about 0.6 of the melting point, and creep of solder joints is a major reliability issue. Polymers, lead and ice also creep near room temperature. Moreover, fine grains that raise strength at room temperature speed up diffusion creep and grain boundary sliding at high temperature. This is why jet engine turbine blades use single crystals with no grain boundaries.

Service lives of real equipment reach tens or hundreds of thousands of hours, so long-term lives are estimated from short tests at higher temperatures or stresses. A typical tool is the Larson–Miller parameter P = T(C + log t_r), where T is absolute temperature, t_r is the rupture time (h), and C of about 20 is commonly used for steels. For example, with C = 20, a condition equivalent to 1000 hours at 600 °C corresponds to about 57 hours at 650 °C. Note, however, that extrapolation errors grow for materials whose microstructure changes over long times.

faq.q: What is the difference between creep and stress relaxation?
faq.a: Creep is the continued increase of strain under a constant load (stress), while stress relaxation is the gradual drop in stress while the strain is held constant. The loss of clamping force in a bolt at high temperature over time is an example of stress relaxation.

faq.q: What is the steady-state creep rate?
faq.a: It is the strain rate in the secondary stage of the creep curve, where the rate is nearly constant, also called the minimum creep rate. In design it is the basis for estimating strain over the service life and predicting rupture time.

faq.q: Does creep occur at room temperature?
faq.a: Yes. The guideline is the ratio to the melting point in kelvin, so for materials with low melting points or glass transition temperatures, such as solders, lead, polymers and ice, creep must be considered even at room temperature.

てこの規則.desc: A rule for finding the mass fraction of each phase in a two-phase region of a phase diagram from ratios of distances along the tie line. The fraction of a phase is proportional to the distance from the alloy composition to the opposite phase.

about.p: Consider an alloy in a two-phase region of a binary phase diagram. If you draw a horizontal line (the tie line) at that temperature, its two ends meet the boundaries of the two phases, and the compositions at those intersections are the compositions of the two phases. The overall alloy composition C₀ lies somewhere along the tie line; because the compositions of the two phases are fixed by temperature alone, changing the alloy composition does not change the phase compositions, only the proportions of the phases. The lever rule gives these proportions and is derived from the overall alloy composition and the conservation of mass of each component.

With Cα the composition of the α phase and C_L that of the other phase (the liquid, say), the mass fraction of liquid is W_L = (Cα − C₀)/(Cα − C_L) and the mass fraction of α is Wα = (C₀ − C_L)/(Cα − C_L). The name comes from the resemblance to the balance of a lever (seesaw): the fraction of a phase is proportional to the distance from the alloy composition to the composition of the opposite phase. A common mistake is to take the distance on the same side. You can check the result by confirming that the two fractions sum to 1. With compositions in wt% you get mass fractions; in at%, fractions by number of atoms.

In eutectic and eutectoid systems it is important to distinguish the fractions of phases from those of microconstituents. For example, a hypoeutectoid steel just below 727 °C has two phases, ferrite and cementite, but two microconstituents, proeutectoid ferrite and pearlite. The fraction of proeutectoid ferrite is found with the lever rule in the α + γ region just above 727 °C, while the fraction of all ferrite as a phase is found in the α + Fe₃C region. Being conscious of which tie line at which temperature you are using prevents mix-ups.

about.h: Relation to real microstructures and caveats
about.p: The lever rule assumes equilibrium. With rapid cooling, as in real casting, diffusion in the solid cannot keep up and segregation remains, so fractions and compositions do not match the calculation. Even so, measuring the area fraction of pearlite in the micrograph of a slowly cooled steel lets you back-calculate its approximate carbon content. Also, when the two phases differ greatly in density, mass fractions do not match the area (volume) fractions seen in a microscope, so convert between mass and volume fractions using the density of each phase as needed.

faq.q: Can the lever rule be used when three phases coexist?
faq.a: In a binary system three phases coexist only at invariant points such as the eutectic temperature, where the fractions are not uniquely determined. Find them with the lever rule in the two-phase regions just above or just below the eutectic temperature.

faq.q: Should I calculate in wt% or at%?
faq.a: If you calculate in the same units as the phase diagram, wt% gives mass fractions and at% gives fractions by number of atoms. The important thing is not to mix units partway through.

faq.q: Why is the distance to the opposite side used?
faq.a: Because the closer the alloy composition is to the composition of one phase, the more of that phase there should be. Solving the conservation of total solute, C₀ = Wα·Cα + W_L·C_L, confirms that the result is the ratio of distances to the opposite side.

ギブスの相律.desc: The rule F = C − P + 2 giving the number of degrees of freedom F at equilibrium from the number of components C and the number of phases P. For condensed systems at constant pressure, F = C − P + 1 is used.

about.h: What the rule means and how it is derived
about.p: The number of degrees of freedom F is the number of intensive variables (temperature, pressure and the composition of each phase) that can be changed independently while equilibrium is maintained. With P phases and C components, fixing the composition of each phase takes C − 1 variables, giving P(C − 1) in all, plus the two variables temperature and pressure. In equilibrium, on the other hand, the chemical potential of each component must be equal in every phase, which imposes C(P − 1) conditions. Subtracting the number of conditions from the number of variables gives F = C − P + 2. The amounts of the phases are not counted as degrees of freedom.

about.h: A one-component example: the phase diagram of water
about.p: For one component (C = 1), F = 3 − P. With only one phase, ice, water or vapor, F = 2, an area of the diagram where temperature and pressure can be varied independently. When two phases coexist, F = 1, a line (the melting curve or vapor-pressure curve) on which fixing the temperature also fixes the pressure. The triple point, where three phases coexist, has F = 0 and is fixed at a single point, 0.01 °C and about 611 Pa for water. The phase rule also shows at once that four phases cannot coexist in equilibrium in a one-component system.

Phase diagrams of metals and ceramics are usually drawn at constant (atmospheric) pressure, and F = C − P + 1, which drops the pressure variable, is used. In a binary system (C = 2), single-phase regions have F = 2 and two-phase regions F = 1; once the temperature is fixed, the compositions of the phases are fixed at the ends of the tie line, and their proportions are found with the lever rule. When three phases coexist, F = 0, and reactions such as eutectic, eutectoid and peritectic reactions appear as horizontal lines at a fixed temperature. In ternary systems, points where four phases coexist at constant pressure are the invariant points.

about.h: Common misconceptions and where it helps
about.p: The phase rule counts phases, not names of microconstituents. Pearlite is a microconstituent made of two phases, ferrite and cementite, not a single phase. The rule also applies to equilibrium states and does not apply to non-equilibrium microstructures such as martensite formed by quenching. The components may be chosen as convenient units, as in the Fe–Fe₃C system. The rule is useful for checking that a phase diagram you have drawn or a cooling curve you have measured does not contradict it, and for identifying how many phases coexist during a temperature arrest.

faq.q: What do the degrees of freedom in the phase rule count?
faq.a: They count the intensive variables, such as temperature, pressure and the composition of each phase, that can be changed independently while equilibrium is maintained. The amounts of the phases and the size of the sample are not included. A point with zero degrees of freedom is an invariant point where both temperature and compositions are fixed.

faq.q: When should F = C − P + 2 and F = C − P + 1 be used?
faq.a: Use +2 when pressure is also treated as a variable, and +1 for condensed systems in which pressure is regarded as constant, such as phase diagrams of metals and oxides. In systems of only solids and liquids, pressure has little effect, so +1 is normally used.

faq.q: When can three phases coexist in a binary system?
faq.a: At constant pressure, only at the specific combinations of temperature and composition where the degrees of freedom become zero. Eutectic, eutectoid and peritectic points are examples, and the cooling curve shows a temperature arrest at that temperature until the reaction is complete.

共晶反応.desc: A reaction in which two solid phases crystallize simultaneously from the liquid on cooling, L → α + β. In a binary system it occurs at a fixed temperature and composition and produces eutectic structures such as lamellae.

about.h: How it appears on a phase diagram, and typical systems
about.p: In a binary system with a eutectic reaction, the point where the liquidus lines descending from both sides meet in a V shape is the eutectic point, and liquid of that composition solidifies all at once at the lowest temperature in the system. The eutectic temperature is lower than the melting point of either component. Typical examples are the Pb–Sn system (183 °C, 61.9 wt% Sn), the Al–Si system (about 577 °C, about 12.6 wt% Si) and the Fe–C system (1147 °C, 4.3 wt% C), whose eutectic structure is called ledeburite. Three phases coexist at the eutectic temperature, and the number of degrees of freedom is zero.

In a eutectic reaction, the two solid phases grow side by side while exchanging solute through the liquid, producing fine lamellar or rod-like structures. The faster the solidification rate v, the smaller the lamellar spacing λ, and the relation that λ²v is nearly constant is well known. If one of the phases tends to form crystal facets, the structure becomes irregular; in Al–Si alloys, Si forms coarse plates and makes the alloy brittle. Adding small amounts of Na or Sr changes the Si into fine fibers (modification), raising elongation and toughness.

about.h: Distinguishing primary crystals from eutectic structure
about.p: In alloys away from the eutectic composition, one solid phase first crystallizes as the primary phase when the liquidus is crossed, and only the liquid remaining when the eutectic temperature is reached becomes eutectic structure. The room-temperature microstructure is therefore "primary phase + eutectic structure", while in terms of phases both consist of the two phases α and β. The fractions of the microconstituents are found with the lever rule just above the eutectic temperature, and the fractions of the phases just below it. In real solidification, segregation can produce a small amount of eutectic in the last regions to solidify, even at compositions that would form no eutectic in equilibrium.

about.h: Use in solders and casting alloys
about.p: Alloys of eutectic composition solidify at a single temperature with no freezing range, so they have good fluidity and are less prone to cracking and segregation during solidification. Eutectic or near-eutectic compositions are therefore used for solders (such as the Sn–Pb eutectic 63Sn–37Pb and Sn–3.0Ag–0.5Cu, which melts at about 217–220 °C), die-casting Al–Si alloys and cast irons. Because eutectics lower the melting point, the eutectic concept is also essential to designing low-melting alloys and brazing filler metals.

faq.q: What is the difference between eutectic and eutectoid reactions?
faq.a: On cooling, a reaction in which two solid phases form simultaneously from a liquid is eutectic (L → α + β), and one in which two solid phases form simultaneously from one solid phase is eutectoid (γ → α + β). A eutectoid reaction proceeds by diffusion in the solid, so its structure tends to be finer than a eutectic one.

faq.q: Is the eutectic temperature always lower than the melting points of the components?
faq.a: Yes. The eutectic point is where the liquidus lines descending from both sides meet, so the eutectic temperature is lower than the melting point of either pure component. For example, the eutectic temperature of Pb (327 °C) and Sn (232 °C) is 183 °C.

faq.q: Why are alloys of eutectic composition suited to casting?
faq.a: Their liquidus and solidus temperatures coincide, so they solidify at a single temperature. With no temperature range in which solid and liquid coexist, the melt flows well and is less likely to crack or segregate during solidification.

共析反応.desc: A reaction in which two solid phases form simultaneously from one solid phase on cooling. In steel, γ → α + Fe₃C occurs at 0.76 wt% C and 727 °C, producing pearlite.

about.h: A three-phase reaction in the solid state
about.p: A eutectoid reaction is one in which one solid phase splits simultaneously into two solid phases on cooling, and it appears on a phase diagram as a horizontal line where three phases coexist (zero degrees of freedom). In steel, at about 0.76 wt% C and 727 °C, austenite (γ) splits into ferrite (α, about 0.022 wt% C) and cementite (Fe₃C, 6.70 wt% C). This temperature is the A1 point, the reference temperature for heat treatment of steel. Besides steel, eutectoid reactions also occur in alloys such as the Cu–Al system (aluminum bronze).

about.h: Easily delayed, since it proceeds by solid-state diffusion
about.p: Unlike a eutectic reaction from a liquid, a eutectoid reaction proceeds by diffusion in the solid, so it takes time. The transformation temperature therefore differs between heating and cooling: Ac1 on heating is above 727 °C, and Ar1 on cooling is below it. The lever rule gives the mass fraction of ferrite in pearlite as (6.70 − 0.76)/(6.70 − 0.022) ≈ 0.89. Because the densities of the two phases are similar, the thickness ratio of the ferrite and cementite layers is about 8:1.

about.h: Hypo- and hypereutectoid steels, and estimating carbon from microstructure
about.p: In hypoeutectoid steels, with less carbon than the eutectoid composition, proeutectoid ferrite forms first and the remaining austenite becomes pearlite at 727 °C. In hypereutectoid steels, with more carbon, proeutectoid cementite precipitates as a network at the grain boundaries. For a slowly cooled hypoeutectoid steel with a pearlite area fraction f, the carbon content can be estimated as about 0.022 + 0.74f wt%, about 0.39 wt% if half the structure is pearlite. A micrograph thus gives a rough idea of a steel's carbon content.

about.h: Effects of alloying elements and cooling rate
about.p: The 727 °C and 0.76 wt% C on the phase diagram are equilibrium values for the pure Fe–C system. Alloying elements shift the eutectoid point: Mn and Ni lower the eutectoid temperature, while Cr, Si, Mo, W and Ti raise it. Most alloying elements also reduce the eutectoid carbon content. With fast cooling, transformation occurs below the A1 point, giving pearlite with a finer lamellar spacing, and with still faster cooling bainite or martensite forms. Practical heat-treatment conditions are set by combining the phase diagram with TTT or CCT diagrams.

faq.q: Is the carbon content of eutectoid steel 0.76%, 0.77% or 0.8%?
faq.a: All are used, and the difference comes from the source of the phase diagram data. Different assessments of the thermodynamic data shift the value slightly, so in textbooks and problems, calculate with the value given there.

faq.q: What is the A1 point?
faq.a: It is the temperature of the eutectoid reaction in iron and steel (727 °C in equilibrium), below which austenite cannot exist stably. Tempering is done below the A1 point, while quenching and normalizing are done after heating above the A1 or A3 point.

faq.q: Is the pearlite formed by the eutectoid reaction a single phase?
faq.a: No, it is a microconstituent in which two phases, ferrite and cementite, alternate in layers. When counting phases with the phase rule or the lever rule, pearlite is treated as two phases.

パーライト.desc: The microstructure formed by the eutectoid reaction in steel, with alternating lamellae of ferrite and cementite. The faster the cooling, the finer the lamellar spacing and the harder the pearlite.

about.p: When austenite of eutectoid composition transforms slightly below the A1 point, pearlite forms mainly from the austenite grain boundaries. Ferrite and cementite grow simultaneously side by side, and just ahead of the growth front, carbon diffuses from the ferrite side to the cementite side and is handed over. A region in which the lamellae share an orientation is called a colony, and many colonies with different orientations form within one austenite grain. The name comes from the pearl-like luster of a polished and etched surface.

The lamellar spacing of pearlite becomes finer the lower the transformation temperature (the greater the undercooling), roughly in inverse proportion to the undercooling, because carbon has to diffuse a shorter distance and more nuclei form. The finer the spacing, the shorter the distance dislocations can travel in the ferrite, so yield strength and hardness rise; a relation in which they are proportional to the inverse square root of the spacing is widely used. Furnace cooling gives coarse pearlite and air cooling (normalizing) gives fine pearlite, so strength changes even at the same carbon content.

about.h: Difference from bainite and spheroidized structures
about.p: Transformation at temperatures below the pearlite range but above the range where martensite forms produces bainite, in which cementite is dispersed not as lamellae but as fine particles or rods in or between the ferrite. When pearlite is held for a long time just below the A1 point, the cementite becomes rounded to lower its surface energy, giving a spheroidized structure. Spheroidized steel is the softest possible at a given carbon content and is easy to machine and cold-work, so this treatment is used on bearing and tool steels before machining.

about.h: Use in piano wire and rails
about.p: High-carbon steel wire rod is transformed isothermally to fine pearlite in a lead bath or similar at about 500–550 °C (patenting) and is then heavily cold-drawn. Drawing makes the lamellar spacing even finer, and piano wire, bridge suspension cables and tire reinforcing cords reach tensile strengths well above 2 GPa. Railway rails also use wear-resistant pearlitic steel, and some have heads heat-treated to fine pearlite. Pearlite is a long-established microstructure, but it remains one of the mainstays of high-strength materials today.

faq.q: What is the difference between pearlite and martensite?
faq.a: Pearlite is a near-equilibrium structure in which carbon has diffused and the steel has separated into ferrite and cementite. Martensite is a non-equilibrium structure formed when quenching prevents diffusion and the steel transforms by shear while retaining carbon in supersaturation; it is far harder and more brittle.

faq.q: Why does pearlite look dark under the microscope?
faq.a: Etching with nital or a similar reagent turns the lamella boundaries into grooves that scatter light. At low magnification the fine lamellae cannot be resolved, so the whole area looks dark. The regions that look white are ferrite or proeutectoid cementite.

faq.q: How can the lamellar spacing of pearlite be made finer?
faq.a: Lower the transformation temperature (cool faster). Normalizing with air cooling and patenting with isothermal transformation around 500 °C give fine pearlite. If cooling is too fast, however, bainite or martensite forms.

マルテンサイト.desc: The microstructure formed by a diffusionless, shear-type transformation when austenite is quenched. In steel it is body-centered tetragonal, supersaturated with carbon, and very hard.

about.p: When steel is cooled from the austenite region faster than the critical cooling rate, carbon atoms have no time to diffuse and form cementite. Instead, a shear-type transformation occurs in which iron atoms shift cooperatively by small amounts, and FCC austenite changes into body-centered tetragonal (BCT) martensite supersaturated with carbon. Atoms move less than an interatomic distance, and the transformation proceeds at nearly the speed of sound. The composition does not change across the transformation, and a distinctive feature is that the amount transformed is set by the temperature reached, not by the holding time.

The martensitic transformation starts at the Ms temperature during cooling, progresses as the temperature falls, and is nearly complete at the Mf temperature. Ms and Mf fall as the carbon and alloy contents increase, and in high-carbon steels Mf is below room temperature, so retained austenite that has not transformed remains. Retained austenite transforms over time and causes dimensional changes, so precision parts are given a subzero treatment, cooling below 0 °C. The volume expansion and temperature differences during quenching also cause quench cracking and distortion.

about.h: The source of hardness and tempering
about.p: The hardness of martensite is determined mainly by its carbon content; the large lattice strain from supersaturated carbon and the high dislocation density strongly obstruct dislocation motion. On the other hand, martensite is very brittle, so it is normally tempered before use. During tempering, the supersaturated carbon precipitates as fine carbides and internal stresses relax, so hardness falls but toughness recovers substantially. Low-temperature tempering is used for tools and high-temperature tempering for shafts and gears (combined with the preceding quench, this is called quenching and tempering), giving a combination of hardness and toughness suited to the application.

The martensitic transformation is not unique to steel. In Ni-Ti alloys, the martensitic transformation and its reverse give the shape memory effect and superelasticity, used in medical wires and actuators. The tetragonal-to-monoclinic transformation of zirconia is also martensitic and is exploited in transformation toughening. All share the same mechanism of cooperative atomic shifts without diffusion, and the crystallography of the transformation determines macroscopic properties. Transformation temperatures vary greatly with alloy composition, so composition control is important.

faq.q: Why is martensite hard?
faq.a: Because carbon dissolved in supersaturation greatly distorts the lattice, and the transformation also introduces many dislocations and twins, making dislocations very hard to move. Its hardness is determined mainly by the carbon content.

faq.q: Does quenching always produce martensite?
faq.a: If the cooling rate is slower than the critical cooling rate, pearlite or bainite forms along the way. The centers of thick sections cool slowly, so alloy steels with high hardenability or quenchants with high cooling power are used.

faq.q: What is retained austenite?
faq.a: In steels whose Mf is below room temperature, it is austenite that remains untransformed after quenching. It transforms over time and changes dimensions, so it is reduced by subzero treatment or tempering.

焼戻し.desc: A heat treatment that reheats quenched steel to a temperature below the A1 temperature (727 °C). It restores toughness and reduces internal stresses at the cost of some hardness.

about.p: When as-quenched martensite is heated, it changes in stages depending on temperature. As a rough guide, at about 100–250 °C supersaturated carbon precipitates as fine carbides such as ε-carbide and the tetragonal distortion of the lattice decreases. At about 200–300 °C retained austenite decomposes, and above about 250 °C cementite forms and the matrix approaches ferrite. In steels containing Mo, V, W or Cr, fine alloy carbides precipitate above 500 °C, causing secondary hardening, a temporary rise in hardness.

The higher the tempering temperature and the longer the time, the lower the hardness and the higher the toughness. Parts that need hardness and wear resistance, such as cutting tools, bearings and carburized parts, keep a high hardness with low-temperature tempering at about 150–200 °C. Machine parts such as shafts and gears that need both strength and toughness receive high-temperature tempering at about 550–650 °C; combined with the preceding quench, this is called quenching and tempering. The effects of temperature and time can be treated together with a tempering parameter of the form T(C + log t) (C is about 20 for steels).

Depending on the tempering temperature, toughness can actually drop. Tempering at about 250–400 °C causes tempered martensite embrittlement, in which carbides precipitate as films at martensite lath boundaries and impact energy falls, so tempering in this range is usually avoided. Also, when Ni–Cr steels and others are cooled slowly through or held in the range of about 375–575 °C, temper embrittlement occurs as impurities such as P, Sb and Sn segregate to prior-austenite grain boundaries. It is prevented by rapid cooling after tempering, reducing impurities, adding Mo and similar measures.

As-quenched steel has large internal stresses and can crack some time after quenching if left standing (delayed cracking), so it is tempered as soon as possible after quenching. Steels with much retained austenite, such as high-speed tool steels, are tempered two or three times at around 550 °C, converting the retained austenite to martensite and then tempering that martensite. For precision parts such as gauges and bearings, where dimensional stability matters, a subzero treatment cooling below 0 °C may be added after quenching before tempering.

faq.q: What is the difference between tempering and annealing?
faq.a: Tempering reheats quenched steel to a temperature below the A1 point to restore toughness. Annealing usually heats steel above the A1 or A3 point and cools it slowly to soften it or refine its structure, and it does not presuppose quenching.

faq.q: What is quenching and tempering?
faq.a: It is a treatment in which quenching is followed by tempering at a high temperature of about 550–650 °C to balance strength and toughness. It gives a tempered martensite structure and is widely applied to shafts and gears of machine structural steels such as S45C and SCM435.

faq.q: Can tempering make steel harder?
