faq.a: Yes. In tool steels containing Mo, V, W and similar elements, fine alloy carbides precipitate around 500–600 °C, causing secondary hardening. Hardness can also rise when retained austenite transforms to martensite on cooling.

析出硬化.desc: Strengthening by dispersing fine precipitates through solution treatment, quenching and aging, so that they obstruct dislocation motion. Used in alloys such as Al-Cu; aging too long causes softening by overaging.

about.p: Precipitation hardening requires a phase diagram in which the solute dissolves well at high temperature and its solubility falls sharply as temperature drops. In the Al–Cu system, the maximum solubility of Cu is about 5.65 wt% at 548 °C, but only a tiny amount dissolves at room temperature. The alloy is therefore solution-treated at about 500 °C to form a uniform solid solution and quenched to carry the supersaturated solid solution to room temperature. Aging at room temperature or at about 100–200 °C then disperses fine precipitates uniformly. Alloys whose solubility hardly changes with temperature cannot be treated this way.

about.h: Precipitate size and the strengthening mechanism
about.p: GP zones and θ″ that form early in aging are small and coherent, with atomic rows continuous with the matrix, and dislocations pass by cutting through them. In this case, the larger the precipitates grow, the higher the stress needed to cut them. As the precipitates grow larger and their spacing widens, dislocations switch to the Orowan mechanism, bowing out between them without cutting, and strength falls in inverse proportion to the spacing. Strength peaks at the size where the two mechanisms cross over, which is the peak-aged condition.

The higher the aging temperature, the faster precipitation proceeds and the sooner peak hardness is reached, but the peak hardness is lower. Aging conditions are chosen to balance the required strength against corrosion resistance and toughness. In aluminum alloy temper designations, natural aging after solution treatment is T4, artificial aging close to peak is T6, and further overaging is T7. For 7000-series alloys, T7-type tempers deliberately overaged for better resistance to stress corrosion cracking, at some cost in strength, are used in aircraft.

about.h: Examples beyond aluminum, and cautions in use
about.p: Precipitation hardening is also used in maraging steels strengthened by Ni₃Ti and similar phases, precipitation-hardening stainless steels such as 17-4PH, nickel-based superalloys strengthened by the γ′ phase, and beryllium copper, the strongest copper alloy. On the other hand, when a precipitation-hardened alloy is used at high temperature or heated by welding, the precipitates coarsen and the alloy overages, losing strength. Parts are designed and materials selected with the softening of weld heat-affected zones and the upper limit of service temperature in mind.

faq.q: Are age hardening and precipitation hardening the same?
faq.a: They are used in almost the same sense. Precipitation hardening is a name focused on the mechanism of strengthening by precipitates, and age hardening a name focused on hardening through the aging treatment.

faq.q: What is the difference between natural and artificial aging?
faq.a: Natural aging advances precipitation at room temperature, while artificial aging advances it by heating to about 100–200 °C. Artificial aging proceeds faster, and in many alloys it gives higher strength.

faq.q: Why does overaging soften the alloy?
faq.a: The precipitates coarsen and become fewer and farther apart, so dislocations can pass between them more easily. The change of coherent metastable phases into the stable θ phase and the like also reduces the strengthening effect.

ホール・ペッチの関係.desc: The relation σy = σ₀ + k/√d in which the yield stress increases in inverse proportion to the square root of the grain size d. Grain boundaries obstruct dislocation motion, so finer grains give higher strength.

about.h: Origin and mechanism of the relation
about.p: The relation in which yield stress increases in inverse proportion to the square root of grain size was shown for steel by Hall in 1951 and by Petch in 1953. Crystal orientation changes at a grain boundary, so dislocations gliding toward it stop in front of it and form a line (a dislocation pile-up). A large stress concentrates at the head of the pile-up, and when it activates dislocation sources in the neighboring grain, yielding spreads. The larger the grain, the longer the pile-up and the greater the stress concentration, so yielding occurs at a lower stress; this picture leads to the d^(−1/2) dependence.

about.h: Size of the coefficients and points to watch in calculation
about.p: σ₀ is the friction stress without grain boundaries, and k is a coefficient expressing how effectively grain boundaries strengthen, in units of MPa·√m. k differs greatly between materials: it is large for BCC iron and steel and small for FCC aluminum and copper, so grain refinement is especially effective in steel. The grain boundary contribution is proportional to 1/√d, so reducing the grain size to 1/100, for example from 100 µm to 1 µm, increases it tenfold. In calculations, remember to convert grain size to meters to match the units of k.

about.h: Range of validity and the inverse Hall–Petch effect
about.p: When the grain size falls below about 10–20 nm, dislocation pile-ups can no longer form within grains and other deformation such as grain boundary sliding takes over, so strength levels off or even decreases (the inverse Hall–Petch effect). At high temperature, finer grains also make diffusion creep and grain boundary sliding easier, so refinement becomes a disadvantage. Relations of the same form are used for hardness, the block size of martensite and the lamellar spacing of pearlite, and grain refinement also lowers the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature.

Grain refinement is one of the few strengthening methods that raise strength and toughness together, and because it does not require more alloying elements, it does not impair weldability. In steel, TMCP, which combines controlled rolling with accelerated cooling, makes ferrite grains a few µm to about 10 µm in size to produce strong, tough heavy plate. In aluminum castings, Al–Ti–B grain refiners are added to increase the number of solidification nuclei. Grain size is evaluated with JIS or ASTM grain size numbers or with the intercept method, which counts the grain boundaries crossed by a line.

faq.q: Why does grain refinement raise both strength and toughness?
faq.a: Grain boundaries obstruct dislocation motion and raise the yield stress, while a cleavage crack must change direction at each grain boundary and propagates with more difficulty, increasing the energy needed for fracture. As a result, the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature also falls.

faq.q: What is the unit of the Hall–Petch coefficient k?
faq.a: MPa·√m (MPa·m^(1/2)). Grain size d is expressed in meters so that k/√d is a stress. Substituting the grain size in µm or mm leads to errors of orders of magnitude.

faq.q: Is a smaller grain size always stronger?
faq.a: No. Below a few tens of nanometers the gain in strength slows, and below about 10–20 nm strength can level off or even decrease, depending on the material and how it is made. At high temperature, finer grains also creep more readily, so a grain size suited to the application must be chosen.

焼入れ性.desc: The depth to which martensite can be obtained by quenching (how readily a steel hardens). It increases when alloying elements such as Mn, Cr and Mo shift the nose of the TTT diagram to longer times.

about.h: Hardenability and as-quenched hardness are different things
about.p: Hardenability expresses how deep martensite can be produced by quenching (how readily the steel hardens). The maximum hardness of the martensite produced (the as-quenched hardness), on the other hand, is determined mainly by carbon content, with little influence from alloying elements. So adding alloying elements to raise hardenability makes the hard layer deeper without changing the maximum surface hardness much. A helpful summary is that carbon content mainly sets hardness, while alloying elements and austenite grain size mainly set hardenability.

Hardenability is evaluated with the Jominy test (end-quench test). A round bar about 25 mm in diameter and 100 mm long is austenitized and then cooled by spraying water onto one end, so the cooling rate varies continuously with distance from that end. After cooling, flats are ground on the side and hardness is measured at each distance from the end, giving the Jominy curve. The more slowly hardness falls, the higher the hardenability; H steels with guaranteed hardenability (such as SCM435H) are specified by upper and lower bands of this curve.

about.h: Critical diameter and the mass effect
about.p: The critical diameter expresses hardenability in terms of part size: it is the largest diameter of a round bar whose center becomes 50% martensite. The value for an ideal quench with infinite cooling power is called the ideal critical diameter, and it can be estimated by finding a base value from carbon content and grain size and multiplying by factors for each alloying element. The phenomenon in which even the same steel hardens less readily in thicker parts, because the center cools more slowly, is called the mass effect, and it is larger in low-hardenability carbon steels. Cooling power also depends on the quenchant, such as water, oil or aqueous polymer solutions.

Alloying elements such as Mn, Cr, Mo and Ni, and tiny amounts of B around 0.001–0.003%, raise hardenability. A coarser austenite grain size raises hardenability by reducing the grain boundary sites for nucleation, but it lowers toughness. Thicker parts need steels with higher hardenability, but too much hardenability makes quench cracking and distortion more likely, and in welding the heat-affected zone becomes hard and prone to cracking. The basic principle is to choose a steel with the minimum hardenability that still hardens to the required depth.

faq.q: Does a steel with higher hardenability become harder?
faq.a: No. Higher hardenability lets hardening reach deeper, but the maximum hardness of martensite is set mainly by carbon content. At the same carbon content, alloy steels and carbon steels have almost the same as-quenched surface hardness.

faq.q: What is the mass effect?
faq.a: It is the phenomenon in which even the same steel hardens less readily in thicker parts because the interior cools more slowly. It is large in low-hardenability carbon steels and small in alloy steels. To harden thick parts through to the center, choose a steel with high hardenability.

faq.q: Why does a very small amount of boron raise hardenability?
faq.a: B segregates to austenite grain boundaries and suppresses the nucleation of ferrite there. It is effective at about 0.001–0.003%, and it is used together with elements such as Ti so that it does not combine with nitrogen.

焼結.desc: The process of heating a powder compact at a high temperature below the melting point so that the particles bond and the compact densifies. The driving force is the reduction in surface energy.

about.p: Sintering can be divided roughly into three stages by how it proceeds. In the initial stage, necks form and thicken at the contacts between particles, and shrinkage is a few percent. In the intermediate stage, the pores form connected tunnels along grain boundaries, and most of the densification occurs here. When the relative density exceeds about 92%, the final stage begins, in which the pores become isolated closed pores and the remaining pores disappear by diffusion to grain boundaries. Once pores close, gas cannot easily escape, so the choice of atmosphere also affects densification.

about.h: Magnitude of the driving force and particle fineness
about.p: The driving force for sintering is the reduction of surface energy, and a curved surface experiences a pressure of about 2γ/r. With a surface energy γ of 1 J/m² and a particle radius of 0.5 µm, this is about 4 MPa. The finer the particles, the greater the driving force and the shorter the diffusion distance over which material moves, so sintering proceeds at lower temperatures and in shorter times. For the same mechanism, Herring's scaling law states that the time needed for sintering is proportional to a power of particle size: the cube for volume diffusion and the fourth power for grain boundary diffusion.

about.h: The competition between densification and grain growth
about.p: Holding at high temperature for a long time also advances grain growth. If grain boundaries move too fast, they leave pores behind and trap them inside grains, and pores away from the boundaries that serve as diffusion paths hardly disappear. It is well known that adding a little MgO to alumina suppresses boundary migration, eliminating pores and producing translucent alumina. Hot pressing, HIP and spark plasma sintering, which applies pressure while passing current, are also methods that supplement the driving force with pressure and promote densification while suppressing grain growth.

about.h: Shrinkage, liquid-phase sintering and density control
about.p: Ceramic green bodies have relative densities of about 50–60%, so they shrink greatly on densification. Going from 55% relative density to full density gives an isotropic linear shrinkage of about 18%, and die dimensions are set to allow for this. Silicon nitride is densified by liquid-phase sintering with Y₂O₃ and Al₂O₃ added to form a liquid, and cemented carbides also use a Co liquid. The density of sintered bodies is measured by the Archimedes method, and some products, such as oil-impregnated sintered bearings, deliberately retain pores to soak up oil.

faq.q: How do sintering and melting differ?
faq.a: Sintering bonds particles together at temperatures below the melting point, mainly by atomic diffusion. Because the whole body is not melted, even materials with very high melting points can be densified while keeping their formed shape. Even in liquid-phase sintering, which forms some liquid, the main skeleton remains solid.

faq.q: What is a typical sintering temperature?
faq.a: It varies widely with the material, particle size and additives, so there is no single value. For example, alumina, which melts at about 2072 °C, is sintered at about 1500–1600 °C, or about 0.75–0.8 times its melting point in kelvin.

faq.q: How is the density of a sintered body measured?
faq.a: The Archimedes method, which finds the volume from the difference between mass in air and in water, is common. Because water penetrates open pores, the pores are sealed before measurement, or the water-saturated mass is used to separate open porosity from apparent density.

ワイブル係数.desc: The parameter m of the Weibull distribution that expresses how small the scatter in strength is. The larger it is, the smaller the scatter: about 5–20 for ceramics and several tens or more for metals.

about.h: The Weibull distribution and the meaning of m
about.p: From the weakest-link idea, in which strength is set by the largest flaw, the strength of brittle materials is often described by the Weibull distribution of failure probability Pf = 1 − exp[−(σ/σ₀)^m]. σ₀ is the scale strength at which the failure probability is about 63.2%, and m is the Weibull modulus, which expresses how small the scatter is. The coefficient of variation of strength (standard deviation/mean) is roughly 1.2/m: about 12% for m = 10 and about 6% for m = 20. Since m reflects how uniform the flaw sizes are, it is also used as an indicator of manufacturing quality.

The strengths of n specimens are ranked from smallest to largest, and the failure probability of the i-th is estimated as (i − 0.5)/n, (i − 0.3)/(n + 0.4) or similar. Plotting ln ln[1/(1 − Pf)] on the vertical axis against ln σ on the horizontal gives a straight line whose slope is m. However, m found by least squares from this plot is easily biased when there are few specimens, so standards such as ASTM C1239 use maximum likelihood estimation. The fewer the specimens, the wider the uncertainty (confidence interval) of m, so a reliable m calls for specimens numbering in the tens.

about.h: Strength and scatter are different things
about.p: A large m means the strength is uniform, not that it is high. A material with high mean strength but small m includes pieces that fail at low stress. Also, m and σ₀ depend on the test method; even for the same material, a tensile test, which stresses a larger volume, gives lower strengths than a bending test. In metals, yielding blunts crack tips, so strength scatter is small and m reaches several tens or more; Weibull statistics are therefore rarely used in their design.

For ceramic parts, the allowable stress is set from a target failure probability. For a failure probability of 10⁻⁶, the allowable stress is (10⁻⁶)^(1/m) times σ₀: about 0.25 times for m = 10 and about 0.50 times for m = 20. This shows that raising m is about as effective in design as raising the strength itself. In addition, the difference in effective volume between part and specimen is corrected for, and proof testing, which applies a stress above the service stress before shipment to weed out weak pieces, is combined to ensure reliability.

faq.q: Why is the failure probability 63.2% at σ₀?
faq.a: Substituting σ = σ₀ into the equation gives Pf = 1 − exp(−1) = 1 − 1/e ≈ 0.632. σ₀ is also called the characteristic strength; it is close to the mean strength but is not the mean itself.

faq.q: How many specimens are needed to find the Weibull modulus?
faq.a: There is no fixed number, but the estimation error grows as the number decreases, so tests on the order of tens of specimens are desirable. With about 10 specimens the estimate of m can deviate greatly from the true value, so a confidence interval should be reported as well.

faq.q: Why is the Weibull modulus not used for the strength of metals?
faq.a: Plastic deformation blunts crack tips in metals, so strength depends little on flaw size and scatters only slightly. Metals are therefore normally handled with ordinary statistics using the mean and standard deviation.

圧電効果.desc: The phenomenon in which applying stress produces polarization and, conversely, applying an electric field produces deformation. It occurs in crystals without a center of symmetry; quartz and PZT are used in sensors and resonators.

about.h: Direct and converse effects, and piezoelectric coefficients
about.p: The appearance of charge on the surface of a crystal under stress is the direct piezoelectric effect, and the straining of a crystal under an electric field is the converse effect; the Curie brothers discovered the direct effect in 1880. The size of the effect is expressed by the piezoelectric coefficient d, in pC/N (charge/force), which has the same dimensions as pm/V (displacement/voltage). It is about 2 pC/N for quartz but reaches several hundred pC/N for PZT ceramics, giving a large response usable in both sensors and actuators.

about.h: Symmetry conditions and the relation to ferroelectrics
about.p: Of the 32 crystal point groups, 21 lack a center of symmetry, and 20 of those show piezoelectricity. Ten of these are polar crystals with spontaneous polarization, which also show pyroelectricity, a change of polarization with temperature. Ferroelectrics are crystals whose spontaneous polarization can be reversed by an electric field. In PZT and BaTiO₃ ceramics, the polarization direction differs from grain to grain, so as made, the piezoelectricity cancels out. Only after poling, in which a strong DC field is applied at high temperature to align the directions, do they become piezoelectric elements.

about.h: Composition of PZT and usable temperature
about.p: In PZT (Pb(Zr,Ti)O₃) there is a boundary between tetragonal and rhombohedral phases (the morphotropic phase boundary) near a Zr/Ti ratio of about 52/48, where the polarization direction changes easily and the piezoelectric coefficient is greatest. Polarization is lost above the Curie temperature, so the service temperature is kept well below it, with about half the Curie temperature as a guideline. Because PZT contains lead, lead-free piezoelectric materials such as those based on potassium sodium niobate (KNN) are also being developed.

The direct effect is used in accelerometers, engine knock sensors, ultrasonic reception and igniters. With the converse effect, the displacement is small but the response is fast and the force large, so it is used for precision positioning and fuel injectors. Applying 100 V to an element with d33 = 500 pm/V gives a displacement of about 50 nm, and stacking 100 layers gives about 5 µm. Quartz crystal resonators produce the reference frequencies of watches and electronic devices, and the high-frequency filters of smartphones use surface acoustic wave devices on LiNbO₃ or LiTaO₃ and AlN thin-film resonators.

faq.q: What is the difference between the piezoelectric and pyroelectric effects?
faq.a: The piezoelectric effect is a change of polarization with stress, while the pyroelectric effect is the appearance of charge as the magnitude of spontaneous polarization changes with temperature. All pyroelectric crystals are also piezoelectric, but some piezoelectric crystals, such as quartz, are not pyroelectric.

faq.q: Are the units pC/N and pm/V for piezoelectric coefficients the same?
faq.a: They have the same dimensions. Converting C/N = (A·s)/(kg·m/s²) and m/V = m/(kg·m²/(A·s³)) to base units gives A·s³/(kg·m) for both. For the direct effect it reads as charge per force, and for the converse effect as displacement per voltage.

faq.q: Why is it hard to measure a static force with a piezoelectric sensor?
faq.a: The generated charge leaks away over time through the insulation resistance of the element and circuit. Piezoelectric sensors are therefore suited to measuring changing forces such as vibration and impact. For quasi-static forces, low-leakage quartz is combined with a charge amplifier.

ペロブスカイト構造.desc: An ABO₃ crystal structure in which the B-site cation sits at the center of an oxygen octahedron (coordination number 6) and the A-site cation in the space between octahedra (coordination number 12). BaTiO₃ is an example.

about.h: Atomic arrangement and origin of the name
about.p: The ideal perovskite structure is cubic and can be drawn with the B-site cation at the body center of the unit cell, oxide ions at the six face centers and A-site cations at the eight corners. The BO₆ octahedra share corners to form a three-dimensional network, and the large A cations sit in the spaces between them. SrTiO₃ is cubic at room temperature, with a lattice parameter of about 0.3905 nm. The name comes from the mineral CaTiO₃, found in the Ural Mountains in 1839 and named after the Russian mineralogist Perovski.

about.h: Estimating stability with the tolerance factor
about.p: The balance of ion sizes is expressed by the Goldschmidt tolerance factor t = (r_A + r_O)/(√2(r_B + r_O)). With t = 1 the ions fit the ideal cubic structure exactly, and empirically the perovskite structure forms readily for t from roughly 0.8 to slightly above 1, while other structures form when t is far outside this range. Calculated with Shannon ionic radii, t is about 1.00 for SrTiO₃, about 1.06 for BaTiO₃ and about 0.97 for CaTiO₃. In BaTiO₃, with t above 1, the Ti moves easily within its octahedron and ferroelectricity appears; in CaTiO₃, with t below 1, the octahedra tilt and the structure becomes orthorhombic.

By changing the combination of A, B and X, the perovskite structure shows a wide variety of properties. BaTiO₃ is used as the dielectric in multilayer ceramic capacitors, PZT in piezoelectric elements and (La,Sr)MnO₃ in the air electrodes of solid oxide fuel cells. Copper-oxide high-temperature superconductors and manganese oxides showing colossal magnetoresistance are also derived from this structure. Furthermore, halide perovskites such as CH₃NH₃PbI₃, in which X is replaced by a halogen, are being researched and commercialized as the light-absorbing layers of solar cells.

about.h: Tuning properties by substitution and defects
about.p: When part of the A or B site is replaced by ions of different valence, oxygen vacancies or electrons and holes form to compensate the charge, allowing electronic and ionic conduction to be tuned. For example, replacing La with Sr increases oxygen vacancies or holes. BaTiO₃ changes from cubic to tetragonal at its Curie temperature of about 120 °C, and additives are used to adjust this temperature and the temperature dependence of permittivity to give capacitors uniform characteristics. There are also many derived structures built from this structure as a basic unit, such as the layered Ruddlesden–Popper type.

faq.q: Is the "perovskite" in perovskite solar cells the same structure?
faq.a: It is the same ABX₃-type structure. Solar cells use halide perovskites in which X is a halogen such as iodine instead of oxygen, A is an organic cation such as methylammonium or Cs⁺, and B is Pb²⁺ or a similar ion.

faq.q: How is the tolerance factor calculated?
faq.a: Insert ionic radii appropriate to the coordination number into t = (r_A + r_O)/(√2(r_B + r_O)). Use 12-coordinate values for A and 6-coordinate values for B; for SrTiO₃ (Sr²⁺ 0.144 nm, Ti⁴⁺ 0.0605 nm, O²⁻ 0.140 nm), t ≈ 1.00.

faq.q: Are all perovskite oxides cubic?
faq.a: No. The ideal cubic form occurs only in some, such as SrTiO₃; many are distorted to tetragonal, orthorhombic or rhombohedral by octahedral tilting or displacement of the B ion. Many substances change crystal system with temperature, and BaTiO₃ undergoes several phase transitions as temperature changes.

変態強化.desc: The mechanism in partially stabilized zirconia by which stress at a crack tip transforms tetragonal to monoclinic, and the accompanying volume expansion closes the crack and raises toughness.

about.h: A phase transformation at the crack tip
about.p: Zirconia (ZrO₂) is cubic, tetragonal and monoclinic in order from high temperature, and the tetragonal-to-monoclinic transformation expands its volume by about 4%. In partially stabilized zirconia, metastable tetragonal grains are retained at room temperature by the constraint of their surroundings. As a crack advances, the tensile stress at its tip transforms grains in a band around the crack (the transformation zone) to monoclinic, and their expansion puts the crack faces under compression and resists opening. Because the zone widens as the crack grows, the material shows R-curve behavior, with resistance increasing as the crack extends.

To retain the tetragonal phase, stabilizers such as Y₂O₃, MgO or CeO₂ are added. Fine-grained tetragonal polycrystals with about 3 mol% Y₂O₃ (3Y-TZP) have a good balance of strength and toughness and are the most widely used. Mg-PSZ, with MgO added, has tetragonal precipitates dispersed in a cubic matrix. If the grains are too large they transform spontaneously to monoclinic during cooling, and if too small they do not transform even under stress, so in Y-TZP the grain size is kept within a suitable submicrometer range.

about.h: Conditions that weaken the effect, and degradation
about.p: Transformation toughening exploits the energy difference between the tetragonal and monoclinic phases, so its effect diminishes as temperature rises and the tetragonal phase becomes more stable. As a high-temperature structural material, the toughness advantage therefore tends to be lost. In moist environments, low-temperature degradation also occurs, in which the transformation to monoclinic proceeds slowly from the surface even near body temperature. Note also that what it raises is mainly fracture toughness rather than strength; the strength levels off at the stress that starts the transformation, so raising toughness does not keep raising strength.

Partially stabilized zirconia has a toughness about twice that of alumina and is used for dental crowns, femoral heads of artificial hip joints, knives, grinding balls and parts of optical fiber connectors. Zirconia-toughened alumina (ZTA), with zirconia particles dispersed in alumina, uses the same mechanism. How much monoclinic phase has formed on a fracture surface can be found from the intensity ratios of XRD peaks. TRIP steel, in which retained austenite transforms to martensite during deformation and increases ductility, is similar in that it also makes use of a phase transformation.

faq.q: Does transformation toughening raise strength as well?
faq.a: Mainly it raises fracture toughness, the resistance to crack growth. In Japanese it is often called by a name meaning transformation strengthening, but strength levels off at the stress that starts the transformation, so it does not rise in step with toughness.

faq.q: Does transformation toughening occur in fully stabilized zirconia?
faq.a: No. Fully stabilized zirconia with a large amount of stabilizer is cubic down to room temperature and has no tetragonal phase to transform. Material with about 8 mol% Y₂O₃ is used for its oxide-ion conduction rather than toughness, as the electrolyte of fuel cells and sensors.

faq.q: What is the fracture toughness of transformation-toughened zirconia?
faq.a: It varies with composition, microstructure and measurement method, but values of roughly 5–10 MPa·√m are reported for partially stabilized zirconia. This is higher than about 3–5 MPa·√m for alumina, making it one of the tougher ceramics.

ガラス転移温度.desc: The temperature at which molecular or atomic motion in an amorphous substance or the amorphous regions of a polymer freezes, switching between the glassy and rubbery (supercooled liquid) states. Written Tg.

about.p: As a liquid or polymer melt is cooled, molecular rearrangement gradually slows. When rearrangement can no longer keep up with cooling, the structure freezes in place and the material enters the glassy state, behaving like a solid. The temperature at which this switch occurs is the glass transition temperature Tg, where the temperature dependence of specific volume, heat capacity and thermal expansion coefficient shows a kink. In polymers, segmental motion, in which several units of the backbone move together, becomes active above Tg, giving a soft, rubbery state.

about.h: How it differs from the melting point
about.p: The melting point Tm is the temperature of a thermodynamic phase transition at which crystals melt, and it has a definite value. Tg, on the other hand, is a kinetic phenomenon determined by the balance between relaxation time and observation time, and its value changes with cooling rate, heating rate and measurement frequency. The faster the cooling, the higher the temperature at which the structure freezes, and the higher Tg. Crystalline polymers have both a melting point Tm for the crystalline regions and a Tg for the amorphous regions; Tg is always lower than Tm, often by a ratio of about 0.5–0.8 in absolute temperature. Amorphous polymers have no Tm, only a Tg.

The harder it is for chains to move, the higher Tg. Polymers with stiff structures such as aromatic rings in the backbone, bulky side groups, strong interchain interactions or many crosslinks have high Tg: about 150 °C for polycarbonate and about 100 °C for polystyrene. Conversely, polyethylene and silicone rubber, with flexible backbones, have Tg far below room temperature. Plasticizers and moisture enter between chains, increase free volume and lower Tg. In epoxy resins, the drop in Tg on moisture absorption is a reliability concern.

Tg is measured from the stepwise change in heat capacity in DSC, the kink in the expansion coefficient in thermomechanical analysis (TMA), and the sharp drop in storage modulus or the peak in the loss tangent tanδ in dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA). Even for the same material, the value can differ by more than 10 °C depending on the method, the heating rate and, for DMA, the frequency, so check the measurement conditions when comparing data. For semiconductor encapsulants and substrate resins, the expansion coefficient and modulus change greatly above Tg, so its relation to temperatures such as reflow matters.

faq.q: Above the glass transition temperature, does a polymer become a liquid?
faq.a: An amorphous polymer first enters a rubbery region above Tg and begins to flow as the temperature rises further. Crosslinked thermosetting resins remain rubbery above Tg and do not flow.

faq.q: Why do DSC and DMA give different Tg values?
faq.a: Tg is a kinetic phenomenon, so its value changes with the time scale of the measurement. The DMA tanδ peak often comes out higher than the DSC midpoint value, so state which definition is used when comparing.

faq.q: Is the Tg of glass the same thing as the Tg of polymers?
faq.a: Both are glass transitions caused by the freezing of structure, and the mechanism is the same. The ranges of values differ widely, however: several hundred °C for silicate glasses versus roughly −100 °C to 200 °C for polymers.

結晶化度.desc: The fraction of a crystalline polymer occupied by crystalline regions. It is determined from density, the heat of fusion by DSC, XRD and so on; higher crystallinity raises density and modulus but lowers transparency.

about.p: The long chains of a polymer are entangled, so the whole material cannot become perfectly ordered. On cooling from the melt, plate-like crystals about 10 nm thick in which the chains are folded (lamellae) alternate with amorphous regions between them, and these further gather radially into spherulites. Crystallinity is the fraction of this crystalline part. The more regular the chain structure, the more readily it crystallizes: lightly branched high-density polyethylene has high crystallinity, while atactic polystyrene and PMMA, with irregularly oriented side groups, hardly crystallize at all.

about.h: Methods of measurement and differences in values
about.p: In DSC, crystallinity is found by dividing the specimen's heat of fusion ΔHm by the heat of fusion of a perfect crystal ΔHm°. For polyethylene, ΔHm° of about 293 J/g is commonly used, so a heat of fusion of 176 J/g gives a crystallinity of about 60%. For specimens such as PET that crystallize during heating (cold crystallization), that exotherm is subtracted. Other methods use density, or separate the areas of the crystalline peaks and the amorphous halo in XRD. Each method counts a different range as crystalline, so values are compared using the same method.

Even for the same resin, fast cooling leaves no time for crystals to grow and gives low crystallinity, while slow cooling or holding below the melting point (annealing) raises it. PET bottles are made by quenching to form a transparent amorphous preform and then stretch-blow molding to align and crystallize the chains, raising strength and gas-barrier performance while staying transparent. In polypropylene, nucleating agents are added to make the spherulites finer, improving transparency and stiffness. When considering the properties of a molded part, the processing conditions matter as much as the resin grade.

Crystalline regions do not melt until the melting point Tm, so even above Tg they tie the chains together and keep the shape. This is why polyethylene and polypropylene, at room temperature above their Tg, are soft yet hold their shape. Higher crystallinity raises modulus, heat resistance, chemical resistance and gas-barrier performance, but tends to lower impact resistance and transparency. Crystalline resins also tend to show larger molding shrinkage than amorphous resins because of the volume decrease on crystallization, which is taken into account in mold design.

faq.q: How is crystallinity related to the glass transition temperature and melting point?
faq.a: Tg is the temperature at which molecular motion begins in the amorphous regions, and Tm the temperature at which the crystalline regions melt. Higher crystallinity makes the change at Tg smaller and the heat of fusion at Tm larger. A completely amorphous polymer has no Tm.

faq.q: Are there polymers with 100% crystallinity?
faq.a: Not in ordinary molded products. Single crystals grown from dilute solution come close, and highly drawn fibers of ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene can reach around 90%, but entanglements and chain ends prevent a perfect crystal.

faq.q: What should I watch for when finding crystallinity by DSC?
faq.a: Use a consistent literature value for the heat of fusion of a perfect crystal, subtract the exotherm of cold crystallization during heating, and note that values change with heating rate and thermal history. The first heating reflects the as-molded state, and the second the state after cooling under fixed conditions.

粘弾性.desc: Behavior that combines properties of an elastic solid and of a viscous fluid. In polymers it appears as stress relaxation and creep and depends on time and temperature.

about.h: Behavior changes with the time scale
about.p: A viscoelastic material behaves like an elastic solid when loaded over a short time and like a liquid when loaded over a long time. Which it appears to be depends on the ratio of the material's relaxation time to the observation time. A familiar example is silicone toy putty, which snaps when pulled quickly, stretches when pulled slowly and flows flat when left alone. In polymers it appears as creep, in which strain increases under constant load; stress relaxation, in which stress falls at constant strain; and hysteresis, in which the loading and unloading curves do not coincide.

When a sinusoidal strain is applied, the stress in a viscoelastic material leads in phase by δ (0–90°). Splitting the stress into components in phase with the strain and 90° out of phase gives the storage modulus E′ (energy stored and returned) and the loss modulus E″ (energy lost as heat), and the ratio tan δ = E″/E′ is called the loss tangent. For a purely elastic solid δ = 0, and for a purely viscous liquid δ = 90°. In dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) with varying temperature, E′ drops sharply near Tg and tan δ shows a maximum.

At small strains, Boltzmann's superposition principle holds, by which the effects of past stresses or strains can simply be added, and this is called linear viscoelasticity. Models of springs and dashpots describe behavior within this range; real polymers are approximated by generalized models with many Maxwell elements of different relaxation times in parallel, and this form is also used as input for finite element analysis. As strain increases, the response departs from linearity and superposition no longer holds.

In polymers, raising the temperature has the same effect as observing over a longer time. Near Tg the WLF equation log a_T = −C₁(T − Tr)/(C₂ + T − Tr) is widely used, and with Tg as the reference temperature, C₁ ≈ 17.44 and C₂ ≈ 51.6 K are the universal values. With these, relaxation proceeds about 700 times faster at 10 K above Tg. Damping materials are designed so that tan δ is large at the temperature and frequency of use, and for tire rubber, tan δ values on the low- and high-temperature sides serve as guides to grip and rolling resistance.

faq.q: What is the difference between viscoelasticity and plasticity?
faq.a: Deformation by linear viscoelasticity includes a component that recovers with time and is proportional to the magnitude of stress. Plasticity is permanent deformation that occurs when the yield stress is exceeded and does not recover on unloading. In polymers both can occur at the same time.

faq.q: What does tan δ express?
faq.a: It corresponds to the ratio of the energy lost as heat to the energy stored in one cycle of deformation, and equals the loss modulus divided by the storage modulus. The larger it is, the better the material absorbs vibration, and it is used to evaluate rubber and damping materials.

faq.q: Do metals show viscoelasticity too?
faq.a: Yes. Even in metals at room temperature, jumps of interstitial carbon atoms and similar processes make strain lag slightly behind stress, which is measured as internal friction. The amount is much smaller than in polymers, but it is relevant to damping in precision springs and resonators and to creep at high temperature.

熱硬化性樹脂.desc: A resin that forms a three-dimensional network by a curing reaction and does not melt when heated after curing. Examples include epoxy and phenolic resins.

about.p: Thermosetting resins harden as a low-molecular-weight base resin reacts with a curing agent to build a three-dimensional network. Epoxy resins cure with amine or acid anhydride hardeners, unsaturated polyesters by radical polymerization with styrene, and phenolic resins by condensation of phenol and formaldehyde. The point at which the reaction has connected molecules throughout the system is the gel point, after which the resin no longer flows. As the reaction continues and the Tg of the network catches up with the curing temperature, the molecules can no longer move and the reaction stops, which is called vitrification.

In thermoplastics the chains are held together only by intermolecular forces, so they flow when heated and can be reshaped any number of times. In thermosets the chains are crosslinked by covalent bonds, so they do not melt when heated and do not dissolve in solvents, only swell. Thermosets do have a glass transition temperature, however, and above it their modulus drops greatly. The Tg of epoxies ranges from around 100 °C to over 200 °C depending on the hardener and curing conditions, and heat resistance is set by the crosslink density and degree of cure.

With insufficient cure, Tg is low and strength and chemical resistance do not fully develop. The curing temperature and time (the cure schedule) are therefore set by measuring the remaining reaction heat by DSC to find the degree of cure and checking Tg by DMA. Where needed, the resin is post-cured at a higher temperature. The curing reaction shrinks the volume, and cooling shrinks it further, producing residual stress and warpage in parts and in CFRP. Epoxies have relatively small cure shrinkage, which suits applications requiring dimensional accuracy.

Thermosets excel in heat resistance, dimensional stability and electrical insulation, and are used as CFRP matrices, glass–epoxy printed circuit boards (FR-4), heavily silica-filled semiconductor encapsulants, adhesives and paints. The phenolic resin (Bakelite) invented by Baekeland in 1907 was the first true synthetic resin. On the other hand, the inability to melt and remold them is a major recycling problem, and research is under way on recovering fibers by pyrolysis or chemical decomposition and on vitrimers, whose bonds can be rearranged by heating.

faq.q: Do thermosetting resins cure only when heated?
faq.a: Not necessarily. The name comes from curing irreversibly on heating, but there are also two-part epoxy adhesives that cure at room temperature and resins that cure with ultraviolet light. What they have in common is that they form a crosslinked network after curing.

faq.q: Do thermosetting resins have a glass transition temperature?
faq.a: Yes. Even in a crosslinked network, partial motion of the chains begins above Tg, and the modulus drops by one to two orders of magnitude to a rubbery state. Because of the crosslinks, however, the resin does not flow, and further heating decomposes it before it melts.

faq.q: Is vulcanized rubber a thermosetting resin?
faq.a: Vulcanized rubber is also a crosslinked network and likewise does not melt on heating. But its crosslink density is low and its Tg is far below room temperature, so it is treated separately from hard thermosets, as an elastomer that shows rubber elasticity at room temperature.

複合則.desc: Expressions that estimate the properties of a composite from the properties and volume fractions of its constituents. Along the fibers, the isostrain form E = VfEf + VmEm applies; perpendicular to them, the isostress form is used as an approximation.

about.h: Thinking in terms of load sharing
about.p: When a material with unidirectionally aligned fibers is pulled along the fibers, the fibers and matrix stretch by the same amount, so the force each carries is proportional to the product of its volume fraction and Young's modulus. Adding the forces gives E = VfEf + VmEm (equal strain, the Voigt equation). When pulled perpendicular to the fibers, the two are in series and carry the same stress, so adding the strains gives 1/E = Vf/Ef + Vm/Em (equal stress, the Reuss equation). Both are derived from an assumption about how each phase carries the force.

about.h: Application to strength, and the minimum volume fraction
about.p: The tensile strength along the fibers can also be estimated as σc ≈ Vfσf + Vmσm′, where σm′ is the matrix stress when the fibers reach their failure strain. With too few fibers, however, the matrix can carry the load after the fibers break, so the strength can even fall below that of the matrix alone. For fibers to strengthen the material, their volume fraction must exceed a minimum value and a critical value needed to surpass the matrix strength. For short fibers, being longer than the critical fiber length is also a condition.

about.h: Use for other properties, and limitations
about.p: Density is simply additive by mass, so ρc = Vfρf + Vmρm holds exactly. Thermal and electrical conductivity also take the same form of equations for parallel and series arrangements. The thermal expansion coefficient, on the other hand, needs an equation weighted by Young's modulus as well as volume fraction, because the stiffer phase constrains the deformation. The Young's modulus of particle-reinforced materials falls between the equal-strain and equal-stress equations, so these serve as upper and lower bounds, and the Hashin–Shtrikman bounds, which give a narrower range, are also used.

about.h: Extension to short fibers and random orientation
about.p: For short fibers or fibers with scattered orientations, the estimate is multiplied by an orientation efficiency factor. With Krenchel's factors, it is 1 for unidirectional fibers, 3/8 for random in-plane orientation and 1/5 for random three-dimensional orientation. For example, a resin (3 GPa) with 20% by volume of glass fibers (72 GPa) randomly oriented in-plane gives E ≈ 3/8 × 0.2 × 72 + 0.8 × 3 ≈ 7.8 GPa, less than half the unidirectional upper bound of 16.8 GPa. In actual molded parts, fiber-length effects and voids can lower it further.

faq.q: Should the rule of mixtures use volume fraction or mass fraction?
faq.a: Use volume fraction, because the fraction of cross-sectional area carrying the load corresponds to the volume fraction. If the formulation was specified by mass fraction, divide by the density of each component to convert to volume fraction first.

faq.q: When can the rule of mixtures not be used?
faq.a: Errors become large when the fiber–matrix interface is debonded, when fibers are too short, when there are many voids, or in strongly nonlinear ranges of stress. Properties determined by local defects, such as fracture, also cannot be expressed by simple addition.

faq.q: Why is the equal-strain equation an upper bound?
faq.a: The condition that the whole material strains equally is an assumption that makes the stiffer phase carry more load than it really does. Conversely, the equal-stress equation assumes the maximum deformation of the softer phase and gives a lower bound, and the actual value lies between the two.

マティーセンの規則.desc: The empirical rule that the resistivity of a metal is the sum of a temperature-dependent component due to lattice vibrations and a temperature-independent component due to impurities and defects.

about.h: Adding the resistivity for each source of scattering
about.p: The electrical resistance of a metal arises from scattering of conduction electrons by lattice vibrations (phonons), impurity atoms, vacancies and dislocations, grain boundaries and so on. If each type of scattering can be regarded as occurring independently, the scattering rates add, so the resistivity is the sum of components, ρ = ρ_th(T) + ρ_i + ρ_d. This is Matthiessen's rule, found by Matthiessen in the 1860s from measurements of the resistance of alloys. Only the lattice-vibration component depends strongly on temperature; the impurity and defect components are nearly independent of it.

The resistivity due to lattice vibrations is nearly proportional to absolute temperature above about the Debye temperature, and at low temperature it falls steeply in proportion to T⁵. At liquid helium temperature (4.2 K), therefore, the lattice-vibration component almost vanishes and only the residual resistivity from impurities and defects remains. The ratio of resistance at room temperature to that at 4.2 K is called the residual resistivity ratio (RRR), and it is larger for metals that are purer and contain fewer defects. For niobium used in superconducting accelerator cavities, values such as an RRR of 300 or more are required as a quality indicator.

about.h: Resistance of alloys, and when the rule fails
about.p: In solid-solution alloys, the impurity component increases greatly with composition; in disordered binary solid solutions it is roughly proportional to x(1 − x) for solute concentration x (Nordheim's rule). When ordering occurs, with atoms arranged regularly as in Cu₃Au, scattering decreases and resistance falls. On the other hand, when scattering differs greatly with electron energy or direction, or when there is a Kondo effect due to magnetic impurities, the components are no longer independent and Matthiessen's rule breaks down. It should be used as an approximate rule.

about.h: Use in conductor materials and precision resistors
about.p: In copper for electric wire, even small amounts of impurities raise resistivity, so high purity and oxygen control are pursued. Conductivity is often expressed in %IACS, with annealed standard copper (resistivity 1.7241 µΩ·cm, about 58.0 MS/m) as 100%. Conversely, in alloys such as manganin and constantan, the temperature-independent residual component makes up most of the resistance, so their temperature coefficient of resistance is very small and they are used in precision resistors and strain gauges. In fine interconnects, scattering components from surfaces and grain boundaries are added and raise the resistivity.

faq.q: What is the residual resistivity ratio (RRR)?
faq.a: It is the ratio of resistivity at room temperature (about 300 K) to that at cryogenic temperature (usually 4.2 K). At cryogenic temperature only the resistance from impurities and defects remains, so a larger RRR shows a purer metal with fewer defects.

faq.q: Why do alloys have small temperature coefficients of resistance?
faq.a: In alloys, the temperature-independent resistance from solute atoms is large, so the temperature-dependent lattice-vibration component is relatively small. By Matthiessen's rule, the fraction of the total resistance that changes with temperature becomes small.

faq.q: Does Matthiessen's rule always hold?
faq.a: It is an approximate rule. When the scattering mechanisms cannot be regarded as independent, for example when the scattering strength changes greatly with electron energy or when magnetic impurities are present, deviations from the sum appear.

キュリー温度.desc: The temperature at which a ferromagnet (or ferroelectric) loses its spontaneous magnetization (or polarization); above it the material is paramagnetic. About 770 °C for iron and about 358 °C for nickel.

about.h: The temperature at which spontaneous magnetization vanishes
about.p: In a ferromagnet, the exchange interaction aligns the magnetic moments of atoms, producing spontaneous magnetization. As temperature rises, thermal motion disturbs this order, the spontaneous magnetization gradually shrinks, and it reaches zero at the Curie temperature. Above it the material is paramagnetic. Curie temperatures are about 770 °C (1043 K) for iron, about 358 °C for nickel, about 1120 °C for cobalt and about 20 °C for gadolinium; Nd₂Fe₁₄B, the main phase of neodymium magnets, is about 310 °C, and magnetite (Fe₃O₄) about 580 °C.

about.h: Behavior above and below the Curie temperature
about.p: Above the Curie temperature, the magnetic susceptibility follows the Curie–Weiss law χ = C/(T − θ), rising sharply as the temperature falls toward θ. θ is called the paramagnetic Curie temperature and is close to the Curie temperature. Ferroelectrics behave similarly, with the permittivity becoming very large near the Curie temperature; BaTiO₃ shows a sharp maximum in permittivity at about 120 °C. The Curie temperature is found by measuring the temperature dependence of magnetization with a magnetic balance, or from small anomalies in DSC or thermal expansion.

Iron loses its ferromagnetism at 770 °C, but its crystal structure remains BCC α-iron; it changes to FCC only at 912 °C. Iron in this range was once called β-iron, but since no structural change is involved, it is no longer regarded as a separate phase. The temperature at which antiferromagnetic order disappears is called the Néel temperature and is distinguished from the Curie temperature. Permanent magnets suffer irreversible demagnetization from falling coercivity at temperatures far below the Curie temperature, so their maximum service temperatures are set well below it.

about.h: Technologies that use the Curie temperature
about.p: The abrupt change in magnetism at the Curie temperature is used for temperature control. Rice cookers, for example, once used a mechanism with a temperature-sensitive ferrite that stops being attracted to a magnet at a certain temperature, cutting the heating when the rice is done and the temperature rises. Some soldering irons keep their temperature constant automatically by using a magnetic material in the tip that heats less readily above its Curie temperature. The way magnetite in rocks records the direction of Earth's magnetic field as it cools below its Curie temperature is the basis of paleomagnetic research.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Curie temperature and the Néel temperature?
faq.a: The Curie temperature is where ferromagnets and ferrimagnets lose their spontaneous magnetization, and the Néel temperature is where antiferromagnets lose their antiparallel order. Above either temperature the material becomes paramagnetic.

faq.q: Does iron change its crystal structure at 770 °C?
faq.a: No. 770 °C is the temperature of the magnetic transformation, at which only magnetic order is lost while the structure stays BCC, and it is called the A2 point on the Fe–C phase diagram. The crystal structure changes to FCC at 912 °C (the A3 point).

faq.q: Does a magnet heated above its Curie temperature recover when cooled?
faq.a: It becomes ferromagnetic again on cooling, but its magnetic domains point in random directions, so its strength as a magnet remains lost. To use it, it must be magnetized again in a strong field. If its microstructure has changed, its performance will not recover either.

保磁力.desc: The strength of the reverse magnetic field needed to bring the magnetization (or flux density) of a magnetized material back to zero. Materials with small coercivity are soft magnetic, and those with large coercivity hard magnetic.

about.h: A quantity that differs by more than six orders of magnitude
about.p: Coercivity expresses how strong a reverse field is needed to reverse the magnetization of a magnetized material, and its unit is A/m (1 Oe ≈ 79.6 A/m). In soft magnetic materials it ranges from below 1 A/m for high-permeability alloys such as Supermalloy to a few to a few tens of A/m for electrical steel sheet. In permanent magnets, ferrite magnets reach a few hundred kA/m and the intrinsic coercivity of neodymium magnets about 1000–3000 kA/m. Such large differences among ferromagnets arise because coercivity depends strongly on microstructure, not just on composition.

The anisotropy field calculated from magnetocrystalline anisotropy is the theoretical upper limit of coercivity, but actual coercivities are much smaller. This is because magnetization reverses when reverse domains nucleate at defects and domain walls move to spread them. The more inclusions, precipitates, grain boundaries and internal stresses catch (pin) domain walls, the larger the coercivity. The goal is a microstructure in which reverse domains hardly nucleate for permanent magnets, and a clean microstructure in which domain walls move easily for soft magnetic materials.

In ordinary soft magnetic materials, grain boundaries hinder domain wall motion, so larger grains lower the coercivity. When the grain size falls below a few tens of nanometers, smaller than the magnetic exchange length, however, the anisotropies of neighboring grains are averaged out and cancel, and coercivity drops sharply in proportion to the sixth power of grain size (Herzer's random anisotropy model). Nanocrystalline soft magnetic alloys exploit this effect. It is a design approach opposite to that for permanent magnets, whose coercivity peaks at the single-domain particle size.

about.h: Measurement and selection for the application
about.p: Coercivity is found by applying a field to a specimen, measuring its magnetization curve (hysteresis loop), and reading the field at which magnetization or flux density becomes zero. For permanent magnets, a closed-circuit BH tracer is used to eliminate the effect of the demagnetizing field, and a vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM) is used for powders and thin films. Magnetic recording media need a coercivity that meets two conditions at once: small enough to be written, yet large enough that thermal fluctuations do not erase the data. Coercivity changes greatly with temperature, so it is evaluated at the service temperature.

faq.q: What is the unit of coercivity?
faq.a: In SI units it is A/m, and kA/m is also common. In the older CGS unit oersted (Oe), 1 Oe = 1000/(4π) A/m ≈ 79.6 A/m. It is sometimes given as µ₀Hc in tesla (T), converted to flux density units.

faq.q: What is the difference between coercivity HcB and intrinsic coercivity HcJ?
faq.a: HcB is the reverse field that brings the flux density B to zero, and HcJ the reverse field that brings the magnetization M to zero; HcJ ≥ HcB always. Whether a magnet resists demagnetization is judged by HcJ, which expresses reversal of the magnetization itself.

faq.q: How can the coercivity of soft magnetic materials be lowered?
faq.a: Reduce impurities and inclusions, remove internal stress and strain by annealing, and enlarge the grains. Other methods are choosing compositions with small magnetocrystalline anisotropy and magnetostriction, or nanocrystallizing to average out the anisotropy.

軟磁性材料.desc: A magnetic material with small coercivity and low hysteresis loss, such as electrical steel, ferrites and amorphous alloys, used for transformer and motor cores.

about.p: "Soft" in soft magnetic material does not mean mechanically soft; it means the material magnetizes easily in a weak field and loses its magnetization quickly when the field is removed. The requirements are low coercivity, high permeability, high saturation flux density and low loss in AC use (core loss). The higher the saturation flux density, the smaller the core can be, and the lower the core loss, the higher the efficiency and the less the heating. No material maximizes all of these at once, however, so materials are chosen according to the frequency of use.

about.h: Components of core loss, and why sheets are thin
about.p: Core loss is divided into hysteresis loss, proportional to the area of the hysteresis loop (and to frequency f), and eddy-current loss, from currents induced in the material by the changing flux. The classical eddy-current loss of a sheet of thickness t is π²t²f²B²/(6ρ), proportional to the square of the thickness and inversely proportional to resistivity ρ. For silicon steel sheet 0.35 mm thick with a resistivity of about 0.48 µΩ·m used at 50 Hz and 1.5 T, this formula gives about 0.3 W/kg; the actual core loss is larger because hysteresis loss and other losses are added. Si is therefore added to raise resistivity, and thin insulated sheets are stacked.

Silicon steel sheet (electrical steel) has a high saturation flux density of about 2 T, is inexpensive, and is the mainstay of transformers and motors at power frequencies. Fe-based amorphous alloys have a somewhat lower saturation flux density of about 1.5 T but very low core loss and are used in distribution transformers. Nanocrystalline alloys of Fe–Si–B with Cu and Nb added (developed in Japan in 1988) combine high permeability with low loss. Ferrites such as Mn–Zn types have low saturation flux densities of about 0.5 T or less, but their very high resistivity keeps losses low at high frequencies.

about.h: Selection by frequency, and cautions in processing
about.p: Large 50/60 Hz transformers use grain-oriented electrical steel, which magnetizes easily in the rolling direction, and motors, which see rotating fields, use non-oriented electrical steel. For switching power supplies from a few kHz to a few MHz, ferrites, nanocrystalline alloys and dust cores are chosen. Soft magnetic materials are sensitive to stress and strain, and punching or bending raises coercivity and increases core loss. Stress-relief annealing is therefore performed after processing, and laminations are not clamped too tightly when stacked.

faq.q: What does "soft" in soft magnetic mean?
faq.a: It means magnetically "soft": the magnetization direction changes easily in a weak field, and almost no magnetization remains when the field is removed. It has nothing to do with mechanical hardness; hard electrical steel sheet is also a soft magnetic material.

faq.q: What is the difference between grain-oriented and non-oriented electrical steel?
faq.a: Grain-oriented steel has the easy <001> magnetization direction of its crystals aligned with the rolling direction (the Goss orientation) and is used in transformers, where the flux direction is fixed. Non-oriented steel has nearly random crystal orientations and is used in motors, where the flux direction rotates.

faq.q: What is the difference between soft ferrite and hard ferrite?
faq.a: Soft ferrites are spinel-type oxides of the Mn–Zn or Ni–Zn type with small coercivity, used in high-frequency transformers and inductors. Hard ferrites are hexagonal magnetoplumbite-type oxides containing Ba or Sr with large coercivity, used for permanent magnets.

間接遷移型半導体.desc: A semiconductor whose conduction band minimum and valence band maximum occur at different crystal momenta. Radiative recombination requires a phonon, so emission efficiency is low. Silicon and germanium are examples.

about.h: The band valley and peak are at different positions
about.p: The energy of electrons in a crystal varies with crystal momentum (the wave vector k). In an indirect-bandgap semiconductor, the lowest point of the conduction band (the valley) and the highest point of the valence band (the peak) lie at different k. In silicon the peak is at the Γ point (k = 0), and the valleys lie about 85% of the way from Γ toward the X point. In germanium the valleys are at the L point. Room-temperature band gaps are about 1.12 eV for Si and about 0.66 eV for Ge, and GaP (about 2.26 eV), AlAs and diamond are also indirect.

The momentum of a photon is very small compared with the crystal momentum of an electron, so k hardly changes when light is absorbed or emitted. To absorb light near the band gap in an indirect semiconductor, a phonon must make up the momentum difference at the same time, which lowers the probability. Silicon therefore has a small absorption coefficient near the band edge, and solar cells need substrates 100 µm or more thick, or surface texturing to trap light. When finding the band gap from measured absorption coefficients, (αhν)^(1/2) is plotted against hν for indirect semiconductors.

The probability that electrons and holes recombine by emitting light is also very small in indirect semiconductors. The radiative recombination coefficient of Si is about four orders of magnitude smaller than that of GaAs, and most injected electrons and holes turn into heat through nonradiative recombination via defect levels. This is why it is hard to make LEDs and lasers from silicon. The green GaP light-emitting diodes of the past made light by localizing electrons at levels created by adding nitrogen, relaxing the momentum constraint. Conversely, long carrier lifetimes are an advantage in solar cells and photodetectors.

about.h: Ways of handling light with silicon
about.p: Although its absorption is weak, silicon detects light well from the visible to a wavelength of about 1.1 µm, so it is the mainstay of image sensors and solar cells. Ways to make it emit are also being studied: in germanium the direct gap (about 0.80 eV) is only about 0.14 eV above the indirect gap, so there are attempts to make it emit using tensile strain and heavy n-type doping. In practical silicon photonics, it is common to bond direct-gap semiconductors such as InP for light sources and to use Ge grown on Si for detection.

faq.q: How can direct and indirect semiconductors be distinguished?
faq.a: Besides band structure calculations and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, they are judged from how the absorption coefficient rises. Direct semiconductors absorb strongly right at the absorption edge and emit strongly. In indirect semiconductors absorption increases gradually and emission is weak.

faq.q: What wavelength of light does silicon emit?
faq.a: Near-infrared light with a wavelength of about 1.1 µm, corresponding to the band gap of about 1.12 eV. It is invisible and the efficiency is extremely low, so it is not used for lighting or displays.

faq.q: Why is indirect-bandgap silicon used for solar cells?
faq.a: Although its absorption is weak, its band gap suits sunlight, the element is abundant, and high-quality crystals can be made cheaply in large volumes. Its long carrier lifetimes, which let electrons and holes generated deep in a thick substrate reach the electrodes, are another advantage.

臨界核半径.desc: The nucleus radius above which growth becomes the more stable path in nucleation. For a spherical nucleus, r* = −2γ/ΔGv, which becomes smaller as the undercooling increases.

about.h: The dividing line for whether a nucleus survives
about.p: A small cluster of atoms (an embryo) that forms in a liquid or a supersaturated parent phase lowers its energy in proportion to its volume, but raises it by the interfacial energy in proportion to its surface area. For a sphere, the free energy change ΔG = (4/3)πr³ΔGv + 4πr²γ first increases at small r, where the surface term wins, reaches a maximum at a certain radius and then decreases. The position of this maximum is the critical nucleus radius r*. An embryo smaller than r* lowers its energy by shrinking, and a nucleus larger than r* by growing, so r* marks the boundary between survival and disappearance.

about.h: Relation to undercooling and typical sizes
about.p: In solidification, the free energy change per unit volume can be approximated as ΔGv ≈ −ΔHf ΔT/Tm (ΔHf is the heat of fusion per unit volume and ΔT the undercooling), so r* = 2γTm/(ΔHf ΔT), inversely proportional to the undercooling. Taking gold as an example, with γ = 0.132 J/m², ΔHf = 1.16×10⁹ J/m³ and Tm = 1337 K, r* is about 3.0 nm at ΔT = 100 K and about 1.5 nm at 200 K. Because the nucleation barrier ΔG* is inversely proportional to ΔT², a small increase in undercooling raises the nucleation rate by orders of magnitude.

about.h: Heterogeneous nucleation, and not confusing r* with grain size
about.p: In heterogeneous nucleation on a mold wall or an impurity particle, the nucleus is a spherical cap with contact angle θ. Its radius of curvature at the critical state is the same r* as in homogeneous nucleation; what decreases is the volume of the nucleus and the barrier. The barrier is multiplied by f(θ) = (2 + cosθ)(1 − cosθ)²/4, which is about 0.16 at θ = 60° and about 0.013 at 30°. Also, r* is the minimum size at which a nucleus becomes stable and is different from the size of grains or precipitates after transformation. The final grain size is set by the number of nuclei formed and how fast they then grow.

about.h: Use in microstructure control and film deposition
about.p: Adding an inoculant in casting refines the grains because it supplies substrates with a small contact angle, lowering the heterogeneous nucleation barrier so that many nuclei form even at small undercooling. In precipitation heat treatment, lowering the aging temperature increases the supersaturation (driving force), which makes r* smaller and gives fine precipitates at high density. The same idea applies to thin-film growth: lowering the substrate temperature or raising the deposition rate increases the supersaturation and shrinks the critical nucleus, so films tend to form with a high island density and a fine microstructure.

faq.q: How is the critical nucleus radius equation derived?
faq.a: Find the radius at which the free energy change of a spherical nucleus, ΔG = (4/3)πr³ΔGv + 4πr²γ, is a maximum. Setting dΔG/dr = 0 gives r* = −2γ/ΔGv, and substituting this back into ΔG gives the barrier height ΔG* = 16πγ³/(3ΔGv²).

faq.q: About how many atoms does a critical nucleus contain?
faq.a: It depends on the material and the undercooling. For gold at ΔT = 100 K, r* is about 3 nm, and a sphere of that size holds about 7000 atoms. At ΔT = 200 K the radius halves and the number of atoms drops to about 1/8, a little under 1000.

faq.q: What happens to the critical nucleus radius when the undercooling is 0?
faq.a: As ΔT approaches 0, ΔGv also approaches 0, so r* becomes infinitely large and no nucleus can form. This is why solidification does not start exactly at the melting point and some undercooling is required.

ストランスキー・クラスタノフ成長.desc: A thin-film growth mode in which, after layer-by-layer growth of a few atomic layers, three-dimensional islands grow to relax the strain from lattice mismatch. It is used to make quantum dots.

about.h: Three growth modes and the wetting condition
about.p: Thin-film growth modes are roughly classified by the substrate surface energy γs, the film surface energy γf and the interface energy γi. If γs ≥ γf + γi, the film wets the substrate and grows one layer at a time (layer-by-layer, or Frank–van der Merwe, growth); in the opposite case islands form from the start (island, or Volmer–Weber, growth). Stranski–Krastanov (SK) growth lies between the two: the film first wets the substrate and grows in layers, but switches to islands beyond a certain thickness. The characteristic feature is this switch from layers to islands partway through growth.

A film whose lattice parameter differs from the substrate's initially grows stretched or compressed in-plane to match the substrate (coherently), so strain energy builds up in proportion to film thickness. Beyond a critical thickness, the energy becomes lower if the film forms islands whose upper parts can relax toward their natural lattice spacing, even at the cost of extra surface area. Three-dimensional islands then sit on a thin layer called the wetting layer. The lattice mismatch is about 7% for InAs/GaAs and about 4% for Ge/Si, and both are classic examples of SK growth.

about.h: How it differs from relaxation by dislocations
about.p: Besides forming islands, strain can be relaxed by introducing misfit dislocations at the film–substrate interface. In combinations with small mismatch, the film stays flat and dislocations appear once the critical thickness is exceeded, so islands are less likely to form. The early islands produced by SK growth are coherent and free of dislocations, which is why they can be used as quantum dots. If growth continues and the islands become larger, dislocations also enter the islands, and the light-emission efficiency drops sharply. SK growth can be seen as a special form of relaxation that relieves strain elastically.

about.h: Self-assembled quantum dots and in-situ monitoring
about.p: Because SK growth makes nanometer-scale islands arrange themselves without lithographic patterning, it is widely used to make self-assembled quantum dots. For InAs/GaAs grown by molecular beam epitaxy (MBE), islands are said to start forming beyond about 1.5–1.7 monolayers; buried in GaAs, they become the active layer of quantum-dot lasers and single-photon sources. The switch from two-dimensional to three-dimensional growth can be identified in situ when the reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED) pattern changes from streaky to spotty. Island size and density are adjusted through the substrate temperature and the amount deposited.

faq.q: What is the difference between SK growth and VW (island) growth?
faq.a: In VW growth the film does not wet the substrate, and islands form from the very beginning. In SK growth the first few atomic layers grow as layers and form a wetting layer, and islands then form on top of it to relax strain.

faq.q: What is a wetting layer?
faq.a: It is the flat film, a few atomic layers thick, that remains beneath the islands in SK growth. It still connects the islands after they form, and because it acts as a thin quantum well itself, it affects light emission and current flow in quantum-dot devices.

faq.q: Why is SK growth well suited to making quantum dots?
faq.a: Because nanoscale islands without dislocations form all at once at high density without any patterning. When buried, they become quantum dots surrounded by interfaces with few defects, and they emit light efficiently.

熱応力.desc: Stress arising from a difference in thermal expansion. For a thin film on a substrate it is estimated as σ = EΔαΔT/(1 − ν); if the film's expansion coefficient is larger, the film is in tension after cooling.

about.p: If a body is heated uniformly and is free to expand, no stress arises. Thermal stress appears when expansion or contraction is prevented, in one of the following cases: (1) materials with different coefficients of linear thermal expansion are joined, (2) there is a temperature difference within the body, or (3) the body is constrained from outside. A thin film on a substrate is the classic example of (1), and the surface of quenched glass of (2). Heating a bar fixed at both ends by ΔT produces a compressive stress of magnitude EαΔT. Because thermal stress arises without any external load, it is easily overlooked.

about.h: Estimating thermal stress in thin films
about.p: A thin film on a sufficiently thick substrate is constrained equally in both in-plane directions, so the biaxial modulus E/(1 − ν) is used and the stress is estimated as σ = EΔαΔT/(1 − ν). For example, cooling a copper film on a silicon substrate (E = 120 GPa, ν = 0.34, α = 17×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) from 400 °C to 25 °C would give a tensile stress of about 1 GPa if it stayed elastic. Real copper films yield partway through, and the stress often ends up at a few hundred MPa. The room-temperature stress of a film deposited at high temperature is frequently set by plastic deformation during cooling.

Residual stress in a thin film is not only thermal stress. Sputtered films tend to develop compressive stress as energetic particles are driven into them, and evaporated films tend to develop tensile stress as islands join together; such stress created during deposition is called intrinsic stress. The measured residual stress is the sum of thermal and intrinsic stress, so trying to explain all of it from the difference between the deposition and room temperatures does not work. The usual approach is to measure the stress while changing the temperature and to separate out the part that varies in proportion to temperature as the thermal stress.

The standard way to obtain the stress in a film on a wafer is from the radius of curvature R of the wafer's bow, using the Stoney equation σ = Es hs²/{6(1 − νs) hf R} (Es and νs are the substrate's Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio, and hs and hf the substrate and film thicknesses). Thermal stress causes hillocks in aluminum interconnects, thermal fatigue of solder joints, spallation of thermal barrier coatings and cracking of substrates in power semiconductors. Countermeasures include choosing materials with similar expansion coefficients, inserting a layer with an intermediate coefficient, and heating and cooling slowly to keep temperature differences small.

faq.q: Why does the thermal stress equation for thin films contain (1 − ν)?
faq.a: A thin film is in a biaxial stress state, constrained in both in-plane directions at once, so it deforms less readily than under uniaxial stress. The biaxial modulus E/(1 − ν) expresses this. For a bar constrained in one direction only, the stress magnitude is EαΔT.

faq.q: How can I tell whether thermal stress in a film is tensile or compressive?
faq.a: After cooling, the film is in tension if its linear expansion coefficient is larger than the substrate's and in compression if it is smaller. On heating the sign reverses. Intrinsic stress also adds to it, so the actual sign is confirmed by measurements such as wafer bow.

faq.q: What is the difference between thermal stress and thermal shock?
faq.a: Thermal stress is the name of the stress caused by differences in expansion or temperature. Thermal shock is the cracking that occurs when rapid heating or cooling creates large temperature differences within a body and the resulting thermal stress breaks it; it is one manifestation of thermal stress.

オストワルド成長.desc: Coarsening in which small particles dissolve and disappear while large particles grow. The driving force is the curvature-dependent difference in solubility (the Gibbs–Thomson effect).

about.p: Atoms at a particle's surface are less stable than those inside by the amount of the interfacial energy. The equilibrium solubility around a particle of radius of curvature r is given by the Gibbs–Thomson equation c(r) ≈ c∞{1 + 2γVm/(rRT)} (c∞ is the solubility at a flat interface and Vm the molar volume), so the smaller the particle, the higher the solubility. As a result, a concentration difference forms in the parent phase from around small particles to around large ones, and solute moves by diffusion. It is coarsening driven by interfacial energy, proceeding in the direction that reduces the total interfacial area.

about.h: The rate of coarsening: r³ proportional to time
about.p: For diffusion-controlled Ostwald ripening, the Lifshitz–Slyozov–Wagner (LSW) theory gives the mean radius as growing according to r̄³ − r̄₀³ = kt. The rate constant k is proportional to the interfacial energy, the diffusion coefficient and the solubility, and rises steeply with temperature. If the initial radius is small enough, doubling the mean radius takes 8 times as long, and over that time the number of particles falls roughly in inverse proportion to time. The size distribution settles into a shape that stays the same over time, and in LSW theory the largest particle is 1.5 times the mean.

about.h: How it differs from coalescence and ordinary growth
about.p: Ostwald ripening is a different mechanism from coalescence, in which particles collide and merge; it proceeds even if the particles do not move, simply by atoms transferring through the parent phase. It also differs from ordinary growth, in which all particles grow by taking solute from a supersaturated parent phase: here the total volume of precipitates stays nearly constant while their number falls and their mean size increases.
