The telltale sign is that small particles actually shrink and vanish. Grain growth after sintering or recrystallization is a separate phenomenon driven by grain-boundary migration, but it shares curvature as its driving force.

When precipitation-strengthened alloys are used at high temperature, Ostwald ripening coarsens the precipitates and lowers the strength (overaging). To suppress it, k must be made small, for example by choosing coherent precipitates with low interfacial energy, or by forming precipitates from elements with low solubility in the matrix and slow diffusion. The γ′ phase in Ni-based superalloys, highly coherent with the matrix and with low interfacial energy, is a classic example of slow coarsening at high temperature. In nanoparticle synthesis, by contrast, Ostwald ripening broadens the size distribution as it proceeds, so the time at which the reaction is stopped is controlled.

faq.q: Is Ostwald ripening the same as Ostwald growth or coarsening?
faq.a: Yes, they refer to the same phenomenon. In English it is usually called Ostwald ripening; in metallurgy the process is often described as particle coarsening, and in colloid science and crystallization as ripening.

faq.q: Are there everyday examples?
faq.a: When ice cream is stored for a long time, small ice crystals disappear and large crystals grow, giving a grainy texture. Along with temperature fluctuations during storage, Ostwald ripening is one of the main causes.

faq.q: Why does it speed up at higher temperature?
faq.a: Because the rate constant is proportional to the diffusion coefficient and the solubility, both of which increase with temperature in Arrhenius fashion. Small temperature differences change the coarsening rate greatly, so controlling service temperature is important when estimating the life of high-temperature parts.

量子サイズ効果.desc: The effect by which energy levels become discrete and the band gap widens when particles or films become as small as the spatial extent of electron waves. It determines the emission color of quantum dots.

about.p: Electrons have a spatial extent as waves, so when they are confined to a small space, the energies they can take are restricted to discrete values. In the simplest model, an infinitely deep well of width L, the levels are Eₙ = n²h²/(8m*L²), rising in inverse proportion to the square of the width. For example, confining an electron in GaAs (effective mass m* = 0.067m₀) in a 10 nm well gives a lowest level of about 56 meV, above the room-temperature thermal energy kT (about 26 meV). Level spacings larger than kT are a rule of thumb for the effect to appear clearly.

Depending on how many directions are confined, a film confined in one direction is called a quantum well, a wire confined in two a quantum wire, and a particle confined in all three a quantum dot. Quantum wells, such as GaAs sandwiched between AlGaAs, are used as the active layers of semiconductor lasers, and the emission wavelength can be tuned by the well width. In quantum dots the density of states becomes sharp atom-like peaks, so the emission linewidth is narrow. In semiconductor particles the effect becomes strong when the size is comparable to or smaller than the exciton Bohr radius, and for CdSe a difference of a few nm in size changes the emission color from blue to red.

Not every size-dependent change in nanoparticles is a quantum size effect. A dispersion of gold nanoparticles looks red because of surface plasmon resonance, a collective oscillation of conduction electrons (absorption near 520 nm), not because of discrete levels. The melting point depression of metal nanoparticles is also a thermodynamic effect of surface energy. The way properties depend on size differs too: the energy shift from the quantum size effect grows roughly in inverse proportion to the square of the particle size, whereas the melting point depression is roughly inversely proportional to the size.

about.h: Designing the emission color of quantum dots, and applications
about.p: The effective band gap of a spherical quantum dot is estimated by the Brus equation E ≈ Eg + (h²/8r²)(1/mₑ* + 1/mₕ*) − 1.8e²/(4πεr), in which the second, confinement term increases in inverse proportion to the square of the radius. In synthesis, the reaction time and temperature are used to make the sizes uniform and the emission narrow. Quantum dots are used in color-conversion films for displays, fluorescent labels in biology and photodetectors, and covering the surface with a shell of a wider-gap material such as ZnS (a core–shell structure) reduces emission losses from surface defects.

faq.q: Below what size does the quantum size effect appear?
faq.a: It depends on the material; the guide is the extent of the exciton (the Bohr radius). It is about 5–6 nm for CdSe, about 18 nm for PbS and about 4–5 nm for silicon, and the effect becomes clear when the particle size is comparable to or smaller than this.

faq.q: Does the quantum size effect occur in metals?
faq.a: It does, but metals have so many electrons that their level spacing is very small, and the effect becomes noticeable only when particles are smaller than about 2 nm. Gold clusters of that size lose their continuous levels, and some emit fluorescence like molecules.

faq.q: What is the difference between a quantum well and a quantum dot?
faq.a: A quantum well is a thin film confined only in the thickness direction, and electrons can move freely in the plane. A quantum dot is a particle confined in all three directions, and its levels are fully discrete, like those of an atom.

XRD(X線回折).desc: An analytical method that shines X-rays on a crystal and uses the angles and intensities of the diffracted X-rays to examine crystalline phases, lattice parameters, crystallite size, strain, texture and more.

about.p: XRD shines X-rays on a crystal, whose atomic spacings are comparable to the X-ray wavelength, and measures the diffracted X-rays that reinforce at angles satisfying Bragg's law. Peak positions give interplanar spacings and lattice parameters, and comparing the pattern with a database identifies the crystalline phases. Peak intensity ratios reveal texture and phase proportions, and peak widths reveal crystallite size and nonuniform strain. Amorphous materials show a broad halo instead of peaks, so XRD can also tell whether a material is crystalline or amorphous.

For powders and polycrystalline specimens, the basic method is θ-2θ measurement (Bragg–Brentano focusing), in which the specimen and detector rotate in step. In this geometry only planes parallel to the specimen surface are seen. For thin films, grazing-incidence measurements that send X-rays in at a shallow angle to probe only the near-surface region, rocking curves for examining texture and lattice tilt, and reciprocal space maps for examining the composition and strain of epitaxial films are used. Cu Kα radiation (wavelength about 0.154 nm) is the most commonly used X-ray source.

Precise lattice parameters obtained from peak positions allow estimates of solid-solution composition (Vegard's law) and residual stress (the sin²ψ method). Proportions of multiple phases are found by comparing peak intensities with standards or by Rietveld analysis, which fits the entire pattern to a calculation. Peak widths give crystallite size through the Scherrer equation, but instrumental broadening must be subtracted and the strain contribution separated. Accurate results require angle calibration and correction for specimen height displacement.

about.h: Use in failure analysis and quality control
about.p: In process work, XRD is used to confirm the phase and texture of deposited films (for example, identifying silicide phases or the (111) texture of Cu interconnects), to confirm crystallization by heat treatment, and to identify corrosion products and foreign matter. Detection generally requires a content of several percent or more and a certain volume, however, so XRD is poor at detecting tiny particles or trace phases. In such cases it is combined with micro-area XRD, electron diffraction in TEM, Raman spectroscopy and the like. A major advantage is that it is nondestructive, so it can be performed before other analyses.

faq.q: Can XRD be used for elemental analysis?
faq.a: XRD reveals crystal structure and cannot directly measure which elements are present. It can distinguish phases of the same elements with different structures, but elemental analysis calls for combining it with EDS, X-ray fluorescence or similar techniques.

faq.q: What happens when an amorphous film is measured by XRD?
faq.a: No sharp peaks appear, only a broad, gentle hump (a halo). If peaks appear after heat treatment, you can conclude that the film has crystallized.

faq.q: How deep does XRD probe?
faq.a: It depends on the material and the incidence angle, but in θ-2θ measurement it reaches several to several tens of micrometers in metals, and deeper still in materials of light elements. To measure only a thin film, use a grazing-incidence geometry.

SEM(走査電子顕微鏡).desc: A microscope that scans a finely focused electron beam across a specimen surface and detects the secondary and backscattered electrons emitted, to observe surface shape and differences in composition.

about.p: In an SEM, an electron beam accelerated to a few kV to about 30 kV is focused down to a few nanometers and scanned across the specimen surface. Displaying the amount of secondary or backscattered electrons emitted from each point as brightness, synchronized with the scan, forms the image. Compared with an optical microscope, the SEM has higher resolution (a few nanometers) and a much greater depth of focus, so rough fracture surfaces and powders can be observed in three-dimensional-looking images that are in focus throughout. Specimens must be conductive; insulators are coated with a thin film of metal or carbon or observed at low accelerating voltage.

Secondary electrons have low energies of 50 eV or less and can escape only from depths of a few nanometers, giving images of shape that strongly reflect surface tilt and edges. Backscattered electrons are incident electrons scattered back out by atoms; they have high energy and come from deeper regions. The backscattered yield increases with atomic number, giving compositional images in which regions of heavy elements are bright, and channeling contrast from crystal orientation can also be obtained. Comparing the two images lets you separate differences in shape from differences in composition.

When the electron beam strikes the specimen, characteristic X-rays with energies specific to each element are also emitted. Analyzing them by EDS or WDS gives elemental distributions as points, lines or maps. Note that characteristic X-rays come from a region of about 1 µm over which electrons spread, so the spatial resolution of elemental analysis is considerably worse than that of the image. In EBSD, the specimen is tilted steeply and the diffraction patterns of backscattered electrons are analyzed to map the orientation of each grain, the character of grain boundaries and the distribution of phases, useful for evaluating texture and recrystallization.

In failure analysis, fracture surfaces are examined to distinguish dimples of ductile fracture, striations of fatigue, cleavage facets of brittle fracture and so on, and to infer the cause of failure. For cross sections, a section is exposed by polishing, ion milling or FIB to examine voids in interconnects, intermetallic compounds in solder joints, film delamination and the like. For foreign particles, EDS confirms the elements present and helps identify their source. Conditions such as accelerating voltage and beam current are chosen with attention to charging, specimen damage and contamination (carbon deposition) by the electron beam.

faq.q: What is the difference between SEM and TEM?
faq.a: SEM observes surface shape and composition with electrons emitted from the surface, and the specimen may be thick. TEM observes the internal crystal structure and defects at the atomic level with electrons transmitted through a thin lamella.

faq.q: How are insulators observed in an SEM?
faq.a: Coat them with a few nanometers of gold, platinum or carbon to make them conductive, or use a low accelerating voltage that reduces charging, or a low-vacuum mode that admits gas into the specimen chamber.

faq.q: What is the resolution of an SEM?
faq.a: Instruments with field-emission electron guns reach around 1 nm, but it varies with the specimen, accelerating voltage and detector. The resolution of elemental analysis by EDS is considerably coarser and can be about 1 µm.

ブラッグの法則.desc: The condition 2d sinθ = nλ for diffraction to reinforce from crystal planes with spacing d. It is the basic equation for finding interplanar spacings from XRD peak angles.

about.p: Think of a crystal as a stack of parallel atomic planes with spacing d. When X-rays of wavelength λ strike the planes at an angle θ, the path difference between X-rays reflected from adjacent planes is 2d sinθ. When this difference is an integer multiple of the wavelength, nλ, the reflections from all planes line up in phase and reinforce. This is Bragg's law, 2d sinθ = nλ. θ is the angle between the planes and the X-rays, so the angle between the incident and diffracted X-rays is 2θ, which is normally plotted on the horizontal axis in XRD.

For example, with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 0.15406 nm) and planes with d = 0.2088 nm, sinθ = 0.15406/(2 × 0.2088) ≈ 0.369, so θ ≈ 21.7° and 2θ ≈ 43.3°. Common mistakes are confusing 2θ with θ and dropping the factor of 2 in the equation. Because sinθ cannot exceed 1, planes with d < λ/2 do not diffract, and shorter wavelengths allow more peaks to be measured. Higher-order reflections (n = 2 and above) are normally treated as first-order reflections from planes with spacing d/n and labeled with indices such as (200).

about.h: Use for cubic crystals and extinction rules
about.p: For cubic crystals the interplanar spacing is d = a/√(h² + k² + l²), so combining it with Bragg's law gives sin²θ = (λ²/4a²)(h² + k² + l²), and the ratios of sin²θ for the peaks reveal the sequence of h² + k² + l². Depending on the arrangement of atoms in the unit cell, however, diffraction from some planes cancels and disappears (the extinction rules). In BCC only planes with h + k + l even appear, and in FCC only planes with h, k and l all even or all odd; from these sequences the structure can be identified and the lattice parameter determined.

Bragg's law is a condition for wave interference, so it applies not only to X-rays but also to electron and neutron diffraction. In TEM electron diffraction, the electron wavelength is very short (about 0.0025 nm at 200 kV) and θ is small, below 1°, so sinθ ≈ θ is used to find interplanar spacings from the spacing of diffraction spots. The same principle is used in EBSD in the SEM, in WDS with its analyzing crystals, and in the spectrometers of X-ray fluorescence analysis, making it a common foundation for many materials analysis techniques.

faq.q: What is the difference between θ and 2θ in Bragg's law?
faq.a: θ is the angle between the crystal planes and the incident X-rays (the Bragg angle), and 2θ is the angle between the incident and diffracted X-rays (the diffraction angle). XRD data are usually plotted against 2θ, so in calculations use half of it as θ.

faq.q: How is an n = 2 reflection treated?
faq.a: 2d sinθ = 2λ is the same equation as a first-order reflection from planes with spacing d/2, so the second-order reflection from (100) planes is treated as a reflection from (200) planes. This way, everything can be calculated with n = 1.

faq.q: What happens if longer-wavelength X-rays are used?
faq.a: For the same spacing θ becomes larger, so peaks are spread farther apart and easier to separate, but the constraint sinθ ≤ 1 reduces the number of planes that can be measured. Radiation such as Cr Kα is used for applications such as residual stress measurement.

消滅則.desc: Rules by which diffraction from certain indices cancels out and disappears because of the arrangement of atoms. In BCC, only planes with h + k + l even diffract; in FCC, only planes whose h, k and l are all even or all odd.

about.h: The structure factor and how extinction happens
about.p: X-rays scattered by each atom in the unit cell overlap with phase differences that depend on the atoms' positions. Their sum is the structure factor F(hkl) = Σ fⱼ exp{2πi(hxⱼ + kyⱼ + lzⱼ)}, and the diffracted intensity is proportional to |F|². In BCC, the 2 atoms at the origin and the body center (1/2, 1/2, 1/2) give F = f{1 + (−1)^(h+k+l)}, which is 0 when h + k + l is odd. In FCC, the 4 atoms give F = 4f when h, k and l are all even or all odd, and 0 when they are mixed. The extinction rules describe how intensity becomes 0 through cancellation within the unit cell even when Bragg's condition is satisfied.

about.h: Identifying the lattice from the peak sequence
about.p: In cubic crystals sin²θ is proportional to h² + k² + l², so the lattice type can be found from the ratios of the peaks' sin²θ. Simple cubic gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8… with 7 missing; BCC gives an evenly spaced 2, 4, 6, 8, 10… (ratios 1:2:3:4…); and FCC gives 3, 4, 8, 11, 12…, a sequence that comes in pairs. In diamond-structure silicon, planes with h + k + l = 4n + 2 also vanish in addition to the FCC condition, so (200) does not appear and the peaks run (111), (220), (311), (400).

about.h: Different atoms do not cancel completely
about.p: The extinction rules assume that identical atoms sit at the positions that cancel. When different atoms occupy the body center and the corners, as in CsCl-type NiAl, reflections such as (100) that vanish in BCC appear as weak peaks proportional to the difference in scattering factors (superlattice reflections). The same happens on ordering of Cu₃Au, and the superlattice intensity serves as a measure of the degree of order. In the NaCl type, the intensity of planes with h, k and l all odd is set by the difference between the two ions' scattering factors; in KCl, where K⁺ and Cl⁻ have equal numbers of electrons, (111) nearly vanishes and the pattern looks simple cubic.

In real measurements, reflections that should be absent (forbidden reflections) are sometimes seen. In single crystals, multiple diffraction, where X-rays diffracted once are diffracted again by another set of planes, can produce sharp peaks at forbidden positions such as silicon (200). Silicon (222) is known to appear very weakly because the distribution of covalent bonding electrons is not spherically symmetric. In crystals with screw axes or glide planes, there are also extinction rules under which only particular rows of indices vanish, and these are used to determine the space group. It is important not to judge only by the presence or absence of a peak but to check the measurement conditions as well.

faq.q: What are the extinction rules for HCP?
faq.a: In HCP, planes with l odd and h + 2k a multiple of 3 vanish. For example, (0001) does not appear, and diffraction from the basal plane is observed as (0002).

faq.q: Do the planes that vanish under the extinction rules not exist?
faq.a: The planes exist, but scattering from the atoms in the unit cell cancels and the intensity becomes 0. For example, the reflection from the BCC (100) planes cancels because it is opposite in phase to the reflection from the planes of body-center atoms lying halfway between them.

faq.q: Do the extinction rules apply to electron diffraction too?
faq.a: Yes. The conditions for absence come from the same structure factor. However, electrons scatter strongly, and forbidden reflections appear easily through multiple scattering, so care is needed when indexing.

シェラーの式.desc: The equation D = Kλ/(β cosθ) for estimating crystallite size from the broadening of XRD peaks, where β is the full width at half maximum in radians and K is about 0.9.

about.p: In a large crystal, scattering from many lattice planes cancels as soon as the angle deviates slightly from the Bragg angle, so the peak is sharp. When the crystallite is small and few planes diffract together, this cancellation is incomplete, and intensity remains over a wider range of angles around the Bragg angle. The Scherrer equation D = Kλ/(β cosθ) expresses the relation between this broadening and crystallite size; the broadening is inversely proportional to the size. For example, with Cu Kα radiation, a peak at 2θ = 30° with a full width at half maximum of 0.25° gives D of about 33 nm with K = 0.9.

β is an angle in radians, taken directly as the width measured on the 2θ scale, while θ is half of the peak position 2θ. The measured peak width also contains the broadening of the instrument itself, so the instrumental width is determined with a standard such as LaB₆ and subtracted (for Gaussian peaks, as the square root of the difference of squares). K depends on the crystallite shape and on whether β is the full width at half maximum or the integral breadth, and values around 0.9 are commonly used. As crystallites grow, the broadening is buried in the instrumental width, so the practical upper limit is roughly 100–200 nm.

What the Scherrer equation gives is the size of the region that behaves as one perfect crystal for diffraction (the crystallite), which may not match the size of grains or particles seen in a microscope. If each particle is polycrystalline and contains several crystallites, the XRD value is smaller than the particle size seen by SEM. If small particles are agglomerated, the size measured by laser diffraction is larger still. The value is a volume-weighted average size and says nothing about the width of the distribution. Comparing it with TEM images or the specific surface area from the BET method gives a more complete picture of the sample.

Non-uniform strain in a crystal spreads the interplanar spacings and also broadens peaks. This broadening is proportional to tanθ, a different angular dependence from crystallite broadening, which is proportional to 1/cosθ. The Williamson–Hall method writes β cosθ = Kλ/D + 4ε sinθ and plots β cosθ for several peaks against 4 sinθ; the intercept gives the crystallite size and the slope the non-uniform strain ε. In samples that have been deformed or ground in a ball mill, strain broadening is large, so calculating with the Scherrer equation alone underestimates the crystallite size.

faq.q: Why is the Scherrer constant K about 0.9?
faq.a: Because the theoretical value for nearly spherical or cubic crystallites, with β taken as the full width at half maximum, is around 0.9. It changes somewhat with shape and the definition of width, so use the same K and the same width definition when comparing samples.

faq.q: Should the peak width be entered in degrees or radians?
faq.a: In radians. Multiply a width measured in degrees by π/180 to convert it. Entering it in degrees makes the crystallite size come out about 1/57 of the correct value.

faq.q: Why is the size from the Scherrer equation smaller than the particle size seen by SEM?
faq.a: Because each particle may consist of several crystallites, or non-uniform strain may be broadening the peaks. Twins and stacking faults also shrink the regions that diffract coherently, and so reduce the value.

EDS(エネルギー分散型X線分光法).desc: A method of elemental analysis that measures the energies of characteristic X-rays excited by an electron beam with a semiconductor detector. It measures all elements simultaneously in a short time, but its resolution is lower than that of WDS.

about.p: When an electron beam knocks an inner-shell electron out of an atom, an electron from an outer shell drops into the vacancy, and the energy difference is emitted as a characteristic X-ray unique to the element. In EDS, these X-rays enter a semiconductor detector, and their energy is measured from the number of electron–hole pairs created. Silicon drift detectors (SDDs) are now standard; they need no liquid-nitrogen cooling and handle high count rates. To excite an inner shell, the accelerating voltage must be well above the absorption-edge (critical excitation) energy, and as a rule of thumb a voltage of at least about twice that energy is chosen.

about.h: Resolution and peaks that tend to overlap
about.p: The energy resolution of EDS is about 125–130 eV as the full width at half maximum of Mn Kα (5.9 keV). Peaks closer together than this are hard to separate: S Kα (2.307 keV) and Mo Lα (2.293 keV) are only 14 eV apart, and Ti Kα (4.511 keV) and Ba Lα (4.466 keV) in BaTiO₃ only 45 eV apart. Spurious peaks specific to the instrument also need attention. With a silicon detector, escape peaks appear 1.74 keV below the true peak, and if the count rate is too high, sum peaks appear at the combined energy of 2 X-rays.

about.h: How large a region is analyzed: spatial resolution
about.p: In a bulk specimen, incident electrons spread as they scatter, so X-rays come from a region much larger than the beam diameter. Estimating the electron penetration depth with the Kanaya–Okayama equation gives about 1.6 µm for iron and about 4 µm for aluminum at an accelerating voltage of 20 kV. Spot analysis of a precipitate smaller than 1 µm therefore also detects elements of the surrounding matrix. Lowering the voltage to 10 kV reduces the depth to about 0.5 µm in iron, but limits which X-rays can be excited. With a thin TEM specimen the spread is small, and regions of a few nm can be analyzed.

EDS quantification uses corrections such as the ZAF correction, which adjusts peak intensities for atomic number, absorption and fluorescence effects. With flat polished specimens and standards, relative errors of a few % can be achieved, but errors grow on rough fracture surfaces and particles. The detection limit is roughly 0.1 wt%, and elements below that are measured by WDS or SIMS. Standard instruments cannot detect H, He or Li, and light elements such as B, C, N and O have low sensitivity and large absorption corrections, so it is safer to treat their values as semi-quantitative. Carbon contamination on the surface also inflates carbon values.

faq.q: Are EDS and EDX the same?
faq.a: Yes, they are the same technique. EDS, EDX and EDXS are just different abbreviations used by different manufacturers and fields, and all of them refer to energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy.

faq.q: When should I use EDS and when WDS?
faq.a: EDS is generally used for qualitative analysis and elemental mapping that survey many elements quickly, and WDS when overlapping peaks must be separated or trace elements quantified precisely.

faq.q: Can EDS determine chemical state (oxidation state)?
faq.a: Hardly at all. Characteristic X-ray energies are set by differences between inner-shell levels, and the changes caused by chemical bonding are much smaller than the resolution. Techniques such as XPS are used to study bonding state.

XPS(X線光電子分光法).desc: An analytical method that determines the elements in the top few nanometers of a surface and their chemical bonding state (oxidation state and so on) from the binding energies of photoelectrons emitted by X-rays.

about.p: In XPS, X-rays such as Al Kα (1486.6 eV) irradiate the specimen, and the kinetic energy E_K of electrons ejected by the photoelectric effect is measured. The binding energy is obtained from E_B = hν − E_K − φ (φ is the work function of the spectrometer), and because it takes a fixed value for each element and core level, the peak position identifies the element. For example, O 1s in oxides is at about 530 eV, so with Al Kα it appears at a kinetic energy of about 950 eV. The 2p and 3d levels are split into 2 by spin–orbit coupling, and the areas of 2p₃/₂ and 2p₁/₂ are in a ratio of about 2:1.

about.h: Why only the top few nm are seen
about.p: The X-rays themselves penetrate deep into the specimen, but photoelectrons readily undergo inelastic scattering, and only those created near the surface escape without losing energy. The inelastic mean free path λ of photoelectrons is about 1–3 nm for kinetic energies of a few hundred to around 1500 eV, and about 95% of the detected signal comes from within a depth of 3λ. Tilting the specimen to increase the take-off angle θ, measured from the surface normal, makes the analysis depth shallower, 3λcosθ. This lets the thickness of thin oxide films and compositional differences with depth be studied without damaging the specimen.

When an atom becomes positively charged because neighboring atoms draw electrons away from it, its core electrons are bound more tightly and the binding energy shifts upward. This is the chemical shift; for Si 2p, elemental Si is at about 99 eV and SiO₂ at about 103 eV. The shifts are small, a few eV, so overlapping peaks are often separated into components by curve fitting. In insulators, the surface charges positively as photoelectrons leave, shifting all peaks upward, so low-energy electrons are used to neutralize it and energies are corrected using the C 1s peak of adventitious surface carbon (about 284.8 eV) as a reference.

XPS detects all elements except H and He, with detection limits of roughly 0.1–1 at% depending on the element. It requires ultra-high vacuum, and the analyzed area ranges from about 10 µm to about 1 mm across, depending on the instrument and conditions. Depth profiles are measured while sputtering with Ar ions, but ion bombardment can reduce oxides or preferentially remove certain elements, changing chemical states and composition. For organic materials, low-damage argon gas cluster ions are used. When smaller areas must be examined, XPS is used alongside Auger electron spectroscopy (AES), which is excited by an electron beam.

faq.q: Are XPS and ESCA the same?
faq.a: Yes, they are the same technique. ESCA (electron spectroscopy for chemical analysis) is a name that emphasizes the ability to determine chemical state; today XPS is the more common name.

faq.q: Can XPS detect hydrogen?
faq.a: No. Hydrogen and helium have no core electrons, and their probability of emitting photoelectrons (photoionization cross-section) is very small. Hydrogen distributions are studied by techniques such as SIMS.

faq.q: What is the difference between XPS and EDS?
faq.a: XPS measures photoelectrons emitted by X-rays and reveals the elements and chemical states in the top few nm. EDS measures characteristic X-rays emitted under an electron beam and gives elemental composition to a depth of around a µm, but reveals almost nothing about chemical state.

SIMS(二次イオン質量分析法).desc: A method that mass-analyzes secondary ions ejected while the specimen is sputtered by primary ions. It can measure depth profiles of trace elements such as dopants with ppm to ppb sensitivity.

about.p: In SIMS, primary ions accelerated to energies from a few hundred eV to tens of keV strike the specimen and knock out surface atoms (sputtering). The small fraction of ejected particles that are ionized is counted by a mass spectrometer to distinguish elements and isotopes. For elements that readily form positive ions, such as B, Al and Na, oxygen ions (O₂⁺) are used, and for elements that readily form negative ions, such as P, As, O, C and H, cesium ions (Cs⁺); this raises the ionization fraction and the sensitivity. A major feature is the ability to measure everything from hydrogen to heavy elements, distinguishing isotopes as well.

Depth profiles of dopants in semiconductors are measured by dynamic SIMS, in which a high dose of primary ions keeps eroding the specimen. After the measurement, the crater depth is measured with a stylus profilometer, and time is converted to depth assuming a constant sputter rate. Static SIMS, by contrast, uses such a low dose that primary ions strike no more than about 1% of the surface atoms; combined with a time-of-flight (TOF-SIMS) mass spectrometer, it examines organic contamination and surface treatments from fragments of molecules on the outermost surface. The same principle is used very differently depending on the information sought.

about.h: Why quantification is hard: the matrix effect
about.p: The fraction of atoms that become secondary ions not only differs by orders of magnitude between elements but also changes greatly with the composition of the surrounding matrix (the matrix effect). Signal intensity alone therefore cannot be converted to concentration; a standard made by implanting a known dose of the element into the same matrix is measured to obtain relative sensitivity factors. The atomic density of silicon is about 5×10²² cm⁻³, so 1 ppb corresponds to about 5×10¹³ cm⁻³. Where the matrix changes, as at an SiO₂/Si interface, apparent steps in concentration are likely, so care is needed.

In mass spectrometry, other ions with the same mass number can overlap. Phosphorus in silicon, ³¹P⁻, differs in mass from ³⁰Si¹H⁻ by only about 0.008, and separating them requires a mass resolution M/ΔM of about 4000. Measures include using an instrument with high mass resolution or detecting the element as a different molecular ion. In depth, mixing, in which primary ions push surface atoms deeper, smooths the profile, so for shallow junctions the primary ion energy is lowered to improve depth resolution. Whether a steep profile is real is checked by changing the conditions.

faq.q: What is the detection limit of SIMS?
faq.a: It depends on the element and conditions, but for boron in silicon and similar cases it reaches about 10¹³–10¹⁴ cm⁻³, that is, the ppb range. For elements also present inside the instrument, such as hydrogen, carbon and oxygen, residual gas raises the limit.

faq.q: Is SIMS a non-destructive technique?
faq.a: No. It is destructive, measuring while eroding the specimen, and the analyzed region does not come back. Static SIMS, however, removes only a tiny fraction of the outermost surface, so it can examine surfaces under nearly non-destructive conditions.

faq.q: What is the difference between SIMS and XPS?
faq.a: SIMS is extremely sensitive, at the ppm to ppb level, and can measure depth profiles and isotopes, but quantification requires standards. XPS has a sensitivity of about 0.1 at%, but it reveals chemical state and allows semi-quantitative analysis without standards.

ステンレス鋼.desc: An alloy steel containing roughly 11% Cr or more, made rust-resistant by a passive surface film. By microstructure it is divided into austenitic, ferritic, martensitic and other grades.

about.p: Stainless steel resists rusting because a passive film consisting mainly of Cr oxide, a few nanometers thick, forms on the surface and prevents the metal from dissolving. Above roughly 11% Cr the film forms stably, and more Cr gives better corrosion resistance. In environments containing oxygen the film spontaneously re-forms even when scratched, but in chloride-rich environments it is broken at weak points, causing pitting and crevice corrosion. For seawater environments, Mo-bearing grades such as SUS316 (AISI 316) are chosen. Note that stainless steel only resists rust; it does not stay rust-free in every environment.

The representative grade SUS304 (18%Cr-8%Ni, JIS; AISI 304) is austenitic, with an FCC structure even at room temperature because Ni stabilizes austenite; it has good ductility and weldability and is nearly nonmagnetic in the annealed condition. Grades such as SUS430 (AISI 430), with almost no Ni, are BCC ferritic, magnetic and relatively inexpensive. Grades such as SUS420J2 (similar to AISI 420), with about 13% Cr and higher carbon, are martensitic and harden on quenching, so they are used for cutlery and blades. In addition, duplex grades, roughly half austenite and half ferrite, have excellent strength and resistance to stress corrosion cracking.

When austenitic stainless steel is heated to about 500–800 °C, Cr carbides precipitate at grain boundaries, depleting the surrounding Cr and weakening passivity. This is called sensitization and causes intergranular corrosion in weld heat-affected zones. Countermeasures include low-carbon SUS304L (AISI 304L) and grades in which carbon is tied up as Ti or Nb carbides. Austenitic grades are also susceptible to stress corrosion cracking in hot chloride environments, and countermeasures include removing residual stress or switching to a duplex grade.

faq.q: Can stainless steel be attracted to a magnet?
faq.a: Ferritic and martensitic grades are attracted to magnets. Even nonmagnetic austenitic SUS304 becomes attracted to a magnet when heavily cold worked, because part of it turns into strain-induced martensite.

faq.q: What is the difference between SUS304 and SUS316?
faq.a: SUS316 (AISI 316) contains about 2–3% Mo, making it more resistant to pitting and crevice corrosion by chloride ions. In seawater or salty environments, SUS316 and similar grades are chosen.

faq.q: Does stainless steel harden on quenching?
faq.a: Martensitic grades harden on quenching, but austenitic and ferritic grades do not transform on cooling and so do not harden by quenching. Austenitic grades are strengthened by cold working.

加工硬化.desc: The increase in the stress needed for deformation as plastic deformation multiplies dislocations, which become entangled with each other. Strength rises but ductility falls. Also called strain hardening.

about.p: When a metal is plastically deformed, dislocations multiply and their density increases by several orders of magnitude; they attract and entangle one another through their stress fields and become harder to move. Further deformation therefore requires a larger stress. This is work hardening. It is why cold-rolled sheet and drawn wire are stronger than before working, and for pure metals that cannot be strengthened by heat treatment, 5000-series aluminum alloys, austenitic stainless steels and the like, work hardening is the main strengthening method. In exchange, ductility and toughness decrease.

For many metals, the relation between true stress and true strain in the plastic region can be approximated as σ = Kεⁿ, where n is called the strain-hardening exponent (work-hardening exponent) and K the strength coefficient. The larger n, the more readily the material strengthens as deformation proceeds and the less localized deformation spreads, so necking is delayed and uniform elongation is larger. Under constant volume, necking can be estimated to begin when the true strain equals n. Annealed FCC copper and austenitic stainless steels have large n and are well suited to stretch forming, where the sheet thins as it stretches (deep drawability depends mainly on the r-value).

When a work-hardened metal is heated, recovery occurs first, as dislocations rearrange and internal stresses fall; at higher temperatures, recrystallization produces new grains, lowering the strength greatly and restoring ductility. Alternating cold working and annealing allows large deformations without cracking. In hot working, done above the recrystallization temperature, recovery and recrystallization proceed during working, so almost no work hardening remains and large deformations can be applied with small forces, though it is inferior to cold working in surface oxidation and dimensional accuracy.

faq.q: What is the difference between work hardening and precipitation hardening?
faq.a: Both strengthen by obstructing dislocation motion, but in work hardening the obstacles are the entanglements of dislocations multiplied by deformation, whereas in precipitation hardening they are fine precipitates formed by aging.

faq.q: How is the amount of working expressed?
faq.a: For drawing and rolling, it is generally expressed as the reduction in cross-sectional area (percent cold work). Note that it is calculated from the area, not the diameter.

faq.q: Can a work-hardened material be returned to its original softness?
faq.a: Annealing above the recrystallization temperature produces new strain-free grains, and strength and ductility return to roughly their condition before working.

固溶強化.desc: A strengthening method in which lattice strain created by solute atoms dissolved in the matrix obstructs dislocation motion and raises the strength of a metal. There are interstitial and substitutional types.

about.h: Interaction between dislocations and strain fields
about.p: Solute atoms differ from the matrix atoms in size and elastic modulus, so they distort the surrounding lattice. A dislocation also has compressive and tensile strain fields around it, and the energy is lowered when large solute atoms gather on its tensile side and small ones on its compressive side. As a result, extra force is needed for a dislocation to move past solute atoms. The magnitude of strengthening depends on the differences in atomic size and modulus, and models in which it is proportional to c^(1/2) (Fleischer) or c^(2/3) (Labusch) in the concentration c are widely used.

Substitutional solutes expand or contract the surrounding lattice almost spherically, so they interact mainly with the hydrostatic component of edge dislocations, and the strengthening is relatively moderate. By contrast, carbon and nitrogen in BCC iron occupy octahedral interstices and create a tetragonal distortion that stretches the lattice strongly in one direction, so they also interact strongly with screw dislocations and produce large strengthening even in small amounts. The yield point phenomenon of mild steel occurs because carbon and nitrogen atoms gather at dislocations and pin them (Cottrell atmospheres), and it gives rise to Lüders bands.

about.h: How it differs from precipitation strengthening
about.p: Solid-solution strengthening comes from solute dispersed as individual atoms, whereas precipitation strengthening comes from particles of clustered solute that obstruct dislocations. Because the state of the solute changes little with heat, solid-solution strengthening tends to remain effective at high temperature and carries little risk of weakening over time, as happens with overaging. On the other hand, solute atoms also scatter electrons and lower electrical and thermal conductivity (Matthiessen's rule). In copper alloys where conductivity matters, designs often precipitate the solute out of the matrix rather than leaving it in solution.

Non-heat-treatable aluminum alloys gain their strength from solid-solution strengthening by Mg and from work hardening. The annealed 5052 alloy, with about 2.5% Mg, has a yield strength of about 90 MPa, more than twice the roughly 35 MPa of annealed pure aluminum (1100). In steels, Mn, Si, P and similar elements contribute solid-solution strengthening and are used in designing the strength of high-strength steel sheet. In Ni-based superalloys, large, slow-diffusing atoms such as W, Mo and Re strengthen the matrix in solution and raise high-temperature creep strength. In every case, adjusting the dissolved amount within the solubility limit is fundamental to the design.

faq.q: Is solid-solution strengthening equally effective for every element?
faq.a: No. Elements with larger differences in size and elastic modulus from the matrix atoms are more effective. However, if the size difference is too large, little can be dissolved, so the attainable strengthening is also limited by the solubility limit.

faq.q: What happens to ductility with solid-solution strengthening?
faq.a: Ductility generally decreases somewhat as strength rises, but the drop is often milder than with precipitation strengthening or work hardening. In some cases, such as brass with up to about 30% zinc, both strength and elongation exceed those of pure copper.

faq.q: What are typical examples of interstitial solid-solution strengthening?
faq.a: Carbon and nitrogen in iron and steel are the typical examples. One of the main reasons martensite is so hard is that supersaturated carbon distorts the lattice strongly and produces intense solid-solution strengthening.

回復.desc: The process, preceding recrystallization when a cold-worked metal is heated, in which dislocations annihilate and rearrange and internal stresses and electrical resistivity decrease. Hardness changes little.

about.p: A cold-worked metal stores many dislocations and point defects. On heating, point defects such as vacancies first migrate and disappear, and then dislocations move by climb and cross-slip, so that dislocations of opposite sign annihilate each other or line up into low-energy arrangements. The process in which dislocations align like walls into low-angle boundaries, dividing grains into small subgrains, is called polygonization. The shape and orientation of the grains themselves remain as they were after working, and the fact that no new grains form is what distinguishes recovery from recrystallization.

about.h: How properties change and how it proceeds
about.p: During recovery, part of the stored energy is released, residual stress falls substantially, and electrical resistivity approaches its value before working. On the other hand, the total number of dislocations does not decrease much, so the drop in hardness and strength is small and much of the strength gained by work hardening remains. Recovery is fastest at the start and slows over time; it does not suddenly take off after an incubation period as recrystallization does. How far recovery goes depends not only on temperature and time but also on the material's stacking fault energy.

about.h: The influence of stacking fault energy
about.p: In metals with high stacking fault energy, such as aluminum and α-iron, dislocations hardly dissociate and cross-slip and climb are easy, so recovery proceeds readily. Even during hot working, recovery balances work hardening and a stable subgrain structure develops (dynamic recovery). In metals with comparatively low stacking fault energy, such as copper, brass and austenitic stainless steel, dislocations dissociate widely and move with difficulty, so recovery does not progress very far at a given temperature. Much of the stored energy therefore remains in the metal, and recrystallization, for which that energy is the driving force, occurs more readily.

Recovery is put to use when only internal stress needs to be lowered while the shape and strength of a part are kept. Examples are stress-relief annealing after welding or bending, and low-temperature annealing to prevent season cracking of brass. For aluminum alloys, tempers that are work hardened and then partially annealed to restore a little ductility are designated H2x, balancing strength and formability. If the annealing temperature is too high or the time too long, recrystallization begins and the material softens greatly, so the temperature and time of the treatment must be controlled carefully.

faq.q: What is the difference between recovery and recrystallization?
faq.a: In recovery only the annihilation and rearrangement of dislocations take place, and the grains remain as they were after working. In recrystallization, new strain-free grains form and replace the deformed structure, so hardness drops greatly.

faq.q: Why does electrical resistivity fall during recovery?
faq.a: Point defects such as vacancies and dislocations added by working scatter electrons and raise the resistivity. During recovery these decrease, and point defects in particular disappear readily, so scattering falls and so does resistivity.

faq.q: What is dynamic recovery?
faq.a: It is recovery that takes place during deformation at high temperature, as in hot working. Because the generation and annihilation of dislocations balance, the stress does not rise much as deformation continues and approaches a nearly constant value.

再結晶.desc: The phenomenon in which new strain-free grains nucleate and grow when a metal storing deformation strain is heated. Strength decreases and ductility is restored.

about.h: Driving force and how nuclei form
about.p: The driving force for recrystallization is the energy of dislocations stored by working. On heating, in regions of high strain, some of the subgrains formed by recovery grow faster than their surroundings and become new grains with high-angle boundaries (recrystallization nuclei). These grains spread by migrating their boundaries into the surrounding dislocation-rich structure, until the whole deformed structure is eventually replaced by grains with little strain. The recrystallized fraction follows an S-shaped curve with time, with a slow start, rapid progress and a slow finish, and is often described by the Johnson–Mehl–Avrami–Kolmogorov (JMAK) equation X = 1 − exp(−ktⁿ).

about.h: Recrystallization temperature and degree of working
about.p: The recrystallization temperature is usually defined as the temperature at which recrystallization is complete in 1 hour, and a rough guide is 0.3–0.5 of the melting point in absolute temperature. It is lower for higher purity; for example, high-purity copper recrystallizes at about 120 °C, about 0.3 of its melting point. Small amounts of solute hinder boundary migration and raise the recrystallization temperature substantially. Heavier working increases the stored energy and the number of nuclei, which lowers the recrystallization temperature and makes the recrystallized grains finer. The time to complete recrystallization depends strongly on temperature, and a small increase in temperature shortens it greatly.

about.h: Distinguishing grain growth and secondary recrystallization
about.p: If heating continues after recrystallization is complete, large grains consume small ones to reduce grain-boundary energy. Its driving force is grain-boundary energy, making it a separate stage from recrystallization, which is driven by stored energy. The phenomenon in which only some grains become abnormally large is called secondary recrystallization (abnormal grain growth); in grain-oriented electrical steel, normal grain growth is suppressed by precipitates and only Goss-oriented grains are allowed to recrystallize secondarily, aligning the orientation. Freshly recrystallized grains are also often biased toward particular orientations (recrystallization texture), which affects sheet formability.

about.h: Role in hot working and manufacturing
about.p: Hot working and cold working are distinguished by whether working takes place above the recrystallization temperature. In hot rolling and forging, recrystallization (dynamic and static) occurs during or right after deformation, turning the coarse cast structure into fine, equiaxed grains. In cold-working processes, material that has work hardened and lost elongation is recrystallized by intermediate annealing to restore ductility before the next step. Changing the temperature and time of the final anneal adjusts the size of the recrystallized grains, so strength and formability can be tailored through the Hall–Petch relationship.

faq.q: What fraction of the melting point is the recrystallization temperature?
faq.a: A rough guide is 0.3–0.5 of the melting point in absolute temperature. However, it varies greatly with purity, degree of working and heating time, so the value for each material needs to be confirmed by experiment.

faq.q: Does recrystallization change the crystal structure?
faq.a: No. Recrystallization replaces highly strained grains with less strained ones within the same phase. It is different from changes that alter the crystal structure, such as the transformation of steel to austenite.

faq.q: What is the critical strain for recrystallization?
faq.a: It is the minimum degree of working needed for recrystallization, often a few %. Annealing after working near this level produces few nuclei, so the grains become very coarse, causing surface roughening (orange peel) and a loss of strength.

黄銅.desc: An alloy of copper with zinc. 70/30 brass, with about 30% Zn, is single-phase α and highly ductile, while 60/40 brass, with about 40% Zn, contains the β phase and is stronger.

about.h: Zinc content and changes in phase
about.p: In the Cu–Zn phase diagram, the FCC α phase can dissolve up to about 39% zinc (around 450 °C), and with more zinc the BCC β phase appears. Below about 450 °C, the β phase becomes the ordered β′ phase, which is hard and difficult to deform cold. As a result, 70/30 brass with about 30% zinc is single-phase α and suited to cold deep drawing, while 60/40 brass with about 40% zinc is two-phase α + β′; at high temperature it contains more β and becomes soft, so it is worked hot. Above about 50% zinc the brittle γ phase appears, so practical brasses are limited to lower zinc contents.

In JIS, 70/30 brass is numbered C2600 and 60/40 brass C2801, among others. 70/30 brass has high elongation and has long been used for deeply drawn parts such as cartridge cases, lamp bases and radiator components. 60/40 brass is stronger and easy to hot forge, so it is used for bolts, nuts and valves. Free-cutting brass (such as C3604) contains a few % lead; the finely dispersed lead breaks up the chips, making it suitable for small parts mass-produced on automatic lathes. For parts in contact with drinking water, brasses using bismuth or silicon instead of lead are also used.

Depending on the environment, brass can undergo dezincification, in which only zinc dissolves selectively and porous copper is left behind. It is a dangerous form of corrosion because the part keeps its shape while losing almost all its strength, and it occurs more readily in brasses containing β, such as 60/40 brass, and in stagnant water or water containing chloride. In α brass, adding small amounts of arsenic, antimony or phosphorus suppresses dezincification. In addition, brass with tensile residual stress in an ammonia-containing environment suffers season cracking (stress corrosion cracking) along grain boundaries, so it is annealed at low temperature after working to remove the stress.

Zinc is cheaper than copper, so brass costs less than copper and is also stronger. Zinc acts as a solid-solution strengthener in copper, and a feature of α brass is that not only its strength but also its elongation exceeds that of pure copper. On the other hand, the dissolved zinc scatters electrons, so electrical and thermal conductivity fall to about 30% of pure copper's, making brass unsuitable for wires or heat dissipation. Its color is a reddish gold at low zinc and grows more yellow with more zinc; thanks to its workability and attractive color, it is also used for ornaments, architectural hardware and brass instruments such as trumpets.

faq.q: Is brass a single alloy?
faq.a: No. Brass is the general name for copper–zinc alloys. In English, 70/30 brass is also called cartridge brass and 60/40 brass Muntz metal, and the term brass band, for an ensemble of brass instruments, comes from the name of this alloy.

faq.q: What is the difference between brass and bronze?
faq.a: Brass is copper with zinc added, and bronze is copper with tin added. Bronze excels in castability, wear resistance and corrosion resistance and is used for bearings, castings and art such as bronze statues. With age, its surface develops a blue-green patina (verdigris).

faq.q: Does brass rust?
faq.a: It does not form red rust like iron, but in air its surface oxidizes and dulls, and moisture or sweat can form green verdigris. Depending on the water environment, dezincification and season cracking also need attention.

チタン合金.desc: An alloy with a density about 60% that of steel, excellent specific strength and corrosion resistance. Depending on the proportions of the HCP α phase and BCC β phase, it is classified as α, α+β or β type.

about.p: Pure titanium takes the HCP α phase below 882 °C and the BCC β phase above it. Alloying elements are divided into α stabilizers (Al, O, N, C), which raise this transformation temperature (the β transus), and β stabilizers (V, Mo, Nb, Ta, Fe, Cr and others), which lower it; Sn and Zr are neutral elements that hardly affect it. Alloys that are mainly α at room temperature are α alloys, those with both phases α+β alloys, and those that retain β to room temperature β alloys. The most widely used is the α+β alloy Ti-6Al-4V, which is said to account for about half of titanium alloy production.

Titanium alloys have a density of about 4.4–4.5 g/cm³, about 60% that of steel but about 1.6 times that of aluminum alloys. Their Young's modulus, about 110 GPa, is also about half that of steel, so their specific stiffness (Young's modulus/density) is almost the same as steel's and aluminum alloys'. Where titanium alloys excel is specific strength: Ti-6Al-4V reaches a tensile strength of about 900–1000 MPa and keeps its strength at temperatures of several hundred °C where aluminum alloys cannot be used, so it is also used for jet engine compressor parts. Titanium is chosen for being light, strong and corrosion resistant rather than light and stiff.

Thanks to its dense passive TiO₂ film, titanium shows very high corrosion resistance in seawater and chloride-containing environments and is used in chemical plant heat exchangers and desalination equipment. It also causes little galvanic corrosion in contact with carbon fiber, which suits it for fasteners in CFRP airframes. On the other hand, its thermal conductivity is low (about 7 W/(m·K) for Ti-6Al-4V), so cutting heat concentrates at the tool edge, and it reacts readily with tools at high temperature, making it difficult to machine. At high temperature it absorbs oxygen and forms a brittle surface layer (alpha case), and absorbed hydrogen causes hydrogen embrittlement.

For α+β alloys, working and heat-treatment temperatures are chosen relative to the β transus (about 1000 °C for Ti-6Al-4V), changing the morphology of the microstructure to balance strength, toughness and fatigue strength. Solution treatment and aging, which precipitate fine α, raise the strength further. Because titanium reacts violently with oxygen and nitrogen at high temperature, melting is carried out in vacuum or inert gas, and titanium sponge is made into ingots by vacuum arc remelting. This is one reason for its high price, and additive manufacturing from powder is now spreading as a way to reduce material waste and make complex parts.

faq.q: Are titanium alloys lighter than aluminum alloys?
faq.a: No. Their density, about 4.4 g/cm³, is higher than the roughly 2.7 g/cm³ of aluminum alloys and lower than the roughly 7.8 g/cm³ of steel, an intermediate value. Compared by specific strength, strength divided by density, they outperform many aluminum alloys.

faq.q: What do the numbers in Ti-6Al-4V mean?
faq.a: They mean the alloy contains about 6% Al and about 4% V by mass. Al stabilizes the α phase and V the β phase, making it the representative α+β alloy. In Japan it is sometimes called “64 titanium”.

faq.q: How are pure titanium and titanium alloys used differently?
faq.a: Pure titanium is weaker but easy to form and highly corrosion resistant, so it is used for chemical equipment, building materials and heat exchanger tubes. Alloys are used where high strength is needed, such as aircraft parts, bolts and artificial joints.

柱状晶.desc: In the solidification of castings, elongated grains that grow inside the surface chill zone in the direction opposite to heat flow. Equiaxed grains form in the center.

about.h: How columnar grains form: competitive growth
about.p: Not every one of the fine chill grains formed at the mold wall grows inward. In cubic metals, dendrites grow fastest along <100>, and grains whose <100> lies closest to the direction opposite to heat flow (the direction of the temperature gradient) advance furthest. Poorly oriented grains are overtaken by their neighbors and stop growing, so the number of grains decreases with distance inward, leaving a zone of elongated grains with aligned <100>. The texture of the columnar zone, whose properties differ with direction, is a result of this competitive growth.

Whether columnar grains give way to equiaxed grains partway through solidification (the CET, columnar-to-equiaxed transition) is determined by the temperature gradient G and growth rate V at the solidification front and by the alloy composition. The smaller G and the larger V, and the more solute, the more the liquid ahead of the front is constitutionally undercooled and the more easily new nuclei form, favoring the switch to equiaxed grains. Conversely, raising the pouring temperature (increasing the superheat) remelts crystal fragments in the liquid, lengthening the columnar zone. Controlling the position of the CET is central to designing cast structures.

about.h: Weaknesses of columnar grains and remedies
about.p: The columnar zone has mechanical properties that differ with direction, and solute, impurities and shrinkage cavities tend to collect on the central plane where columnar grains growing from both sides meet (centerline segregation). In continuous casting of steel, electromagnetic stirring is therefore used to move the liquid and break off columnar tips, increasing the fraction of equiaxed grains. In aluminum alloys, Al-Ti-B grain refiners are added to multiply heterogeneous nucleation sites, preventing columnar growth and giving fine equiaxed grains. If a casting is hot worked afterward, the columnar structure is converted into fine grains by recrystallization.

about.h: Making columnar grains on purpose: directional solidification
about.p: Columnar grains are not only a drawback. Jet engine turbine blades are made by directional solidification, in which the mold is cooled from the bottom so that heat flows in one direction and the blade consists only of columnar grains running along its length. At high temperature, grain boundaries perpendicular to the stress readily become sites of creep fracture, so eliminating them greatly extends life. Furthermore, if a helical passage (a grain selector) is used to select and grow a single grain, the result is a single-crystal blade with no grain boundaries at all. Here too, the fast growth along <100> is put to use.

faq.q: What is the difference between columnar and equiaxed grains?
faq.a: Columnar grains are elongated in one direction along the heat flow, while equiaxed grains are roughly the same size in every direction. Equiaxed grains show less directional variation in properties and spread segregation more evenly, so they are preferred in many castings.

faq.q: Why do columnar grains grow along <100>?
faq.a: Because in cubic metals, anisotropy in the solid–liquid interface energy and in how readily atoms attach makes dendrite trunks grow fastest along <100>. Grains with this direction close to the heat flow survive the competitive growth.

faq.q: Do columnar grains form in welds too?
faq.a: Yes. Heat in the weld pool escapes into the surrounding base metal, so columnar grains grow from the fusion boundary toward the weld centerline. Impurities collect on the plane where they meet at the center, which can cause solidification cracking.

標準電極電位.desc: The equilibrium potential of an electrode reaction, such as that between a metal and its ions, under standard conditions, relative to the standard hydrogen electrode at 0 V. The more negative it is, the more easily the metal is oxidized.

about.h: The reference and what the potential means
about.p: The standard electrode potential is the equilibrium potential of the electrode reaction Mⁿ⁺ + ne⁻ ⇄ M under standard conditions, such as 25 °C and unit ion activity, expressed relative to the standard hydrogen electrode (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇄ H₂) at 0 V. For example, Cu²⁺/Cu is +0.34 V, Fe²⁺/Fe is −0.44 V and Zn²⁺/Zn is −0.76 V. Active metals with more negative values tend to give up electrons and become cations readily, while noble metals with more positive values tend to resist ionization. The emf of a cell combining two electrodes is the potential of the noble side minus that of the active side.

about.h: Relation to the likelihood of corrosion
about.p: For a metal to corrode, a cathodic reaction must be paired with its dissolution. In neutral water this is oxygen reduction and in acidic solutions hydrogen evolution; if the metal's potential is below the potential of those reactions, corrosion is thermodynamically possible. Gold and platinum hardly corrode because their potentials are very noble. Zinc and magnesium, on the other hand, with active potentials, are used as sacrificial anodes to protect steel. Which metal dissolves when dissimilar metals are in contact can also be judged from their relative potentials.

The standard electrode potential is determined by equilibrium thermodynamics and tells you nothing about the rate of corrosion. Aluminum, at −1.66 V, and titanium, at −1.63 V, are very active, yet they resist real environments well thanks to their dense surface oxide films. Also, real solutions differ from standard conditions in ion concentration and temperature, and the potential changes according to the Nernst equation. When evaluating combinations of dissimilar metals, it is therefore common to use the ranking of corrosion potentials measured in real environments such as seawater (the galvanic series).

faq.q: What do “active” and “noble” mean?
faq.a: Metals whose electrode potentials lie on the negative side are called active (base), and those on the positive side noble. The more active a metal, the more readily it ionizes, and when dissimilar metals are in contact, the more active one dissolves.

faq.q: Is the ionization tendency the same as the standard electrode potential?
faq.a: The order of ionization tendency (the activity series) roughly corresponds to arranging standard electrode potentials from low to high. You can think of the standard electrode potential as expressing it numerically.

faq.q: Why does aluminum resist corrosion even though its potential is active?
faq.a: A dense, stable oxide film forms on its surface and prevents further reaction. The standard electrode potential shows only a tendency and does not include differences in rate caused by films.

不動態.desc: A state in which a dense oxide film a few nanometers thick forms on a metal surface and dissolution of a metal that should thermodynamically dissolve almost stops.

about.p: Iron, chromium, nickel, titanium, aluminum and other metals can, under the right conditions, form dense oxide (or hydroxide) films a few nanometers thick on their surfaces, reducing the dissolution rate by several orders of magnitude. This state is passivity. Even for metals that are active in potential, the film separates the metal from the environment, so actual corrosion becomes very slight. In stainless steel a Cr-rich film plays this role, and in titanium a TiO₂ film. The film is thin and invisible, so the metallic luster is preserved.

about.h: Conditions that maintain or break it
about.p: In environments containing oxygen or oxidizers, the passive film re-forms spontaneously even when scratched. Iron, for example, becomes passive in concentrated nitric acid and hardly dissolves. On the other hand, in oxygen-poor crevices or reducing acids such as hydrochloric acid, the film re-forms with difficulty, and once broken, active dissolution proceeds. Chloride ions in particular break the film locally at weak points, so pitting and crevice corrosion are problems for stainless steel in seawater. For passive materials, localized corrosion requires more attention than uniform corrosion.

about.h: Passivity seen through potential and current
about.p: In a polarization curve, which measures the dissolution current while the metal's potential is raised step by step, the current first increases with potential, but above a certain potential (the passivation potential) it drops abruptly and stays small over a wide range of potential. This range is the passive region. Raising the potential further reveals the transpassive region, where the film breaks down and the current rises again, or, with chlorides present, the pitting potential. The higher the pitting potential, the more resistant the material is to pitting, and it is used as an index for selecting and evaluating grades. Even for the same material, the pitting potential falls as temperature and chloride concentration rise.

faq.q: How thick is the passive film?
faq.a: In stainless steel it is a very thin film of a few nanometers. It is different from the thick oxide scale that forms during high-temperature oxidation.

faq.q: What is passivation treatment?
faq.a: A treatment in which stainless steel is immersed in an oxidizing solution such as nitric acid to remove surface contamination and iron particles and to ensure that a dense passive film forms.

faq.q: Why does stainless steel sometimes rust in seawater?
faq.a: Chloride ions break the passive film locally, causing pitting and crevice corrosion. Grades with a stronger film, such as Mo-bearing SUS316 (AISI 316), are the countermeasure.

局部電池.desc: On the surface of a single metal, anodic and cathodic regions formed by inclusions, strain, oxygen concentration differences and the like, through which corrosion proceeds as in a battery.

about.h: Tiny cells on a single metal
about.p: A metal surface is never perfectly uniform. Inclusions, grain boundaries, regions strained by working and flaws in surface films give slightly different potentials, and the regions of lower potential become anodes and those of higher potential cathodes. The metal itself acts as the wire and the surrounding water as the electrolyte, so many small cells form on the surface: at the anodes the metal dissolves, and at the cathodes oxygen is reduced or hydrogen evolved. If the anodes and cathodes shift position over time, the surface wastes away uniformly; if they stay fixed, the metal is dug out locally and deeply.

Local cells arise not only from non-uniformity of the metal but also from non-uniformity of the environment. The typical case is the oxygen concentration (differential aeration) cell, set up by differences in dissolved oxygen: the region with less oxygen becomes the anode and the region with more oxygen the cathode. When a drop of salt water is placed on an iron plate, the edge of the drop, which is easily reached by air, becomes the cathode and the center, which oxygen reaches with difficulty, the anode, so the center corrodes (Evans's drop experiment). This mechanism is why places that oxygen reaches poorly, such as deep in crevices, under deposits and where soil changes along buried pipes, corrode selectively.

about.h: Thinking about corrosion rate with mixed potentials
about.p: While local cells are operating, the metal's potential settles at the value where the anodic dissolution current equals the cathodic reduction current. This is the corrosion potential (mixed potential), and the current at that point is the corrosion current. The corrosion rate depends strongly on the rate of the cathodic reaction. For example, in dilute acid high-purity zinc dissolves only slowly, whereas zinc containing impurities such as copper dissolves vigorously, because hydrogen evolves easily on the impurities and they act as effective cathodes. In neutral water, the supply of dissolved oxygen sets the rate, so removing the oxygen almost stops corrosion.

about.h: How it differs from galvanic corrosion
about.p: Galvanic corrosion between dissimilar metals in contact is the case where the anode and cathode are different metals and form a cell of visible size. A local cell refers to anodes and cathodes too small to see distributed over a single metal; the principle is the same electrochemical cell. Manganese sulfide (MnS) inclusions in stainless steel, sensitized grain boundaries, and differences in microstructure between a weld and the base metal also create local cells. Corrosion protection measures include making the surface uniform, blocking the electrolyte with films or paint, and removing dissolved oxygen.

faq.q: Why do local cells form even on pure metals?
faq.a: Because even at high purity, grain boundaries, differences between crystal orientations, strain and surface scratches give slightly different potentials. Non-uniformity on the environment side, such as differences in oxygen concentration, also creates cells.

faq.q: How can corrosion by local cells be prevented?
faq.a: Methods include separating the metal from the electrolyte with paint or plating, removing dissolved oxygen, adding inhibitors (corrosion inhibitors), and making the whole metal a cathode by cathodic protection.

faq.q: What is the difference between local cells and macrocell corrosion?
faq.a: Local cells have tiny anodes and cathodes close together, while macrocells form large cells between distant locations, as with reinforcing bars in concrete or long pipelines. In macrocells, corrosion tends to concentrate at particular spots.

ガルバニック腐食.desc: Accelerated corrosion of the more active metal, acting as the anode, when metals of different potential are in contact in an electrolyte. Also called dissimilar-metal corrosion.

about.h: Potential differences and which metal corrodes
about.p: When different metals are electrically connected and immersed in the same electrolyte, the metal with the lower (more active) corrosion potential becomes the anode and the one with the higher (more noble) potential the cathode. Corrosion of the active metal speeds up compared with when it is alone, while corrosion of the noble metal slows down. To judge which metal will dissolve, the ranking of corrosion potentials measured in real environments such as seawater (the galvanic series) is used rather than standard electrode potentials. In seawater, the metals become more noble roughly in the order magnesium, zinc, aluminum alloys, steel, copper alloys, passive stainless steel, titanium and graphite.

about.h: Effects of area ratio and distance
about.p: The corrosion rate changes greatly not only with the potential difference but also with the area ratio of anode to cathode. The larger the cathode and the smaller the anode, the more the large dissolution current, matched to the oxygen reduced at the cathode, is concentrated on the small anode. Painting only the anode can therefore backfire, since a small flaw in the coating becomes a small anode and is dug out deeply; if painting, the cathode side is painted too. In fresh water or thin moisture films in air, which have high electrical resistance, corrosion concentrates near the contact, while in well-conducting environments such as seawater the effect extends over a wider area.

The surest method is to combine metals that are close together in the galvanic series. When different metals must be used, measures include insulating them electrically with plastic washers or sleeves, designing joints so that water does not collect, and cutting off the electrolyte path with sealants. Fasteners are made of a material more noble than the parts they join, so that no small anode is created. For combinations of aluminum alloys and CFRP, a glass fiber layer is inserted between them for insulation, or titanium alloy fasteners are used.

about.h: Using it for protection, and a historical example
about.p: Used well, galvanic action becomes a means of protection. In hot-dip galvanized steel sheet, even if a scratch exposes the steel, the surrounding zinc dissolves first and protects it (sacrificial protection). The sacrificial anodes attached to ship hulls and harbor structures work on the same principle. A well-known failure is the Statue of Liberty: the insulation between its copper skin and iron framework broke down in the damp, the iron framework corroded, and in the 1980s restoration the iron bars supporting the skin were replaced with stainless steel. It is important to determine at the design stage which way a potential difference will act.

faq.q: Are galvanic corrosion and bimetallic corrosion the same?
faq.a: Yes, they are the same phenomenon. It is called galvanic corrosion because it works like a galvanic cell, and bimetallic or dissimilar-metal corrosion when the emphasis is on its cause. It should be distinguished from stray-current corrosion, which is driven by external currents.

faq.q: Is it all right to connect stainless steel and carbon steel?
faq.a: In environments exposed to rain or seawater, the carbon steel side corrodes more easily. It is especially dangerous when the carbon steel area is small, as when carbon steel bolts fasten stainless steel plates; insulate the joint or make the fasteners stainless steel as well.

faq.q: Does galvanic corrosion occur in dry air?
faq.a: Without an electrolyte no current flows, so it hardly occurs. However, it does occur when condensation or salt deposits form a thin film of water, so care is needed outdoors and near the sea.

孔食.desc: Localized corrosion in which chloride ions or similar species locally break down the passive film and small pits are dug deeper. It is a problem for stainless steels and aluminum.

about.h: How pitting starts and accelerates itself
about.p: Pitting begins when chloride ions locally break down weak points in the passive film. In stainless steels, sites where inclusions such as manganese sulfide (MnS) have dissolved are known to be favored starting points. Most small pits repassivate partway and stop (metastable pitting), but inside a pit that keeps growing, dissolved metal ions hydrolyze and make the solution acidic, and chloride ions gather to maintain electrical neutrality, so the film can no longer repair itself. The inside of the pit becomes a small anode and the wide passive surface around it the cathode, so only the bottom of the pit advances rapidly.

about.h: Choosing a grade: PREN and critical pitting temperature
about.p: The pitting resistance equivalent number PREN = Cr + 3.3Mo + 16N (each element in mass%) is widely used as a guide to the pitting resistance of stainless steels. SUS304 is about 18–20, SUS316 about 24, and the duplex stainless steel SUS329J3L (equivalent to 2205) about 35; for long exposure to seawater, grades of 40 or more are sometimes chosen. The critical pitting temperature (CPT), found by raising the temperature in a solution such as ferric chloride until pitting begins, is also used for comparison. PREN is a guide calculated from composition, so actual resistance varies with welds and surface condition.

about.h: Weight loss does not reveal the danger
about.p: In pitting, even if only a tiny amount of metal has dissolved overall, a single pit that penetrates the wall makes a pipe or tank leak and puts it out of service. Service life therefore cannot be assessed from weight loss or average corrosion rate as with uniform corrosion. Pits are small, and the surface is often covered with rust or deposits, so they are easily missed in visual inspection. In practice, the maximum pit depth measured on limited areas is used with extreme value statistics (the Gumbel distribution) to estimate the maximum depth over the whole installation.

Aluminum is also a passive metal and pits in neutral water containing chloride. In particular, when the water contains traces of copper ions, copper deposits on the aluminum surface and acts as a cathode, promoting pitting. For this reason, layouts that place aluminum parts downstream of copper piping, where dissolved copper can reach them, are avoided. Countermeasures include forming a thick oxide film by anodizing, covering heat exchanger tubes and similar parts with a zinc-containing layer that sacrifices itself (clad material), and simply avoiding aluminum in environments with high chloride concentrations.

faq.q: What is the difference between pitting and crevice corrosion?
faq.a: Both are forms of corrosion in which the passive film breaks down locally, but pitting can start anywhere on a flat surface, whereas crevice corrosion occurs inside crevices, such as under bolt heads or gaskets.
