Crevice corrosion generally occurs at lower temperatures and chloride concentrations than pitting.

faq.q: How is the pitting resistance equivalent number (PREN) calculated?
faq.a: In mass%, it is calculated as Cr + 3.3 × Mo + 16 × N. For example, Cr 17%, Mo 2.2% and N 0.05% give about 25. Higher values tend to mean greater pitting resistance, but it should be used only as a guide.

faq.q: Why is pitting hard to predict?
faq.a: Because where and when it starts is decided probabilistically by small film defects, inclusions and local differences in the environment. Once a pit starts growing it advances quickly, so both material selection and inspection are needed to guard against it.

応力腐食割れ.desc: Crack growth at stresses below the yield stress when a susceptible material under tensile stress is exposed to a specific corrosive environment.

about.h: It occurs in specific material–environment combinations
about.p: Stress corrosion cracking (SCC) does not occur in just any environment but in specific combinations of material and environment. Typical examples are austenitic stainless steel in hot chloride-containing water (said to occur readily above about 60 °C), brass in ammonia (season cracking), carbon steel in concentrated alkali (caustic embrittlement), and high-strength aluminum alloys in humid air or chloride. Chloride cracking of stainless steel is often transgranular, branching through the grains, while season cracking of brass is often intergranular, following grain boundaries, so the crack morphology observed in a failed part is also a useful clue to the cause.

When the crack growth rate da/dt in SCC is plotted against the stress intensity factor K at the crack tip, the crack hardly grows below a threshold K_ISCC; above it the rate rises steeply and then reaches a region where it is nearly constant regardless of K. The rate in this region is set by the rate of the corrosion reaction or of hydrogen diffusion at the crack tip. K_ISCC is often much smaller than the fracture toughness in air, K_IC, so a crack can grow little by little under a constant load until it finally reaches K_IC and fails suddenly. In design, the allowable crack size is chosen so that K does not exceed K_ISCC.

The mechanisms of SCC are broadly considered in 2 groups. One is the dissolution type (slip–dissolution), in which plastic deformation at the crack tip ruptures the film and the freshly exposed metal dissolves, advancing the crack. The other is the hydrogen embrittlement type, in which hydrogen produced by corrosion enters the highly stressed region ahead of the tip and embrittles the material; it is a problem in high-strength steels. The distinction bears directly on countermeasures: cathodic protection suppresses dissolution-type cracking by making the metal a cathode, but for the hydrogen type it can increase hydrogen generation and promote cracking.

about.h: Difference from corrosion fatigue, and the approach to prevention
about.p: Cracking under combined cyclic stress and corrosion is called corrosion fatigue; it differs from SCC in that it occurs without a specific environment and that a clear fatigue limit no longer appears. Preventing SCC means removing one of its 3 requirements: material, stress or environment. For the material, options include changing to higher-Ni grades or duplex stainless steels, or using a crack-resistant microstructure at a small cost in strength, as in the overaged T73 temper of 7075 alloy. For stress, stress-relief annealing and shot peening are used; for the environment, reducing chloride and dissolved oxygen or lowering the temperature.

faq.q: Why is stress corrosion cracking dangerous?
faq.a: Because parts crack suddenly at stresses below the yield stress, even though they show almost no visible corrosion from outside. The cracks are fine and only small portions reach the surface, so they are hard to find without searching with methods such as penetrant testing.

faq.q: Are stress corrosion cracking and hydrogen embrittlement the same?
faq.a: They overlap but are not the same. Crack growth caused by hydrogen generated by corrosion is regarded as one form of SCC, but hydrogen embrittlement can also be caused by hydrogen introduced during plating or welding and can occur without any corrosive environment.

faq.q: What tests are used to study stress corrosion cracking?
faq.a: They include the U-bend test, in which a specimen bent into a U shape is immersed in the environment; constant-load tests, in which a fixed load is maintained; and the slow strain rate test (SSRT), in which the specimen is pulled slowly to detect a loss of ductility.

犠牲陽極.desc: An anode of zinc, aluminum alloy, magnesium or another metal more active than the metal to be protected, connected electrically so that it dissolves first and protects the metal as the cathode.

about.h: Galvanic anode systems and impressed current systems
about.p: Cathodic protection comes in 2 forms: the galvanic (sacrificial) anode system, which connects a metal more active than the one to be protected and uses the current produced as it dissolves, and the impressed current system, which drives current from a DC power supply. Sacrificial anodes need no power source or wiring management, are simple to install, and carry little risk of sending stray currents into other structures. On the other hand, the voltage they provide is small, so the current tends to be insufficient in high-resistance soil or fresh water, and impressed current systems are chosen for large structures and high-resistance environments.

In seawater, anodes of zinc and of aluminum alloys containing In and Zn are mainly used. Pure aluminum forms a passive film and stops dissolving readily, so elements such as In are added to hinder film formation and let it dissolve steadily. Magnesium has the most active potential and provides a large driving voltage, so it is used for pipelines in high-resistance soil and for freshwater equipment. In seawater, however, too much current flows, it is consumed quickly and can overprotect the steel, so it is seldom used there. Anodes are chosen by potential, charge available per unit mass and price.

The charge an anode can deliver is set by Faraday's law; the theoretical values are about 820 Ah/kg for zinc, about 2980 Ah/kg for aluminum and about 2200 Ah/kg for magnesium. In practice, part of the anode is lost to self-corrosion without contributing to protection, so the usable charge is less than theoretical; for magnesium in particular it is said to be about half. For example, supplying 1 A of protection current for 1 year requires 8760 Ah, so even on the theoretical value about 11 kg of zinc is needed. In design, the number of anodes and their replacement interval are determined from the required current, the number of years and the usable fraction of the anode.

Whether sacrificial anodes are protecting a structure is judged by measuring its potential with a reference electrode. Common protection criteria for steel are a potential more negative than −0.80 V against a silver/silver chloride electrode in seawater, and more negative than −0.85 V against a saturated copper sulfate electrode in soil. If the potential becomes too negative, hydrogen evolves on the surface and can cause hydrogen embrittlement of high-strength steel or disbonding of coatings, so overprotection must also be avoided. Anodes are consumables, so the remaining amount is inspected regularly and they are replaced before they are used up.

faq.q: Do sacrificial anodes and zinc galvanizing work on the same principle?
faq.a: Yes. Galvanizing can be thought of as a layer of sacrificial anode over the whole steel surface; even if a scratch exposes the steel, the surrounding zinc dissolves first and protects it.

faq.q: How long do sacrificial anodes last?
faq.a: It depends on the current needed for protection and the mass of the anodes, and designs range from a few years to several decades. On ship hulls, it is common to inspect wear and replace the anodes each time the ship is drydocked.

faq.q: Why must sacrificial anodes not be painted?
faq.a: Because an anode produces current by dissolving itself, and covering its surface with paint stops the current and destroys its protective action. When a hull is repainted, the anodes are left unpainted.

ファラデーの法則.desc: The law that the amount of substance changed by an electrode reaction is proportional to the charge passed. The mass dissolved or deposited is m = ItM/(nF).

about.h: What the law says and the equation
about.p: Faraday's laws of electrolysis state that the amount of substance reacting at an electrode is proportional to the charge passed (first law), and that the amount reacting for the same charge is proportional to the substance's molar mass divided by the number of electrons in the reaction (second law). Combined, the mass dissolved or deposited when a current I flows for a time t is m = ItM/(nF). F is the Faraday constant, the charge of 1 mol of electrons, 96485 C/mol, equal to the product of the Avogadro constant and the elementary charge, F = N_A·e. Faraday found these relations by experiment in the 1830s.

about.h: From corrosion current to corrosion rate
about.p: Corrosion is also an electrochemical reaction, so once the corrosion current is known, Faraday's law converts it into a corrosion rate. Using the current density per unit area i, the rate of thickness loss is iM/(nFρ) (ρ is density). When iron dissolves as Fe²⁺, a corrosion current density of 1 µA/cm² corresponds to a loss of about 11.6 µm per year, or about 0.012 mm/y. Obtaining the corrosion current by polarization resistance measurement or Tafel extrapolation and converting it to annual thickness loss this way is a standard procedure in corrosion assessment. It is important for n to match the charge of the ions actually formed.

about.h: Use in plating and electrolytic smelting
about.p: In electroplating, Faraday's law is used to estimate film thickness. Plating in a copper sulfate bath at a current density of 2 A/dm² (0.02 A/cm²) for 10 minutes deposits about 4.4 µm of copper, assuming all the current goes into copper deposition. In practice part of the current goes into hydrogen evolution and other reactions, so the result is multiplied by the fraction used for deposition, the current efficiency. Acidic copper and zinc baths have high current efficiencies, whereas chromium plating is known for low efficiency. In electrolytic smelting of aluminum, producing 1 kg of aluminum requires about 2980 Ah of charge, which is why the process uses so much electric power.

Battery capacity is also determined by Faraday's law. If an electrode material exchanges n mol of electrons per mol, its theoretical capacity per unit mass is nF/M, which converts to nF/(3.6M) mAh/g using 1 mAh = 3.6 C. The 372 mAh/g of graphite and the roughly 170 mAh/g of LiFePO₄ are values obtained from this calculation. In the same way, the charge a sacrificial anode can deliver and the charge obtained from 1 mol of hydrogen in a fuel cell (2F) can be calculated. As the basic relation linking charge and amount of substance, it appears in every area of electrochemistry.

faq.q: What is the value and meaning of the Faraday constant?
faq.a: It is about 96485 C/mol, the magnitude of the charge carried by 1 mol of electrons. It equals the elementary charge, 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C, multiplied by the Avogadro constant, 6.022×10²³ mol⁻¹.

faq.q: What goes into n in the equation?
faq.a: It is the number of electrons exchanged per particle of the reacting substance: 2 for deposition of Cu²⁺, 3 for Al³⁺ and 1 for Ag⁺. For metals such as iron that can form both Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺, choose it to match the actual reaction.

faq.q: Why is the deposited amount smaller than calculated?
faq.a: Because part of the current is used in reactions other than the intended one, such as hydrogen evolution or reactions of impurities. This fraction is expressed as the current efficiency, and multiplying the calculated value by it brings the result closer to the actual amount.

理論容量.desc: The maximum charge an electrode material can store, expressed per unit mass. It is calculated as Q = nF/(3.6M) mAh/g; for graphite it is 372 mAh/g.

about.p: When 1 mol of electrode material reacts and exchanges n mol of electrons, the charge passed is nF coulombs (F is the Faraday constant, 96485 C/mol). Dividing by the formula weight M gives the charge per unit mass, and converting with 1 mAh = 3.6 C gives Q = nF/(3.6M) mAh/g. For graphite, 1 mol of C₆ (72.06 g/mol) takes up one Li⁺, giving 372 mAh/g; for LiCoO₂, extracting all of the one Li gives about 274 mAh/g. The value changes depending on which mass is used in the denominator, so it is important to check which state's mass the capacity is quoted per.

Not all of the calculated theoretical capacity can necessarily be used. In layered LiCoO₂, extracting more than about half the Li destabilizes the crystal structure and degradation proceeds through oxygen release and phase transitions, so practical capacity has been limited to about 140–150 mAh/g, roughly half the theoretical value. Graphite and LiFePO₄, by contrast, can be used close to their theoretical values. On the first charge, an SEI film forms on the anode surface and some lithium is lost, so the capacity obtainable from the cell is slightly smaller still.

The energy stored in a battery is the product of capacity and voltage. The larger the potential difference between the positive and negative electrodes, the more energy is stored for the same capacity. LiFePO₄ has a theoretical capacity of about 170 mAh/g, but its average voltage of about 3.4 V is lower than that of layered oxides (about 3.7–3.8 V), so its energy per mass is smaller. In addition, the whole cell includes the mass of the electrolyte, separator, current collectors and casing, so the energy density of a cell is far smaller than the value calculated from the active materials.

faq.q: Is a material with a larger theoretical capacity always a better electrode material?
faq.a: Capacity alone does not decide it. Voltage, cycle life, volume change, safety and cost also matter. Silicon has about ten times the theoretical capacity of graphite, but its large volume change makes it difficult to use on its own.

faq.q: What is the difference between mAh/g and Wh/kg?
faq.a: mAh/g is the charge stored per unit mass, and Wh/kg the energy stored per unit mass. Multiplying charge by the average voltage gives energy, and the value of mAh/g × V is numerically the value in Wh/kg.

faq.q: Do the capacities of the positive and negative electrodes need to match?
faq.a: The capacity of the cell is set by the electrode with the smaller capacity. In real cells, the anode capacity is generally designed to be slightly larger than the cathode's so that lithium metal does not plate on the anode.

層状岩塩型構造.desc: A structure in which Li layers and transition-metal layers alternate within close-packed oxygen. LiCoO₂ and LiNiO₂-based cathodes take this structure, and Li⁺ moves two-dimensionally between the layers.

about.h: From rock salt to layered order
about.p: In the rock salt (NaCl-type) structure, cations fill all the octahedral interstices of cubic close-packed oxygen. In LiCoO₂, Li⁺ and Co³⁺ together occupy these interstices, but the 2 kinds of cation are not arranged randomly; they are ordered so that Li layers and Co layers alternate on every cubic (111) plane. This ordering lowers the symmetry to rhombohedral (space group R-3m, α-NaFeO₂ type), and the structure is called layered rock salt. The CoO₂ layers form a robust framework of edge-sharing octahedra, and Li⁺ moves two-dimensionally within the planes between these layers.

LiCoO₂ was reported as a cathode material by Goodenough and coworkers in 1980 and became the first cathode of the lithium-ion battery commercialized in 1991. Its average voltage is high, about 3.9 V, but Co is expensive and its resources are limited. This led to the development of LiNi_xMn_yCo_zO₂ (NMC), in which part of the Co is replaced by Ni and Mn, and LiNi_xCo_yAl_zO₂ (NCA), which adds Co and Al to Ni. The more Ni, the larger the capacity, but thermal stability and cycle life tend to decrease, so the composition is chosen to balance the two.

about.h: Cation mixing and degradation at high states of charge
about.p: The ionic radius of Ni²⁺ (about 0.69 Å) is close to that of Li⁺ (about 0.76 Å), so in Ni-rich materials cation mixing, in which Ni enters the Li layers, occurs easily. Ni in the Li layers blocks the Li⁺ pathways and lowers capacity and power. In XRD, the intensity ratio of the (003) and (104) peaks is often used as a measure of the degree of mixing. In addition, when much Li has been removed, a phase transition that abruptly contracts the interlayer spacing causes microcracks in particles, and lattice oxygen is released and reacts with the electrolyte, causing degradation and heat generation.

LiCoO₂ has a theoretical capacity of about 274 mAh/g, but removing all the Li destroys the structure, so only part of it can be used; raising the upper charging voltage increases capacity at the cost of faster degradation. Small amounts of elements such as Al, Mg and Ti are therefore added to stabilize the structure, and particle surfaces are coated with oxides to suppress reactions with the electrolyte. To make internal cracking less likely, cathodes made of large single-crystal particles, rather than secondary particles made of many small primary particles, have also come into use.

faq.q: What does “rock salt” mean in layered rock salt?
faq.a: It means the structure has the same framework as sodium chloride (rock salt), with cations in the octahedral interstices of cubic close-packed oxygen. “Layered” is added because the cations are arranged in separate layers by kind.

faq.q: What do the numbers in NMC532 and NMC811 mean?
faq.a: They are the molar ratios of Ni, Mn and Co. NMC811 is Ni:Mn:Co = 8:1:1, a Ni-rich high-capacity composition, and NMC532 is 5:3:2, with less Ni and more Co.

faq.q: Why do layered rock salt cathodes tend to generate heat?
faq.a: Because when much Li has been removed, the oxidation state of the transition metal is high and lattice oxygen becomes unstable and is easily released at high temperature. If the released oxygen reacts with the electrolyte and generates heat, it can lead to thermal runaway.

スピネル型構造.desc: A structure of composition AB₂O₄ in which cations occupy tetrahedral and octahedral sites in cubic close-packed oxygen. The cathode LiMn₂O₄ has three-dimensional Li⁺ pathways.

about.p: The spinel structure is named after the mineral spinel, MgAl₂O₄. Its unit cell contains 8 AB₂O₄ units, with 32 oxygens forming cubic close packing. Of the 64 tetrahedral interstices among them, 8 are occupied by A, and of the 32 octahedral interstices, 16 by B. The arrangement with A in tetrahedral and B in octahedral sites is called normal spinel, and the one in which half of B occupies tetrahedral sites and A octahedral sites is called inverse spinel; magnetite, Fe₃O₄, is the classic inverse spinel. Which arrangement forms depends on ion size and on differences in crystal field stabilization.

The cathode LiMn₂O₄ is a normal spinel with Li⁺ in tetrahedral sites (8a) and Mn in octahedral sites (16d). Li⁺ moves to a neighboring 8a site via an empty octahedral site (16c), and because these pathways connect in 3 directions, the material can be charged and discharged quickly, suiting high-power uses. Its average voltage is about 4.0 V and its theoretical capacity about 148 mAh/g; it uses no Co, is inexpensive, and is comparatively thermally stable. The Mn₂O₄ framework hardly collapses when Li⁺ is removed, and the fully delithiated form is called λ-MnO₂.

about.h: Causes of degradation: Mn dissolution and the Jahn–Teller effect
about.p: The weakness of LiMn₂O₄ is capacity fade, especially at high temperature. Through the action of hydrogen fluoride and similar species in the electrolyte, Mn³⁺ disproportionates into Mn²⁺ and Mn⁴⁺; the Mn²⁺ dissolves into the electrolyte, deposits on the anode, and damages the SEI, accelerating degradation. In addition, discharging to around 3 V inserts excess Li⁺ and raises the fraction of Mn³⁺, and the Jahn–Teller effect distorts the octahedra, causing a large phase change from cubic to tetragonal. Replacing part of the Mn with Al, Ni or similar elements, and coating the surface, are used to suppress this degradation.

about.h: High-voltage cathodes and the spinel anode
about.p: In LiNi₀.₅Mn₁.₅O₄, in which a quarter of the Mn is replaced by Ni, the Ni²⁺/Ni⁴⁺ reaction is used and a high voltage of about 4.7 V is obtained. At this voltage, however, ordinary electrolytes decompose easily, so developing suitable electrolytes is a challenge. On the anode side, spinel Li₄Ti₅O₁₂ reacts at about 1.55 V, and its lattice size hardly changes as Li is inserted and removed (zero strain), so it has a very long life, forms little SEI and is safe. Its higher voltage lowers the energy density, but it is used for fast charging and applications such as buses.

faq.q: What is the difference between normal and inverse spinel?
faq.a: In normal spinel, A occupies tetrahedral sites and B octahedral sites. In inverse spinel, half of B occupies tetrahedral sites and the remaining B and all of A occupy octahedral sites. Fe₃O₄ and nickel ferrite, NiFe₂O₄, are inverse spinels.

faq.q: How is the theoretical capacity of LiMn₂O₄ calculated?
faq.a: Assuming 1 Li⁺ is removed per mol of LiMn₂O₄, with a formula weight of about 180.8 g/mol, the capacity is 96485/(3.6 × 180.8) ≈ 148 mAh/g.

faq.q: Why are spinel cathodes suited to high power?
faq.a: Because the Li⁺ pathways are connected in three dimensions, so the ions can move in any direction. Li⁺ enters and leaves the particles easily regardless of their orientation, making charge and discharge at high current easier.

オリビン型構造.desc: The structure of the mineral olivine, taken by the cathode LiFePO₄. Strong covalent bonds in PO₄ make it thermally stable, but Li⁺ diffusion is one-dimensional and electronic conductivity is low.

about.p: LiFePO₄ is orthorhombic (space group Pnma), with Fe²⁺ and Li⁺ in octahedral sites and P in tetrahedral sites within slightly distorted hexagonal close-packed oxygen. PO₄ tetrahedra link the FeO₆ octahedra, and the resulting framework is very robust. On the other hand, Li⁺ can use only the pathways running along the crystal's b axis (the [010] direction), so its diffusion is one-dimensional. A weakness of one-dimensional diffusion is that a defect in which Fe enters a pathway (an antisite defect) blocks the entire channel, so that the Li in it can no longer be used.

about.h: Why the voltage is flat: a two-phase reaction
about.p: Charge and discharge of LiFePO₄ proceed by a two-phase reaction, in which the two phases LiFePO₄ and FePO₄ coexist while their proportions change. At constant temperature and pressure, when 2 phases coexist in a 2-component system, the Gibbs phase rule leaves no degrees of freedom, so the potential stays constant even as the Li content changes. The result is a very flat voltage curve at about 3.4 V. A stable voltage is convenient for device design, but it also makes it difficult to estimate the state of charge (SOC) from the voltage. The volume change between the two phases is about 6–7%.

LiFePO₄ has very low electronic conductivity (about 10⁻⁹ S/cm or less), and Li⁺ diffusion is one-dimensional, so as is it cannot be charged and discharged at high current. The keys to its commercialization were shrinking the particles to tens to hundreds of nm to shorten the distances Li⁺ and electrons must travel, and coating the particle surfaces with a thin carbon film to provide paths for electrons. Making plate-like particles that are thin along the b axis shortens the pathways further. With these improvements, capacities close to the theoretical value of about 170 mAh/g can be obtained even at relatively high currents.

about.h: Safety and where it is used
about.p: In LiFePO₄ the oxygen is strongly covalently bonded to P, so even fully charged FePO₄ hardly releases oxygen at high temperature, making the material less prone to thermal runaway than layered oxide cathodes. Fe and P are abundant and inexpensive, and the absence of Co and Ni is another advantage. On the other hand, its voltage is low at about 3.4 V and its density is small, so its energy per unit volume and mass is lower than that of layered cathodes. It is therefore widely used where safety, life and cost matter most, such as stationary storage batteries, electric buses and some electric vehicles. Goodenough and coworkers reported it as a cathode material in 1997.

faq.q: What is a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery?
faq.a: It is a lithium-ion battery that uses olivine-type LiFePO₄ as the cathode. Its energy density is somewhat lower than that of batteries with layered oxide cathodes, but it excels in safety, cycle life and cost.

faq.q: Why is the voltage of LiFePO₄ higher than that of iron oxides?
faq.a: Because the oxygen in PO₄ is strongly covalently bonded to P, which makes the Fe–O bond more ionic and lowers the energy of the Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ redox couple (the inductive effect). As a result, a voltage of about 3.4 V is obtained, higher than with simple iron oxides.

faq.q: Is the olivine structure related to the mineral olivine?
faq.a: Yes. Olivine is a mineral of composition (Mg,Fe)₂SiO₄, and LiFePO₄ takes the same type of structure, so it is called olivine type. The gemstone peridot is also olivine.

固体電解質.desc: A material that conducts ions while remaining solid but conducts almost no electrons. Examples include sulfide and oxide electrolytes for all-solid-state batteries and stabilized zirconia for fuel cells.

about.p: A solid electrolyte is a material in which specific ions move through a crystal, glass or polymer to carry current, while electrons are hardly conducted at all. Ions need vacant sites or connected interstitial pathways to move, and the conductivity rises steeply with temperature, as in σT = A exp(−Ea/kT). For a material with an activation energy of 0.3 eV, cooling from 25 °C to −20 °C lowers the conductivity to about 1/7, and for 0.5 eV to about 1/27. A classic example is α-AgI, in which Ag⁺ moves almost like a liquid above 147 °C; such materials are called superionic conductors.

about.h: Typical materials and the ions they conduct
about.p: Yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ), which conducts oxide ions, is used in oxygen sensors and solid oxide fuel cells and needs about 700 °C or more for sufficient conductivity. β-alumina, which conducts Na⁺, is the electrolyte of sodium–sulfur batteries operating at about 300 °C. For all-solid-state lithium batteries, sulfides such as Li₁₀GeP₂S₁₂ (LGPS), with conductivities on the order of 10⁻² S/cm at room temperature, oxides such as garnet-type Li₇La₃Zr₂O₁₂ (LLZO), which are comparatively stable in air, and soft, easily processed polymers such as polyethylene oxide (PEO) are all being researched, and some have been commercialized.

about.h: How they differ from liquid electrolytes
about.p: In a liquid electrolyte both cations and anions move, and in lithium-ion battery electrolytes the fraction of current carried by Li⁺ (the transference number) is generally less than half. In many inorganic solid electrolytes, the framework stays put and only Li⁺ moves, so the transference number is nearly 1 and concentration gradients hardly form near the electrodes. Being non-flammable and leak-free are further advantages. On the other hand, contact between solids tends to be at points or along lines, so interfacial resistance tends to be high, and contact is secured by applying pressure or using soft materials.

The ionic conductivity of solid electrolytes is measured by AC impedance spectroscopy, and the response at different frequencies is used to separate the resistance of the grain interiors from that of the grain boundaries. The electronic conductivity is found by applying a DC voltage with ion-blocking electrodes and measuring the remaining current. Even a small electronic current causes self-discharge and makes lithium more likely to deposit inside the electrolyte. Indeed, lithium dendrites, once expected to be stopped by a solid, have been found to grow through solid electrolytes along grain boundaries and defects, a major challenge for realizing safe all-solid-state batteries.

faq.q: What is the difference between a solid electrolyte and a liquid electrolyte?
faq.a: A liquid electrolyte is a lithium salt dissolved in an organic solvent and can burn or leak. A solid electrolyte conducts ions while remaining solid, is hard to ignite, and in many cases only Li⁺ moves.

faq.q: How do sulfide and oxide electrolytes differ?
faq.a: Sulfides have high conductivity and are soft, so interfaces can be formed simply by pressing, but they react with moisture to release hydrogen sulfide. Oxides are comparatively stable in air but hard, and high-temperature sintering is needed to make them dense.

faq.q: What is a superionic conductor?
faq.a: It is a material that, while solid, shows a high ionic conductivity close to that of liquid electrolytes. α-AgI and some of the sulfides used in all-solid-state batteries are examples.

固体高分子形燃料電池.desc: A fuel cell whose electrolyte is a polymer membrane with sulfonic acid groups that conducts protons when hydrated. Abbreviated PEFC (also PEMFC); it is humidified to keep the membrane from drying and operates at about 80 °C.

about.p: In a PEFC, hydrogen is oxidized at the anode as H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻; protons pass through the electrolyte membrane and electrons through the external circuit to the cathode, where oxygen is reduced as O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O. The overall reaction forms water from hydrogen and oxygen; the standard Gibbs energy change for forming liquid water at 25 °C is −237.1 kJ per mol of water, so the theoretical emf is E° = −ΔG°/(2F) ≈ 1.23 V. The water produced is discharged on the air side, and no carbon dioxide is emitted during operation.

about.h: Why the voltage falls short of theory
about.p: When current is drawn, the actual voltage of a single cell drops to about 0.6–0.8 V. The largest loss is the activation overpotential caused by the slowness of the oxygen reduction reaction at the cathode, which remains large even with platinum catalysts. As current increases, losses from the resistance of the membrane and contacts are added, and at high currents mass transport losses appear as oxygen and water cannot move fast enough. The upper limit of theoretical efficiency, ΔG/ΔH, is about 83% on a higher heating value basis, but operating at 0.7 V gives a voltage efficiency of about 47%. The required voltage is obtained by stacking hundreds of single cells.

about.h: The membrane electrode assembly and water management
about.p: A membrane electrode assembly (MEA) consists of the electrolyte membrane (about 10–50 µm thick) with, on each side, a catalyst layer of carbon carrying fine platinum particles mixed with polymer electrolyte, and a gas diffusion layer; it is sandwiched between separators with flow channels to make a cell. The membrane conducts protons poorly when dry, but too much water fills the pores of the catalyst and gas diffusion layers and stops gas from reaching them (flooding). Electro-osmotic drag, in which protons carry water with them to the cathode, also occurs, so water management, balancing humidification against drainage, is key to performance.

In a PEFC operating at low temperature, carbon monoxide adsorbs strongly on the platinum surface and blocks the catalyst (CO poisoning). The international standard for hydrogen for fuel cell vehicles (ISO 14687) requires CO to be kept to 0.2 ppm or less, and home systems that produce hydrogen by reforming city gas must include a step to remove CO. Because PEFCs start quickly at low temperature and have high power density, they are used in fuel cell vehicles and in home fuel cells such as the ENE-FARM systems sold in Japan since 2009. Reducing the amount of platinum is a major cost challenge.

faq.q: Are PEFC and PEMFC the same?
faq.a: Yes. In Japan the name polymer electrolyte fuel cell (PEFC) is common, while in English-speaking countries proton exchange membrane fuel cell (PEMFC) is often used; both refer to fuel cells with a polymer membrane as the electrolyte.

faq.q: What is the difference between a PEFC and an SOFC?
faq.a: A PEFC uses a polymer membrane that conducts protons and operates at about 80 °C, so it starts quickly and suits vehicles. An SOFC uses a ceramic that conducts oxide ions and operates above 700 °C, so it needs no platinum and generates power efficiently, but it takes time to start up.

faq.q: Why does a PEFC need platinum?
faq.a: Because at the low temperature of about 80 °C, the oxygen reduction and hydrogen oxidation reactions are slow, and sufficient current cannot be obtained without a highly active catalyst such as platinum. Research is under way on catalysts that use less platinum or none at all.

ショックレー・クワイサー限界.desc: The upper limit on the theoretical efficiency of a single-junction solar cell. Balancing the transmission of light below the band gap against thermalization losses, it reaches a maximum of about 33% at about 1.34 eV under terrestrial sunlight.

about.p: In 1961, Shockley and Queisser treated a solar cell as a body that receives sunlight and also emits light according to its own temperature, and derived the upper limit of efficiency from the balance of light in and out (detailed balance). The assumptions were that every photon with energy above the band gap is absorbed and creates one electron–hole pair, that the only recombination is radiative recombination, which emits light, and that carriers instantly cool to the band edges. The important point is that even an ideal cell, with no defect recombination or resistive losses, retains the unavoidable loss of radiative recombination.

Photons with energy below the band gap Eg are not absorbed and are lost by transmission. Photons above Eg are absorbed, but their excess energy is lost as heat while the electrons fall to the band edge (thermalization). For example, when a 2.5 eV photon is absorbed by a 1.1 eV gap, 1.4 eV becomes heat. A smaller gap absorbs more light but lowers the voltage, while a larger gap raises the voltage but absorbs less light. Balancing these, the maximum for terrestrial sunlight (AM1.5) is about 33% at about 1.34 eV.

The Shockley–Queisser limit is not an upper bound on all conversion of sunlight, like the Carnot efficiency of heat engines. It is the limit under assumptions such as a single junction, one carrier pair per photon and no concentration, and it can be exceeded if those assumptions are dropped. Multijunction solar cells, which stack cells with different gaps, absorb each part of the spectrum in the layer best suited to it and reduce thermalization, and efficiencies well above 40% have been reported under concentration. Also, silicon (1.12 eV) lies close to the maximum of the limit, but as an indirect-gap material it absorbs light weakly and needs a thick absorber, so unavoidable Auger recombination becomes the main loss, and its practical limit is estimated at about 29%.

The limit curve serves as a yardstick for evaluating new solar cell materials. Many perovskite solar cells use materials with band gaps of about 1.5–1.6 eV because that range is close to the maximum of the limit. Comparing a real cell's open-circuit voltage, short-circuit current and fill factor with the limiting values for the same gap shows where the losses lie. A shortfall in open-circuit voltage in particular indicates a large amount of non-radiative recombination. Tandem cells that stack a wide-gap perovskite on silicon are being developed with the aim of exceeding the single-junction limit.

faq.q: What is the value of the Shockley–Queisser limit?
faq.a: For the terrestrial solar spectrum (AM1.5), the maximum is about 33% at a band gap of about 1.34 eV. The original 1961 paper treated the sun as a 6000 K blackbody and gave about 30% at about 1.1 eV.

faq.q: Why can multijunction solar cells exceed the limit?
faq.a: Because they stack cells with different band gaps, absorbing short-wavelength light in the upper layer with a large gap and long-wavelength light in the lower layer with a small gap, which reduces thermalization and transmission losses at the same time.

faq.q: Why does concentrating sunlight raise the efficiency?
faq.a: Because stronger light increases the current proportionally, and the open-circuit voltage also rises with the logarithm of the light intensity, so efficiency increases. At the ideal maximum concentration, the limit even for a single junction rises to about 40%.

熱電性能指数.desc: The dimensionless value ZT = S²σT/κ that expresses the conversion performance of a thermoelectric material. It is larger the higher the Seebeck coefficient and electrical conductivity and the lower the thermal conductivity.

about.h: The quantities that make up ZT
about.p: S is the Seebeck coefficient, the voltage generated per kelvin of temperature difference; σ is the electrical conductivity, κ the thermal conductivity and T the absolute temperature. S²σ in the numerator is called the power factor and is a measure of how much electrical power can be extracted from the material. The smaller κ in the denominator, the easier it is to maintain the temperature difference between the hot and cold sides. The units in S²σT/κ cancel, so ZT is dimensionless. For example, a material with S = 200 µV/K, σ = 1.0×10⁵ S/m and κ = 1.5 W/(m·K) has ZT = 0.8 at 300 K.

The maximum efficiency of thermoelectric power generation is expressed as the Carnot efficiency, set by the hot- and cold-side temperatures, multiplied by a factor determined by ZT. The larger ZT, the closer the efficiency approaches the Carnot efficiency, but even at ZT = 1 the efficiency is only about 20% of the Carnot efficiency (about 17–24% depending on the temperatures). Bi₂Te₃-based materials near room temperature, PbTe- and Mg₂Si-based materials at intermediate temperatures, and SiGe, silicides and oxides at high temperatures are researched and used, so the materials with high ZT differ by operating temperature range.

about.h: Why ZT is hard to raise
about.p: S, σ and κ are not independent of one another. Raising the carrier concentration increases σ but lowers S, and the thermal conductivity carried by electrons also increases according to the Wiedemann–Franz law. The optimum carrier concentration therefore lies in the range of heavily doped semiconductors, about 10¹⁹–10²⁰ cm⁻³. Efforts are thus made to lower the lattice thermal conductivity by scattering only the phonons, which carry much of the heat, using nanostructured interfaces, point defects or atoms rattling inside cage-like crystals, while disturbing electron conduction as little as possible.

faq.q: Why are metals unsuitable as thermoelectric materials?
faq.a: Metals have high electrical conductivity, but their Seebeck coefficients are small, a few µV/K, and their electronic thermal conductivity is large, so ZT is extremely small. Heavily doped semiconductors are used as thermoelectric materials.

faq.q: Does ZT change with temperature?
faq.a: Yes. S, σ and κ all depend on temperature, and the ZT expression itself contains T. Each material has a temperature range where ZT is highest, so materials are chosen to match the operating temperature.

faq.q: Does ZT also matter for Peltier cooling?
faq.a: Yes. The coefficient of performance of thermoelectric cooling (Peltier devices) also increases with ZT, so ZT is the index of material performance for both power generation and cooling.

CFRP(炭素繊維強化プラスチック).desc: A composite of carbon fibers bound with epoxy or another resin. With low density and high modulus and strength, it excels in specific stiffness and is used in aircraft, automobiles and sporting goods.

about.p: CFRP is a composite of carbon fibers about 5–7 µm in diameter bound with a thermosetting resin such as epoxy or with a thermoplastic. Carbon fiber has a low density of about 1.8 g/cm³ and a Young's modulus of about 230 GPa for standard grades and several hundred GPa for high-modulus grades. In the fiber direction of unidirectional material, its specific stiffness (Young's modulus/density) is more than three times that of steel or aluminum alloys, and it also resists fatigue well, so it is used for the wings and fuselages of aircraft where weight must be saved, automobiles, wind turbine blades, fishing rods, golf clubs and more.

Unidirectional material is strong and stiff along the fibers, but perpendicular to the fibers and in in-plane shear it shows only low values close to those of the resin. Real parts are therefore made as laminates stacking plies of different orientations, such as 0°, ±45° and 90°, placing fibers to match the directions of load. When similar in-plane properties are wanted in every direction, a quasi-isotropic layup is used. The through-thickness direction is supported by the resin alone, so interlaminar strength is low and impact readily causes internal delamination, which requires attention.

Carbon fiber conducts electricity and has a noble electrode potential, so direct contact with aluminum alloys readily causes galvanic corrosion of the aluminum. At joints, a layer of glass fiber is interposed or titanium alloy fasteners are used. CFRP made with thermosetting resin cannot be melted after curing, so recycling is difficult, and technologies to recover the fibers by pyrolysis and other methods are being developed. Voids and fiber waviness from molding reduce strength, so parts are inspected by ultrasonic testing and similar methods.

faq.q: Is CFRP stronger than steel?
faq.a: In specific strength and specific stiffness, the tensile strength and Young's modulus in the fiber direction divided by density, it far exceeds steel. But its strength perpendicular to the fibers and through the thickness is low, so it is not stronger than steel in every direction.

faq.q: How are CFRP and GFRP chosen between?
faq.a: CFRP is generally used for parts where lightness and stiffness are critical and a high price is acceptable, and GFRP for parts where cost must be kept down or where electrical insulation or transparency to radio waves is required.

faq.q: Does CFRP rust?
faq.a: CFRP itself does not rust as metals do, but the resin can degrade from moisture absorption and ultraviolet light. It can also promote galvanic corrosion of metals it contacts, so joints with dissimilar materials need countermeasures.

GFRP(ガラス繊維強化プラスチック).desc: A composite of glass fibers bound with resin. It is less stiff than CFRP but inexpensive, electrically insulating and transparent to radio waves, and is used for boat hulls, bathtubs, printed circuit boards and more.

about.p: GFRP mainly uses fibers of E-glass (an aluminoborosilicate glass developed for electrical insulation), with a Young's modulus of about 72 GPa, a density of about 2.55 g/cm³ and diameters of roughly 10–20 µm. Stronger and stiffer S-glass fibers also exist and are used for parts such as aircraft components. The resins include thermosets, such as inexpensive unsaturated polyester, highly corrosion-resistant vinyl ester and epoxy with excellent strength and adhesion, as well as thermoplastics such as polyamide. The fiber surfaces are treated with silane coupling agents to improve adhesion to the resin.

about.h: Specific stiffness on a par with steel, or lower
about.p: GFRP is strong, but not especially stiff. For a unidirectional laminate with 60% fiber volume fraction, the rule of mixtures gives a Young's modulus in the fiber direction of about 45 GPa and a density of about 2.0 g/cm³, so its specific stiffness is somewhat lower than steel's. In mats with randomly oriented fibers, the modulus falls further, to a fraction of that. GFRP parts are therefore often sized by deflection before strength, and sections are enlarged or reinforced with ribs. The key to design is how to make up for the lack of stiffness while exploiting the strength.

Glass fibers are used as bundled rovings, chopped strand mats made of short scattered strands, woven fabrics and other forms. Molding methods include hand lay-up, in which fibers are laid in a mold and resin is applied layer by layer; SMC, in which sheets of fiber and resin are press-molded; and filament winding, in which fibers are wound onto pipes and tanks. Uses are wide-ranging: boat hulls, bathtubs, septic tanks, piping, wind turbine blades, automotive body panels and printed circuit boards (FR-4, made of glass cloth and epoxy). Because it transmits radio waves, GFRP is also used for radar domes (radomes).

Under sustained load in a moist environment, small surface cracks in glass fibers can grow slowly, and the fibers may break at stresses below their short-term strength (static fatigue). E-glass is vulnerable to acids and can suffer stress corrosion cracking of the fibers in acidic environments, so acid-resistant glasses such as ECR glass are used. Degradation of the resin by water absorption and ultraviolet light also needs attention. GFRP made with thermosetting resins is hard to recycle, and discarded wind turbine blades and similar items are crushed and used as raw material or fuel for cement production.

faq.q: Are FRP and GFRP the same?
faq.a: FRP refers to fiber-reinforced plastics in general; with glass fibers it is GFRP and with carbon fibers CFRP. In Japan, plain “FRP” often means the GFRP used for boats and bathtubs.

faq.q: What is the fiber content of GFRP?
faq.a: It varies greatly with the molding method; as a rough guide, hand lay-up mats are around 20% by volume, while pultrusion and filament winding reach about 50–60%. The higher the content, the stronger and stiffer the material.

faq.q: Does GFRP conduct electricity?
faq.a: No. Both glass fibers and resin are insulators, so it can be used for parts that need electrical insulation and for radomes that must transmit radio waves. This is a major difference from CFRP, which uses conductive carbon fibers.

臨界繊維長.desc: The length needed for the stress at the middle of a short fiber to reach the fiber's tensile strength through interfacial shear. It is given by lc = σf·d/(2τc); fibers shorter than this pull out.

about.h: Why there is a critical length
about.p: Load is transferred to a short fiber in a matrix mainly through shear at the interface along the fiber's sides. At the fiber ends the stress is nearly zero; moving away from an end, load enters gradually through the interfacial shear stress τc and the fiber stress increases. The length at which load entering from both ends brings the stress at the fiber's middle exactly to its tensile strength σf is the critical fiber length lc, and force balance gives lc = σf·d/(2τc) (d is the fiber diameter). For carbon fiber in epoxy, lc is a few tenths of a millimeter to about 1 mm.

If a fiber is shorter than lc, its stress never reaches the tensile strength, and the fiber pulls out of the matrix before it breaks, so its strength cannot be fully exploited. If the fiber is much longer than lc, the low-stress end portions make up a small fraction, and reinforcement close to that of continuous fibers is obtained. As a rough guide, fibers more than about fifteen times lc are regarded as close to continuous. The stronger the interfacial adhesion, the larger τc and the shorter lc, and the thinner the fiber, the shorter lc.

In injection-molded short-fiber-reinforced plastics, fibers break and shorten during compounding and molding, and when the average fiber length approaches lc, the reinforcing effect drops sharply. Long-fiber pellets that keep fibers long and adjustments to molding conditions are therefore used. Pull-out also absorbs energy during fracture, so a certain amount of pull-out can help toughness. In ceramic matrix composites, the interface is made weak to deliberately induce pull-out, preventing sudden fracture and raising toughness.

faq.q: Does strengthening the interface shorten the critical fiber length?
faq.a: Yes. lc is inversely proportional to the interfacial shear strength τc, so strengthening adhesion with a coupling agent or similar shortens it, letting even short fibers use their strength.

faq.q: What changes if the fibers are made thinner?
faq.a: lc is proportional to the fiber diameter d, so thinner fibers have shorter critical lengths. For fibers of the same length, thinner ones have a larger ratio of length to lc, improving reinforcing efficiency.

faq.q: Can the critical fiber length be ignored for continuous fibers?
faq.a: Even with continuous fibers, when a single fiber breaks somewhere along its length, a length of about lc/2 on each side of the break, about lc in total, is needed for the stress to recover. This length also bears on how a fiber break affects neighboring fibers and on how strength scatter is treated.

疑似等方積層.desc: A laminate, such as [0/±45/90]ₛ, stacked from plies whose fiber directions are divided at equal angles. The in-plane Young's modulus is nearly equal in all directions, but the through-thickness direction remains weak.

about.p: When unidirectional plies are stacked in equal numbers in n directions (n ≥ 3) at equal intervals of 180°/n, the in-plane stiffness becomes independent of direction. For n = 3 the minimum set is [0/60/−60], and for n = 4 it is [0/45/−45/90]. Calculating with classical laminate theory for carbon fiber/epoxy with E₁ = 140 GPa, E₂ = 10 GPa, G₁₂ = 5 GPa and ν₁₂ = 0.3, both [0/±45/90]ₛ and [0/60/−60]ₛ give a Young's modulus of about 54 GPa in every direction. For [0/90]ₛ, by contrast, the modulus is about 75 GPa at 0° but falls to about 18 GPa at 45°.

The in-plane Young's modulus of a quasi-isotropic laminate is about 40% of the fiber-direction value of the unidirectional material. In the example above it is about 54 GPa against 140 GPa: the laminate can take loads from any direction, but the stiffness in any particular direction drops considerably. Even so, with high-performance carbon fibers, a modulus close to that of aluminum alloys (about 70 GPa) is obtained at about 60% of the density. For members with a clear load direction, it is more rational to add 0° plies to raise stiffness and strength in that direction; making everything quasi-isotropic is not always the answer.

Even when the in-plane extensional stiffness is isotropic, the material does not truly become isotropic. Bending stiffness changes with the stacking order, and because the orientation of the outer plies dominates, the bending stiffness differs with direction. Strength also varies somewhat with direction, and interlaminar stresses concentrate at ply edges and around holes. Moreover, through-thickness stiffness and strength are carried by the resin and remain far lower than in-plane values. Stacking symmetrically about the midplane (the subscript s) is done to prevent coupling between extension and bending, which would make the plate warp or twist on cooling or under load.

In aircraft structures, load directions vary from place to place and unexpected loads also occur, so quasi-isotropic or near-quasi-isotropic laminates are often used as a baseline. Design conventions include placing at least about 10% of the plies in each of the 0°, ±45° and 90° directions, not stacking many plies of the same orientation in a row, and using equal numbers of +45° and −45° plies (balanced laminates). Thick blocks of plies with the same orientation produce large shear stresses between plies, making resin cracking and delamination more likely. Around bolt holes, the proportion of ±45° plies is sometimes increased to ease stress concentration.

faq.q: How is the notation [0/±45/90]ₛ read?
faq.a: The bracket lists the ply orientations of one half of the laminate from the outside inward; ±45 means 2 plies at +45° and −45°, and the subscript s means the sequence is mirrored about the midplane. The full laminate is the 8 plies [0/45/−45/90/90/−45/45/0].

faq.q: How is the Young's modulus of a quasi-isotropic laminate found?
faq.a: It is found by classical laminate theory, which transforms the stiffness of each ply according to its angle using the 4 elastic constants of the unidirectional material and averages over the thickness. For carbon fiber/epoxy it is often about 40% of the unidirectional fiber-direction value.

faq.q: Does a quasi-isotropic layup prevent delamination?
faq.a: No. The through-thickness direction is carried by the resin and remains weak, and delamination can start from impacts, ply edges and holes. Choosing the stacking sequence carefully can make it less likely.

層間はく離.desc: Damage in which the resin or interface between plies of a laminate cracks and the plies separate. It occurs because the through-thickness strength is low, and when caused internally by impact it is hard to detect from outside.

about.h: Why the region between plies is weak
about.p: In-plane loads in a laminate are carried by the fibers, but there are no fibers between plies; they are connected only by resin and by the fiber–resin interface. As a result, the strength against through-thickness tension (peeling forces) and interlaminar shear is lower than the fiber-direction strength by a factor of several tens. In laminates, interlaminar stresses arising from the differences in ply orientation concentrate at free edges, around holes, at ply drops and in curved sections, and delamination starts there. Voids and foreign matter introduced during molding also act as starting points.

Delamination is treated by fracture mechanics as the growth of a crack between plies. The interlaminar fracture toughness in the opening mode (mode I), G_Ic, is measured by the double cantilever beam (DCB) test, and that in the sliding mode (mode II), G_IIc, by tests such as the end-notched flexure (ENF) test. For carbon fiber laminates with brittle epoxy, G_Ic is roughly 100–300 J/m², orders of magnitude smaller than the fracture toughness of metals expressed in the same energy terms. Toughened epoxies containing thermoplastic particles, or thermoplastic matrices, can raise G_Ic substantially.

about.h: Invisible impact damage and compressive strength
about.p: Even an impact as minor as a dropped tool or a flying stone can spread many delaminations of different orientation, ply by ply, in a cone shape inside a laminate. Only a slight dent remains on the surface, so the damage can hardly be found visually (BVID: barely visible impact damage). Delaminated regions buckle easily as thin sublaminates under compression, so compressive strength drops much more than tensile strength. Aircraft design therefore uses compression after impact (CAI) strength, measured on laminates that have been deliberately impacted, as one of its criteria.

Internal delaminations are usually found by ultrasonic inspection (C-scan), which examines the waves reflected from delamination surfaces; infrared thermography and tap testing are also used. To prevent them, besides using toughened resins, there are methods that put fibers in the through-thickness direction to tie the plies together, such as stitching with thread, inserting fine Z-pins and three-dimensional weaving. However, through-thickness fibers can disturb the in-plane fibers and reduce in-plane properties, so the choice is a trade-off between the two. Separation at interfaces in semiconductor packages and coatings is likewise called delamination, from the same idea of layers coming apart.

faq.q: Does delamination only apply to composites?
faq.a: No. Besides laminated composite plates, the word is used for interface separation in anything built up in layers, such as semiconductor packages, paint films and laminated glass.

faq.q: How is delamination detected?
faq.a: Because internal damage often cannot be seen from outside, it is usually examined by ultrasonic inspection. Ultrasound reflects from delamination surfaces, so their position and depth can be imaged.

faq.q: Can delaminated parts be repaired?
faq.a: Small delaminations are sometimes repaired by injecting resin to rebond them. For larger damage, the damaged area is machined away and new plies are laid up and bonded, as in doubler or scarf repairs.

シランカップリング剤.desc: A compound with, in a single molecule, a group that bonds to inorganic materials and a group that reacts with resin. It is used to treat the surface of glass fibers, improving interfacial adhesion and water resistance.

about.h: What each end of the molecule does
about.p: A silane coupling agent is generally a molecule that can be written Y−R−Si(OR′)₃. The Si(OR′)₃ part carries alkoxy groups such as methoxy or ethoxy groups; these hydrolyze in water to silanols (Si−OH), which condense with hydroxyl groups on the surface of glass or metal oxides to form strong bonds such as Si−O−Si. At the other end, Y is an organic functional group such as amino, epoxy, methacryl or vinyl, which reacts or entangles with the resin. In this way the molecule links inorganic and organic materials by covalent bonds, chemically bridging the interface.

about.h: Choosing one to match the resin
about.p: The effect of a coupling agent depends greatly on whether its organic functional group can react with the resin. For epoxy resins, amino silanes, which react like a curing agent, or epoxy silanes, which carry the same epoxy group, are often used; for unsaturated polyester and vinyl ester, methacryl silanes, which can copolymerize by radical reactions, are common. Typical molecules include 3-aminopropyltriethoxysilane and 3-glycidoxypropyltrimethoxysilane. In dental composite resins as well, filler surfaces are treated with methacryl silanes so that they bond chemically to the resin. In combinations that cannot react, the agent has almost no effect.

about.h: Materials it works on and materials it does not
about.p: Silane coupling agents bond strongly to materials with many surface hydroxyl groups, such as glass, silica, alumina and many metal oxides. They work poorly on carbon fibers, which have few surface hydroxyl groups, or on hard-to-oxidize gold; for carbon fibers, the surface is electrochemically oxidized to create functional groups and then coated with a sizing, and for gold, compounds with thiol groups are used. Applying too thick a layer can backfire, as the condensed silane layer itself becomes a weak layer and weakens adhesion. It is important to cover the surface thinly and evenly with a small amount.

Without silane treatment, water readily penetrates the interface between glass fibers and resin, and strength drops sharply in humid environments or boiling water. The bonds formed by the silane and the hydrophobic layer created at the interface suppress water ingress and hydrolysis of the interface, greatly improving strength retention in wet conditions. This effect is exploited not only in glass-fiber-reinforced plastics but also in plastics filled with inorganic powders, primers for adhesives and paints, and silica-filled automobile tires. In tires, sulfur-containing silanes link the silica filler to the rubber during vulcanization.

faq.q: How are silane coupling agents applied?
faq.a: There are 2 approaches: making a dilute aqueous or alcohol solution, applying it to or dipping the surface, and then drying and heating to form bonds; or mixing the agent directly into the resin. For glass fibers, it is included in the sizing applied right after spinning.

faq.q: What is the difference between a silane coupling agent and a sizing agent?
faq.a: Sizing refers to the whole treatment applied to fiber surfaces, including components that bind the fibers into strands, lubricants and coupling agents. The silane coupling agent is the component within it that is responsible for bonding at the interface.

faq.q: Why is it called a “coupling” agent?
faq.a: Because a single molecule couples, or joins, inorganic and organic materials with completely different properties. It is not an adhesive itself but a molecule that chemically mediates the interface between 2 materials.

金属基複合材料.desc: A composite (MMC) with a metal matrix such as aluminum reinforced by SiC particles or fibers. It can raise stiffness and wear resistance and lower thermal expansion.

about.p: A metal matrix composite (MMC) uses a metal such as aluminum, magnesium, titanium or copper as the matrix, reinforced with particles, short fibers or continuous fibers of materials such as SiC and Al₂O₃. Particle-reinforced aluminum alloys are the most widely used, with particle contents ranging from about 10–20% by volume up to more than 60% in heat-dissipation materials. MMCs aim at properties between those of polymer matrix composites and ceramics: higher heat resistance than the former, and higher toughness and thermal conductivity than the latter. Cemented carbides, in which WC particles are bonded by Co, are sometimes regarded as MMCs in a broad sense.

The Young's modulus of a particle-reinforced composite lies between the upper bound of the rule of mixtures (equal strain in each phase) and the lower bound (equal stress). For aluminum (70 GPa) with 20 vol% SiC particles (410 GPa), the upper bound is about 138 GPa and the lower bound about 84 GPa, and actual values often fall in between, around 100 GPa. The linear expansion coefficient also falls with particle content, and with a large particle fraction it can be reduced from the matrix's roughly 23×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ to values close to those of semiconductors and ceramic substrates. Being able to lower expansion alone while keeping thermal conductivity high is the advantage in heat-dissipation materials.

MMCs are made by stir casting, in which particles are mixed into molten metal and cast; powder metallurgy, in which metal and reinforcement powders are mixed and consolidated; and pressure infiltration, in which molten metal is forced into a preform of the reinforcement. Molten metals often wet particles poorly, so particles tend to cluster and distribute unevenly, and voids tend to remain. Also, prolonged contact at high temperature makes SiC react with aluminum to form brittle Al₄C₃, so the temperature, time and Si content of the matrix are controlled. Dislocations multiplied around particles by the expansion mismatch on cooling also affect the strength.

Aluminum alloy/SiC MMCs have been used for baseplates of power semiconductor modules, structural parts of precision equipment, brake components and bicycle frames. Their weaknesses, however, are that the hard particles wear cutting tools quickly so that diamond tools are needed, that ductility and toughness are lower than the matrix's, that they are expensive, and that the particles make recycling difficult. They are therefore generally reserved for parts where stiffness, wear resistance or low thermal expansion is particularly important and no other material can meet the requirements at a reasonable cost.

faq.q: What is the difference between MMCs and FRP?
faq.a: The matrix differs. FRP uses resin and MMCs use metal, so MMCs have higher heat resistance and conduct heat and electricity well. On the other hand, their density is higher and manufacturing tends to be more expensive.

faq.q: Are MMCs stronger than ordinary aluminum alloys?
faq.a: Their Young's modulus and wear resistance rise greatly and their yield strength is often higher too, but elongation and toughness fall. If strength alone is the goal, a heat-treated aluminum alloy is often sufficient.

faq.q: What is AlSiC?
faq.a: It is an MMC of aluminum with a high SiC content, used for heat-dissipating baseplates and packages of electronic components. It conducts heat well while bringing thermal expansion close to that of semiconductors and ceramic substrates, reducing thermal stress in solder joints.

セラミックス基複合材料.desc: A composite (CMC) with a ceramic matrix such as SiC reinforced by ceramic fibers. A weak interface lets fibers pull out, giving a material that does not fail suddenly.

about.p: Ceramics have excellent heat resistance, but their greatest weakness is brittleness: they fail all at once from a small crack. A CMC is reinforced with ceramic fibers so that it does not fail immediately even when the matrix cracks. Whereas composites with polymer or metal matrices add fibers mainly to raise strength or stiffness, the main aim in CMCs is to change how they fail and so raise toughness. Fibers bridge matrix cracks and absorb energy as they debond at the interface and pull out, so the stress–strain curve continues smoothly instead of breaking off.

about.h: Main types and how they are made
about.p: CMCs include SiC/SiC, with silicon carbide fibers and matrix; C/SiC, reinforced with carbon fibers; C/C, with carbon fibers and matrix; and oxide/oxide, with alumina-based fibers and oxide matrices. SiC fibers were made possible by a method announced in 1975 by Seishi Yajima and coworkers at Tohoku University, in which an organosilicon polymer is spun and fired, and they were industrialized in Japan. C/C withstands very high temperatures but oxidizes easily and is used with surface protection. Matrices are produced by chemical vapor infiltration (CVI) from gases, polymer infiltration and pyrolysis (PIP), and melt infiltration of molten silicon.

When a CMC is loaded, many fine cracks begin to form in the matrix at a certain stress (the proportional limit), and beyond that the fibers carry most of the load. Once cracks form, oxygen and water vapor enter through them to the fibers and interfaces and accelerate degradation, so designs often keep CMCs below the proportional limit. In addition, SiC forms a protective SiO₂ film in high-temperature oxygen, but in environments rich in water vapor, such as combustion gases, the SiO₂ volatilizes and recedes. The surface is therefore covered with an environmental barrier coating (EBC).

SiC/SiC CMCs are about a third of the density of Ni-based superalloys and withstand higher temperatures, so their use in the hot sections of jet engines is advancing. Since the mid-2010s, CMCs have begun to be used in commercial aircraft engines for parts such as the shrouds that surround the turbine. Because less air is needed to cool the parts, fuel efficiency improves. The challenges are that manufacturing is slow and expensive and that internal damage is hard to inspect, calling for design and inspection approaches different from those for metal parts. For brakes, C/SiC discs are used in high-performance cars.

faq.q: How do CMCs differ from ordinary ceramics?
faq.a: Ordinary ceramics fail all at once when a crack forms. In CMCs, fibers bridge cracks and absorb energy as they pull out, so the material does not fail suddenly when cracks form and can tolerate a certain amount of damage.

faq.q: Why is the fiber–matrix interface made weak in CMCs?
faq.a: Because if the interface is too strong, a matrix crack runs straight through the fibers and the material fails like a monolithic ceramic. A coating such as BN makes the interface suitably weak, deflecting the crack and letting the fibers pull out.

faq.q: Up to what temperature can CMCs be used?
faq.a: It depends on the type and environment, but SiC/SiC aims at use around 1200–1300 °C and is said to be usable at higher temperatures than Ni-based superalloys. C/C withstands temperatures above 2000 °C in the absence of oxygen.

比表面積.desc: The surface area per unit mass of a powder or porous body, in m²/g. For spherical particles S = 6/(ρd), increasing in inverse proportion to particle size.

about.p: Specific surface area is the total surface area of 1 g of a powder or porous body, usually given in m²/g. The rate and extent of anything that happens at surfaces, such as catalytic reactions, gas adsorption, dissolution, sintering and the oxidation of powders, is roughly proportional to surface area, so the same substance can behave like a different material when its specific surface area differs. The more surface there is per unit volume, the more excess energy, in the form of surface energy, the material holds, and this is also the driving force for sintering and agglomeration. Much of the way the properties of nanomaterials change with particle size can be explained by this increase in specific surface area.

about.h: Estimating it from size and density
about.p: For dense spheres all of diameter d, dividing the surface area πd² by the mass ρπd³/6 gives S = 6/(ρd). The same formula holds for cubes of edge d. For example, gold (density 19.3 g/cm³) with a diameter of 10 nm gives about 31 m²/g, while amorphous silica (about 2.2 g/cm³) of the same diameter gives about 270 m²/g, so the lower the density, the larger the specific surface area. To compare fineness without the effect of the substance, the surface area per unit volume (m²/cm³) is sometimes used; this is ρS = 6/d and depends only on size. For a diameter of 10 nm it is 600 m²/cm³.

about.h: Why calculated and measured values differ
about.p: The actual specific surface area often does not match the value from the formula. When particles sinter together and join at necks, the surface there is lost, so the measured value is smaller. Conversely, pores and surface roughness make it much larger than the value calculated from the outer shape. In porous bodies such as activated carbon and zeolites, the walls of internal pores account for most of the surface area even when the particles are large, and some activated carbons exceed 1000 m²/g. A large specific surface area is not the same thing as small particles.

Specific surface area is usually measured by the BET method, which uses the amount of a gas such as nitrogen that is adsorbed. There is also the air permeability method, which uses how hard it is to pass air through a bed of powder, as for the fineness of cement; by convention this is given in cm²/g. In processing, powders with a larger specific surface area sinter at lower temperatures and need more solvent or binder to wet them, which changes the viscosity of slurries and their formability. Metal powders with a large specific surface area oxidize easily and can even ignite in air. For catalysts and battery materials, specific surface area for each lot is a basic quality-control item.

faq.q: What is the unit of specific surface area?
faq.a: The most common is m²/g per unit mass. In SI units it is m²/kg, with 1 m²/g = 1000 m²/kg. Values per unit volume in m²/cm³ are also used; multiplying the value per unit mass by the density gives the value per unit volume. For cement and some other materials, cm²/g is used by convention.

faq.q: How is particle size found from specific surface area?
faq.a: Assuming all particles are dense spheres of the same size, d = 6/(ρS). For example, a density of 4.0 g/cm³ and a specific surface area of 60 m²/g give d = 25 nm. Pores make the result too small, and a wide size distribution gives a value different from the mean, so treat it as a guide.

faq.q: How does specific surface area differ from surface area?
faq.a: Surface area is the area of the whole sample and is proportional to the amount of sample. Specific surface area is that divided by the mass (or volume) and expresses the fineness or porosity of the material regardless of amount. Specific surface area is used to compare materials, and total surface area for designing, for example, the amount to load into a reactor.

BET法.desc: A method that physically adsorbs a gas such as nitrogen onto a powder at low temperature, fits the BET equation to the adsorption isotherm, and obtains the specific surface area from the monolayer capacity.

about.p: The BET method is based on a theory by Brunauer, Emmett and Teller that extends Langmuir's monolayer adsorption to handle multilayer adsorption. After the specimen is heated and degassed to remove surface moisture and the like, it is cooled to liquid-nitrogen temperature (about 77 K), and the amount adsorbed is measured while the relative pressure p/p₀ of nitrogen gas is varied. Fitting the resulting adsorption isotherm with the BET equation gives the monolayer capacity vm, the amount needed to cover the surface with exactly one layer. Converting vm to a number of molecules and multiplying by the area occupied by one nitrogen molecule, about 0.162 nm², gives the surface area.

about.h: The range over which the BET equation is fitted
about.p: The BET equation usually holds well over a relative pressure range of about 0.05–0.3. At lower pressures, surface heterogeneity, and at higher pressures, capillary condensation in pores, become significant, causing deviations from linearity. vm and the constant C are found from the slope and intercept of the straight line in the BET plot, and you also check, for example, that C is positive. For highly porous materials the value can change with the choice of fitting range, so it is important to record the measurement conditions when comparing. To measure small surface areas precisely, krypton is sometimes used instead of nitrogen.

about.h: Conversion to particle size and comparison with other methods
about.p: Assuming the particles are dense spheres of equal size, the particle size (BET diameter) can be estimated from the specific surface area S as d = 6/(ρS). The BET method counts all surface that gas molecules can reach, so even when primary particles are gathered with point contacts, nearly all their surface is measured. The BET diameter is therefore close to the primary particle size seen by TEM and usually comes out smaller than sizes from dynamic light scattering or laser diffraction, which measure whole agglomerates in liquid. Conversely, a BET diameter much smaller than the TEM size indicates open pores or roughness on the particle surfaces.

faq.q: Can the BET method measure the surfaces of closed pores?
faq.a: No. The inner surfaces of closed pores that gas molecules cannot enter from outside do not take part in adsorption, so they are not included in the BET specific surface area.

faq.q: How does the BET diameter differ from the crystallite size from the Scherrer equation?
faq.a: The BET diameter is a size derived from the surface area of the particles, while the Scherrer equation gives the size of coherent crystal domains (crystallites). When a single particle consists of several crystallites, the BET diameter is larger than the crystallite size.

faq.q: Why is the specimen heated and degassed before measurement?
faq.a: If moisture or gases adsorbed on the surface remain, the area available for nitrogen adsorption is reduced and the specific surface area is underestimated. The temperature is chosen within a range that does not alter the specimen.

ナノ粒子の融点降下.desc: The lowering of the melting point of nanoparticles below that of the bulk due to the surface energy contribution. The depression is roughly inversely proportional to particle size and becomes pronounced for particles a few nanometers across.

about.p: When particles of metals or semiconductors are made as small as a few nanometers, they melt at temperatures well below the melting point of the bulk. For gold, electron diffraction and other methods have confirmed that particles a few nanometers in diameter melt several hundred K below the bulk melting point (1337 K). The melting point is usually treated as a constant characteristic of a substance, but for nanoparticles it becomes a quantity that depends on size. Wherever nanoparticles are heated in use, as in sintering, the degradation of catalysts or the temperature of joining, applying the bulk value can lead to wrong conclusions.

about.h: Why it is inversely proportional to size
about.p: Whether the solid or the liquid is stable is decided by which has the lower free energy, and in a particle the energy of surfaces and interfaces is added on top. The ratio of surface to volume is inversely proportional to particle size, so the depression of the melting point is also roughly inversely proportional to size and can be written as Tm(d) = Tm∞(1 − β/d), where β is a length set by the substance and conditions. From this relation, a particle whose melting point falls by 5% at 10 nm in diameter would fall by about 10% at 5 nm and by about 2.5% at 20 nm. The depression grows rapidly as size decreases, so it is especially noticeable in the range of a few nanometers.

about.h: How it differs from similar effects
about.p: The mechanism differs from the freezing-point depression of solutions. Freezing-point depression occurs because a dissolved solute lowers the chemical potential of the liquid, and it is set by the solute concentration. Melting point depression in nanoparticles occurs in a pure substance through size alone. Nanoparticles also begin to melt at the surface first (surface melting), so melting often proceeds over a range rather than at a single temperature, and the heat of fusion becomes smaller as well. On the other hand, there are reports of superheating, in which particles embedded with coherent interfaces in a substance of higher melting point do not melt until above the bulk melting point.

about.h: Effects on low-temperature sintering and heat resistance
about.p: Because a lower melting point means atoms move more easily, nanoparticles sinter at temperatures far below the bulk melting point. Techniques that print inks or pastes of silver or copper nanoparticles and heat them at relatively low temperatures to form wiring or joints exploit this. Another advantage is that the wiring or joints formed by sintering are no longer made of small particles, so in service they show heat resistance close to that of the bulk. Conversely, in metal nanoparticle catalysts, particles can move, merge and coarsen even at the operating temperature, reducing surface area and activity, so measures such as strengthening the bond to the support are taken.

faq.q: At what size does melting point depression become noticeable?
faq.a: Because the depression is roughly inversely proportional to size, it grows rapidly as particles get smaller. For particles of tens of nanometers the depression is slight, but it becomes large below about 10 nm, and at a few nanometers there are cases several hundred K below the bulk. The size at which it matters depends on the substance and the application.

faq.q: Is the freezing point of nanoparticles lowered too?
faq.a: Yes. The temperature at which liquid nanoparticles solidify is also lower than in the bulk, for the same reason. In addition, crystal nuclei form less easily inside small particles, so they often stay liquid while strongly supercooled below the melting point, and the difference between the melting and freezing temperatures tends to be large.

faq.q: Won't a joint made from low-melting nanoparticles melt at a low temperature?
faq.a: Once the particles sinter and join into larger bodies, the fraction of surface becomes small, so the melting point approaches the bulk value. A joint made at a low temperature can therefore be used even above the joining temperature. If sintering is incomplete and fine particles or voids remain, however, the microstructure can change in service.

カーボンナノチューブ.desc: A carbon material formed by rolling graphene into a tube about 1 nm to several tens of nanometers in diameter. Depending on the rolling direction (the chiral indices) it can be metallic or semiconducting, and its strength along the axis is extremely high.

about.p: A carbon nanotube (CNT) has the structure of graphene, carbon atoms arranged in hexagons by sp² bonds, rolled seamlessly into a cylinder. There are single-walled CNTs with just one layer and multiwalled CNTs with many concentric layers; the interlayer spacing of multiwalled CNTs is about 0.34 nm, close to that of graphite.
