The rolling direction is given by the pair of integers (n, m) of the chiral vector Ch = na₁ + ma₂, which becomes the circumference; n = m is called armchair, m = 0 zigzag, and the rest chiral. The diameter can be calculated as d = a√(n² + nm + m²)/π (a = 0.246 nm), and most single-walled CNTs are about 1–2 nm.

The electronic states of a single-walled CNT are determined by which of graphene's band states survive, namely only the wave vectors allowed as standing waves around the circumference. When a line of allowed wave vectors passes through the K point, where graphene's conduction and valence bands touch, that is, when n − m is a multiple of 3, the tube is metallic; otherwise it is semiconducting. All armchair tubes are metallic. The band gap of semiconducting CNTs is roughly inversely proportional to the diameter, a few tenths of an eV to about 1 eV at a diameter of about 1 nm. Ordinary synthesis produces a mixture of metallic and semiconducting tubes, so separation or selective growth is a challenge for applications such as transistors.

about.h: Mechanical and thermal properties and uses
about.p: Along their axis, CNTs are joined only by strong sp² bonds, so they have a very high Young's modulus of about 1 TPa and tensile strengths of several tens of GPa, with a low density of about 1.3–2 g/cm³. Their axial thermal conductivity is also high. Exploiting these properties, they are used as small additions to resins and rubbers to raise conductivity and strength, as conductive additives in lithium-ion battery electrodes, in transparent conductive films and as interconnect materials. To bring out the outstanding properties of a single CNT in large materials such as bundles, yarns and composites, however, dispersion, alignment and load transfer between CNTs must be engineered.

faq.q: How are carbon nanotubes made?
faq.a: Besides arc discharge and laser ablation, mass production mainly uses chemical vapor deposition (CVD), in which hydrocarbons are decomposed and CNTs grow from fine catalyst particles of iron, cobalt and the like. The CNT diameter can be controlled to some extent by the size of the catalyst particles.

faq.q: If (n, m) are chosen at random, what fraction is metallic?
faq.a: n − m is a multiple of 3 about one third of the time, so about one third are metallic and about two thirds semiconducting.

faq.q: Can multiwalled carbon nanotubes be semiconducting too?
faq.a: Multiwalled CNTs contain a mixture of metallic and semiconducting layers, and the band gaps of the wide outer layers are small, so overall they usually show metallic conduction.

グラフェン.desc: A single atomic layer of carbon atoms arranged in a honeycomb lattice by sp² bonds. Its band gap is essentially zero, its electron mobility is high, and its theoretical specific surface area counting both sides is about 2630 m²/g.

about.p: Graphene is a single atomic layer of carbon, one layer peeled from graphite. In 2004 Geim and Novoselov isolated single layers by peeling graphite with adhesive tape and measured their electrical properties, and the two received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2010. The carbon atoms form a network of regular hexagons, with a C–C bond length of about 0.142 nm and a lattice constant a = √3 × 0.142 ≈ 0.246 nm. The area per atom is about 0.0262 nm², from which the areal density works out to about 0.76 mg/m² and the specific surface area counting both sides to about 2630 m²/g.

In graphene the conduction and valence bands meet at the K points with the apexes of two cones touching, and near them the electron energy is proportional to the wavenumber. Electrons behave like massless particles, and in clean samples the mobility far exceeds 10000 cm²/(V·s) even at room temperature. Mechanically, experiments pressing a tip into a suspended single layer give an estimated Young's modulus of about 1 TPa, among the stiffest of known materials. A single layer absorbs only about 2.3% of light, so it is also a candidate for transparent conductive films.

about.h: How it differs from graphite and graphene oxide
about.p: Graphite is many layers of graphene stacked, with an interlayer spacing of about 0.335 nm. As the number of layers increases, interlayer interactions change the band structure, and at about 10 layers the properties are said to be essentially those of graphite. Products sold as graphene therefore range from single layers to flakes of a few or tens of layers. Graphene oxide (GO), made by oxidizing and exfoliating graphite, has many oxygen-containing functional groups, is insulating and disperses easily in water; reduced graphene oxide (rGO), made by reducing it, still contains many defects and does not reach the conductivity of single-layer graphene.

about.h: How it is made and used
about.p: High-quality single layers for research can be made by mechanical exfoliation with adhesive tape, but the areas are small and unsuited to mass production. For large-area films, a widely used method grows graphene by CVD, decomposing methane or similar gases on copper foil at high temperature, and transfers it to another substrate using a polymer support film. There is also a method that heats silicon carbide to high temperature to drive off silicon. Powdered multilayer flakes are made by chemical exfoliation of graphite or by sonication in liquids and are used as conductive additives in batteries, as additives to polymers and in heat-dissipating materials. When discussing properties, it is important to check how the material was made and how many layers it has.

faq.q: How thick is graphene?
faq.a: Being one atom thick, its thickness cannot be defined sharply, but the graphite interlayer spacing of about 0.335 nm is commonly taken as the thickness of one layer. When a single layer on a substrate is measured by atomic force microscopy, it often appears thicker than this because of adsorbates on the surface and the gap to the substrate.

faq.q: How does graphene differ from carbon nanotubes?
faq.a: Both are hexagonal networks of sp²-bonded carbon, but graphene is a flat two-dimensional sheet, while a carbon nanotube is that sheet rolled seamlessly into a one-dimensional cylinder. Nanotubes can be metallic or semiconducting depending on how they are rolled (the chiral indices), whereas flat graphene has a band gap of essentially zero.

faq.q: Why is graphene said to be strong?
faq.a: Because in-plane carbon atoms are joined without gaps by strong sp² covalent bonds. Indentation of suspended single layers gives estimates of a Young's modulus of about 1 TPa and a breaking strength above 100 GPa. These are values for small defect-free regions, however; large-area films containing grain boundaries and defects, and composites with polymers, are far weaker.

量子ドット.desc: A semiconductor nanocrystal a few nanometers across that confines electrons and holes in three dimensions. The confinement energy is roughly inversely proportional to the square of the size, so the emission wavelength can be tuned by size.

about.h: Why the color changes with size
about.p: When a semiconductor crystal is made a few nanometers across, comparable to or smaller than the extent of an electron–hole pair (an exciton), the electron and hole behave as waves confined in a small box and their energies take discrete values. Even the lowest level is raised by the confinement energy, so the effective band gap becomes larger than in the bulk and smaller particles emit shorter wavelengths of light. Tuning the emission color by changing only the size of the same material is the defining feature, and the 2023 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to three researchers for discovering this effect and establishing methods of synthesis.

The lowest energy of a particle confined in a spherical box of radius R is ħ²π²/(2m*R²), where m* is the effective mass, so it is inversely proportional to the square of the radius and larger for a smaller effective mass. Adding the contributions of both electron and hole and subtracting their Coulomb attraction gives the estimate known as the Brus equation. Confinement acts strongly when the radius is comparable to or smaller than the exciton Bohr radius (about 5 to 6 nm for CdSe). Below a few nanometers, however, the bands depart from parabolic shape, so the relation between actual size and gap is usually read from a calibration curve built from measurements.

about.h: What is and is not called a quantum dot
about.p: Quantum dots include colloidal quantum dots, synthesized in solution with surfaces covered by organic molecules (ligands), and self-assembled quantum dots, which use island structures that form during crystal growth. The latter use Stranski–Krastanov growth, in which a film on a substrate with a different lattice constant turns into islands, and are used in systems such as InAs/GaAs for semiconductor lasers and single-photon sources. On the other hand, although gold and silver particles are also nanometers in size, their colors come from collective oscillations of surface electrons (plasmons), a phenomenon separate from the confinement effect of quantum dots.

Many of a quantum dot's atoms are at the surface, so when surface defects trap electrons or holes, energy is lost without emitting light. The CdSe core is therefore wrapped in a shell of a wider-gap material such as ZnS, a core–shell structure that raises emission efficiency and stability. In displays, quantum dots are used in color-conversion layers that turn the light of blue LEDs into red and green, and their narrow emission widens the range of reproducible colors. Because cadmium is a restricted substance, replacement by quantum dots with InP cores is advancing, and applications as fluorescent labels in biology and in solar cells are also being studied.

faq.q: What is the difference between quantum dots and nanoparticles?
faq.a: Nanoparticle is a broad term for any particle about 1 to 100 nm in size. Quantum dots are those, mainly semiconductor nanocrystals, whose energy levels and band gap change with size through the confinement of electrons and holes. Even the same substance is not called a quantum dot if it is too large for confinement to act.

faq.q: What decides the emission color of a quantum dot?
faq.a: Mainly the material and the particle size. The material sets the approximate position of the bulk band gap, and the smaller the particle, the more confinement widens the gap and shifts emission toward blue. The more uniform the sizes, the narrower the emission, and the type of shell and the surface state also affect small wavelength shifts and emission efficiency.

faq.q: Do quantum dots degrade?
faq.a: When light, heat, oxygen or moisture oxidize the surface or strip off ligands, defects increase and emission efficiency falls. Besides wrapping them in shells, quantum dots are therefore sealed in polymers or glass, or sandwiched between films that block oxygen and water. Ensuring stability is said to be more difficult for cadmium-free materials.

ボトムアップ法.desc: Methods of making nanomaterials by assembling atoms and molecules through nucleation and growth, such as liquid-phase reduction and thermal decomposition, the sol-gel method and CVD. The counterpart of top-down methods, which break down larger materials.

about.p: Bottom-up synthesis is the general term for methods that build nanomaterials by gathering atoms, ions and molecules. They include reducing metal ions in solution, thermal decomposition of organometallic precursors, the sol-gel method that hydrolyzes and condenses metal alkoxides, condensation of atoms from the vapor, CVD that decomposes source gases on a substrate, and ALD that deposits one atomic layer at a time. Compared with top-down methods, which cut or crush large materials, they produce less disorder in the arrangement of atoms, and their strength is that particles of uniform size and shape can be designed through chemical conditions.

The key to uniform particle size is to separate nucleation and growth in time. When the monomer concentration in solution exceeds the critical supersaturation, nuclei form all at once; as the concentration falls, nucleation stops and only the existing nuclei grow (the LaMer model). The hot-injection method reported in 1993 creates this situation by rapidly injecting precursors into a hot solvent and spread as a way of obtaining semiconductor nanocrystals of uniform size. In the growth stage, the final size is adjusted through temperature, time and precursor concentration, and the reaction is stopped by cooling at the right moment.

In liquid-phase synthesis, molecules with long chains such as oleic acid and oleylamine, as well as citric acid and polymers, adsorb on particle surfaces. These ligands (capping agents) prevent particles from agglomerating, and because they adsorb strongly on particular crystal faces and slow the growth of those faces, they allow cubes, rods, plates and other shapes to be made selectively. The synthesis of gold nanorods, in which small seed crystals are grown in one direction with the help of a surfactant, is an example. On the other hand, when the particles are used as catalysts or electronic materials, the surface ligands hinder reactions or the flow of current, so a step is needed to remove them by heat treatment or ligand exchange.

The challenges of bottom-up methods are mass production and control of placement. Liquid-phase synthesis yields only small amounts per reaction and can require large volumes of organic solvent and purification steps. Placing the resulting particles at defined positions on a substrate is also difficult. Top-down methods such as lithography can define position and shape precisely, but making dimensions of a few nanometers or surfaces smooth at the atomic level is hard. Methods combining the two are therefore also widely used, such as self-assembling molecules along patterns drawn by lithography, or printing nanoparticle inks to form wiring.

faq.q: What is the difference between bottom-up and top-down methods?
faq.a: Bottom-up methods build materials from atoms and molecules by nucleation and growth, while top-down methods make large materials smaller by grinding, etching or machining. The former easily produce particles of uniform size and shape with few defects, while the latter are strong in mass production and control of position.

faq.q: Is the sol-gel method a bottom-up method?
faq.a: Yes. It hydrolyzes and condenses metal alkoxides or similar compounds to make a dispersion of particles (a sol) from molecules and then a connected network (a gel), so it is a typical bottom-up method. In the method that makes silica spheres with ammonia as the catalyst, particles of very uniform size can be obtained under suitable conditions.

faq.q: How can particle sizes be made uniform?
faq.a: The basic approach is to concentrate nucleation in a short time and then let only growth proceed under conditions where no new nuclei form. Methods include rapidly injecting precursors into a hot solvent and making seed crystals first and then growing them. After growth, the distribution can be narrowed further by size-selective precipitation, in which a poor solvent is added to precipitate particles by size.

ゼータ電位.desc: The potential at the slipping plane outside the layer that moves with a particle in a liquid. The larger its absolute value, the stronger the electrostatic repulsion between particles and the more stable the dispersion. It is nearly zero at the isoelectric point.

about.h: The electrical double layer and the slipping plane
about.p: The surface of a particle in a liquid becomes charged through dissociation of surface groups or adsorption of ions, and ions of opposite sign gather around it to form an electrical double layer. Ions close to the surface are held strongly and move with the particle, while those farther out are spread by thermal motion. When the particle moves, the boundary between the layer moving with it and the stationary liquid is called the slipping plane, and the potential there is the zeta potential. The potential of the surface itself cannot be measured directly, but the zeta potential can be found from the motion of particles, so it is used as a measure of the electrostatic repulsion particles feel as they approach each other.

The zeta potential is found from how fast particles move in an applied electric field (the electrophoretic mobility µ). When the double layer is much thinner than the particle, the Smoluchowski equation ζ = ηµ/ε is used, where η is the viscosity of the liquid and ε its permittivity. In water at 25°C, a mobility of 1 µm·cm/(V·s) corresponds to about 12.8 mV. The thickness of the double layer is indicated by the Debye length, which in aqueous solutions of a 1:1 salt at 25°C is about 9.6 nm at 1 mmol/L and about 0.96 nm at 100 mmol/L. Adding salt shrinks the double layer and shortens the range of the repulsion.

Unlike the surface potential, the zeta potential is the value at the slipping plane, so its magnitude is smaller than that of the surface potential. Also, the isoelectric point (the pH at which the zeta potential is zero) and the point of zero charge (where the surface charge is zero) coincide when no ions adsorb specifically, but they differ when such adsorption occurs. The rule of thumb that dispersions are stable when the magnitude exceeds 30 mV is widely used, but it depends on salt concentration and particle size. Steric repulsion from adsorbed polymers does not show up in the zeta potential, so a dispersion can be stable even when the magnitude is small.

Measurement commonly derives the mobility from the Doppler shift of scattered laser light. Because the result depends strongly on pH and salt concentration, these must always be recorded. The isoelectric point differs with the substance and its surface state; typically it is low for silica, at about 2 to 3, and high for alumina, at around 9. The zeta potential is used to design against agglomeration by choosing pH and dispersants for slurries for slip casting and tape casting of ceramics, CMP polishing slurries for semiconductors, paints and pharmaceutical dispersions. Conversely, in water treatment, coagulants bring the zeta potential close to zero so that particles agglomerate on purpose and settle.

faq.q: What is the unit of zeta potential?
faq.a: As a potential, its unit is the volt, usually expressed in mV. Its sign corresponds to the sign of the particle's surface charge; for oxides it is positive when the pH is below the isoelectric point and negative above it. Reports should ideally state the pH, salt concentration, temperature and conversion equation used.

faq.q: How is zeta potential related to the isoelectric point?
faq.a: Measuring the zeta potential while changing the pH, the pH at which it becomes zero is the isoelectric point. Near the isoelectric point there is almost no electrostatic repulsion, so particles agglomerate most easily. To disperse particles, choose a pH far from the isoelectric point; to agglomerate them, set it near the isoelectric point.

faq.q: Is a dispersion always stable if the zeta potential is large?
faq.a: Not always. At high salt concentration the double layer shrinks and the range of repulsion becomes short, so particles can agglomerate even at the same zeta potential. Large, heavy particles also settle even when dispersed. Stability is confirmed by measuring settling and changes in particle size over time in addition to the zeta potential.

材料選択図(アシュビーの図).desc: A chart that plots two properties, such as Young's modulus and density, on log–log axes and shows the range of each material family. Lines of constant performance index are straight, and the chart is used to compare candidates.

about.p: A materials selection chart plots two properties on the vertical and horizontal axes, such as Young's modulus versus density, strength versus density or fracture toughness versus strength, and shows the ranges of values for many materials. Because the values span many orders of magnitude, both axes are logarithmic. Members of the same material family cluster together; on the modulus–density chart, ceramics and metals occupy the upper right, polymers and woods the middle, and foams the lower left. Individual materials are shown as ellipses or bubbles covering the range of variation with composition and processing, and material families as larger envelopes around them.

Writing the condition for a constant performance index in logarithms gives a straight line. For example, E/ρ = C gives log E = log ρ + log C, a line of slope 1; √E/ρ = C gives a line of slope 2; and ∛E/ρ = C a line of slope 3. Materials on a line parallel to it perform equally in that application, and performance increases as the line is shifted toward the upper left. Drawing such a line on the chart and moving it step by step narrows the field to the materials remaining above the line as promising candidates. Because the slope changes with the loading mode, the winning materials on the same chart change with the application.

about.h: Its role in the selection procedure
about.p: In Ashby's method, the design requirements are first organized into function, constraints, objective and free variables, and candidates are screened by constraints such as service temperature and corrosion resistance. Next, the surviving candidates are ranked by the performance index derived from the objective, and finally the top candidates are researched for ease of fabrication into the actual shape, joining, price fluctuations, service history and so on before deciding. The selection chart is a tool for doing this screening and ranking visually. A major advantage of using it is that candidates can be surveyed across material families without fixing on a particular material from the start.

faq.q: Why are log–log axes used?
faq.a: Because Young's modulus spans many orders of magnitude, from about 0.001 GPa for foams to about 1000 GPa for diamond. Also, power-law performance indices appear as straight lines, which makes comparison simple.

faq.q: Can a material be chosen from the chart values alone?
faq.a: No. The chart is a tool for narrowing down candidates, and its values are typical ranges for material families. The final decision is made by researching data for specific alloys and grades, processing methods, cost and service history.

faq.q: Are there charts that use strength?
faq.a: Yes. On strength–density charts, guidelines for σf/ρ or ∛(σf²)/ρ are drawn, and on fracture toughness–strength charts, lines of K_IC/σy, to look for light, strong materials or materials resistant to fracture.

材料選択の性能指数.desc: The combination of material properties to be maximized in materials selection: E/ρ for a stiffness-limited tie, √E/ρ for a beam, ∛E/ρ for a plate, and σf/ρ for a strength-limited tie.

about.p: A performance index emerges when the free variables (such as section dimensions) are eliminated, using the constraints (specified stiffness or strength), from the equation expressing the objective (such as mass). For a tie of specified stiffness, the extension condition fixes the cross-sectional area as A ∝ 1/E, and the mass is m = ρAL ∝ ρ/E. So the larger E/ρ, the lighter the tie can be made. In this way, performance separates into the product of three parts, the functional requirements such as load and length, a factor for the shape of the cross section, and the material properties, and the material part alone is the performance index. Even after the shape and dimensions are optimized, the ranking of materials is determined by this index.

For a beam of square section whose dimensions can be varied freely, bending stiffness is proportional to the fourth power of the dimension, so mass is proportional to ρ/√E and the performance index is √E/ρ. For a plate of fixed width whose thickness alone can be varied, stiffness is proportional to the cube of the thickness, giving ∛E/ρ. When strength is the constraint, the indices become σf/ρ for a tie, ∛(σf²)/ρ for a beam and √σf/ρ for a plate. The deeper the root in the index, the relatively greater the influence of density, so low-density materials such as wood, magnesium alloys, CFRP and foams are favored for beams and plates in bending.

about.h: Extension to cost and environmental impact
about.p: When the objective is material cost instead of mass, density multiplied by the price per kg Cm, ρCm, is used, and for a stiffness-limited tie, E/(ρCm) is maximized. When the objective is the energy or CO₂ emissions of production, the per-kg value is multiplied in the same way. In thermal design, indices combining thermal conductivity and thermal diffusivity are used. Note, however, that performance indices are derived on assumptions such as keeping the shape geometrically similar, so they may not be directly comparable when the cross-sectional shape differs greatly between materials or when there is a lower limit on dimensions.

faq.q: If the specific stiffness E/ρ is the same, is the performance as a beam also the same?
faq.a: No. The performance index for a beam is √E/ρ, so even with the same E/ρ, the lower-density material is better as a beam. Steel and aluminum alloys have almost the same E/ρ, but as beams the aluminum alloy is lighter.

faq.q: Does a performance index have units?
faq.a: Yes. For example, the unit of √E/ρ is something like √GPa/(Mg/m³). Indices with the same units can be compared in magnitude, but the value of an index itself has no particular physical meaning.

faq.q: What if there are two or more constraints?
faq.a: Calculate the required dimensions and mass for each constraint, and for each material compare using the larger mass (the more restrictive constraint). Which constraint is active varies from material to material.

比剛性.desc: Young's modulus divided by density, E/ρ, also called specific modulus. Steel, aluminum alloys and titanium alloys are all roughly the same, at about 25 GPa/(g/cm³).

about.p: Specific stiffness E/ρ expresses how resistant to deformation a component of a given mass can be made. It is used to compare materials for components that must be both light and stiff, such as in aircraft, cars, robot arms and parts that rotate at high speed. It is commonly given in GPa/(g/cm³), which corresponds to 10⁶ m²/s². √(E/ρ) is the speed of longitudinal waves along a thin bar, about 5200 m/s in steel. The natural frequency of components of the same shape is also proportional to √(E/ρ), so materials of high specific stiffness are preferred for parts that must avoid vibration and for loudspeaker diaphragms.

Steel (E = 210 GPa, ρ = 7.8 g/cm³) gives about 27, aluminum alloys (70 GPa, 2.7 g/cm³) about 26, titanium alloys (110 GPa, 4.5 g/cm³) about 24 and magnesium alloys (45 GPa, 1.74 g/cm³) about 26, so the specific stiffness of the main structural metals is almost the same. Adding alloying elements changes Young's modulus and density only slightly, and Al-Li alloys and beryllium (about 160) are exceptions. The ceramic alumina (about 380 GPa, 3.95 g/cm³) gives about 96, and unidirectional CFRP reaches several times the value of metals along the fibers.

The material with the largest specific stiffness E/ρ does not always give the lightest component. E/ρ itself is the performance index only when the cross-sectional area alone can change, as for a bar (tie) of specified tensile stiffness. For beams whose cross-section size can change the index is √E/ρ, and for plates whose thickness alone can change it is ∛E/ρ, which favor materials of lower density. So even though steel and aluminum alloys have almost the same specific stiffness, aluminum alloys give lighter beams and plates. Specific stiffness is also a separate quantity from specific strength σ/ρ, and one must first decide whether stiffness or strength is required.

Each 1 mass% of lithium added to aluminum is said to lower the density by about 3% and raise Young's modulus by about 6%, and Al-Li alloys are used for aircraft skins and structural members. Other approaches combine stiff reinforcements, as in metal matrix composites reinforced with particles such as silicon carbide and in CFRP reinforced with carbon fibers. Because the specific stiffness of CFRP changes greatly with fiber direction, the orientation of the plies is designed to match the direction of loading. In terms of shape, making components as hollow tubes or honeycomb sandwich structures, which move material away from the neutral axis, also raises stiffness for the same mass.

faq.q: What is the difference between specific stiffness and specific strength?
faq.a: Specific stiffness is Young's modulus divided by density, E/ρ, and expresses resistance to deformation per unit of lightness. Specific strength is a strength (tensile or yield) divided by density, σ/ρ, and expresses resistance to failure or yielding per unit of lightness. Compare specific stiffness when deflection or vibration is the issue, and specific strength when failure is.

faq.q: What is the unit of specific stiffness?
faq.a: Because it is Young's modulus divided by density, it is usually given in GPa/(g/cm³) or MPa/(kg/m³). In SI units it is m²/s², and 1 GPa/(g/cm³) is 10⁶ m²/s². Its square root has units of speed and corresponds to the speed of longitudinal waves along a bar.

faq.q: Are specific modulus and specific stiffness the same thing?
faq.a: When they refer to E/ρ as a material property, they are used with the same meaning. In structural mechanics, however, stiffness can mean the ratio of load to deformation including the shape of the component (in N/m, for example), and specific stiffness is sometimes used for a component's stiffness divided by its mass. It is safest to check the context.

破壊前降伏.desc: The condition in which, even with a crack present, the whole component yields first and sudden brittle fracture does not occur. The allowable crack size is proportional to (K_IC/σy)², so K_IC/σy serves as the performance index.

about.p: When a cracked component is loaded, one of two things happens first: the stress intensity factor K at the crack tip reaches the fracture toughness K_IC and the component fails suddenly, or the stress in the whole component reaches the yield stress σy and it deforms plastically. Yield before fracture is the design approach of ensuring that the latter always comes first. A component that yields deforms visibly, so the abnormality can be noticed before sudden brittle fracture. Solving K = Yσ√(πa) for the crack length at which K = K_IC when σ = σy gives a = (1/π)(K_IC/(Yσy))², and for cracks smaller than this, yielding comes first.

about.h: Raising strength shrinks the allowable crack
about.p: Because the critical crack length is proportional to (K_IC/σy)², raising the yield stress while K_IC stays the same shrinks the allowable crack with the square. For example, a material with K_IC = 40 MPa·√m and σy = 400 MPa (Y = 1) has a limit of about 3.2 mm, but raising σy to 600 MPa at the same K_IC gives about 1.4 mm. In practice, raising strength by heat treatment and similar means often lowers toughness as well, so the allowable crack becomes smaller still. Stronger materials are not necessarily safer, and materials must be chosen by comparison with the crack sizes that inspection can find.

The ratio K_IC/σy appears elsewhere in fracture mechanics too. The size of the plastic zone at a crack tip is proportional to (K/σy)², and in plane stress it is about (1/2π)(K/σy)². To obtain a valid plane-strain K_IC in a fracture toughness test, the specimen thickness and crack length must be at least 2.5(K_IC/σy)² (ASTM E399). For K_IC = 40 MPa·√m and σy = 400 MPa this is 25 mm. A material with a large K_IC/σy can deform plastically to a large extent at a crack tip and, in components of ordinary thickness, is unlikely to fail in a brittle manner.

The yield-before-fracture approach is often used in choosing materials for pressure vessels and piping. When yield before fracture is the objective, the performance index is K_IC/σy, and on Ashby charts K_IC and σy are plotted on logarithmic axes and compared using lines of slope 1. Under the leak-before-break approach, which ensures that even when a crack penetrates the wall and the contents leak out, sudden fracture does not yet occur, the index becomes K_IC²/σy. For steels, whose K_IC drops as temperature falls, it is important in both cases to judge using values at the lowest service temperature.

faq.q: What is the difference between yield before fracture and leak before break?
faq.a: Yield before fracture is the approach of making the whole component yield before it fails from a crack, with the performance index K_IC/σy. Leak before break ensures that even when a crack penetrates the wall and a leak occurs, a crack of that length still does not cause sudden fracture; for pressure vessels the index is K_IC²/σy.

faq.q: Does a component never fail once it yields?
faq.a: Yielding first means that sudden brittle fracture is avoided, not that failure cannot occur. If the load increases further, ductile fracture occurs after large deformation. Also, if a crack grows by fatigue or stress corrosion cracking, it can exceed the critical length so that the condition no longer holds.

faq.q: What is the geometry factor Y in the critical crack length formula?
faq.a: It is a dimensionless factor expressing how the stress intensity factor depends on the shape and position of the crack and the dimensions of the component, written as K = Yσ√(πa). For a central through crack in an infinitely wide plate Y = 1, and it departs from 1 for surface cracks or plates of limited width. The larger Y is, the smaller the critical crack length.

ライフサイクルアセスメント.desc: A method (LCA) for quantitatively evaluating energy consumption and environmental impact at each stage: material production, product manufacture, use, and disposal or recycling.

about.p: Life cycle assessment (LCA) is a method that evaluates environmental impact by counting the energy and resources used and the greenhouse gases and pollutants emitted over a product's whole life: extraction of raw materials and production of materials, manufacture of the product, transport, use, and disposal or recycling. Judging something to be good for the environment from one stage alone can mean the burden has merely moved to another stage, so the aim is to compare across the whole life. In materials selection, it is used for judgments such as whether a material that takes a lot of energy to produce pays off overall by saving energy in the use stage.

The LCA procedure is defined in the international standards ISO 14040 and ISO 14044 and consists of four phases. First comes goal and scope definition, which sets the unit for counting the function of what is compared (the functional unit) and how far the count extends (the system boundary). Next, inventory analysis totals the energy and materials going into and out of each process. Impact assessment groups these into impact categories such as climate change, acidification and eutrophication; greenhouse gases, for example, are expressed in kg-CO₂eq converted to CO₂. Finally, interpretation checks the reliability and sensitivity of the results and presents conclusions and limitations.

LCA results change greatly with the choice of functional unit and system boundary. To compare drink containers, for example, the comparison must be per function, delivering the same amount of drink, rather than per container. Counting up to material production (cradle to gate) and including disposal (cradle to grave) can even reverse the conclusion. How the burden of recycled material is allocated among products and assumptions about how electricity is generated also affect the results. The carbon footprint, which counts only greenhouse gases, is one impact category taken out of an LCA.

In the early stages of design, before a detailed LCA, a common approach is to roughly estimate the burden of each stage from data on production energy or CO₂ emissions per 1 kg of material together with the mass of each part. Once it is known which stage dominates, efforts can be concentrated on reducing it. For products dominated by the use stage, lightweighting and better efficiency are effective; for products dominated by material production, materials with low production energy and the use of recycled material are effective. LCA results are also used in environmental product declarations (EPDs), which publish a product's environmental performance after third-party verification.

faq.q: What is the functional unit in LCA?
faq.a: It is a reference that defines the function of the products being compared as a quantity. It is set, for example, as delivering 1000 L of drink to consumers or covering 1 m² of floor for 50 years, and all burdens are counted per this unit. Without a common functional unit, products of different life or performance cannot be compared correctly.

faq.q: What is the difference between LCA and a carbon footprint?
faq.a: LCA evaluates several impact categories together, including climate change, acidification, eutrophication and resource depletion. A carbon footprint takes out only greenhouse gas emissions and expresses them converted to CO₂. A product with low greenhouse gas emissions can still have large other impacts.

faq.q: How does using recycled material change LCA results?
faq.a: In general it lowers the burden, because the production energy is smaller than making new material. However, the burdens of collection, sorting and transport must also be counted, and the result depends on whether the benefit of recycling is credited to the side using the material or the side whose material is recovered (allocation). Comparisons should use the same allocation method.

トランプエレメント.desc: Elements such as copper and tin that get mixed into steel scrap, are hard to remove by refining, and accumulate in steel with each recycling. They cause quality problems such as surface cracking during hot working.

about.p: When steel scrap is melted in an electric arc furnace, elements mixed in with the scrap dissolve along with it. In refining, oxygen is blown in to remove elements more easily oxidized than iron, such as silicon, manganese, phosphorus and carbon, as oxides or gases, but elements less easily oxidized than iron, such as copper, tin, nickel and molybdenum, remain in the steel. Elements that cannot be removed by refining in this way and end up in the steel unintentionally are called tramp elements. The problem is that, because they cannot be removed, they build up little by little each time steel is made from scrap and that steel becomes scrap again.

The best-known harm is surface cracking during hot working caused by copper. When steel is heated before rolling, iron at the surface oxidizes preferentially to form scale, and copper, which oxidizes less easily, becomes concentrated at the interface with the scale. Above the melting point of copper (about 1085°C), the concentrated copper becomes liquid and penetrates the grain boundaries, and the surface cracks during rolling. Tin reduces how much copper dissolves in iron and also lowers the temperature at which liquid forms, so even small amounts make this cracking worse. Nickel, conversely, suppresses the cracking, and some steels contain copper and nickel added together.

Besides hot shortness, copper and tin lower the ductility of steel and make demanding forming such as deep drawing difficult. Tin, antimony, arsenic and similar elements tend to segregate to grain boundaries and also cause temper embrittlement. Products with strict quality requirements, such as automotive sheet steel, therefore tolerate only small amounts, and steel from scrap tends to go to products with relatively relaxed requirements, such as reinforcing bars for construction. This lowering of the grade of use with each round of recycling is called downcycling. On the other hand, copper is also a useful element when added on purpose, as in weathering steels.

about.h: Countermeasures and examples in other metals
about.p: Countermeasures fall into three kinds: not mixing them in, removing them and diluting them. Copper-rich parts such as motors and wiring harnesses from end-of-life vehicles are removed at the dismantling stage, and copper is removed after shredding by magnetic separation and hand sorting. What remains is diluted by adding pig iron or direct reduced iron low in impurities. Methods for removing copper in refining have been studied, but none is yet in wide practical use. In aluminum recycling too, iron and silicon are similarly hard to remove and are a problem as elements that build up with each remelting, so collecting scrap sorted by alloy type is important.

faq.q: Which elements are tramp elements?
faq.a: In steel, copper, tin, nickel, molybdenum and others are listed, and copper and tin are particular problems. What they have in common is that in refining by blowing oxygen they are not oxidized before iron and cannot be moved into the slag. Which elements are controlled, and to what level, depends on the type of steel and its use.

faq.q: Why can they not be removed by refining?
faq.a: Steel refining removes impurities by oxidizing them with oxygen into slag or gas, so elements less easily oxidized than iron cannot be removed without oxidizing the iron first. Evaporating them in vacuum is also very slow when the copper concentration in the steel is low and is considered hard to put into practice. Keeping them out at the scrap stage is therefore the basic approach.

faq.q: Is electric arc furnace steel inferior to blast furnace steel?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Steel made from iron ore by blast furnace and converter contains almost no copper or tin, but electric arc furnace steel can also be of high quality if the scrap is selected and diluted with reduced iron or similar. Because electric arc furnaces emit less CO₂ in production, the challenge is to widen the range where they can be used while controlling tramp elements.

パレート最適.desc: A state in which improving any one of several objectives necessarily worsens another. For competing objectives, candidates are chosen from the Pareto front using an exchange constant.

about.p: In materials selection with two or more objectives, a candidate is said to dominate another if it is equal or better in every objective and strictly better in at least one. Candidates that are not dominated by any other are Pareto-optimal, named after the Italian economist Pareto. When mass and cost are plotted on the horizontal and vertical axes, the Pareto-optimal candidates line up along the lower-left edge, called the Pareto front (trade-off curve). Dominated candidates lying to the upper right of the front are never chosen whatever the weighting, so they can be removed at the start.

about.h: Narrowing to one with an exchange constant
about.p: To choose one candidate on the front, a rate of exchange between objectives is set. For mass m and cost C, the candidate minimizing the penalty function Z = αm + C is chosen, where α is the amount one is willing to pay to save 1 kg of mass (the exchange constant). For example, among three candidates, A (10 kg, 2000 yen), B (6 kg, 4000 yen) and C (4 kg, 20000 yen), A is the minimum for α = 300 yen/kg, B for 2000 yen/kg and C for 10000 yen/kg. α is set by the nature of the product and is far larger for aircraft and spacecraft, where lightness translates directly into fuel savings, than for cars.

Pareto-optimal does not mean best but rather that neither objective can be improved further without the other getting worse, and usually there is more than one candidate. Where on the front to choose is decided only by adding a value judgment such as an exchange constant. Adding objectives in different units without normalizing them lets the result be driven by the size of the numbers. Selection by a weighted sum also has the property that when the front has a dented shape, candidates in the dent are never chosen however the weights are changed. Incidentally, the Pareto principle, that the top 20% account for 80% of the whole, is a different concept named after the same person.

On materials selection charts, two performance indices are plotted on logarithmic axes, candidate materials are plotted and the Pareto front is drawn. On logarithmic charts, lines of constant Z = αm + C are curves rather than straight lines, so reading the points where they touch the front for several values of α shows how the choice changes with the exchange constant. In materials informatics, which searches alloy compositions and process conditions, competing objectives such as strength and ductility or performance and cost are often handled together, and methods are used that find the Pareto front by multi-objective optimization such as genetic algorithms and choose the candidates to test experimentally from it.

faq.q: What is a Pareto front?
faq.a: It is the line (a surface for three or more objectives) joining the Pareto-optimal candidates, those not dominated by any other. When both objectives are to be minimized, it is the lower-left edge of the chart. Along the front, improving one objective always worsens the other.

faq.q: How is the exchange constant decided?
faq.a: It is set by converting the value gained from saving 1 kg of mass into money, from fuel savings, extra payload and the like. It varies greatly with the type of product, being larger for aircraft than for ordinary cars and larger for spacecraft than for aircraft. If its value is uncertain, check whether the chosen candidate changes as α is varied.

faq.q: Is it related to the Pareto principle (the 80/20 rule)?
faq.a: The name comes from the same Pareto, but the content is different. The Pareto principle is a rule of thumb that a small number of factors account for most of the whole, as in the distribution of income. Pareto optimality is an optimization concept referring to a state in which one objective cannot be improved without worsening another.

磁区.desc: A small region inside a ferromagnet or ferrimagnet in which the magnetization points in one direction. The material splits into many domains to lower the magnetostatic energy of its surface poles.

about.h: Why a material splits into domains
about.p: Inside a ferromagnet, the exchange interaction tends to align the magnetic moments of neighboring atoms parallel. If the whole crystal is magnetized in one direction, however, large magnetic poles appear on its surface, creating fields in the surrounding space and inside, with a large magnetostatic energy. Splitting into domains with different directions lets the poles cancel and lowers this energy greatly. Triangular closure domains can also form near the surface so that the flux closes on itself. This is why iron, though ferromagnetic, does not act as a magnet when no external field has been applied.

The boundary between domains is called a domain wall, and within it the magnetic moments turn gradually over a width of tens to hundreds of atoms. Turning abruptly raises the exchange energy, while turning slowly increases the number of moments tilted away from the easy axis and raises the anisotropy energy, so the wall thickness is set by the balance between the two and is proportional to √(A/K), where A is the exchange stiffness and K the anisotropy constant. A wall has an energy per unit area, so dividing into too many domains does not pay. The actual domain size is set by the balance between the decrease in magnetostatic energy and the increase in wall energy.

When a field is applied to a demagnetized ferromagnet, the domains oriented closest to the field first grow by domain-wall motion. As the field is increased further, the magnetization inside the domains rotates from the easy axis toward the field, approaching the saturation magnetization. Domain walls get caught at grain boundaries, precipitates and sites of internal stress, so how easily the walls move governs the coercivity and permeability. In soft magnetic materials, impurities and strain are reduced so the walls move easily; in permanent magnets, microstructures are created in which reversed domains are hard to nucleate or grow.

Domains can be observed by the Bitter method, in which a liquid of fine magnetic particles is applied to the surface and the particles gathering at the walls are viewed; by magneto-optical Kerr effect microscopy, which uses the rotation of polarized light; and by magnetic force microscopy (MFM), which detects the stray field from the surface with a magnetic tip. In electron microscopes, Lorentz microscopy and electron holography reveal the distribution of magnetization inside a specimen. In grain-oriented electrical steel, a technique is used in which fine grooves or strain are introduced on the surface by laser to refine the domains and lower the loss due to eddy currents.

faq.q: Are magnetic domains the same as grains?
faq.a: No. A grain is a region in which the atoms are arranged with the same orientation, and a domain is a region in which the magnetization points in the same direction. One grain can contain many domains, and a small particle can be a single domain as a whole (single-domain). Domain walls, the boundaries between domains, move under an applied field independently of grain boundaries.

faq.q: What happens to the domains when a magnet is heated?
faq.a: As the temperature rises the spontaneous magnetization decreases, and above the Curie temperature the spontaneous magnetization itself disappears and the material becomes paramagnetic, so the domains vanish as well. Cooling below the Curie temperature forms domains again, but without an external field they split into many domains with unaligned directions, so the magnet's magnetization does not return.

faq.q: What is a single-domain particle?
faq.a: In particles smaller than a certain size (the critical size), the energy needed to create a domain wall exceeds the reduction in magnetostatic energy, so the whole particle becomes a single domain. This is a single-domain particle. Reversing its magnetization requires rotating the whole magnetization, so the coercivity is large. Making it smaller still, however, leads to superparamagnetism, in which the magnetization reverses thermally.

磁壁.desc: The transition layer at the boundary between neighboring domains, across which the direction of the magnetic moments rotates gradually. Its thickness is set by the balance between exchange and anisotropy energies.

about.h: What happens inside a domain wall
about.p: A domain wall is the transition layer between two domains of different orientation, across which the magnetic moments rotate gradually to change direction. Besides 180° walls, with opposite magnetization on the two sides, 90° walls also form in cubic crystals such as iron, whose easy axes lie along three mutually perpendicular directions. Inside thick specimens the walls are Bloch walls, in which the moments rotate within the plane of the wall, so no magnetic poles appear on the wall. In magnetic thin films thinner than the wall width, Néel walls, in which the moments rotate within the plane of the film, have the lower energy.

For a 180° wall in a material with uniaxial anisotropy, the thickness can be estimated as about δ = π√(A/K) and the energy per unit area as γ = 4√(AK), using the exchange stiffness A and anisotropy constant K. Applying these to iron (A ≈ 2×10⁻¹¹ J/m, K ≈ 4.8×10⁴ J/m³) gives δ of about 64 nm and γ of about 4 mJ/m². In Nd₂Fe₁₄B, whose anisotropy is extremely large (A ≈ 8×10⁻¹² J/m, K ≈ 4.9×10⁶ J/m³), δ is as thin as about 4 nm. The thinner the wall, the more easily it is caught even by small inhomogeneities.

Much of the change in magnetization under an applied field occurs by domain-wall motion. Impurities, precipitates, strain and the like in a material make the wall energy vary from place to place, and walls get caught at places of low energy (pinning). A caught wall breaks free suddenly and jumps as the field increases, so the magnetization changes in fine steps that can be heard as noise when picked up by a coil. This is the Barkhausen effect. Permanent magnets are considered in two types: the pinning type, such as Sm₂Co₁₇-based magnets, whose coercivity comes from pinning of walls, and the nucleation type, such as Nd-Fe-B and SmCo₅ magnets, which suppress the formation of reversed domains.

Because how easily walls move reflects the internal state of a material, measuring Barkhausen noise in steels is used to examine residual stress and grinding burn nondestructively. The walls themselves can be observed by magnetic force microscopy and Lorentz microscopy. In devices, racetrack memory has been proposed, in which walls lined up in a nanowire are moved by current to store information, and research on moving walls by current-driven spin transfer is advancing. Microstructures are designed to make walls move easily in soft magnetic materials and with difficulty in pinning-type magnets, so domain walls are a central object of materials design.

faq.q: What is the difference between Bloch walls and Néel walls?
faq.a: In a Bloch wall the magnetic moments rotate within the plane of the wall, so no magnetic poles appear on the wall. In a Néel wall the moments rotate within the plane of the film, and poles appear on the wall. Bloch walls are stable in thick specimens, and Néel walls in films thinner than the wall width.

faq.q: Is a domain wall the same as the boundary between domains?
faq.a: Yes. The boundary between domains is not a plane of zero width but a layer of finite thickness across which the magnetic moments change direction gradually, and that layer is called a domain wall. Its thickness differs with the material and is estimated at tens of nanometers in iron and a few nanometers in permanent magnet materials of high anisotropy.

faq.q: What kind of material has easily moving domain walls?
faq.a: One with small magnetocrystalline anisotropy and magnetostriction and few impurities, precipitates, internal strains and fine grain boundaries to catch the walls. Soft magnetic materials such as permalloy and grain-oriented electrical steel are examples, and walls are made to move easily by raising purity and removing strain by annealing.

飽和磁化.desc: The magnetization when a strong field aligns all the magnetic moments in the same direction. For iron it is about 1.7×10⁶ A/m (about 2.2 T as µ₀Ms), and it decreases as the temperature rises.

about.p: Saturation magnetization Ms is the magnetic moment per unit volume when a strong field aligns all the moments in one direction, in units of A/m. Because it is set by the moment per atom and the number density of atoms, for a given composition and temperature it hardly depends on grain size or the degree of working. In this it differs in character from coercivity and permeability, which change greatly with microstructure, and it is treated as a structure-insensitive quantity. In designing magnetic materials, the magnitude of the saturation magnetization is first fixed by composition, and coercivity and permeability are then adjusted by controlling the microstructure.

Compared as the room-temperature saturation flux density µ₀Ms, iron gives about 2.15 T, cobalt about 1.8 T and nickel about 0.6 T, with moments per atom at 0 K of about 2.22, 1.72 and 0.61 µB respectively. An alloy of iron with about 35% cobalt reaches about 2.4 T, the highest value among practical materials. Iron-based amorphous alloys, by contrast, are lower at about 1.5 to 1.6 T, and Mn-Zn ferrites at about 0.5 T. The value is sometimes given per unit mass instead of per unit volume; expressed this way, the saturation magnetization of iron is about 218 A·m²/kg (218 emu/g).

As temperature rises, thermal fluctuations make it harder for the moments to stay aligned, and the saturation magnetization decreases. On heating from 0 K it falls slowly at first, then rapidly near the Curie temperature, where it reaches 0. The Curie temperature is about 770°C for iron, about 358°C for nickel and about 1120°C for cobalt. Room-temperature values are somewhat smaller than those at 0 K; for nickel, for example, the 0 K value calculated from the atomic moment is about 0.64 T, compared with about 0.61 T at room temperature. For motor and transformer materials used at high temperature, the saturation magnetization at the service temperature must be considered.

Because flux density is B = µ₀(H + M), the flux density at saturation Bs is µ₀Ms plus µ₀H, but in soft magnetic materials µ₀H is small, so Bs ≈ µ₀Ms is used. Remanence is the magnetization left when the field is returned to 0; it is smaller than the saturation magnetization and depends strongly on microstructure and shape. In measurement, the magnetization curve is taken with a vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM) or a SQUID magnetometer and the saturated value is read at high field. A demagnetizing field due to the specimen's shape means a strong field is needed for saturation, so measures are taken such as placing a long, thin specimen along the field.

faq.q: What is the difference between saturation magnetization and saturation flux density?
faq.a: Saturation magnetization Ms is the density of magnetic moment in the material, in A/m, and saturation flux density Bs is the flux density at saturation, in T. From B = µ₀(H + M), Bs is larger than µ₀Ms by µ₀H, but the difference is small, so the two are sometimes used almost interchangeably.

faq.q: How are units of saturation magnetization converted?
faq.a: In SI units it is A/m and in CGS units emu/cm³, with 1 emu/cm³ = 1000 A/m. Expressed as flux density, µ₀Ms (T) is used, or 4πMs (G) in CGS, with 1 T = 10000 G. Values per unit mass have the same number in A·m²/kg and emu/g.

faq.q: Does heat treatment or working change the saturation magnetization?
faq.a: Hardly at all, as long as the composition and phases do not change. If heat treatment forms precipitates or a phase transformation or ordering produces a different phase, however, the overall saturation magnetization changes because each phase has a different value. Austenitic stainless steel becoming martensite on working and starting to stick to magnets is an example.

フェリ磁性.desc: Magnetism in which the moments of two antiparallel sublattices differ in size, leaving a spontaneous magnetization equal to the difference. Ferrites such as magnetite are typical examples.

about.p: Ferrimagnetism is magnetism in which moments on two kinds of sites in a crystal (sublattices) align antiparallel, leaving a spontaneous magnetization equal to the difference in their sizes. Magnetic oxides such as magnetite had long been known as magnets, but the fact that their magnetization is much smaller than that of ferromagnetic metals was first explained by this idea. The Frenchman Néel set out the theory in 1948, and for this work together with that on antiferromagnetism he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1970. In oxides, superexchange through the oxygen ions between metal ions acts to align the moments antiparallel.

The magnetizations of the two sublattices decrease differently with temperature, so the temperature dependence of the total magnetization can take shapes unlike those of ferromagnets. In some rare-earth iron garnets, one sublattice dominates at low temperature and the other at high temperature, and in between a compensation temperature appears where the two cancel and the magnetization is 0; for gadolinium iron garnet it lies near room temperature. The temperature at which the spontaneous magnetization vanishes is called the Curie temperature and is about 580°C for magnetite. Another feature is that in the paramagnetic range above it, the inverse susceptibility plotted against temperature is not a straight line but a curve.

about.h: How it differs from ferro- and antiferromagnetism
about.p: Seen from outside, ferrimagnets closely resemble ferromagnets: they have domains, show hysteresis and stick to magnets. To tell them apart, the orientation of the moments on each sublattice is examined by neutron diffraction, or the saturation magnetization is compared with the sum of the atomic moments. That the measured saturation magnetization of magnetite Fe₃O₄ is about 4 µB per formula unit, far smaller than the sum of the moments of three iron ions, is typical evidence of ferrimagnetism. In antiferromagnetism the moments of the two sublattices are equal and cancel completely, so no spontaneous magnetization remains.

The typical ferrimagnetic materials are ferrites, including the spinel type MFe₂O₄, the magnetoplumbite (hexagonal) types BaFe₁₂O₁₉ and SrFe₁₂O₁₉, and the garnet type Y₃Fe₅O₁₂. Being oxides, their electrical resistivity is orders of magnitude higher than that of metals and eddy currents hardly flow even at high frequencies, so Mn-Zn and Ni-Zn spinel ferrites are used in transformers for switching power supplies and in parts for noise suppression. Hexagonal ferrites have large magnetocrystalline anisotropy and are used in huge quantities in motors and elsewhere as cheap permanent magnets that do not rust, and garnets are used in microwave devices.

faq.q: Is ferrite in magnetic materials the same as ferrite in steel microstructures?
faq.a: No. Ferrite in magnetic materials is the general name for iron oxides that show ferrimagnetism. Ferrite in steel is the name of the microstructure of body-centered cubic iron (α-iron) and its solid solutions, which is ferromagnetic. The name is the same, but the substance and the type of magnetism are different.

faq.q: Why is the saturation magnetization of ferrimagnets small?
faq.a: Because the moments of the two sublattices align antiparallel and only the difference remains. In oxides, moreover, oxygen ions with no magnetic moment occupy much of the volume, so there is less moment per unit volume as well. The saturation flux density of ferrites is therefore around 0.5 T, smaller than the roughly 2.2 T of iron.

faq.q: What is a compensation temperature?
faq.a: In a ferrimagnet whose two sublattice magnetizations change differently with temperature, it is the temperature at which their sizes are exactly equal and the total magnetization is 0. Above and below it, the sublattice that sets the direction of the total magnetization switches. Materials for magneto-optical recording made use of properties near this temperature.

結晶磁気異方性.desc: The property that the ease of magnetization depends on the crystal direction. In iron, <100> is the easy axis. A large value raises coercivity, and a small one raises permeability.

about.p: Magnetocrystalline anisotropy is the property that a material's energy depends on which crystal direction the magnetization points along. In cubic crystals, with α₁, α₂ and α₃ as the direction cosines of the magnetization, it is written E = K₁(α₁²α₂² + α₂²α₃² + α₃²α₁²) + …. Iron has a positive K₁ ≈ 4.8×10⁴ J/m³ (room temperature) with <100> as the easy axis, and nickel has a negative K₁ with <111> as the easy axis. For uniaxial materials such as hexagonal cobalt it is written E = K_u sin²θ, with θ the angle from the c axis, and K_u for cobalt is about 4×10⁵ J/m³. The unit is energy per unit volume, J/m³.

Magnetization is carried mainly by spin, but spin is coupled to the orbital motion of electrons by spin–orbit interaction, and the orbitals have preferred orientations in the crystal field created by the surrounding ions. Through this coupling, the direction of magnetization comes to distinguish crystal directions. The 4f electrons of rare earths have a large orbital contribution, giving extremely large anisotropy, as in Nd₂Fe₁₄B (K₁ ≈ 4.9×10⁶ J/m³) and SmCo₅. A guide to the field needed to pull the magnetization away from the easy axis is the anisotropy field HA = 2K/(µ₀Ms); µ₀HA is about 0.06 T for iron but reaches about 7.5 T for Nd₂Fe₁₄B.

about.h: How it differs from other anisotropies
about.p: Magnetocrystalline anisotropy is not the only reason energy depends on the direction of magnetization. In elongated particles and thin films, the demagnetizing field makes the magnetization prefer the long direction or the film plane; this is shape anisotropy. The coercivity of alnico magnets comes mainly from the shape anisotropy of an elongated ferromagnetic phase. There is also stress-induced anisotropy from the combination of stress and magnetostriction, and induced anisotropy created by heat treatment in a magnetic field. The difference is that magnetocrystalline anisotropy is a property of the substance itself, set by composition and temperature, whereas shape anisotropy and induced anisotropy can be changed through microstructure and processing.

In permanent magnets, larger anisotropy makes the magnetization harder to reverse and raises the upper limit of coercivity, so materials with large K are chosen and sintered with the easy axes of the grains aligned. In soft magnetic materials anisotropy is instead made small; in permalloy, K₁ is brought close to 0 by composition. In nanocrystalline soft magnetic alloys, the grain size is made smaller than the magnetic correlation length so that the anisotropies of individual grains average out and cancel. Grain-oriented electrical steel, which aligns iron's easy axis <100> with the rolling direction, is an example of putting anisotropy to use. Because anisotropy constants fall faster than saturation magnetization as temperature rises, values at the service temperature matter for magnets used hot.

faq.q: What are the easy and hard axes of magnetization?
faq.a: The easy axis is the crystal direction of lowest magnetocrystalline anisotropy energy, along which saturation is reached at low field; the hard axis is the direction of highest energy, which needs a strong field to saturate. In iron, <100> is the easy axis and <111> the hard axis, which can be measured as differences in the magnetization curves of a single crystal along each direction.

faq.q: How is magnetocrystalline anisotropy measured?
faq.a: A common method uses a torque magnetometer, which rotates a single-crystal specimen in a magnetic field and measures the torque pulling the magnetization back toward the easy axis. Other methods measure magnetization curves along the easy and hard axes and obtain the anisotropy energy from the area between them, or derive it from the ferromagnetic resonance frequency.

faq.q: Is a magnetic material better the larger its anisotropy?
faq.a: It depends on the application. In permanent magnets, larger anisotropy allows higher coercivity and is an advantage. In soft magnetic materials such as transformer cores, the magnetization must change at low field, so the smaller the anisotropy the better. In magnetic recording there is a balance: large enough to keep the recorded data, but moderate enough to write.

超常磁性.desc: The state of very small ferromagnetic particles in which the barrier to reversal, KV, is small compared with the thermal energy, so the magnetization reverses thermally and the coercivity is almost zero.

about.h: A magnet whose direction is changed by heat
about.p: In small single-domain particles, the magnetization of the whole particle behaves as one large magnetic moment and can switch between the two directions along the easy axis by crossing an energy barrier KV. If the barrier is not sufficiently large compared with the thermal energy kT, the magnetization reverses frequently by thermal activation and appears to be 0 on average. This is superparamagnetism, and ferromagnetic order is preserved inside the particle. The moment of a single magnetite particle 10 nm in diameter is about 27000 times the Bohr magneton, so the susceptibility is far larger than that of paramagnetic atoms. The super in the name comes from this large moment.

The mean time before the magnetization reverses (the Néel relaxation time) is τ = τ₀ exp(KV/kT), where τ₀ is of the order of 10⁻⁹ s. Whether a particle appears superparamagnetic depends on how τ compares with the time taken by the measurement. In DC magnetization measurements (about 100 s) the boundary is KV ≈ 25kT, and the temperature that satisfies this is called the blocking temperature T_B. T_B is proportional to volume, so for the same material, doubling the particle volume also doubles T_B. In Mössbauer spectroscopy, whose measurement time is much shorter, the same particles show a higher T_B, so it is important to state the method of measurement.

The magnetization curve of an assembly of superparamagnetic particles has no hysteresis and approaches saturation in the form of a Langevin function, which resembles paramagnetism. But because each moment is large, it approaches saturation at fairly modest fields even at room temperature. Below the blocking temperature, reversal of the magnetization is frozen and coercivity appears. Experimentally, the ZFC curve, measured after cooling without a field, is compared with the FC curve, measured after cooling in a field, and blocking is examined from the temperature at which the two begin to separate. A distribution of particle sizes spreads T_B, so analysis is combined with the size distribution.

The property of retaining no magnetization once the field is switched off is useful in medicine and biology. Superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles are used as MRI contrast agents, in hyperthermia, where they are heated by an AC field, and in separating cells and molecules by collecting them with magnets; an advantage is that once the field is off the particles do not readily cluster magnetically. In hard disks, on the other hand, the limit at which shrinking the bits makes the grains superparamagnetic and the data disappear (the superparamagnetic limit) is a problem. Keeping data for 10 years with τ₀ = 10⁻⁹ s requires KV/kT of about 40 or more by a simple estimate, and heat-assisted recording, which temporarily makes high-anisotropy FePt easier to write by heating, was developed.

faq.q: What is the difference between superparamagnetism and paramagnetism?
faq.a: Paramagnetism is a state in which the small moments of individual atoms point in random directions; superparamagnetism is a state in which the large moment of each whole ferromagnetic particle is randomized by heat. Because the moments are thousands to tens of thousands of times larger, superparamagnetic particles magnetize strongly even in weak fields. They also differ in that coercivity appears on cooling.

faq.q: How small must particles be to become superparamagnetic?
faq.a: It depends on the material's anisotropy constant, the temperature and the measurement time. Taking KV ≈ 25kT as a guide, at room temperature the limit is a diameter of roughly 20 to 30 nm or less for iron oxides with small anisotropy, and a few nanometers or less for ordered FePt with large anisotropy. The larger the anisotropy, the smaller the particle that can keep a stable magnetization.

faq.q: Do superparamagnetic particles stick to magnets?
faq.a: Yes. They magnetize strongly when an external field is applied, so particles in a liquid can be collected with a magnet. When the field is removed, the magnetization returns almost to 0 and the particles disperse again. This property is used in magnetic fluids and magnetic separation.

最大エネルギー積.desc: The value (BH)max at which the magnitude of the product of flux density B and field H is greatest on the demagnetization curve of a permanent magnet. In kJ/m³, it measures a magnet's strength.

about.h: Why it measures a magnet's capability
about.p: Permanent magnets are usually used to create a field in an air gap. Ignoring leakage, the magnet volume needed to create a field of flux density Bg in a gap of volume Vg is Vm = Bg²Vg/(µ₀|BH|), where |BH| is the magnitude of the product of B and H at the magnet's operating point. So using the magnet at a point of large |BH| keeps it small, and the maximum of this product is (BH)max. Besides kJ/m³, the CGS unit MGOe is also used, with 1 MGOe being about 7.96 kJ/m³. It is the value most often compared in discussions of making magnets smaller or raising motor output.

The operating point of a magnet is the intersection of the demagnetization curve with a straight line (the permeance line) set by the shapes of the magnet and gap. The permeance coefficient Pc = −B/(µ₀H), which expresses the slope of this line, becomes small when the demagnetizing field is large, as when a thin plate magnet is magnetized through its thickness. For an ideal magnet with a straight demagnetization curve, |BH| is largest at the point where B = Br/2 (Pc = 1), giving (BH)max = Br²/(4µ₀). Estimating the upper limit with this formula, Br = 1.6 T gives about 510 kJ/m³ (about 64 MGOe), close to the theoretical limit for Nd₂Fe₁₄B, the main phase of neodymium magnets.

(BH)max is usually given at room temperature, and performance at high temperature and resistance to demagnetization must be judged by other indicators. As temperature rises, remanence and coercivity fall, and magnets with a small intrinsic coercivity HcJ are partly demagnetized irreversibly by reverse fields or heat. So even with a large (BH)max, grades with a large HcJ are chosen for motors used at high temperature. Sm-Co magnets fall short of neodymium magnets in (BH)max, but their properties change little with temperature, so they are used in high-temperature applications. Price, susceptibility to rust and the supply of resources also influence the actual choice.

(BH)max grew throughout the 20th century each time a new magnet material appeared. In Japan, Kotaro Honda's KS steel (1917) and Tokushichi Mishima's MK steel (1931) are well known, and alnico, ferrite and Sm-Co magnets followed. In 1982 Masato Sagawa and colleagues developed sintered Nd-Fe-B magnets, and some commercial products today exceed about 400 kJ/m³. As a guide to typical values, ferrite magnets give about 10 to 40 kJ/m³, Sm-Co magnets about 130 to 250 kJ/m³ and sintered neodymium magnets about 250 to 440 kJ/m³, and each is chosen according to the demands of the application.

faq.q: How are MGOe and kJ/m³ converted?
faq.a: 1 MGOe is about 7.96 kJ/m³. For example, 50 MGOe is about 398 kJ/m³, and dividing a value in kJ/m³ by about 8 gives the approximate MGOe. MGOe is the megagauss-oersted of the CGS system and is still widely used in magnet catalogs.

faq.q: Does a magnet with a larger (BH)max hold more strongly?
faq.a: For the same shape and size, a magnet with a larger (BH)max can generally create a stronger field. But holding force varies greatly with the magnet's shape, the direction of magnetization, the thickness of the iron it attracts and the gap between them, and is not set by (BH)max alone. Making a magnet thin can lower the operating point through the demagnetizing field, so its performance is not fully used.

faq.q: Does (BH)max change with temperature?
faq.a: Yes. As temperature rises the remanence falls, so (BH)max also becomes smaller. Neodymium magnets show a relatively large drop with temperature, while Sm-Co magnets show a small one. In addition, insufficient coercivity causes irreversible demagnetization at high temperature, so the demagnetization curve at the service temperature should be checked.

渦電流損失.desc: The loss due to Joule heating by eddy currents induced in a magnetic material when the flux changes under AC. It is proportional to the square of thickness and frequency and inversely proportional to resistivity.

about.p: In the cores of transformers and motors used with alternating current, energy is lost as heat each time the material is magnetized back and forth; this is called core loss (iron loss). Core loss is broadly divided into hysteresis loss, which corresponds to the area of the hysteresis loop, and eddy-current loss, from the Joule heating of currents induced in the core by the changing flux. Hysteresis loss per cycle is nearly constant, so hysteresis loss is proportional to frequency, while eddy-current loss is proportional to the square of frequency. As frequency rises, the share of eddy-current loss grows, so in high-frequency applications suppressing eddy currents becomes central to materials selection.

about.h: The classical formula for thin sheet
about.p: When a sinusoidal flux of frequency f and peak flux density Bm passes through a thin sheet of thickness t and resistivity ρ, the eddy-current loss per unit volume is P = π²t²f²Bm²/(6ρ), where the skin effect can be neglected. For example, a 3% silicon steel sheet with t = 0.35 mm and ρ = 4.8×10⁻⁷ Ω·m at 50 Hz and 1.5 T gives about 0.31 W/kg, taking the density as 7.65 g/cm³. Raising the frequency to 400 Hz in the same sheet makes the loss (400/50)² = 64 times larger. Because the loss is proportional to the square of thickness and inversely proportional to resistivity, making sheets thinner and raising resistivity are the basic countermeasures.

about.h: The gap from the classical formula (anomalous loss)
about.p: Subtracting the hysteresis loss and the classical eddy-current loss from the core loss measured on real electrical steel leaves a considerable amount. This is called anomalous eddy-current loss (excess loss), and it arises because eddy currents do not flow uniformly through the whole sheet but concentrate near moving domain walls. The larger the domains and the fewer the walls, the faster each wall must move, and the larger this loss becomes. Fine grooves or strain introduced by laser on the surface of grain-oriented electrical steel to refine the domains serve to reduce this loss. In analyses that separate the losses, it is sometimes treated as a term proportional to frequency to the power 1.5.

To reduce eddy currents, the paths for current are cut finely or the resistivity of the material is raised. Electrical steel is made of thin sheets with insulating coatings stacked together, and about 3% silicon is added to iron to raise the resistivity to several times that of pure iron. There are also sheets with silicon raised to 6.5%. At frequencies of kHz and above, amorphous alloy ribbons about 20 to 30 µm thick, dust cores made by compacting insulated powder, and ferrites of extremely high resistivity are used. On the other hand, the Joule heat of eddy currents is put to active use in induction heating and induction cooktops, eddy-current braking, and eddy-current testing to find flaws at metal surfaces.

faq.q: What is the difference between eddy-current loss and hysteresis loss?
faq.a: Hysteresis loss comes from the irreversibility of domain-wall motion and rotation of magnetization; the value per cycle depends little on frequency, so the loss is proportional to frequency. Eddy-current loss is the Joule heat of induced currents; it is proportional to the square of frequency and depends strongly on sheet thickness and resistivity.

faq.q: Why is silicon added to electrical steel?
faq.a: Because silicon greatly raises the electrical resistivity of iron, reducing eddy-current loss. It also lowers magnetocrystalline anisotropy and magnetostriction, helping to raise permeability. Adding too much, however, lowers the saturation flux density and makes the sheet brittle and hard to roll, so it is usually kept to around 3%.

faq.q: What materials are used as frequency rises?
faq.a: Electrical steel is common at power frequencies (50/60 Hz), thin electrical steel and amorphous alloys from several hundred Hz to several kHz, and nanocrystalline alloys and ferrites at tens of kHz and above. The higher the frequency, the thinner and more resistive the material must be. The boundaries vary with the application and flux density, however.

引け巣.desc: A void in a casting where solidification shrinkage could not be made up by melt. It tends to form in thick sections that solidify last and is prevented by the design of risers and the order of solidification.
