about.p: Between pouring the melt into the mold and reaching room temperature, a metal shrinks in three stages: liquid contraction while it cools as a liquid, solidification shrinkage as it changes from liquid to solid, and solid contraction as the solid cools to room temperature. The first two cause shrinkage cavities; if melt cannot be supplied to make up for them, voids remain. Solidification shrinkage is as large as about 7% for pure aluminum and several percent even for steel. Solid contraction, on the other hand, reduces the overall dimensions of the casting and is compensated by a shrinkage allowance that makes the mold dimensions larger. Shrinkage cavities and dimensional shrinkage differ in the stage that causes them and in how they are dealt with.

To prevent shrinkage cavities, the riser must solidify after every part of the casting, with solidification progressing in order toward the riser. A guide to solidification time is Chvorinov's rule t = B(V/A)², where V is the volume, A the surface area that contributes to cooling, and V/A is called the modulus. For example, a cube with 100 mm edges has a modulus of about 16.7 mm. Making the riser modulus about 1.2 times that of the casting, as experience suggests, gives a solidification time 1.2² ≈ 1.44 times longer, so melt remains until after the casting has solidified. Chills that speed cooling of thick sections and insulating or exothermic sleeves that keep the riser liquid longer are also used.

The form of shrinkage cavities depends on how the alloy solidifies. Pure metals and eutectic alloys, which solidify over a narrow temperature range, grow a solid shell from the outside inward, so a large cavity tends to gather at the center that solidifies last. Alloys with a wide freezing range have a broad region where solid and liquid coexist, melt can no longer reach between the dendrites, and fine cavities form dispersed through the casting (microshrinkage). Gray cast iron is notable in that the expansion when graphite forms at the end of solidification offsets the shrinkage, so smaller risers suffice and castings tend to have few shrinkage cavities.

Internal shrinkage cavities cannot be seen from outside, so they are examined by radiography and ultrasonic testing, with X-ray CT also used for precise evaluation. At the design stage, casting simulation predicts the order of solidification and where solidification ends, and the positions of risers and chills are decided accordingly. Shrinkage cavities impair pressure tightness and act as initiation sites for fatigue cracks, so they are controlled especially strictly in parts that carry pressure and in rotating parts. Internal cavities not connected to the surface can be closed by hot isostatic pressing (HIP), but those open to the surface cannot, so they are repaired by welding or the casting is rejected.

faq.q: How can shrinkage cavities be told apart from gas pores?
faq.a: The inner surface of a shrinkage cavity is rough, with dendrite tips visible, and such cavities gather in the thick sections that solidify last. Gas pores form when dissolved gas comes out, so their inner surfaces are smooth and round and they appear throughout the casting. On radiographs, shrinkage cavities show as irregular shapes and pores as round shadows.

faq.q: Is the shrinkage allowance of a pattern related to shrinkage cavities?
faq.a: They arise at different stages. The shrinkage allowance is a dimensional margin that makes the mold larger to allow for contraction of the solid as it cools to room temperature after solidification. A shrinkage cavity is a void formed when the earlier shrinkage during liquid cooling and solidification is not made up by feeding melt, and it is prevented by designing the risers and the order of solidification.

faq.q: How large should a riser be?
faq.a: So that the riser solidifies after the casting, its modulus (volume divided by cooling surface area) is made larger than that of the thick sections of the casting, often about 1.2 times or more by experience. Enough melt must also remain to make up the casting's shrinkage. Insulating or exothermic sleeves keep even small risers liquid for longer.

インベストメント鋳造.desc: A precision casting method in which a wax pattern is coated with refractory and hardened, and melt is poured into the mold left after the wax is melted out. Also called the lost-wax process; used for turbine blades and the like.

about.p: In investment casting, wax is first injected into a metal die to make patterns of the same shape as the product, and many of them are attached to wax bars that will become the runners, forming a tree. This is dipped into a slurry containing fine refractory powder, coarse refractory grains are sprinkled on the surface and it is dried, and this is repeated many times to build a shell. The wax is then melted out, for example in a steam autoclave, and the shell is fired at high temperature to strengthen it and burn off remaining wax. Melt is poured while the fired shell is still hot, and after solidification the shell is broken away, the castings are removed, cut from the runners and finished.

Because the pattern is removed by melting, the mold need not be split, and shapes that could not be withdrawn from a mold, fine grooves and thin blade-like forms can be made in one piece. Fine refractory powder copies the pattern surface, so surfaces are smooth and dimensional accuracy is good, greatly reducing the amount of machining. If ceramic cores are set in the wax die so that they end up inside the pattern, and are dissolved away chemically after casting, hollow parts with complex internal cooling passages can also be made. On the other hand, each pattern and shell is made individually, so the process is long, the cost per part is high and making large parts is harder than with sand casting.

about.h: How it differs from similar casting methods
about.p: Lost foam casting (the full mold process), in which a foamed polystyrene pattern is buried in sand and vanishes in the heat of the melt as it is poured, also uses a disappearing pattern, but investment casting, which removes the pattern before pouring, gives higher surface and dimensional accuracy. In jewelry and dental casting, the pattern is embedded in a plaster-based investment, while ceramic shells are the mainstream for industrial parts. Die casting, which injects melt into metal dies at high pressure, excels in productivity but is unsuited to high-melting alloys and complex hollow shapes.

Turbine blades for jet engines and gas turbines, made of Ni-based superalloys, are a typical example of investment casting. Withdrawing the shell gradually downward from the furnace so that it solidifies from bottom to top gives directionally solidified blades with aligned columnar grains, and adding a narrow passage partway that selects only one crystal gives single-crystal blades. The aim is to eliminate grain boundaries perpendicular to the load, which are weak points in high-temperature creep. Recently, making wax or polymer patterns by 3D printing and casting prototypes and small batches without a die has also spread. The method is also used for medical implants and golf club heads.

faq.q: Are investment casting and the lost-wax process the same thing?
faq.a: They are used with almost the same meaning. Lost-wax process emphasizes that the wax pattern is melted and lost, while investment casting emphasizes that the pattern is wrapped (invested) in refractory. Industry usually says investment casting, while art and craft usually say lost wax.

faq.q: Which materials suit investment casting?
faq.a: Because the refractory shell withstands high temperatures, it can be used for high-melting alloys such as steels, stainless steels, Ni-based and Co-based superalloys and titanium alloys. Titanium melt reacts easily, so the inner face of the shell uses an unreactive refractory such as yttria, and the metal is melted and cast in vacuum. Aluminum and copper alloys are cast this way too.

faq.q: Why is it called precision casting?
faq.a: Because patterns of consistent dimensions made in a die are copied by fine refractory powder, dimensional accuracy is higher and surfaces smoother than with other casting methods. Many surfaces can be used as cast, reducing machining. The die dimensions must allow for the shrinkage of wax and metal, however, and accuracy is harder to keep for larger parts.

押出し.desc: Plastic working in which a billet in a container is pushed by a ram through a die opening to make long products of constant cross section. Aluminum profiles are a typical example.

about.p: Extrusion is a process in which a heated billet placed in a container is pushed by a ram and forced out through a die opening. Besides direct extrusion, in which the billet slides forward within the container, and indirect extrusion, in which the die side moves to eliminate friction between billet and container, there is also hydrostatic extrusion, in which pressure is applied through a liquid surrounding the billet. The amount of working is expressed by the extrusion ratio R = A₀/A, the ratio of the original cross-sectional area to that of the product, and for aluminum alloys ratios of more than several tens are possible. Because the material is under compressive stress, a large deformation can be given in one pass.

Drawing also reduces the cross-section by passing material through a die, but because it pulls on the product, the product tears if the drawing stress exceeds the material's strength. Even in the ideal case, ignoring friction and other effects, the drawing stress is Y ln R (with Y the flow stress), so ln R cannot exceed 1 and the reduction in area in one pass is limited to at most about 63%. Extrusion pushes the billet from behind and has no such limit; for R = 40 the ideal pressure is Y ln R ≈ 3.7Y. The required pressure is higher, but a large change in cross-section can be given at once.

Hollow sections such as aluminum window frames and heat-exchanger tubes are made with porthole dies (bridge dies). Inside the die the material is first split into several streams, which rejoin around a mandrel and are pressure-welded together, so the product retains longitudinal weld seams. For 6000-series aluminum alloys the billet is heated to about 400 to 500°C, and the section leaves the die even hotter because of deformation heating; if it is cooled by air or water right after leaving the die and then aged, it gains strength without a separate solution treatment (T5 temper). If the extrusion speed or temperature is too high, heat from friction and deformation causes fine surface cracks, so conditions are controlled for each alloy.

Pushing the billet out to the very end creates a defect in which surface oxides and dirt are drawn into the center, so the end portion is discarded rather than used as product. Under conditions of low extrusion ratio and large die angle, arrowhead-shaped internal cracks (chevron cracks) can also form. Besides aluminum alloy sections, extrusion is used for copper alloy rods and tubes, seamless steel tubes and titanium alloy members. For materials extruded at high temperature such as steel, glass powder can be used as a lubricant. Extrusion molding, which feeds polymers or foods continuously with a screw, follows the same idea of making products of constant cross-section.

faq.q: What is the extrusion ratio?
faq.a: It is the cross-sectional area of the billet before extrusion divided by that of the extruded product. For round bar it is the square of the ratio of diameters. The larger the extrusion ratio, the larger the deformation and the required extrusion pressure, which in the ideal case is proportional to the natural logarithm of the extrusion ratio.

faq.q: How are direct and indirect extrusion used differently?
faq.a: Direct extrusion uses simpler equipment and suits products of many shapes, but needs extra force to overcome friction between billet and container. Indirect extrusion has little friction, so less force is needed, the billet heats up less and quality is more uniform, but because the product is taken out through a hollow ram, its size and shape are restricted.

faq.q: Why do extruded sections have a constant cross-section?
faq.a: Because the material passes straight through the shape of the die opening. Changing the shape of the opening allows L shapes, H shapes and complex hollow sections. If material flows at different speeds through thick and thin parts of the section, however, bending and twisting result, so the die is designed to even out the flow.

スプリングバック.desc: The partial recovery of shape by elastic recovery when the load is removed after bending or other working. It is larger for materials with a higher yield stress and a lower Young's modulus.

about.p: When a sheet is bent, the outside is stretched and the inside compressed, and most of the cross-section deforms plastically. Even so, stresses of about the yield stress remain in the cross-section, and when the part is taken out of the die the shape recovers by the elastic strain corresponding to these stresses. This is springback. Its size is roughly set by the ratio of yield stress to Young's modulus, Y/E, and it is larger for materials with a higher yield stress and a lower Young's modulus. It occurs not only in bending but also in press drawing and stretch forming, and because it distorts the dimensions and shape of parts, it is one of the most troublesome problems in designing press forming.

Ignoring work hardening and assuming the whole cross-section has yielded, the bending moment per unit width is Yt²/4 and the bending stiffness is Et³/12, so the recovery of curvature on unloading is Δ(1/R) = 3Y/(Et), where t is the sheet thickness. For example, bending a sheet with Y = 300 MPa and t = 1 mm to a radius of 10 mm gives a radius after springback of about 10.45 mm for steel (E = 210 GPa) and about 11.5 mm for an aluminum alloy (E = 70 GPa). With one-third the Young's modulus, the recovery is about three times larger. Because the recovery of curvature is fixed, the gentler the bend, the larger the recovery relative to the original shape.

Car bodies use high-strength steel sheets to save weight, but their Young's modulus is almost the same as mild steel while only the yield stress is higher, so springback becomes large. When hat-shaped sections are pressed, not only do the corner angles open, but shape distortions such as curling of the side walls (wall curl) and twisting of the whole part also occur. In V-bending, depending on conditions, negative springback (spring-go), in which the part closes further than the bent angle, can also occur. Because simple bending formulas cannot fully predict this, forming simulation is used in practice.

The basic countermeasure is to bend extra by the amount that will spring back (overbending). Other effective methods press the bend hard with the die at the end of bending to compress it and make the whole cross-section yield (bottoming, coining), or bend while applying tension so that the stress distribution across the section becomes closer to uniform. Today it is common to compensate the die shape in advance so as to cancel the springback predicted by forming simulation. On the material side, warm forming, which lowers the yield stress by heating, and hot stamping (press hardening), which forms at high temperature and quenches in the die, also suppress springback in high-strength parts.

faq.q: What determines the size of springback?
faq.a: Mainly the ratio of yield stress to Young's modulus Y/E, the sheet thickness and the bend radius. The larger Y/E, the thinner the sheet and the larger the bend radius, the larger the relative recovery. It also changes with the amount of work hardening, friction with the die and the bending method.

faq.q: Is springback larger for thicker sheet?
faq.a: For the same bend radius, the thicker the sheet, the smaller the recovery of curvature, because the recovery Δ(1/R) ≈ 3Y/(Et) is inversely proportional to thickness. Bending thick sheet needs large forces, however, and cracking on the outside or wrinkling on the inside becomes more likely, so other problems need attention.

faq.q: Do titanium and aluminum alloys show large springback?
faq.a: They tend to. Titanium alloys, with about half the Young's modulus of steel, and aluminum alloys, with about one-third, spring back about two to three times as much as steel at the same yield stress. Titanium alloys also have a high yield stress, so their springback is especially large, and forming them hot is common.

溶接熱影響部.desc: The part of the base metal that did not melt during welding but whose microstructure and properties were changed by the welding heat. Also called the HAZ; hardening, softening, grain coarsening and sensitization can occur there.

about.p: A joint made by fusion welding such as arc welding is divided into the weld metal, which melted and solidified; the heat-affected zone (HAZ) outside it, which did not melt but received heat; and the base metal, which is hardly affected by heat. Within the HAZ, the peak temperature is higher closer to the boundary with the weld metal (the fusion line) and lower farther away. According to the peak temperature, the HAZ of steel is divided into bands such as a coarse-grained zone where grains have grown large, a fine-grained zone refined by transformation, an intercritical zone where only part transformed, and a tempered zone that does not transform, each with different hardness and toughness.

about.h: Hardening and cold cracking in the HAZ of steel
about.p: The part of the HAZ of steel heated into the austenite range is quenched as the surrounding cold base metal draws off its heat, so in steels of high hardenability it becomes hard martensite. When a hard microstructure, diffusible hydrogen from the weld metal and tensile stress from restraint coincide, cold cracking occurs some time after welding. The guide to hardenability is the carbon equivalent; in steels where it is high, preheating or postheating slows the cooling and lets hydrogen escape. Increasing the heat input also slows the cooling, but the grains in the coarse-grained zone can grow too large and the toughness can fall.

The problems that arise in the HAZ depend on the material. In austenitic stainless steels, Cr carbides precipitate at grain boundaries in the band exposed to about 500 to 800°C, causing sensitization and intergranular corrosion. In precipitation-hardened aluminum alloys and in materials strengthened by cold working, precipitates coarsen or the material recrystallizes, softening the HAZ so that the joint is weaker than the base metal. Even in high-strength steels strengthened by quenching and tempering, parts heated above the tempering temperature can soften. Joint design must allow for such strength loss in the HAZ.

faq.q: How wide is the heat-affected zone?
faq.a: It varies greatly with the welding process and heat input. In arc welding it is often a few mm, while in laser welding and electron beam welding, which have high energy density, the heat input is small and the zone is much narrower. The larger the heat input, and the thinner the plate so that heat escapes less easily, the wider the heat-affected zone.

faq.q: Can the properties of the heat-affected zone be restored after welding?
faq.a: To some extent. In steel, postweld heat treatment (stress-relief annealing) lowers residual stresses and tempers the hardened regions to restore toughness. Sensitization of stainless steel can be reversed by a solution heat treatment that dissolves the carbides again. In large structures, however, heat-treating the whole is difficult, so the basic approach is to prevent problems through the choice of material and welding conditions.

faq.q: Does friction stir welding also have a heat-affected zone?
faq.a: Yes. The material does not melt, but it is heated by friction, so outside the stir zone there form a thermo-mechanically affected zone, which received both heat and deformation, and a heat-affected zone, which received heat only. In precipitation-hardening aluminum alloys, precipitates coarsen and soften the material in this region, and it can be the weakest part of the joint.

炭素当量.desc: The sum of the effects of a steel's alloying elements on hardenability, converted into an amount of carbon. The higher the Ceq, the more the weld heat-affected zone hardens and the more likely cold cracking is.

about.p: Carbon equivalent is the sum of the effects of the alloying elements in a steel on hardenability, that is, on how readily it becomes martensite on rapid cooling, converted into an amount of carbon. In welding, the heat-affected zone of the base metal is cooled rapidly, so the higher the hardenability of a steel, the harder and more brittle that zone becomes. Carbon equivalent is a convenient indicator for estimating from chemical composition alone whether a steel tends to harden in welding, and it is the starting point for deciding whether preheating is needed and at what temperature. The coefficient of each element was determined experimentally by comparing its hardening effect with that of 1% carbon.

The International Institute of Welding (IIW) formula Ceq = C + Mn/6 + (Cr + Mo + V)/5 + (Ni + Cu)/15 is used for steels with somewhat higher carbon, and Pcm = C + Si/30 + (Mn + Cu + Cr)/20 + Ni/60 + Mo/15 + V/10 + 5B, proposed by Ito and Bessyo, for high-strength steels low in carbon. For a steel with C 0.12%, Si 0.30%, Mn 1.40%, Cu 0.20%, Ni 0.20%, Cr 0.10% and Mo 0.05%, Ceq is about 0.41% and Pcm about 0.22%. The value differs with the formula, so always state which formula was used.

about.h: The carbon equivalent of cast iron is different
about.p: Although it has the same name, carbon equivalent means something different for cast iron. The carbon equivalent of cast iron is expressed as CE = C + (Si + P)/3 or similar, converting into carbon the effect of silicon and phosphorus in shifting the eutectic point to lower carbon contents. A CE of about 4.3% is the eutectic composition; irons below it are called hypoeutectic and those above it hypereutectic. For example, a cast iron with C 3.4%, Si 2.4% and P 0.1% has a CE of about 4.23%, close to eutectic. The CE of cast iron is used to estimate how the iron solidifies, how graphite forms and how well the metal flows, a different purpose from the carbon equivalent for weldability of steel.

about.h: Use in preheating and steel development
about.p: The higher the carbon equivalent, the higher the preheating temperature needed to prevent cold cracking in welding. The actual preheating temperature is set by methods in standards and guidelines that combine carbon equivalent with plate thickness (thicker plates cool faster), the amount of diffusible hydrogen in the weld metal and the degree of joint restraint. On the steelmaking side, thermo-mechanical controlled processing (TMCP), with controlled rolling and accelerated cooling, refines the grains so that strength is kept while carbon and alloying elements are reduced, producing easily welded plates of low carbon equivalent. Some standards for steels for buildings and bridges set upper limits on carbon equivalent or Pcm.

faq.q: How are Ceq and Pcm used differently?
faq.a: The IIW Ceq is widely used as a guide to the hardenability of steels with relatively high carbon, while Pcm is said to represent well the susceptibility to cold cracking of high-strength steels low in carbon. Because Pcm has smaller coefficients, it gives a smaller value than Ceq for the same steel. Which is used depends on the steel grade and the standard followed.

faq.q: Can steels with a high carbon equivalent not be welded?
faq.a: They can be welded. Slowing cooling with preheating and postheating, using dried low-hydrogen welding consumables and controlling heat input make welding possible. Condition control becomes stricter, however, adding work and cost, so steels of low carbon equivalent are generally chosen for welded structures.

faq.q: Why does the IIW carbon equivalent formula not include silicon?
faq.a: In the IIW formula, silicon is omitted because its effect on hardenability is small. Some formulas, such as Pcm and those in Japanese standards, include silicon with a small coefficient. Which elements are included and with what coefficients depends on the range of steels in the experiments the formula was based on.

鋭敏化.desc: The phenomenon in which stainless steel heated to about 500 to 800°C precipitates Cr carbides at grain boundaries, depleting the Cr around them and making the steel prone to intergranular corrosion.

about.p: Stainless steel resists rusting because a passive film of Cr oxide forms on its surface, which is said to require roughly 11 to 12% Cr or more. When austenitic stainless steel is held at about 500 to 800°C, dissolved carbon combines with Cr and carbides such as Cr₂₃C₆ precipitate at grain boundaries. Carbon diffuses quickly but Cr moves only slowly, so a band forms along the grain boundaries right next to the carbides in which the Cr concentration has fallen too low to maintain passivity. In a corrosive environment this band dissolves preferentially, and corrosion advances along the grain boundaries.

about.h: The relation between time and temperature
about.p: Sensitization occurs through a combination of temperature and holding time. If the temperature is too high, carbon stays in solution and carbides form less readily; if it is too low, diffusion is too slow. It therefore occurs fastest at an intermediate temperature, giving a C-shaped curve on a time–temperature diagram. The higher the carbon content, the more the curve shifts to shorter times, and the more easily sensitization occurs even with short heating such as welding. Given enough time, carbides grow slowly even at lower temperatures, so low-temperature sensitization must also be watched for in welded piping and similar equipment used for long periods at moderate temperatures.

SUS304L and SUS316L, with carbon reduced to about 0.03% or less, form carbides less readily and largely prevent sensitization from welding. Stabilized steels containing Ti or Nb (SUS321, SUS347) tie up carbon first as Ti or Nb carbides. Even in stabilized steels, however, if the region right next to the fusion line reaches very high temperatures, the Ti or Nb carbides dissolve, and later reheating precipitates Cr carbides, so corrosion can advance in a narrow band along the weld line (knife-line attack). Ferritic grades dissolve little carbon and diffusion in them is fast, so they tend to sensitize even while cooling from high temperature.

Whether a steel is sensitized is examined by methods such as electrolytic etching in oxalic acid to see the shape of grooves at grain boundaries, the Strauss test, in which the steel is boiled in a sulfuric acid–copper sulfate solution with copper and checked for cracks on bending, and measuring the current of electrochemical reactivation. Sensitized steel can be restored by solution heat treatment, heating to about 1000 to 1100°C to redissolve the carbides and then quenching. Sensitized grain boundaries are also paths for stress corrosion cracking, and intergranular stress corrosion cracking in the piping of boiling water reactors is known as a case that prompted a review of measures against sensitization.

faq.q: What is the difference between sensitization and weld decay?
faq.a: Sensitization is the term for the condition in which Cr carbides precipitate at grain boundaries, forming Cr-depleted zones and making the steel prone to intergranular corrosion. Weld decay is the phenomenon in which welding heat sensitizes the heat-affected zone and intergranular corrosion occurs in that band. The cause is the same; weld decay is the name for the case that arises from welding.

faq.q: Does using an L grade prevent sensitization?
faq.a: It makes sensitization unlikely during short heating such as welding, but does not prevent it completely. If the steel is held in the sensitization range for a long time, carbides precipitate even with low carbon. For long service at high temperature, choose a stabilized steel or check whether sensitization occurs at the service temperature and time.

faq.q: Do ferritic and martensitic stainless steels also sensitize?
faq.a: Yes. Ferritic grades dissolve little carbon and nitrogen, so Cr carbides and nitrides precipitate at grain boundaries even while cooling from high temperature, and steels with very low carbon and nitrogen or with Ti and Nb added are used. Martensitic grades can also lose corrosion resistance when carbide precipitation at some tempering temperatures depletes Cr.

熱間静水圧プレス.desc: A method that applies an equally high pressure from all directions with an inert gas at high temperature, to densify powder or eliminate closed internal pores in castings and sintered bodies. Abbreviated HIP.

about.p: HIP is a treatment in which parts, or capsules filled with powder, are placed in a pressure vessel and an equal pressure is applied from all directions at high temperature, using an inert gas such as argon as the pressure medium. Pressures of about 100 to 200 MPa are used, with the temperature chosen for each material below its melting point but high enough for diffusion and creep to proceed, held for several hours. Examples are temperatures in the 900s°C for titanium alloys and around 1100 to 1200°C for Ni-based superalloys. Closed internal pores collapse by plastic deformation, creep and diffusion of the surrounding material, and the facing surfaces bond by diffusion and disappear. Because the pressure is equal from all directions, the shape of the part hardly changes.

HIP can only close pores that are closed, that is, not connected to the surface. Gas from the pressure medium enters open pores and balances the pressure inside and out. Sintered bodies are therefore treated after the relative density exceeds roughly 92 to 95% and the pores have closed, and there is also a method that carries out sintering and HIP in succession in one furnace (sinter-HIP). When making parts directly from powder, the powder is packed into a metal capsule, which is evacuated and sealed and then consolidated as a whole. Densifying powder with a packing fraction of 65% to full density shrinks it by about 13% in length, so the capsule shape is designed to allow for this shrinkage.

about.h: How it differs from similar methods
about.p: Isostatic pressing also includes cold isostatic pressing (CIP), which compacts powder in a rubber mold at room temperature using a liquid as the pressure medium. CIP is a forming step that makes the density of the compact uniform, with densification done later by sintering, whereas HIP treats at high temperature and densifies close to full density on the spot. Hot pressing, which applies pressure in one direction to material in a graphite or similar die, uses simpler equipment, but shapes are limited to simple ones such as disks and plates, and density tends to vary with direction. The strength of HIP is that it applies equal pressure even to parts of complex shape.

about.h: Where it is used and its limits
about.p: HIP is widely used to remove internal shrinkage cavities and pores in cast parts for aircraft engines and so reduce scatter in fatigue strength, and it has become indispensable as a post-treatment for parts made by metal additive manufacturing. It is also used in PM-HIP, which makes large near-net-shape parts from powder, and in HIP bonding, which joins different materials by diffusion. However, inclusions such as oxides and pores with oxidized inner surfaces do not bond well even when collapsed and can remain as defects. Because the material is held at high temperature, grain growth and changes in precipitates also occur, so conditions are set together with the heat treatment after HIP.

faq.q: What is the difference between HIP and CIP?
faq.a: Both apply equal pressure from all directions, but HIP uses an inert gas at high temperature as the pressure medium and goes as far as densification, while CIP uses water or oil at room temperature as the pressure medium and forms powder in a rubber mold uniformly. Compacts made by CIP are then densified by sintering.

faq.q: Does HIP remove pores completely?
faq.a: Closed pores mostly collapse to near full density. However, open pores connected to the surface do not collapse, and pores with oxidized inner surfaces may not bond. If gas such as argon was trapped inside pores, they can also swell again when the part is later reheated.

faq.q: How high is the pressure in HIP?
faq.a: Pressures of about 100 to 200 MPa are common, about 1000 to 2000 times atmospheric pressure. If the pressure is too low, pores take a long time to collapse, and if the temperature is too low, the material deforms with difficulty, so temperature, pressure and time are combined for each material.

ギブスエネルギー.desc: A state function defined by G = H − TS. At constant temperature and pressure, changes proceed spontaneously in the direction that lowers G, and the state of minimum G is equilibrium.

about.h: Why G can decide the direction
about.p: What decides the direction of natural change is the increase in entropy of the system and surroundings together. At constant temperature and pressure, the heat −ΔH given off by the system is received by the surroundings at temperature T, so the entropy of the surroundings changes by −ΔH/T. The condition that the total entropy change ΔS − ΔH/T is positive becomes, on multiplying both sides by −T, ΔH − TΔS < 0, that is, ΔG < 0. The Gibbs energy is the quantity that lets the direction of change be decided from properties of the system alone, without considering the surroundings. It is named after the American Gibbs, who laid the foundations of chemical thermodynamics in the 1870s.

The Gibbs energy change of a reaction can be written ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, using the standard-state value ΔG° and the reaction quotient Q, which expresses the actual composition. At equilibrium ΔG = 0, so ΔG° = −RT ln K, and the equilibrium constant K follows from the standard value. At 298 K, K increases tenfold for every roughly 5.7 kJ/mol by which ΔG° becomes more negative, and at 1000 K for every roughly 19.1 kJ/mol. Differences of tens of kJ/mol in ΔG° thus shift the position of equilibrium by many orders of magnitude. Reading oxide stability and equilibrium oxygen partial pressures from Ellingham diagrams is also based on this relation.

A positive ΔG° does not mean a reaction cannot proceed at all. ΔG° is the value when all components are in their standard states; under conditions where products are scarce or gaseous products are continually removed, Q is small, ΔG is negative and the reaction proceeds. Conversely, a negative ΔG does not mean a reaction is fast. At room temperature graphite has a lower Gibbs energy than diamond (the difference is about 2.9 kJ/mol), so diamond is thermodynamically unstable, but the change is so slow that diamond effectively does not transform. The Gibbs energy decides the direction, and kinetics decides the rate.

about.h: Use in phase diagrams and materials design
about.p: In materials science, the Gibbs energy of each phase is expressed as a function of temperature and composition, and phase diagrams are drawn from the phases or combinations of phases that give the lowest G. The melting point of a pure substance is the temperature at which the G of solid and liquid are equal, and for alloys the compositions of coexisting phases are found by drawing common tangents to the G–composition curves of the phases. The CALPHAD method fits expressions for the G of each phase to experimental data and calculates phase diagrams and phase fractions of multicomponent systems. In undercooled liquids and supersaturated solid solutions, the difference in G is the driving force for nucleation and precipitation and the starting point for considering the rates of phase transformations.

faq.q: What is the difference between Gibbs energy and Helmholtz energy?
faq.a: The Gibbs energy G = H − TS is used to decide the direction of change at constant temperature and pressure, and the Helmholtz energy F = U − TS at constant temperature and volume. Experiments and processes with materials are usually carried out at atmospheric pressure, so G is used more often. For solids the difference between the two, pV, is often small.

faq.q: Are Gibbs free energy and Gibbs energy the same thing?
faq.a: Yes. Free energy used to be the usual name, but IUPAC recommends calling it Gibbs energy. Textbooks and papers use both names, so it is safe to take both as referring to G = H − TS.

faq.q: What is the unit of Gibbs energy?
faq.a: Being an energy, its unit is the joule (J). Per amount of substance, J/mol or kJ/mol is used, and the Gibbs energy change of a reaction is usually given in kJ/mol for the reaction as written with its coefficients. The value therefore changes with how the coefficients of the equation are chosen, which needs attention.

エリンガム図.desc: A diagram plotting the standard Gibbs energy change of formation of oxides and similar compounds, normalized per mol of O₂, against temperature. The lower its line, the more stable the oxide a metal forms.

about.h: How the diagram is drawn and the slope of the lines
about.p: An Ellingham diagram takes oxide formation reactions such as 2M + O₂ → 2MO, normalizes the standard Gibbs energy change ΔG° per mol of O₂, and plots it against temperature. Since ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° and ΔH° and ΔS° hardly depend on temperature, each reaction gives a straight line whose slope is −ΔS°. In metal oxidation gaseous O₂ is taken into a solid and ΔS° is negative, so almost all lines slope upward, and oxides become less stable at higher temperature. At the temperatures where a metal or oxide melts or boils, ΔS° changes and the line bends.

At a given temperature, the lower the line, the more negative ΔG° is and the more stable the oxide. The vertical distance between 2 lines equals the ΔG° of the reaction in which the metal of the lower line reduces the oxide of the upper line, so metals near the bottom, such as Al, Mg and Ca, can reduce many oxides. The line for carbon, 2C + O₂ → 2CO, slopes downward because the number of gas molecules increases and ΔS° is positive, and at higher temperatures it lies below the lines of more and more metal oxides. This is why iron ore can be reduced with coke in a blast furnace. Above the temperature where a line crosses ΔG° = 0, the oxide decomposes even in 1 bar of oxygen.

about.h: The oxygen partial pressure scale and how to use it
about.p: At equilibrium ΔG° = RT ln pO₂, so joining a point on a line at a given temperature to the point ΔG° = 0 at 0 K and extending the line lets you read the equilibrium oxygen partial pressure. Many Ellingham diagrams carry an oxygen partial pressure scale for this purpose, and some also have scales for H₂/H₂O and CO/CO₂ ratios. They can be used to estimate the conditions that prevent steel from oxidizing in a heat-treatment atmosphere, whether an oxide decomposes in vacuum, and the conditions under which Cr is selectively oxidized in stainless steel. However, the diagram shows equilibria between pure substances; reaction rates and differences in activity within alloys must be considered separately.

faq.q: Does a metal lower in the Ellingham diagram always reduce the oxides above it?
faq.a: Thermodynamically it can, since the ΔG° of the reaction in that direction is negative, but whether it actually proceeds depends on the reaction rate, the removal of products and the activities. Reactions between solids proceed poorly if contact is poor, and they can stop when the oxide formed covers the surface. There are also examples, such as the thermite reaction, that proceed all at once with a large release of heat.

faq.q: Why is the Ellingham diagram drawn per mol of O₂?
faq.a: Because when the amount of oxygen is the same, taking the difference between 2 formation reactions cancels the O₂, and the vertical distance between the lines is directly the ΔG° of the redox reaction. If it were drawn per mol of oxide, the number of oxygen atoms would differ with the formula, and the lines could not be compared directly. Diagrams for sulfides and nitrides are drawn per mol of S₂ or N₂ on the same idea.

faq.q: Can the rate of oxidation be read from an Ellingham diagram?
faq.a: No. An Ellingham diagram shows the equilibrium ΔG° and only indicates the thermodynamic tendency for an oxide to form. Aluminum corrodes little even though its ΔG° is strongly negative, because a dense oxide film blocks diffusion; the rate is set by kinetics such as diffusion through the film.

平衡酸素分圧.desc: The oxygen partial pressure at which a metal and its oxide coexist in equilibrium. It is found from ΔG° = RT ln pO₂; above it the metal is oxidized, and below it the oxide is reduced.

about.p: For 2M + O₂ → 2MO written per 1 mol of O₂, if the metal and oxide are pure solids, the equilibrium constant is 1/pO₂. From ΔG° = −RT ln K it follows that ΔG° = RT ln pO₂, so the equilibrium oxygen partial pressure is found from the standard value alone. For example, for a reaction with ΔG° = −400 kJ/mol, at 1200 K log pO₂ = −400000/(2.303 × 8.314 × 1200) ≈ −17.4, that is, about 4×10⁻¹⁸ bar. When the metal or oxide is in an alloy or solid solution and its activity is not 1, the activity is included in the equilibrium constant.

about.h: Why metals oxidize even in vacuum
about.p: The equilibrium oxygen partial pressure is extremely low for metals whose oxides are stable. For example, at 1000°C the ΔG° of 4/3 Cr + O₂ → 2/3 Cr₂O₃ is about −530 kJ/mol, and the equilibrium oxygen partial pressure is of the order of 10⁻²² bar. Even in a vacuum of 1 Pa, by contrast, the oxygen partial pressure of the remaining air is as much as about 2×10⁻⁶ bar, far higher. So even in vacuum or in high-purity inert gas, the surfaces of alloys containing Cr, Al, Ti and similar elements oxidize when heated. In bright heat treatment of such metals, reducing gases such as hydrogen are used to lower the effective oxygen partial pressure of the atmosphere.

about.h: Setting the oxygen partial pressure of an atmosphere
about.p: Lowering the oxygen partial pressure directly to something like 10⁻²⁰ bar is difficult, so in practice the oxygen partial pressure of an atmosphere is set by the ratio in mixed gases of H₂/H₂O or CO/CO₂. From the equilibrium 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, fixing the ratio of H₂O to H₂ fixes the oxygen partial pressure at that temperature. In industrial furnaces, the amount of water vapor in hydrogen is controlled through the dew point, and the lower the dew point, the lower the oxygen partial pressure. Which metals oxidize can be judged by comparing the oxygen partial pressure of the atmosphere with each metal's equilibrium oxygen partial pressure, and selective oxidation, in which only the easily oxidized components of an alloy oxidize at the surface, is treated with the same idea.

The oxygen partial pressure in atmospheres and molten metals can be measured with oxygen sensors using a zirconia solid electrolyte. When gases with oxygen partial pressures p₁ and p₂ are on the two sides of the zirconia, oxide ions move and an electromotive force E = (RT/4F) ln(p₁/p₂) arises, where F is the Faraday constant. At 1000 K each order of magnitude difference in oxygen partial pressure gives about 49.6 mV, so with air on the reference side even extremely low oxygen partial pressures can be measured as a voltage. Such sensors are used to control the air–fuel ratio from car exhaust, in probes that measure the oxygen content of molten steel in steelmaking, and to control the atmosphere of heat-treatment furnaces.

faq.q: Are equilibrium oxygen partial pressure and dissociation pressure the same?
faq.a: They refer to the same thing. In the reaction in which an oxide decomposes into metal and oxygen, the oxygen pressure at equilibrium is called the dissociation pressure of the oxide. If the oxygen partial pressure of the atmosphere is below it, the oxide decomposes (is reduced); if above, the metal oxidizes. The equilibrium pressure of the gas from decomposing carbonates and similar compounds is also called the dissociation pressure.

faq.q: How does the equilibrium oxygen partial pressure change with temperature?
faq.a: For most metal oxidation reactions ΔS° is negative, so as temperature rises ΔG° approaches 0 and the equilibrium oxygen partial pressure increases. In other words, oxides decompose more readily at higher temperature. For example, raising the temperature from 1000 K to 1200 K increases the equilibrium oxygen partial pressure of Ni/NiO by about four orders of magnitude.

faq.q: How does the equilibrium oxygen partial pressure change for a metal in an alloy?
faq.a: Because the activity of the metal is less than 1, the oxygen partial pressure in equilibrium with the oxide is higher than for the pure metal. In other words, a metal in an alloy oxidizes less readily in the same atmosphere than the pure metal. Conversely, when the oxide is in a solid solution and its activity is small, the oxide forms more readily.

活量.desc: The thermodynamic effective concentration of a component in a solution or solid solution, satisfying μ = μ° + RT ln a. It is 1 for the pure substance and equals the mole fraction in an ideal solution.

about.p: When the chemical potential of component i in a solution is written μi = μi° + RT ln ai, ai is the activity. μi° is the chemical potential in the reference state; in materials science the pure solid or liquid at the same temperature is often taken as the reference (ai = 1), and for gases the partial pressure divided by the standard pressure corresponds to the activity. In an ideal solution ai = xi (the mole fraction) by Raoult's law, and for real solutions one writes ai = γi·xi, with the activity coefficient γi expressing the deviation from ideality. Equilibrium constant expressions contain activities in place of concentrations.

When unlike atoms attract each other more weakly than like atoms, the component escapes from the solution more easily, giving γ > 1 (positive deviation from Raoult's law), and in extreme cases the solution separates into 2 phases. Conversely, when unlike atoms attract strongly, γ < 1 (negative deviation), indicating a tendency toward ordering or compound formation. In the regular solution model, it can be written RT ln γA = Ω(1 − xA)² using the interaction parameter Ω. In the dilute range of a solute, γ becomes nearly constant, and Henry's law, in which activity is proportional to concentration, holds.

The equilibrium of metal oxidation 2M + O₂ → 2MO is expressed by ΔG° = −RT ln K with K = a(MO)² ÷ (a(M)² × pO₂). If the activity of metal M in an alloy is less than 1, the equilibrium oxygen partial pressure is higher for the same ΔG°, and M becomes harder to oxidize. Conversely, if the oxide formed dissolves in another oxide and its activity falls, oxidation proceeds more easily. Removing impurity oxides by dissolving them into slag in smelting, and finding the amount of hydrogen or nitrogen dissolved in a molten metal from the gas partial pressure (Sieverts' law), are also based on equilibrium thinking with activities.

faq.q: How is activity different from concentration?
faq.a: Concentration expresses how much of a component is present, while activity expresses how strongly that component acts in chemical reactions and phase equilibria. In an ideal solution the mole fraction and activity coincide, but in real solutions with atomic interactions they differ by the activity coefficient. It is activity that is used in the expressions for equilibrium constants and chemical potentials.

faq.q: Why is the activity of a pure solid 1?
faq.a: Because the pure solid itself is chosen as the reference state. If the chemical potential of the reference state is μ°, then for the pure substance μ = μ°, so ln a = 0, that is, a = 1. Choosing another reference changes the value, but in equilibrium calculations ΔG° is put on the same reference, so the result does not change.

faq.q: Can activity exceed 1?
faq.a: With the pure substance as the reference, it does not exceed 1 in a solution in stable equilibrium. If it did, the free energy would be lowered by precipitating that component as the pure substance. In supersaturated states, or with another reference based on Henry's law (such as a dilute 1 wt% solution), values above 1 can occur.

化学ポテンシャル.desc: The rate at which the Gibbs energy of a system increases when 1 mol of a component is added (the partial molar Gibbs energy). In phase equilibrium, the chemical potential of each component is equal in all phases.

about.p: The chemical potential is the rate at which the Gibbs energy increases when a little of component i is added at constant temperature, pressure and amounts of the other components, µᵢ = (∂G/∂nᵢ). Its unit is J/mol. Moving a small amount of a component from phase α to phase β changes G by (µᵢ(β) − µᵢ(α)) × the amount moved, so components tend to move from where their chemical potential is high to where it is low. Just as a difference in electric potential drives charge and a difference in temperature drives heat, a difference in chemical potential is the driving force that moves matter. For a pure substance, the chemical potential equals the Gibbs energy per mole.

about.h: Relation to activity and reading it from a diagram
about.p: The chemical potential of a component in a solution can be written µ = µ° + RT ln a, using its value in the reference state µ° and the activity a. For an ideal gas a = p/p°, and for an ideal solution a = x. For a binary solution, if G per mole is plotted against composition and a tangent is drawn at a given composition, the values where the tangent meets the vertical axes at x = 0 and x = 1 are the chemical potentials of the components. The chemical potentials of the two components also cannot be changed independently; they are linked by the Gibbs–Duhem equation x_A dµ_A + x_B dµ_B = 0, so measuring the activity of one gives the other.

Diffusion usually proceeds from high to low concentration, but the true driving force is the gradient in chemical potential. In 1949 Darken showed that when two steels with almost the same carbon concentration but different silicon contents are joined and heated, carbon moves into the side with less silicon, creating a large difference in carbon concentration near the interface. Silicon raises the activity of carbon, so carbon on the silicon-rich side had a higher chemical potential and escaped from it. Uphill diffusion in spinodal decomposition is another example of atoms moving because of differences in chemical potential rather than concentration.

The chemical potential also changes with particle size and charge. For a particle of radius r, the surface energy γ raises the chemical potential by 2γV_m/r, where V_m is the molar volume. Supposing γ = 1 J/m² and V_m = 1×10⁻⁵ m³/mol, at r = 10 nm it is about 2 kJ/mol higher, and the solubility into the surroundings at 1000 K is about 1.27 times that at a flat surface. Ostwald ripening, in which small particles dissolve and large ones grow, is driven by this difference. For charged particles, the electrochemical potential, which adds a term for electric potential, is used, and for electrons in a solid this corresponds to the Fermi level.

faq.q: What is the difference between chemical potential and Gibbs energy?
faq.a: The Gibbs energy belongs to the whole system and is proportional to the amount of material. The chemical potential is how much it increases when 1 mol of a component is added; it is also called the partial molar Gibbs energy and is an intensive quantity independent of amount. The G of the whole system is the sum of the products of each component's amount and chemical potential, G = Σnᵢµᵢ.

faq.q: What is the unit of chemical potential?
faq.a: As an energy per mole, it is J/mol. In physics it is sometimes given as an energy per particle, for example in eV, in which case it is the value in J/mol divided by the Avogadro constant. 1 eV per particle corresponds to about 96.5 kJ/mol.

faq.q: How does chemical potential change with temperature?
faq.a: At constant pressure, its rate of change with temperature is minus the partial molar entropy, so the chemical potential falls as temperature rises, and falls faster for phases of higher entropy. So even if the solid has the lower chemical potential at low temperature, at high temperature the liquid or gas has the lower value, and melting or evaporation occurs.

正則溶液.desc: A solution model in which the entropy of mixing is the same as for an ideal solution and the enthalpy of mixing is Ωx(1 − x). When Ω is positive, a miscibility gap appears at low temperature.

about.p: The regular solution is a model that assumes atoms mix randomly, so that the entropy of mixing is the same as for an ideal solution, and adds only the enthalpy of mixing from bonds between unlike atoms. Hildebrand named it in 1929. Considering only bonds between nearest neighbors, the interaction parameter is Ω = zN_A[ε_AB − (ε_AA + ε_BB)/2], where z is the number of nearest neighbors and ε the energy of each bond. If unlike bonds are weaker than the average of like bonds, Ω is positive and atoms of the same kind tend to cluster. If they are stronger, Ω is negative, showing a tendency toward ordering, in which unlike atoms sit next to each other.

about.h: Activity coefficients and the miscibility gap
about.p: In a regular solution, the activity coefficient of component A is given by RT ln γ_A = Ω x_B². For example, with Ω = 10 kJ/mol at 1000 K, γ_A ≈ 1.35 at x_B = 0.5 and γ_A ≈ 3.33 in the limit where A is very dilute, so the activity is larger than in an ideal solution. When Ω is positive and the temperature is low enough, a miscibility gap appears. The critical temperature at its top is Tc = Ω/(2R). At T = 0.8Tc, the compositions of the two coexisting phases are x ≈ 0.145 and 0.855, and the spinodal compositions are x ≈ 0.276 and 0.724.

The regular solution is an inconsistent approximation in that it assumes atoms mix randomly even though they interact. When the magnitude of Ω is large compared with RT, short-range order actually forms in which like or unlike atoms gather, and the entropy of mixing is smaller than for an ideal solution. In real alloys, Ω also changes with temperature and composition, and miscibility gaps are often not symmetric. More precise treatments therefore use the quasi-chemical approximation or subregular solution expressions that extend Ω to a polynomial in composition. Even so, the value of this model is that it shows the tendency toward phase separation or ordering with a single number.

about.h: Links to CALPHAD and experimental data
about.p: In the CALPHAD method, the excess Gibbs energy of a solution phase is expressed by a Redlich–Kister polynomial of the form x_A x_B Σ L_k (x_A − x_B)^k, whose first term L₀ corresponds to Ω of the regular solution. Ω can be obtained from calorimetric measurements of the heat of mixing, from activities measured by vapor pressure or electromotive force, from the shape of miscibility gaps and so on. It is also sometimes estimated from bond energies found by empirical methods or first-principles calculations. For systems with a miscibility gap in the solid solution, such as Fe-Cr, the regular solution approach gives a rough estimate of the range of temperature and composition where phase separation occurs.

faq.q: What is the difference between a regular solution and an ideal solution?
faq.a: An ideal solution has zero enthalpy of mixing and mixes through the entropy of mixing alone. A regular solution keeps the entropy of mixing of an ideal solution and adds an enthalpy of mixing Ωx(1 − x). With Ω = 0, a regular solution reduces to an ideal solution.

faq.q: What happens when Ω is negative?
faq.a: Unlike atoms attract, so the enthalpy of mixing is negative and no miscibility gap forms at any temperature. The activity coefficients are less than 1 and the activities lower than in an ideal solution. In systems where Ω is strongly negative, superlattices and intermetallic compounds actually form readily, and the assumption of random mixing no longer holds.

faq.q: What shape is the miscibility gap of a regular solution?
faq.a: Because the enthalpy of mixing has the form x(1 − x), symmetric in composition, the gap is also symmetric about x = 0.5, with its top at x = 0.5 and T = Ω/(2R). In real alloys the gap is often asymmetric, and then it is described by expressions in which Ω varies with composition.

混合エントロピー.desc: The entropy that arises because mixing increases the number of ways atoms can be arranged. In an ideal solution it is −R[x ln x + (1 − x) ln(1 − x)], with its maximum at x = 0.5.

about.p: The number of ways to place N_A atoms of A and N_B atoms of B on the lattice sites of a crystal is W = N!/(N_A!N_B!), while a pure substance can be arranged in only one way. Applying Stirling's approximation to Boltzmann's formula S = k ln W gives the entropy of mixing per mole as ΔS_mix = −R[x ln x + (1 − x) ln(1 − x)]. This is configurational entropy and does not include entropy from atomic vibrations or magnetism. It takes its maximum value R ln 2 ≈ 5.76 J/(mol·K) at x = 0.5. The same form of expression applies to mixing ideal gases.

about.h: Small amounts of solute and the effect of temperature
about.p: The entropy of mixing is not negligible even for small amounts of solute. For example, at x = 0.01, ΔS_mix ≈ 0.47 J/(mol·K), which at 1000 K lowers the Gibbs energy by −TΔS_mix ≈ −470 J/mol. As x approaches 0, the slope of the curve becomes infinitely steep, so even sparingly soluble elements always dissolve to a tiny extent, and removing impurities becomes harder the closer purity is pushed to its limit. Because the entropy of mixing acts on G in the form −TΔS, the drive toward mixing is stronger at higher temperature, which is why in many alloys the solubility limit widens at higher temperatures.

Mixing equal amounts of n elements gives an entropy of mixing of R ln n; for five elements it is R ln 5 ≈ 13.4 J/(mol·K) (about 1.61R). Since around 2004, alloys containing many principal elements in nearly equal proportions have been studied as high-entropy alloys. The name comes from the idea that a large entropy of mixing suppresses the formation of intermetallic compounds and stabilizes simple solid solutions, and one definition calls alloys with an entropy of mixing of 1.5R or more high-entropy alloys. In practice, however, many cases have been found in which compounds or multiple phases form because of the enthalpy of mixing and differences in atomic size.

about.h: Smaller for polymers and ordered alloys
about.p: When long-chain polymers are mixed, the atoms in each chain move together while connected, so the number of arrangements is far smaller than for small molecules of the same mass. In Flory–Huggins theory, the entropy of mixing becomes smaller in inverse proportion to the degree of polymerization, which is why polymer blends phase-separate readily even with a slightly positive heat of mixing. Also, when an alloy orders, the positions of atoms become fixed, so its configurational entropy becomes smaller and reaches 0 for complete order. Order–disorder transformations can be understood as a competition between enthalpy, which favors order at low temperature, and the entropy of mixing, which wins at high temperature.

faq.q: What is the maximum entropy of mixing?
faq.a: For ideal mixing of two components it is largest at x = 0.5, where its value is R ln 2 ≈ 5.76 J/(mol·K). For n components mixed in equal amounts it is R ln n, which grows as the number of components increases, but only slowly because the growth is logarithmic.

faq.q: Does the entropy of mixing change with temperature?
faq.a: The configurational entropy of an ideal solution depends only on composition, not on temperature. Its contribution to the Gibbs energy, however, is −TΔS_mix, so its effect grows with temperature. In real solutions the degree of short-range order changes with temperature, so the entropy of mixing also changes somewhat with temperature.

faq.q: If the entropy of mixing is positive, do substances always mix?
faq.a: Not always. Whether they mix is decided by the Gibbs energy of mixing ΔH_mix − TΔS_mix, and if the enthalpy of mixing is large and positive, separation is more stable at low temperature. If ΔH_mix = 0, as in an ideal solution, they mix at every composition.

スピノーダル分解.desc: Phase separation into 2 phases at compositions where the free energy curve is convex upward, in which composition fluctuations grow without a nucleation barrier. Uphill diffusion produces a periodic structure.

about.p: A solid solution quenched into a miscibility gap can separate into two phases by two routes. At compositions where the G–composition curve is concave upward, small composition fluctuations raise G, so separation does not start until nuclei above a certain size form, and it proceeds by nucleation and growth. At compositions where it is convex upward (d²G/dx² < 0), even the smallest fluctuations lower G, so they simply grow. This is spinodal decomposition: at first the composition undulates smoothly, and with time the amplitude grows and approaches the compositions of the two phases. A feature is that there is no waiting time as in nucleation, and the microstructure forms uniformly throughout.

about.h: Theory and the scale of the microstructure
about.p: The theory of spinodal decomposition was built up from the late 1950s into the 1960s by Cahn, Hilliard and others. The growth rate of fluctuations depends on wavelength: long wavelengths grow slowly because atoms must move far, and short wavelengths do not grow because the energy from sharp changes in composition (gradient energy) is large. One wavelength therefore grows fastest, producing microstructures with periods of a few to tens of nanometers. In crystals, the elastic strain energy from differences in lattice constant between regions of different composition also opposes decomposition, so the actual boundary (the coherent spinodal) lies at a lower temperature than the chemical spinodal.

Microstructures from spinodal decomposition often consist of two interwoven phases forming continuous networks, seen in transmission electron microscopy as striped or mottled contrast. In X-ray diffraction, small peaks called satellites appear on both sides of the main reflections, corresponding to the periodic variation in composition. Small-angle scattering also shows a scattering maximum at the position corresponding to the period. Recently, atom probes have been used to examine the three-dimensional distribution of atoms and to distinguish spinodal decomposition from nucleation by whether the compositional amplitude grows with time. Often, however, the form of the microstructure alone cannot decide which mechanism operated.

Spinodal decomposition is used to build properties into materials. In Fe-Cr-Co magnets and alnico magnets, heat treatment in a magnetic field aligns the ferromagnetic phase into elongated shapes, and shape anisotropy provides coercivity. Cu-Ni-Sn alloys are strengthened by spinodal decomposition and used for springs and connectors. Heat-treating borosilicate glass to separate it into two phases and dissolving one with acid gives porous silica glass. On the other hand, the ferrite phase of duplex stainless steels becomes brittle by spinodal decomposition during long service at roughly 300 to 500°C, the so-called 475°C embrittlement, so upper limits are set on the service temperature.

faq.q: What is the difference between the spinodal and the solubility line (binodal)?
faq.a: The solubility line is the boundary of compositions where two phases determined by the common tangent coexist in equilibrium; inside it, separation into two phases is more stable. The spinodal is the boundary where d²G/dx² = 0 and lies inside the solubility line. Between the two, phase separation proceeds by nucleation and growth, and inside the spinodal by spinodal decomposition.

faq.q: In which materials does spinodal decomposition occur?
faq.a: It occurs in systems with a miscibility gap in the solid solution. Besides alloys such as Fe-Cr, Cu-Ni-Fe, Cu-Ni-Sn, Au-Ni and Al-Zn, it is known in borosilicate glasses and polymer blends. The condition is that the material can be quenched to a temperature inside the spinodal before nucleation occurs.

faq.q: How does a spinodal microstructure change with time?
faq.a: At first the compositional amplitude grows and the compositions of the two phases approach their equilibrium values. After that the microstructure coarsens to reduce interfacial area, and the period becomes longer. There is therefore a time and temperature that give the best strength or magnetic properties, and the scale of the microstructure is adjusted through the aging conditions.

生体適合性.desc: The ability of a material to perform the required function in a specific application with an appropriate host response. It is evaluated including not only the material but also its shape, surface condition and location of use.

about.p: Biocompatibility is defined as "the ability of a material to perform with an appropriate host response in a specific application". In the past the emphasis was on not reacting and doing no harm in the body, but as materials that exploit active responses of the body increased, such as ceramics that bond to bone and polymers that are resorbed and replaced by tissue, it came to be judged by whether the desired response occurs for the application. Even the same material faces different requirements inside bone, in contact with blood and on the skin, so biocompatibility is an evaluation of a combination of material and application.

about.h: Host responses and the classification of materials
about.p: When a material is placed in the body, proteins first adsorb on its surface, and cells respond on top of them. Around bioinert materials a thin fibrous membrane often forms, separating the material from the surrounding tissue. Bioactive materials bond chemically to bone at their surface, and bioresorbable materials gradually degrade and are replaced by tissue. For materials in contact with blood, hemocompatibility, which suppresses platelet adhesion and thrombus formation, is important. Released ions and wear debris can cause inflammation or allergy, so not only the surface but also what is produced by degradation is evaluated.

Biocompatibility is evaluated by combining cytotoxicity tests, in which cells are exposed to the material or its extract, tests for sensitizing (allergic) and irritant reactions, genotoxicity tests, implantation tests in animals and others, and the framework is set out in the international standard for the biological evaluation of medical devices (the ISO 10993 series). Which tests are needed depends on the part of the body contacted and the duration. For implants, mechanical compatibility also matters: too little strength leads to failure, and too much stiffness relative to bone thins the bone by stress shielding. Only when both chemical safety and mechanical properties are in place is biocompatibility achieved for that application.

faq.q: Is a biocompatible material safe wherever it is used?
faq.a: No. Biocompatibility is an evaluation for each application, so a material that works without problems in bone may form thrombi where it contacts blood. The shape, surface condition, duration of use, wear debris and ion release also affect the outcome, so it must be confirmed for each application.

faq.q: Is a material more biocompatible the less it reacts in the body?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Some applications, such as the femoral heads of artificial joints, are best served by no reaction, but bioactive materials that bond to bone work well as bone defect fillers, and materials that are resorbed and disappear work well as sutures. Biocompatibility requires that the response needed in that application occurs.

faq.q: Why is titanium used so widely as a biomaterial?
faq.a: Because the TiO₂ passive film on its surface is stable in body fluids and gives high corrosion resistance, and because osseointegration, in which bone contacts the surface directly, occurs. Its high specific strength and its lower Young's modulus than stainless steel or Co-Cr alloys are also advantages.

応力遮蔽.desc: A phenomenon in which an implant far stiffer than bone carries most of the load, the mechanical stimulus to the surrounding bone falls, and the bone is resorbed and thins.

about.p: When bone and an implant are joined and carry a load together, both strain by nearly the same amount, so the stress is shared in proportion to Young's modulus. The Young's modulus of cortical bone is about 10–30 GPa, whereas stainless steel is about 200 GPa, Co-Cr alloys about 210 GPa and Ti-6Al-4V about 110 GPa. When a high-modulus metal carries most of the load, the stress on the surrounding bone becomes smaller than it should be. From the bone's point of view the load is shielded, so the phenomenon is called stress shielding. It is a problem with the stems of artificial hip joints and with plates that fix fractures.

Bone changes the balance of formation and resorption according to the mechanical stimulus it receives, becoming thicker where it is used heavily and thinner where it is not (Wolff's law). Where stress shielding reduces the stimulus, resorption outpaces formation, bone density falls and the bone thins. As a result, loosening develops between implant and bone, or the bone becomes prone to fracture after the implant is removed. The weakening of bone during long bed rest or in weightlessness has the same mechanism. In artificial hip joints, bone loss is often said to be most noticeable near the upper end of the femur.

The basic remedy is to bring the stiffness of the implant closer to that of bone. On the materials side, β titanium alloys with a Young's modulus of about 55–80 GPa and porous metals whose modulus is lowered by pores have been developed. The Young's modulus of a porous body with open pores falls roughly with the square of the relative density, and bone growing into the pores also strengthens fixation. On the shape side, stems are made thinner and shorter, or designed to transfer load at a position close to the bone. However, lowering the stiffness too far risks implant deformation and fatigue failure, so it is decided in balance with strength.

faq.q: If the aim is a lower Young's modulus, why not make implants from polymers?
faq.a: Polymers often have a Young's modulus too far below that of bone, or cannot withstand the load in terms of strength, creep and fatigue, so on their own they are unsuitable for sites that carry large loads. Composites whose modulus is brought close to that of bone, such as carbon-fiber-reinforced PEEK, are used in spinal fixation devices and similar applications.

faq.q: Is stress shielding a change that makes bone stronger?
faq.a: No, the opposite. The implant takes over the load, so the stimulus to the bone falls, and the bone is resorbed and weakens. It is the opposite problem to bone failing under excessive stress.

faq.q: How is stress shielding investigated?
faq.a: Clinically, changes in bone mass around the implant are followed with X-ray images and bone density measurements. At the design stage, the stress distribution in bone and implant is calculated by the finite element method, and the drop in bone stress compared with the case without an implant is evaluated.

ハイドロキシアパタイト.desc: A calcium phosphate with the formula Ca₁₀(PO₄)₆(OH)₂. Close to the mineral component of bones and teeth, it is used as a bioactive ceramic that bonds directly to bone. Its Ca/P ratio is 1.67.

about.h: Relation to the mineral of bone and teeth
about.p: Hydroxyapatite is a hexagonal crystal in which Ca²⁺, PO₄³⁻ and OH⁻ are arranged regularly. The mineral of bone is an apatite close to it, but it contains carbonate ions, magnesium, sodium and other ions, and consists of plate-like crystallites a few tens of nm long aligned along the collagen fibers. Tooth enamel is more than 90% mineral by mass, with larger, denser crystals. Synthetic hydroxyapatite is close to stoichiometric and has larger crystals, so it is less soluble than bone apatite. The way synthetic materials become integrated with bone owes much to this closeness in composition.

When hydroxyapatite is placed in a bone defect, slight dissolution and reprecipitation occur at its surface, and a layer of apatite similar to that of bone forms from the calcium and phosphate in body fluid. Bone-forming cells act on this layer and new bone forms, so the material and bone bond without a fibrous membrane in between. Bioactive glasses and some glass-ceramics likewise form an apatite layer on their surface and bond to bone. A common way to predict whether a material can bond to bone is to soak it in simulated body fluid, whose ion concentrations are close to human blood plasma, and see whether apatite forms on the surface, but this is only a guide.

about.h: Weakness in strength and how it is used
about.p: Even densely sintered hydroxyapatite has a low fracture toughness of about 1 MPa·√m and is brittle, so it cannot carry large loads on its own. It is therefore used as a filler for bone defects that carry no load, as porous bodies that bone can grow into, and as thin coatings on titanium alloy stems and dental implants. Coatings are often made by plasma spraying; if part of the material decomposes or becomes amorphous at the high temperature, it dissolves more easily in the body, so crystallinity and adhesion strength are controlled. The metal provides the strength and the coating provides the bond to bone.

There are many calcium phosphate compounds with different Ca/P ratios. Hydroxyapatite (Ca/P = 1.67) is the least soluble in body fluid near neutral pH and remains in the body for a long time. β-TCP (1.50) is more soluble and is gradually resorbed and replaced by bone. In biphasic calcium phosphates, which mix the two, the rate of resorption can be adjusted through the mixing ratio. In synthesis, if the Ca/P ratio of the powder deviates from 1.67, other phases form on firing, so the phases are checked by X-ray diffraction. Bone defect fillers are chosen among these according to how long they should remain.

faq.q: How are hydroxyapatite and β-TCP used differently?
faq.a: As a rule, hydroxyapatite is used where the material should keep its shape for a long time and bond to bone, and as coatings on metals, while β-TCP is used for bone defects where the material should be resorbed and replaced by the patient's own bone. The two are sometimes mixed to give an intermediate rate of resorption.

faq.q: Why are artificial joints not made of hydroxyapatite alone?
faq.a: Its fracture toughness is low, about 1 MPa·√m, and it is brittle, so it could crack under large repeated loads such as walking. The load is carried by metals such as titanium alloys, and hydroxyapatite is used as a surface coating or as a filler in places that carry no load.

faq.q: Is bone apatite the same as synthetic hydroxyapatite?
faq.a: They belong to the same crystal structure, but bone apatite contains carbonate and other ions, has a Ca/P ratio below 1.67 and consists of nanometer-sized crystals. It is therefore more soluble than synthetic stoichiometric hydroxyapatite and is repeatedly resorbed and formed in the metabolism of bone.

オッセオインテグレーション.desc: A state in which living bone and the implant surface are in direct contact without intervening fibrous tissue and can transfer load. It was discovered with titanium dental implants.

about.p: Osseointegration is a phenomenon found by Brånemark in Sweden in the 1950s, when titanium observation chambers placed in rabbit bone became so firmly united with the bone that they could not be removed. It is defined as a state in which living bone and the implant surface are in direct contact, without fibrous tissue between them at the magnification of the light microscope, and can transmit load. Building on this idea, clinical use of titanium dental implants began in the 1960s. Today the same idea is also used in orthopedics, for example in fixing artificial joints without cement.

Whether osseointegration is achieved is not decided by the material alone. The surface properties, a surgical technique that does not damage the bone, and the way load is applied during healing must all be right. Heat when drilling bone is a major enemy: it has been reported that bone cells are damaged if the bone is held at about 47 °C for only about 1 minute, so drilling is done slowly with cooling. If the implant moves a lot relative to the bone early in healing, it becomes surrounded by fibrous tissue instead of bone. Micromotion beyond roughly 50–150 µm is generally said to hinder bone formation, so good fixation right after placement (primary stability) is important.

The osseointegration of titanium refers mainly to a state in which bone and surface are in direct contact and interlock, and it is distinguished from bioactivity, in which bone bonds chemically through an apatite layer formed on the surface, as with hydroxyapatite and bioactive glass. However, the titanium surface is also covered by a thin passive film of TiO₂ that adsorbs calcium and phosphate from body fluid, so the boundary between the two is not entirely clear. It is known that treating the surface with acid or moderately roughening it by blasting increases the fraction of bone contact and shortens the healing period.

In animal studies, the implant is removed together with the bone, sections are prepared, and the fraction of the surface length in direct contact with bone (bone-implant contact) is measured. Clinically, the strength of fixation is evaluated from the torque needed to turn the implant or from the resonance frequency of a small transducer attached to it. Once achieved, osseointegration is not necessarily maintained forever. In dentistry, bone can be lost through peri-implantitis, a bacterial inflammation around the implant, and excessive load can also cause bone resorption. Cleaning and control of load are conditions for long service.

faq.q: How long does osseointegration take?
faq.a: In Brånemark's original protocol, the guideline was to wait without load for about 3 months in the lower jaw and about 6 months in the upper jaw. The period depends on bone quality and surface treatment, and with roughened implants or good primary stability, protocols that load the implant earlier are also used.

faq.q: Does it occur with materials other than titanium?
faq.a: Yes. Direct contact of bone without intervening fibrous tissue has also been reported for tantalum, niobium, zirconia ceramics and others. Titanium and its alloys are the most widely used because they combine strength, corrosion resistance, ease of processing and a long clinical record.

faq.q: Why does an implant feel different from a natural tooth?
faq.a: A natural tooth is attached to bone through a thin fibrous tissue, the periodontal ligament, which lets it move slightly to cushion impacts and senses biting forces. An osseointegrated implant is fixed directly to bone with no periodontal ligament, so it hardly moves and its sensation differs from that of a natural tooth.

β型チタン合金.desc: A titanium alloy containing large amounts of β-stabilizing elements such as Nb, Ta and Mo, so that it has the BCC β phase even at room temperature. Its low Young's modulus reduces stress shielding in medical use.

about.h: Phases of titanium and β-stabilizing elements
