about.p: Pure titanium has the HCP α phase below 882 °C and the BCC β phase above it. Mo, V, Nb and Ta dissolve widely in the β phase and lower the transformation temperature, while Fe, Cr and others act as eutectoid-type β stabilizers. When enough of these elements is added, the β phase is retained to room temperature on quenching or air cooling, and such alloys are called β titanium alloys. Most are metastable at room temperature, and aging precipitates fine α phase and other phases. Al, O and N, on the other hand, stabilize the α phase, and Ti-6Al-4V is an α+β alloy consisting of the two phases. Which phase dominates changes the properties greatly.

about.h: Why the Young's modulus is low
about.p: The Young's modulus of β alloys is about 55–80 GPa for biomedical compositions, lower than the roughly 110 GPa of Ti-6Al-4V. The closer the composition of the BCC β phase is to the limit at which it can exist stably, the lower its resistance to deformation that shears atomic planes, and the lower its Young's modulus. Tuning the composition so that the β phase is only just retained therefore gives a low Young's modulus. Ti-Nb-Ta-Zr and Ti-Mo alloys are examples. They still do not reach bone (about 10–30 GPa), but compared with stainless steel (about 200 GPa) or Co-Cr alloys they are much closer to bone.

about.h: Heat treatment and the balance of modulus and strength
about.p: A β alloy that has only been solution treated and quenched has a low Young's modulus but not very high strength. Aging to precipitate fine α phase raises the strength greatly, but because the α phase has a higher Young's modulus, the overall modulus also rises. Aging at lower temperatures can also form a fine phase called the ω phase, which raises the Young's modulus and causes embrittlement. For biomedical use, therefore, cold working and aging conditions are chosen to adjust the microstructure so that the required strength and fatigue strength are obtained while keeping the Young's modulus low. Combining low modulus with strength is at the heart of alloy design.

Because β alloys are BCC, they are easy to cold work and can be heat treated to high strength, so they have also been used for aircraft springs and fasteners and for sheet that is formed cold. For biomedical use, another advantage is that compositions can avoid V and Al and be made of elements regarded as having low cytotoxicity, such as Nb, Ta and Zr. On the other hand, Nb and Ta are heavy and expensive elements, which raise density and cost. Like titanium alloys in general, they also have poor wear resistance and are unsuitable for sliding parts. Ni-free superelastic and shape memory alloys are also being studied in β-type Ti-Nb and related systems.

faq.q: What is the difference between α, α+β and β alloys?
faq.a: The classification is by which phase mainly makes up the alloy at room temperature. α alloys consist of the HCP α phase and excel in high-temperature strength, creep strength and weldability. The α+β alloy Ti-6Al-4V balances strength and workability well and is the most widely used. β alloys are BCC, easy to cold work, can be heat treated to high strength and can have a low Young's modulus.

faq.q: Why are alloys without V and Al sought for biomedical use?
faq.a: Because concerns have been raised about the cytotoxicity of V and about the effects of Al on the nervous system in Ti-6Al-4V. Problems have not been confirmed in normal use, but for implants left in the body for a long time, alloys using elements regarded as having small effects if they dissolve, such as Nb, Ta and Zr, have been developed.

faq.q: Can the Young's modulus of a β titanium alloy be made equal to that of bone?
faq.a: Not as a dense alloy: even the lowest-modulus compositions are about 40–50 GPa and cannot reach the roughly 10–30 GPa of cortical bone. To get closer, this is combined with making a porous body whose pores lower the Young's modulus. Increasing porosity also lowers strength, however, so the two are balanced.

超弾性.desc: The property, above the reverse transformation finish temperature, of recovering large strains of several percent on unloading through stress-induced martensitic transformation and its reverse. Ni-Ti alloys are the typical example.

about.p: When a superelastic alloy is loaded in tension above Af, the parent phase first deforms elastically in the ordinary way, and at a certain stress a flat region (plateau) appears in which large strain develops at almost constant stress. This is the range in which the parent phase transforms to stress-induced martensite. On unloading, the martensite reverts to the parent phase along a plateau at a lower stress, and the strain returns almost to zero. The difference in stress between the loading and unloading plateaus is called hysteresis, and in each cycle an energy corresponding to the area enclosed by the curve is lost as heat.

The plateau stress depends strongly on temperature: the higher the temperature, the more stable the parent phase, so a larger stress is needed for transformation. This relation is expressed by the Clausius–Clapeyron equation, and for Ni-Ti the plateau stress is reported to rise by a few MPa per K (roughly 5–8 MPa/K). At or above the temperature Md, where the stress needed for transformation exceeds the stress for slip, slip occurs instead of transformation and the strain no longer recovers. Superelasticity can therefore be used between Af and Md. The transformation temperatures of Ni-Ti change greatly with slight differences in Ni content, so they are tuned precisely through composition and heat treatment.

about.h: Difference from the shape memory effect and ordinary elasticity
about.p: If the same alloy is deformed in the martensitic state below Mf, the strain remains after unloading, and the shape recovers when it is heated above Af. This is the shape memory effect; the difference from superelasticity is whether the reverse transformation is caused by removing the stress or by heating. Also, while the elastic strain limit of most metallic materials is less than 1%, superelasticity recovers strains of about 6–8%. The essential difference is that the strain arises not from stretching interatomic distances, as in ordinary elasticity, but from a change of crystal structure. A nearly constant force partway through deformation is also a feature that ordinary elastic bodies lack.

In orthodontic wires, the stress on the unloading plateau is nearly constant, so the force on the teeth changes little even as the teeth move and the strain decreases. Self-expanding stents are folded thin, carried into a blood vessel by a catheter and, when pushed out, expand to their original diameter and hold the vessel open with a constant force. For this, Af is set below body temperature. Guidewires and the files used in root canal treatment exploit the fact that they recover even after large bending. On the other hand, evaluation of long-term reliability, such as fatigue under repeated deformation and surface treatments that suppress Ni release, is essential.

faq.q: What is the difference between superelasticity and the shape memory effect?
faq.a: Both come from martensitic transformation and its reverse. Superelasticity is used above Af, and the shape recovers simply on unloading; the shape memory effect involves deforming below Mf and recovering the shape by heating. Even in the same Ni-Ti alloy, which one appears depends on the relation between the service temperature and the transformation temperatures.

faq.q: How far can a superelastic alloy be bent and still recover?
faq.a: For Ni-Ti the limit of recoverable strain is about 6–8%. Beyond this, dislocation slip occurs even in the martensite and permanent strain remains. Above Md superelasticity itself does not occur, so the range of service temperature also needs attention.

faq.q: How are the transformation temperatures measured?
faq.a: The usual method is differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), which gives Ms, Mf, As and Af from the exothermic and endothermic peaks accompanying transformation on heating and cooling. For products, Af is also found by bending a specimen at low temperature, heating it and finding the temperature at which its shape has fully recovered.

生分解性高分子.desc: A polymer broken down in the body or the environment by hydrolysis or the action of microorganisms. Polylactic acid and polyglycolic acid are used in absorbable sutures and bone fixation devices.

about.h: Two meanings: in the body and in the environment
about.p: The term biodegradable polymer is used in two settings. In medicine it means materials that are broken down and absorbed in the body, also called bioresorbable materials. Typical examples are poly(lactic acid) (PLA), poly(glycolic acid) (PGA), their copolymer PLGA and polycaprolactone (PCL), used for sutures, bone fixation devices and carriers that release drugs gradually. In the environmental field it means plastics broken down by microorganisms ultimately to carbon dioxide, water and the like. The difference is that degradation in the body proceeds mainly by hydrolysis by water, whereas in the environment the action of microbial enzymes plays a large part.

In hydrolysis, polymer chains are first cut at random and the molecular weight falls, then strength is lost, and finally small fragments dissolve and the mass decreases. When water penetrates quickly into the interior and the whole material degrades almost uniformly, this is called bulk erosion; when the surface reaction is faster than water penetration and the material thins gradually from the surface, it is called surface erosion. Aliphatic polyesters such as PLA and PGA mainly undergo bulk erosion, and in large parts acid accumulates inside and degradation speeds up from the center. Materials that show surface erosion, such as polyanhydrides, are suited to carriers that release a drug at a constant rate.

The rate of degradation varies greatly with chemical structure, crystallinity, molecular weight and part size. PGA is highly hydrophilic and loses its strength within a few weeks, so it suits short-term sutures. Crystalline poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA) has a glass transition temperature of about 60 °C and a melting point of about 170–180 °C, and takes several years to be fully absorbed in the body. PCL has a low glass transition temperature of about −60 °C, is soft at room temperature and also degrades slowly, on a scale of years. Depending on the use, the material and composition are chosen so that strength is kept until the bone or tissue heals and the material is absorbed afterward.

Biodegradable describes whether a material is broken down, and biobased describes whether its raw material comes from plants or other biomass; the two are separate matters. Polyethylene made from plants does not biodegrade, while petroleum-based PBAT and PCL do. Biodegradability tests are also carried out under defined conditions. For example, PLA degrades in industrial compost at about 58 °C, but in soil or seawater, below its glass transition temperature, it degrades only very slowly. Even products labeled biodegradable are not necessarily broken down in the environment where they are discarded, so it is important to check under what conditions they are biodegradable.

faq.q: Do bioresorbable and biodegradable mean the same thing?
faq.a: In medicine they are often used almost interchangeably, but strictly, biodegradable means the material is broken down, while bioresorbable also includes removal of the products from the body by metabolism or excretion. A material that only breaks into small pieces that remain in the body cannot be called bioresorbable.

faq.q: Is the lactic acid released by degradation harmful?
faq.a: Lactic acid and glycolic acid are metabolized to carbon dioxide and water, so they are usually not a problem. However, if a large part degrades in a short time, acid can build up locally and cause an inflammation-like reaction, so the rate of degradation and the size of the part are adjusted.

faq.q: How is the rate of degradation adjusted?
faq.a: The basic method is copolymerization to change crystallinity and hydrophilicity; PLGA, made by copolymerizing glycolic acid with PLA, has a degradation period that can be changed through its composition. Molecular weight, crystallinity, part thickness and porosity also have an effect. Raising crystallinity or molecular weight slows degradation.

骨セメント.desc: A material made by mixing PMMA powder with liquid methyl methacrylate and polymerizing it in the body to fix artificial joints to bone. It fixes them not by adhesion but by filling the gap and interlocking mechanically.

about.h: Its role in fixing artificial joints
about.p: Bone cement became widespread after Charnley introduced it around 1960 for fixing artificial hip joints. It is packed into the bone while still soft just after mixing, and when a stem or other component is inserted, the cement flows into the gaps between the spongy irregularities of the bone and the implant and hardens. Its role is not to bond chemically but to penetrate the irregularities, interlock mechanically and transfer load to the bone over a large area, which is why it is likened to a grout that fills gaps. Being able to bear weight right after surgery is a major advantage over cementless fixation.

The powder consists mainly of PMMA particles and contains the initiator benzoyl peroxide and a radiopacifier, barium sulfate or zirconia, which makes the cement visible on X-ray images. The liquid is methyl methacrylate monomer with an aromatic amine accelerator that lets the reaction proceed at room temperature and a stabilizer that prevents polymerization during storage. When the two are mixed, the accelerator decomposes the initiator to form radicals, the monomer polymerizes and binds the powder particles together, and the whole mass hardens. The time to pass from liquid through a dough-like state to hardening changes greatly with temperature, so the temperature of the operating room and of stored materials is controlled.

The properties of bone cement are set by ISO 5833 and ASTM F451, which require, among other things, a maximum exotherm temperature in the test mold of no more than 90 °C, a setting time of 5–15 minutes (ASTM F451) or 3–15 minutes (ISO 5833), and a compressive strength of at least 70 MPa; ISO 5833 also specifies a bending strength of at least 50 MPa and a bending modulus of at least 1800 MPa. PMMA is strong in compression but weak in tension and fatigue, and air bubbles trapped during mixing become origins of fatigue cracks. Mixing under vacuum to reduce bubbles is therefore widely used.

about.h: Refinements in use and remaining issues
about.p: Some bone cements contain antibiotics to prevent infection and are used, for example, in revision surgery for infected artificial joints. For spinal compression fractures caused by osteoporosis, there is also a treatment that injects bone cement into the collapsed vertebral body to relieve pain. On the other hand, in long-term use, loosening at the interfaces between cement and bone or implant, cracking of the cement by fatigue and bone resorption caused by wear debris become problems. A complication is also known in which the pressure of packing drives monomer and marrow fat into blood vessels and lowers blood pressure. For these reasons, whether to use cement is decided according to the patient's age and bone condition.

faq.q: Is bone cement an adhesive?
faq.a: No. Bone cement does not bond chemically to bone or implant but fixes them by filling the gaps and interlocking with the irregularities. Washing blood and fat off the bone surface and pressurizing the cement so that it penetrates deep into the irregularities therefore determine the strength of fixation.

faq.q: Does the heat of setting damage the bone?
faq.a: Polymerization is exothermic, and in the test mold the temperature rises considerably, but in the body the cement layer is thin and cooled by blood flow, so the peak is lower. Even so, the surrounding bone cells may be damaged, so it is recommended not to make the cement layer thicker than necessary.

faq.q: How does it differ from calcium phosphate cement?
faq.a: Calcium phosphate cement hardens when its powder is mixed with an aqueous solution and turns into apatite or other phases by a hydration reaction; it bonds to bone and may be replaced by bone over time. Its strength is lower than that of PMMA bone cement, however, so it is used not for fixing artificial joints but for filling bone defects that carry little load.

応力拡大係数.desc: A quantity expressing the strength of the stress field at a crack tip. Given by K = Yσ√(πa), it depends on both the stress and the crack length, and the crack grows unstably when it reaches a critical value.

about.h: The stress field at a crack tip
about.p: Near the tip of a crack in an elastic body, the stress grows in inverse proportion to the square root of the distance r from the tip, taking the form σ ∝ K/√(2πr). The shape of this distribution is the same regardless of the shape of the crack or the part, and only its strength is set by the stress intensity factor K. So even for a part and a test specimen of different shapes, the crack tips can be regarded as being in the same state if K is the same. This is why fracture toughness measured on small specimens can be used to design real structures. In reality the region near the tip yields and becomes a plastic zone, so this idea holds when the plastic zone is small enough.

about.h: The geometry factor Y and superposition
about.p: The stress intensity factor can be written K = Yσ√(πa), where the geometry factor Y depends on the shape and position of the crack, the width of the part and how the load is applied. For a central crack (length 2a) in an infinitely wide plate, Y = 1; for a short crack entering from the edge of a plate (an edge crack) it is about 1.12, and Y rises as the crack becomes large compared with the width of the part. Y for many geometries is compiled in handbooks as formulas and tables. Within the elastic range, when several loads such as tension and bending act together, K values of the same mode can be added, and the K from residual stress is also included in the assessment.

about.h: Relation to the energy release rate
about.p: The elastic energy released when a crack advances by a unit area is called the energy release rate G, related to K by G = K²/E in plane stress and G = K²(1 − ν²)/E in plane strain. Griffith's condition, that G equals the energy needed to create surfaces, is equivalent when written with K to K reaching a critical value K_c. The critical value for Mode I is the fracture toughness K_IC, and under repeated loading the range of K, ΔK, determines the fatigue crack growth rate. In this way, K is the quantity that links the assessment of both static fracture and fatigue.

faq.q: How does the stress intensity factor differ from the stress concentration factor?
faq.a: The stress concentration factor Kt is a dimensionless number giving how many times the average stress the maximum stress at a rounded hole or notch root is. When the tip is sharp, as at a crack, the maximum stress is in theory infinite and cannot be expressed by Kt, so the strength of the stress field at the tip is expressed by the stress intensity factor K (in MPa·√m).

faq.q: What do the units MPa·√m mean?
faq.a: In K = Yσ√(πa), σ is the stress (MPa) and a is the crack length (m), and since its square root is multiplied in, the units become MPa·√m. Even at the same stress, a crack 4 times longer doubles K. The square root of a length appears in the units because the effect of crack size is included.

faq.q: When can the stress intensity factor not be used?
faq.a: When the plastic zone at the crack tip is large compared with the crack length, the plate thickness or the remaining cross-section. In highly ductile materials, thin plates or under high loads, the plastic zone spreads and K alone cannot describe the state. In that case, elastic-plastic fracture mechanics quantities that include plasticity, such as the J-integral or the crack tip opening displacement (CTOD), are used.

グリフィスの理論.desc: The theory that fracture proceeds when the elastic energy released as a crack extends exceeds the energy of the new surfaces. The fracture stress is given by √(2Eγs/(πa)).

about.h: Treating fracture as an energy balance
about.p: In 1920 Griffith proposed judging whether a crack grows not from the stress at its tip but from an energy balance. When a crack grows slightly in a stressed plate, the elastic strain energy stored around it is released. On the other hand, creating new fracture surfaces requires surface energy. While the crack is short, the energy needed to create surface is larger and the crack does not grow, but the released energy increases faster the longer the crack is, so beyond a certain length the released energy wins and the crack runs through all at once, accelerating as it goes.

When a stress σ acts perpendicular to a crack of length 2a in a wide plate, in plane stress an elastic energy of πσ²a²/E per unit thickness is released, and the surface energy is 4aγs. Differentiating the total energy with respect to a and setting it to zero gives the fracture stress σf = √(2Eγs/(πa)). In plane strain, E is replaced by E/(1 − ν²). For example, for a glass with E = 70 GPa and γs = 1.0 J/m², a = 10 µm gives σf of about 67 MPa, roughly a hundredth of the theoretical strength of about 7 GPa. The strength is inversely proportional to √a.

Griffith's equation works well for glass, in which almost no plastic deformation occurs, but applied to metals it greatly underestimates the strength. Orowan and Irwin proposed adding the work consumed in the plastic zone at the crack tip to the surface energy. In ductile steels this plastic work is thousands of times the surface energy or more and accounts for most of the energy needed for fracture. Irwin further expressed the energy balance by the energy release rate G and the stress field at the crack tip by the stress intensity factor K, showed the relation between the two and laid the foundation of linear elastic fracture mechanics.

about.h: Why the strength of brittle materials scatters
about.p: Griffith's theory shows that the strength of a brittle material is set less by the material itself than by the largest crack it contains. This is why the strength of the same glass differs greatly depending on how it has been scratched, and why specimens made by the same process show scattered strengths. Larger parts are more likely to contain large cracks, so their average strength is lower. The Weibull distribution treats this scatter and size effect statistically. Griffith himself showed by experiment that thinner glass fibers are stronger. This is why controlling crack size and proof testing are emphasized in the design of ceramics.

faq.q: Why is the strength inversely proportional to the square root of crack length in Griffith's equation?
faq.a: The released elastic energy grows with the square of the crack length, while the surface energy grows in proportion to the length. Solving the condition at which their rates of increase balance gives the square of the stress inversely proportional to crack length, so the strength is inversely proportional to √a.

faq.q: How is Griffith's equation related to the fracture toughness K_IC?
faq.a: Griffith's equation can be rewritten as σf√(πa) = √(2Eγs). The left side has the form of the stress intensity factor K and the right side is a constant of the material, so the fracture condition is the same as K reaching a critical value. For brittle materials such as glass, K_IC ≈ √(2Eγs).

faq.q: For which materials can Griffith's theory be used?
faq.a: It can be used directly for materials such as glass and ceramics, in which almost no plastic deformation occurs before fracture. For metals and polymers, the energy consumed by plastic deformation and other processes at the crack tip must be included, and the theory extended in that form is the basis of present-day fracture mechanics.

エネルギー解放率.desc: The elastic energy released when a crack advances by a unit area. Written G, it equals K²/E in plane stress, and the crack advances when it reaches the critical value G_c.

about.p: The energy release rate G is the energy released from the system of the body and its loading when a crack extends by unit area, and its unit is J/m². Despite the word rate in its name, it is not a quantity per unit time but per unit crack area. The value of G for a small crack extension is the same whether the load is held constant or the displacement is fixed. A crack grows when G reaches the energy needed to advance it, that is, the material's resistance R, so its critical value G_c is the fracture toughness expressed as an energy: the material's resistance to fracture.

about.h: Relation to the stress intensity factor and differences between materials
about.p: In the linear elastic range, G and the stress intensity factor K are related by G = K²/E in plane stress and G = K²(1 − ν²)/E in plane strain. Converting fracture toughness into energy with these equations shows the differences between materials clearly. For soda-lime glass (K_IC about 0.75 MPa·√m, E about 70 GPa), G_c is about 8 J/m², the same order as the surface energy. For a steel with K_IC of about 50 MPa·√m and E of about 210 GPa, it is about 1×10⁴ J/m², showing that orders of magnitude more energy is used in plastic deformation at the crack tip.

If the ratio of load-point displacement to load P is taken as the compliance C (displacement/load), then for a specimen of thickness B, G = (P²/2B)(dC/da). By measuring or calculating how the compliance changes with crack length, G can be found without solving the stress distribution in detail. This method is often used for problems in which K is hard to obtain, such as delamination between the layers of fiber-reinforced plastics. For example, in the double cantilever beam (DCB) test, in which a starter crack is placed at the end of a laminate and the two arms are pulled apart, the mode I interlaminar fracture toughness G_IC is found.

In ductile materials and some ceramics, the resistance R to crack growth increases as the crack extends, because the plastic zone grows or bridging between the crack faces increases. This is called the R-curve. In such materials, fracture does not occur as soon as G reaches R; the crack grows a little and stops. The crack grows unstably when the rate at which G increases with crack extension exceeds the rate at which R increases. Under constant load G increases with crack length more readily than under fixed displacement, making instability more likely, so the test method and the way a structure is supported also affect how fracture proceeds.

faq.q: Should I use G or K?
faq.a: In the linear elastic range with a small plastic zone, both carry the same information and can be converted by G = K²/E in plane stress. K is often used in the design of metals, while G is often used to evaluate delamination of composites and adhesive joints. When modes are mixed, G, which can be added as an energy, is sometimes easier to handle.

faq.q: How does G_c differ from the surface energy?
faq.a: The surface energy is the minimum energy needed to create new surface, while G_c is the energy actually needed to advance a crack. In glass the two are of the same order, but in metals the work of plastic deformation is added, so G_c is orders of magnitude larger than the surface energy.

faq.q: Are the units J/m² and N/m of the energy release rate the same?
faq.a: Yes. Since J = N·m, J/m² can be written as N/m. G can also be thought of as a force per unit length of the crack front that tries to push the crack forward, and in that sense it is sometimes called the crack extension force.

応力集中係数.desc: The number Kt giving how many times the average stress the maximum stress at a hole or notch root is. For an elliptical hole it is 1 + 2√(a/ρ), and for a circular hole it is 3.

about.h: Definition and choice of nominal stress
about.p: The stress concentration factor Kt is the maximum stress σmax at the root of a notch or hole divided by a reference nominal stress σn: Kt = σmax/σn. The nominal stress may be calculated on the gross section without the hole or on the net section reduced by the hole, and the value of Kt depends on which is used as the reference. When using handbook values, therefore, always check how the reference was taken. Kt is determined by elastic calculation and depends only on geometry and the way the load is applied, not on the kind of material. For the same geometry, it has the same value for steel and for aluminum alloys.

about.h: Stress distribution around a circular hole
about.p: When uniaxial tension acts on a circular hole in an infinitely wide plate, the stress is greatest at the two points on the edge of the hole lying across the load direction, and Kt = 3. Away from the edge the stress falls quickly; with hole radius a and distance r from the center, the stress on the section beside the hole is σ(2 + a²/r² + 3a⁴/r⁴)/2. At r = 2a, that is, only one radius from the edge, it has already fallen to about 1.22 times. The value also changes with the type of loading: Kt = 2 for equal biaxial tension and 4 for pure shear. What matters is that the high stress is confined very close to the hole.

about.h: Fatigue uses the fatigue notch factor
about.p: The drop in fatigue strength is often not as large as Kt would predict. The fatigue notch factor Kf, the fatigue limit of an unnotched specimen divided by that of a notched specimen, is therefore used, and the relation between the two is expressed by the notch sensitivity q = (Kf − 1)/(Kt − 1). q takes values from 0 to 1 and tends to be smaller for smaller notch root radii and for softer, lower-strength materials. High-strength steels are notch sensitive, with q close to 1, and feel almost the full effect of Kt. The sharper the notch, the larger the gap between Kf and Kt, and designing on Kt alone can be overly conservative.

When a static load acts on a ductile material, the stress redistributes to the surroundings even if the notch root yields, so the effect of Kt is small and strength can often be evaluated from the average stress on the net section. For brittle materials, for fatigue, and for materials that become brittle at low temperature, however, Kt translates directly into a loss of strength. In design, measures include giving large fillets to the corners of stepped shafts, avoiding abrupt changes of section and adding relief grooves nearby to smooth the flow of stress. The emergency measure of drilling a small hole at a crack tip to blunt it and stop its growth is based on the same idea.

faq.q: Does the stress concentration factor depend on the material?
faq.a: Not in the elastic range. Kt is obtained from elasticity theory and depends only on geometry and loading. How much that concentration affects strength, however, differs between materials: little for the static strength of ductile materials and a lot for brittle materials and fatigue.

faq.q: Why is the stress concentration factor of a circular hole 3?
faq.a: Because stress that cannot pass through the hole detours around its sides and concentrates near the edge. In the formula for an elliptical hole, Kt = 1 + 2√(a/ρ), a = ρ for a circle, so Kt = 1 + 2 = 3. It does not depend on hole size: in a wide plate, a small hole and a large hole both give 3.

faq.q: How is the stress concentration factor found?
faq.a: For simple shapes it is taken from elasticity solutions or handbook charts, and for complex shapes it is calculated by the finite element method. Experimentally, the strain at the notch root is measured with strain gauges, photoelasticity or digital image correlation. In finite element analysis, the maximum stress is underestimated unless the elements at the notch root are fine enough.

パリス則.desc: The empirical law da/dN = C(ΔK)ᵐ, stating that the fatigue crack growth rate is proportional to a power of the stress intensity factor range. It is used to estimate crack growth life.

about.h: The three regions of the crack growth curve
about.p: Plotting the fatigue crack growth rate da/dN against the stress intensity factor range ΔK = K_max − K_min on log-log axes gives an S-shaped curve. In the region of small ΔK, the rate drops sharply as ΔK approaches the threshold ΔK_th, and below it the crack effectively does not grow. In the intermediate region the curve is a straight line, and expressing it as da/dN = C(ΔK)ᵐ is the Paris law. In the region where ΔK is large and the maximum stress intensity factor approaches the fracture toughness, the rate rises sharply and finally leads to unstable fracture. The region used to estimate life in design is mainly the intermediate one.

about.h: The exponent m and the constant C
about.p: The exponent m is roughly 2–4 for metals and can exceed 10 for ceramics. The larger m is, the more the growth rate changes with a small increase in stress or crack length. The value of the constant C changes with the unit system, so the data are used with consistent units, such as da/dN in m/cycle and ΔK in MPa·√m. It is also known that, among steels, differences in the intermediate-region rate due to microstructure and strength are relatively small. On the other hand, the rate is affected by mean stress (the stress ratio R), environment and temperature, so it is important to choose data measured under the conditions of use.

Substituting ΔK = YΔσ√(πa) into the Paris law and integrating from the initial crack length a₀ to the critical crack length a_f gives the number of cycles needed for the crack to grow. The critical length is set by the condition K_max = K_IC. Because growth is slow while the crack is short, most of the life is spent early on, and the result depends strongly on the estimate of a₀. In damage-tolerant design for aircraft and similar structures, a crack of a size that nondestructive inspection could miss is assumed to exist, and the inspection interval is set so that it is found at the next inspection before it reaches the critical size.

faq.q: Is the Paris law derived from theory?
faq.a: No, it is an empirical law obtained by organizing a large body of experimental data. There are models that try to explain the exponent from plastic deformation and blunting at the crack tip, but C and m are usually determined by tests on each material. Note also that it holds only in the intermediate region.

faq.q: If ΔK is below ΔK_th, will a crack never grow?
faq.a: Under constant-amplitude loading it is a guide below which the crack can be regarded as effectively not growing. However, when the crack is very short, when occasional large loads are mixed in, or in corrosive environments, cracks can grow even below ΔK_th.

faq.q: How does crack growth change when the stress ratio R changes?
faq.a: Even at the same ΔK, the larger R = σmin/σmax is (the higher the mean stress), the faster the growth rate tends to be and the smaller ΔK_th becomes. One main reason is crack closure: when the crack faces touch partway through unloading, the ΔK actually acting at the tip becomes smaller, but this effect weakens as R increases.

マイナー則.desc: The rule that adds up damage at different stress amplitudes as the sum of the ratios n/N of applied cycles to life, and regards fatigue failure as occurring when the sum reaches 1.

about.h: The idea of adding up damage
about.p: Real machines and structures experience repeated stresses of different sizes. Miner's rule takes the life at stress amplitude σi as Ni, regards the damage from ni cycles at that amplitude as ni/Ni, and assumes failure when the summed damage D = Σni/Ni reaches 1. Because Palmgren presented it in 1924 for estimating bearing life and Miner in 1945 for aircraft materials, it is also called the Palmgren–Miner rule. As long as an S-N curve at constant amplitude is available, the life under varying loads can be estimated, so it is widely used in design.

about.h: How the calculation proceeds, with an example
about.p: Real load records are irregular, so first the number of cycles of each size is counted with a method such as rainflow counting. Next, the life at each amplitude is read from the S-N curve and the damage is summed. For example, for a part that each day experiences 1000 cycles at stress amplitude σ1 (life 1.0×10⁵ cycles) and 1.0×10⁴ cycles at σ2 (life 1.0×10⁶ cycles), the daily damage is 0.010 + 0.010 = 0.020, and the life is estimated at about 50 days. Although σ2 occurs 10 times as often, its contribution to damage is the same. This shows that large-amplitude cycles, though rare, strongly affect life.

Miner's rule assumes that damage accumulates uniformly in proportion to the number of cycles, regardless of the order of loading. In reality, when a low stress follows a high one, the crack formed earlier can grow even under the low stress, so failure tends to occur before the damage reaches 1. Conversely, in a low-to-high sequence, failure may not occur even beyond 1. A single large tensile overload can also create compressive residual stress at the crack tip that temporarily slows subsequent growth. In experiments, the damage at failure often deviates greatly from 1, so the estimate should be regarded as having a range.

about.h: Treating stresses below the fatigue limit
about.p: In constant-amplitude tests, stresses below the fatigue limit cause no failure however many times they are applied, so the original Miner's rule counts their damage as zero. Under varying loads, however, a crack formed by large stresses can grow even under stresses below the fatigue limit, and ignoring that damage overestimates life. Methods such as the modified Miner's rule, which extends the S-N curve below the fatigue limit and counts the damage there, are therefore used. Design codes for welded structures and others combine such methods with the idea of taking the damage limit smaller than 1, to give conservative estimates.

faq.q: Does a part always fail when the Miner damage reaches 1?
faq.a: No. D = 1 is an average guide, and in experiments the damage at failure can be smaller or larger than 1 depending on load sequence, material and mean stress. The scatter of the S-N curve itself is also large, so in design the rule is used with a margin.

faq.q: Is the linear cumulative damage rule the same as Miner's rule?
faq.a: Yes. Because damage is assumed to accumulate linearly, in proportion to the cycle ratio n/N, and can be added up, it is also called the linear cumulative damage rule. Rules that make damage accumulation nonlinear to represent sequence effects have also been proposed, but for its simplicity the linear Miner's rule is the most widely used.

faq.q: Can Miner's rule be used for loads whose mean stress varies?
faq.a: Yes, but the effect of mean stress must be corrected first. The usual procedure is to convert each cycle into an equivalent stress amplitude at zero mean stress with a modified Goodman diagram or similar, read the life from the fully reversed S-N curve and then sum the damage.

ストライエーション.desc: Fine lines seen on a fracture surface where a fatigue crack has advanced. Their spacing corresponds roughly to the crack growth per cycle, and they are observed with an electron microscope.

about.p: In a fatigue crack in a ductile metal, the crack tip opens by slip and becomes blunt and rounded on each loading, sharpens again as it closes on unloading, and advances by one cycle's worth. This process leaves steps on the fracture surface, and the fine lines lying perpendicular to the direction of crack growth are fatigue striations. The lines follow the shape of the crack front in arcs, and the direction in which the arcs bulge usually indicates the direction of crack growth. The spacing is often below a micrometer, and they are observed with a scanning electron microscope. They appear clearly in highly ductile materials such as aluminum alloys and may be indistinct in high-strength steels.

In the intermediate ΔK region, the striation spacing agrees well with the macroscopically measured crack growth rate da/dN, so in failure analysis ΔK at that location can be estimated from the spacing. For example, for a steel with Paris-law constants C = 1.0×10⁻¹² (da/dN in m/cycle, ΔK in MPa·√m) and m = 4, a spacing of 0.50 µm gives ΔK of about 27 MPa·√m. If the crack length at that location is 5.0 mm and the geometry factor is taken as 1, the stress range is estimated at about 210 MPa. By measuring the spacing at several places on the fracture surface, the magnitude of the stress that acted on the part can be worked back.

about.h: When they are not visible, and cautions
about.p: Not seeing striations does not mean that the failure was not fatigue. Near the threshold, where growth is very slow, striations are not visible or one line forms over several cycles, so one line no longer corresponds to one cycle. In the region of fast growth near the fracture toughness, ductile dimples are mixed in. If the fracture surfaces rub against each other or corrode, the lines disappear. Conversely, some patterns resemble striations, such as machining marks and steps from slip bands, so they are distinguished by checking the regularity of the spacing and its relation to the direction of crack growth.

Ordinary striations form by plastic deformation at the crack tip and are called ductile striations. In fatigue in corrosive environments, by contrast, brittle striations are sometimes seen: on flat, cleavage-like facets, lines perpendicular to the growth direction cross river-like markings running along it. Which of the two types is seen is therefore a useful clue for judging whether the environment played a part. In failure analysis, observations of striations, beach marks, the origin and the final fracture zone are combined to reconstruct when and from where the crack grew and under what loading.

faq.q: Does one striation correspond to one load cycle?
faq.a: In the intermediate growth-rate region, roughly one line corresponds to one cycle. In the region of very slow growth, however, one line may form over several cycles, and under variable loading only the large loads may leave distinct lines, so care is needed when taking the number of lines directly as the number of cycles.

faq.q: How are striations distinguished from beach marks?
faq.a: By their size. Beach marks are widely spaced patterns visible to the naked eye or at low magnification, with many cycles between one mark and the next. Striations are often spaced below a micrometer and become visible only at magnifications of a few thousand times in a scanning electron microscope.

faq.q: Are striations visible on the fatigue fracture surface of every material?
faq.a: No. They are clear in highly ductile metals such as aluminum alloys, copper alloys and austenitic stainless steels, but often indistinct in high-strength steels and cast irons. Even if they are not visible, whether the failure was fatigue is judged together with other features such as the location of the origin and beach marks.

修正グッドマン線図.desc: A diagram expressing the effect of mean stress. It joins the fully reversed fatigue limit and the tensile strength with a straight line, taking σa = σw(1 − σm/σB) as a guide to the allowable stress amplitude.

about.p: With mean stress σm on the horizontal axis and stress amplitude σa on the vertical axis, the modified Goodman line is the straight line joining the fatigue limit at zero mean stress σw (the fully reversed fatigue limit) on the vertical axis and the tensile strength σB on the horizontal axis. A stress combination below this line is judged to be on the safe side of the fatigue limit. If the mean stress reaches the tensile strength, the part fails statically even with zero amplitude, so the end point on the horizontal axis is the tensile strength. A diagram of this form, showing constant life in terms of mean stress and amplitude, is generally also called a Haigh diagram, and a line can be drawn for each life.

about.h: Finding the safety factor, with an example
about.p: With the modified Goodman line, the safety factor n is found from 1/n = σa/σw + σm/σB. For example, if a cyclic stress with σm = 200 MPa and σa = 120 MPa acts on a steel with σw = 250 MPa and σB = 700 MPa, then 1/n = 0.48 + 0.29 = 0.77, and n is about 1.3. This means the line is reached if the mean stress and the amplitude are both increased by about 1.3 times in the same ratio. However, if the maximum stress σm + σa exceeds the yield stress, plastic deformation occurs on the first loading, so the yield condition σm + σa ≤ σy is also checked.

There are other lines representing the effect of mean stress. The Gerber line is the parabola σa = σw{1 − (σm/σB)²}, which often passes through the middle of test data for ductile steels; the modified Goodman line lies inside it, on the safe side. The Soderberg line is a straight line whose end point on the horizontal axis is the yield stress σy, giving an even more conservative estimate. In design, the modified Goodman line is often used because it is simple and conservative. However, for brittle materials test data may fall inside the modified Goodman line, so it is important to check against data for the material.

about.h: Cautions when applying it to real parts
about.p: For σw in the diagram, the fatigue limit of test specimens is not used as is but is lowered to account for the size of the part, the surface finish and the service environment. For notched parts, the stress amplitude is multiplied by the fatigue notch factor Kf, and the treatment of mean stress is decided according to the ductility of the material. Residual stresses from quenching or welding also act as mean stress, so they are included in the evaluation. And although compressive mean stress often benefits fatigue, its effect scatters, so in design the allowable amplitude on the compressive side is usually kept at the fully reversed value and the benefit is not counted.

faq.q: Should I use the modified Goodman line or the Gerber line?
faq.a: For ductile steels, test data often fall near the Gerber line, but in design the conservative modified Goodman line is commonly used. If test data for the material are available, choose the line that fits them; with little data or for brittle materials, the basic rule is to use the conservative line.

faq.q: Why is it called the modified Goodman diagram?
faq.a: The relation Goodman presented in his 1899 book is said to have differed from today's diagram in both its assumptions and its form. Because it was later revised into the present form, which represents the relation between mean stress and stress amplitude by a straight line, it is called modified, although accounts of who devised which diagram differ.

faq.q: Can the modified Goodman diagram be used for finite life?
faq.a: Yes. Instead of σw on the vertical axis, take the fully reversed fatigue strength at the target number of cycles and join it to the tensile strength; the line then represents the combinations allowed for that life. Drawing a line for each life gives a diagram from which the life can be read for any combination of mean stress and amplitude.

フォノン.desc: A particle-like quantum of the lattice vibrations of a crystal. Phonons carry heat and heat capacity in insulators and also cause the scattering of electrons.

about.p: The atoms in a crystal are bound to one another as if joined by springs, and their vibrations can be expressed as a superposition of waves spread through the whole crystal. The energy of each wave is quantized in units of ħω, and a unit of this excitation is called a phonon, just as a photon is the quantum of an electromagnetic wave. There are acoustic phonons, in which neighboring atoms move in the same direction, and optical phonons, in which atoms within the unit cell move in opposite directions. The Debye temperature is a rough measure of the energy of the highest-frequency phonon converted to a temperature, and it is higher for stronger bonds and lighter atoms.

At high temperatures all vibrations are excited, each atom holds an energy of 3kT, and the molar heat capacity is about 3R (the Dulong–Petit law). As the temperature falls, phonons stop being excited in order from the highest energy, and the heat capacity shrinks. At temperatures well below the Debye temperature, only long-wavelength acoustic phonons are excited, and the heat capacity is proportional to T³. This quantum behavior of the heat capacity, which classical theory could not explain, was the starting point when Einstein and Debye explained the heat capacity of solids.

In insulators and semiconductors heat is carried mainly by phonons, and the thermal conductivity is expressed through the heat capacity, the speed of sound and the mean free path, as in κ = (1/3)Cvl. Phonons are scattered by other phonons, point defects and isotopes, dislocations, and grain boundaries and surfaces. At high temperatures umklapp processes between phonons dominate and κ falls roughly as 1/T, while at very low temperatures scattering at surfaces and grain boundaries dominates. Thermoelectric materials deliberately scatter phonons with nanostructures and heavy atoms to lower thermal conductivity, whereas heat-dissipating materials use crystals with little scattering instead.

faq.q: Is a phonon a real particle?
faq.a: It is a quantum of the collective vibration of atoms, not a particle that can be taken out on its own, and it is called a quasiparticle. Even so, it carries energy and crystal momentum and collides with and scatters electrons and photons, so treating it as a particle explains many phenomena simply.

faq.q: Do phonons carry heat in metals too?
faq.a: They do, but in pure metals the heat carried by conduction electrons is far larger, and the phonon share is usually only part of the total. In alloys and in intermetallic compounds with few electrons, the phonon share can become large.

faq.q: How are phonons related to electrical resistance?
faq.a: The main cause of the temperature dependence of the electrical resistance of metals is the scattering of conduction electrons by phonons. As temperature rises, phonons increase and so does scattering, and near room temperature the resistivity increases nearly in proportion to temperature. The fall in semiconductor mobility with temperature has the same cause.

デュロン・プティの法則.desc: The law that the molar heat capacity of many solid elements near room temperature is about 3R (about 25 J/(mol·K)). It corresponds to the classical limit of lattice vibrations at high temperature.

about.h: Content and history of the law
about.p: The Dulong–Petit law is an empirical rule presented in 1819 by Dulong and Petit, who found that the product of specific heat and atomic weight is nearly constant for many solid elements. In today's terms, the molar heat capacity of solid elements is about 3R, or about 25 J/(mol·K). Atomic weights were not yet accurately established at the time, so the law was also used to estimate atomic weights from measured specific heats and to correct wrong values. For copper, for example, dividing 3R by the molar mass of 63.55 g/mol gives about 0.39 J/(g·K), in good agreement with the measured value of about 0.385 J/(g·K).

about.h: Classical explanation and its place in quantum theory
about.p: By the equipartition theorem of classical statistical mechanics, each atom in a solid can be regarded as a harmonic oscillator in three directions and has an energy of 3kT, kinetic and potential energy combined. Differentiating this with respect to temperature gives a heat capacity of 3N_A k = 3R per mole. In this explanation, however, the heat capacity should not depend on temperature, and its decrease at low temperature cannot be explained. Einstein and Debye explained the low-temperature behavior from the quantization of vibrational energy, and the Dulong–Petit law came to be understood as the high-temperature limit in which all vibrations are fully excited.

about.h: Elements that deviate from the law
about.p: Elements whose room-temperature values deviate strongly from 3R are those in which light atoms are strongly bonded and the Debye temperature is far above room temperature. The molar heat capacity of diamond at room temperature is about 6.1 J/(mol·K), only about a quarter of 3R, and beryllium (about 16 J/(mol·K)) and silicon (about 20 J/(mol·K)) are also below 3R. In these, the high-energy vibrations are not fully excited even at room temperature. Well above room temperature, on the other hand, the constant-pressure heat capacity of many elements slightly exceeds 3R, because the effects of thermal expansion, vibrational anharmonicity and, in metals, conduction electrons are added.

about.h: Extension to compounds and practical use
about.p: According to the Neumann–Kopp rule, the molar heat capacity of a compound is nearly equal to the sum of the molar heat capacities of its elements, and combined with the Dulong–Petit law this gives about 3R per atom in the formula unit. NaCl, for example, has two atoms and is estimated at about 6R ≈ 50 J/(mol·K), close to the measured room-temperature value of about 50.5 J/(mol·K). Even for materials without heat capacity data, a rough value can be estimated this way if the Debye temperature is not much above room temperature. Expressed per unit mass, materials made of elements with smaller atomic weights have larger specific heats.

faq.q: Is the Dulong–Petit law about the heat capacity at constant pressure or at constant volume?
faq.a: The theoretical 3R is the value at constant volume. In solids, the difference between constant-pressure and constant-volume heat capacities is small at room temperature, a few percent, so comparisons are often made with the more easily measured constant-pressure value. At high temperature the difference grows and the constant-pressure heat capacity exceeds 3R.

faq.q: Why is the heat capacity of diamond small?
faq.a: Because carbon atoms are light and very strongly bonded, the lattice vibration frequencies are high and the Debye temperature, about 1900–2200 K, is far above room temperature. At room temperature many vibrations are not excited and few vibrations can take up energy, so the molar heat capacity stays at about 6.1 J/(mol·K).

faq.q: How do I estimate the specific heat per unit mass?
faq.a: Divide 3R ≈ 24.9 J/(mol·K) by the molar mass. For iron (55.85 g/mol), for example, this gives about 0.45 J/(g·K), in good agreement with the measured value of about 0.45 J/(g·K). The larger the atomic weight of an element, the smaller its specific heat per unit mass.

デバイ温度.desc: The highest frequency of lattice vibration converted, via its energy, to a temperature. Well below it, the lattice heat capacity is proportional to T³, and at high temperatures it approaches about 3R.

about.h: The idea of the Debye model
about.p: Debye regarded the lattice vibrations of a crystal as a collection of waves traveling at the speed of sound in an elastic body, and assumed that vibrational modes exist, starting from the lowest frequencies, up to three times the number of atoms. Calling the highest of these frequencies ωD, the Debye temperature is defined as θD = ħωD/k. If the temperature is well above θD, all modes are excited and the heat capacity approaches 3R; if it is well below θD, only low-frequency modes are excited. θD is a guide temperature marking the boundary between classical and quantum behavior of the lattice vibrations of that substance.

about.h: Typical values and what determines them
about.p: The Debye temperature is higher the stronger the interatomic bonds and the lighter the atoms. Typical values are about 105 K for lead, about 165 K for gold, about 343 K for copper, about 428 K for aluminum, about 470 K for iron, about 645 K for silicon and about 1900–2200 K for diamond. In a substance with low θD such as lead, the heat capacity is nearly 3R even at room temperature, whereas in diamond it is far below 3R even at room temperature. θD can also be calculated from the speed of sound obtained from elastic constants and density, and roughly agrees with the value from heat capacity. The value changes somewhat, however, depending on the temperature of the heat capacity data it is fitted to.

about.h: The low-temperature T³ law, with a numerical example
about.p: Well below θD, the lattice heat capacity is C ≈ (12π⁴/5)R(T/θD)³, that is, about 1944(T/θD)³ J/(mol·K). For copper at 10 K, for example, it is about 0.048 J/(mol·K), about 1/500 of the room-temperature value. The T³ law holds accurately roughly below θD/50. On the other hand, even at T = θD the heat capacity reaches about 95% of 3R, and above θD it can be regarded as nearly 3R. At very low temperatures the heat capacity becomes very small and a tiny amount of heat changes the temperature greatly, a property used in radiation and light detectors that operate at cryogenic temperatures.

about.h: Measuring and analyzing the heat capacity of metals
about.p: In metals, the contribution of conduction electrons γT is added to the low-temperature heat capacity, so C = γT + βT³. Plotting the measured C/T against T² therefore gives a straight line; the intercept gives the electronic heat capacity coefficient γ and the slope gives β, from which θD is obtained. Below a few K the electronic contribution is the larger. Besides heat capacity, the Debye temperature appears in the analysis of thermal conductivity, the temperature dependence of electrical resistance and the temperature dependence of X-ray diffraction intensities (the Debye–Waller factor), and it correlates with the melting point. It is used as a convenient index that expresses the stiffness of lattice vibrations by a single temperature.

faq.q: Does something change at the Debye temperature?
faq.a: No. The Debye temperature is not a phase transition temperature but a guide that converts the highest energy of lattice vibrations into a temperature. The heat capacity changes smoothly around the Debye temperature and approaches 3R from about that point on.

faq.q: What characterizes materials with a high Debye temperature?
faq.a: Their atoms are light and strongly bonded, so they tend to have large elastic moduli and hardness and high sound velocities. In insulators, phonons are scattered less readily and the thermal conductivity tends to be high. Diamond, cubic boron nitride and silicon carbide are examples.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Einstein model and the Debye model?
faq.a: The Einstein model assumes that all atoms vibrate at the same single frequency and predicts that the heat capacity falls exponentially at low temperature. The Debye model treats the vibrations as a collection of sound waves with a range of frequencies, so it correctly reproduces the experimental result that the heat capacity is proportional to T³ at low temperature.

熱拡散率.desc: The quantity α = κ/(ρc), the thermal conductivity divided by the heat capacity per unit volume. It expresses how quickly a change in temperature spreads through a material and has units of m²/s.

about.h: How it differs from thermal conductivity
about.p: Thermal conductivity κ expresses how much heat flows under a temperature gradient, that is, how easily heat flows in a steady state. Thermal diffusivity α = κ/(ρc), by contrast, is the ratio of conducting heat easily to being hard to warm up (the heat capacity per unit volume ρc), and it expresses how quickly a change in temperature spreads. The transient heat conduction equation is ∂T/∂t = α∇²T, so the change of temperature with time is set by α, not by κ alone. A rough time for the temperature to change through a plate of thickness L is L²/α, which can be used to estimate heating and cooling times.

Near room temperature, the thermal diffusivity is about 1.1×10⁻⁴ m²/s for copper, about 1×10⁻⁴ m²/s for aluminum, about 1×10⁻⁵ m²/s for carbon steel, about 4×10⁻⁶ m²/s for stainless steel, about 5×10⁻⁷ m²/s for glass, and about 1×10⁻⁷ m²/s for wood and polymers. Diamond exceeds 10⁻³ m²/s. The heat capacity per unit volume differs only by a few times among solids, so thermal diffusivities rank broadly in the same order as thermal conductivities. Gases have low thermal conductivity but also low density, so their thermal diffusivity is larger than that of solid polymers.

Thermal diffusivity is commonly measured by the laser flash method. A pulse of light is applied to the front of a disk sample, and α is found as α = 0.1388L²/t½ from the time t½ for the temperature rise of the back face to reach half its maximum. Because the sample can be small and measurements can be made up to high temperatures, the thermal conductivity is often obtained by multiplying the measured α by the density and specific heat, as κ = αρc. Thermal diffusivity matters in heat problems that involve time, such as the spread of temperature in welding and heat treatment, the temperature difference between surface and interior on quenching, and estimates of transient heating in semiconductor devices.

faq.q: Does a material with a large thermal conductivity always have a large thermal diffusivity?
faq.a: Among solids this is often so, but materials with a large heat capacity per unit volume ρc have a small thermal diffusivity for their thermal conductivity. Choose the quantity according to whether the aim is to compare steady heat flow or the speed of temperature change.

faq.q: How does thermal diffusivity differ from thermal effusivity?
faq.a: Thermal diffusivity κ/(ρc) expresses how quickly a change in temperature spreads through a material, while thermal effusivity √(κρc) expresses how much heat a surface absorbs when heat is applied to it. The coldness felt on touching and the momentary temperature rise of a surface depend on the effusivity.

faq.q: Why does thermal diffusivity have the same units, m²/s, as a diffusion coefficient?
faq.a: Because the transient heat conduction equation ∂T/∂t = α∇²T has the same form as Fick's second law for the diffusion of matter, ∂C/∂t = D∇²C. The spread of temperature can be treated like the diffusion of atoms, with a characteristic distance of √(αt).

ヴィーデマン・フランツの法則.desc: The law that the ratio of a metal's thermal conductivity κ to its electrical conductivity σ is proportional to absolute temperature, κ = LσT, where L is the Lorenz number, about 2.44×10⁻⁸ W·Ω/K².

about.h: Content of the law and the Lorenz number
about.p: In 1853 Wiedemann and Franz found that at room temperature the ratio of thermal conductivity to electrical conductivity is nearly the same for many metals, and Lorenz later showed that the ratio is proportional to absolute temperature. The proportionality constant L = κ/(σT) is called the Lorenz number. The quantum theory of free electrons gives L = (π²/3)(k/e)² ≈ 2.44×10⁻⁸ W·Ω/K², a value independent of the kind of metal. Electrons carry both charge and heat, and both are hindered by the same scattering, so the ratio of the two is constant regardless of the details of the scattering mechanism.

about.h: When it holds and when it fails
about.p: The law holds when scattering hardly changes the electrons' energy. This is the case above the Debye temperature and at very low temperatures, where impurity scattering dominates. At intermediate temperatures, scattering by phonons changes the electrons' energy bit by bit and impedes the flow of heat more readily, so L becomes smaller than 2.44×10⁻⁸ W·Ω/K². In substances where phonons carry a large share of the heat, such as alloys and semimetals, that share is added to the measured κ, so the apparent L becomes larger. In semiconductors, L changes further depending on the state of the carriers.

about.h: Estimating thermal conductivity from electrical resistance
about.p: Because thermal conductivity takes effort to measure, for metals it is often estimated from the electrical resistivity ρ as κ ≈ LT/ρ. For example, aluminum with a resistivity of about 2.7×10⁻⁸ Ω·m at 293 K gives about 265 W/(m·K), in rough agreement with the measured value of about 237 W/(m·K). One reason for the difference is that room temperature is below the Debye temperature of aluminum, so L is somewhat smaller. On the other hand, an austenitic stainless steel with a resistivity of about 7.2×10⁻⁷ Ω·m gives about 10 W/(m·K), smaller than the measured value of about 16 W/(m·K). In alloys the phonon contribution matters.

about.h: Use in thermoelectric materials and semiconductors
about.p: Raising the figure of merit of thermoelectric materials requires lowering the thermal conductivity, but the part carried by charge carriers is fixed in proportion to the electrical conductivity. The lattice thermal conductivity is therefore evaluated separately by subtracting LσT from the measured thermal conductivity. Here, in degenerate semiconductors L is close to the metallic value, but in nondegenerate semiconductors with low carrier concentrations it can fall to about 1.5×10⁻⁸ W·Ω/K², and methods that estimate L from the Seebeck coefficient are also used. That raising the electrical conductivity also raises the thermal conductivity is one reason thermoelectric materials are hard to design.

faq.q: Is the Lorenz number the same for every metal?
faq.a: The theoretical value of 2.44×10⁻⁸ W·Ω/K² does not depend on the metal, but measured values vary with temperature and purity. Near room temperature, most pure metals fall within about 2.2–2.6×10⁻⁸ W·Ω/K², though some metals are higher, and in alloys the phonon contribution makes it larger.

faq.q: Can the Wiedemann–Franz law be used for insulators?
faq.a: No. In insulators heat is carried almost entirely by phonons and there are almost no electrons to carry current, so thermal and electrical conductivity are not linked. Some substances, such as diamond, conduct almost no electricity yet have a higher thermal conductivity than metals.

faq.q: Why is the ratio proportional to temperature?
faq.a: Because the electronic thermal conductivity is proportional to the electronic heat capacity, and the electronic heat capacity of a metal is proportional to temperature. The electrical conductivity is set by the electron charge and does not depend on the heat capacity. The electron speed and mean free path act on both alike and cancel, so the ratio κ/σ is proportional to temperature.

ウムクラップ過程.desc: Phonon-phonon scattering in which the total momentum changes by a reciprocal lattice vector. It counteracts heat flow and is the main reason the thermal conductivity of insulators falls at high temperatures.

about.p: In collisions between phonons, two phonons merge into one or one splits into two. Energy is conserved, but the sum of the wave vectors (crystal momentum) may change by a reciprocal lattice vector G. Collisions in which the sum is conserved as is, k₁ + k₂ = k₃, are called normal processes (N processes), and those with k₁ + k₂ = k₃ + G are called umklapp processes (U processes). Umklapp is German for flipping over and expresses that the resulting phonon points nearly opposite to the original flow. The idea was introduced by Peierls in 1929.

In normal processes the total crystal momentum of all the phonons does not change, so a population of phonons aligned with the direction of heat flow keeps that flow even when they collide. With normal processes alone, therefore, the thermal conductivity would be infinite. In umklapp processes the sum changes by a reciprocal lattice vector and crystal momentum in the flow direction is lost, so the heat flow is impeded. In other words, a defect-free insulating crystal has a finite thermal conductivity mainly because of umklapp processes. Normal processes play the role of redistributing phonons and assisting umklapp processes and scattering by defects.

For an umklapp process to occur, the colliding phonons must have wave numbers close to the size of the Brillouin zone boundary, corresponding to energies of roughly kθD/2. At high temperature such phonons are plentiful and the number of phonons grows in proportion to temperature, so the thermal conductivity falls roughly as 1/T. As the temperature is lowered, the number of such phonons drops sharply, roughly in the form exp(−θD/2T), so the thermal conductivity increases steeply. At still lower temperatures the phonon mean free path is capped by the sample size or grain spacing, and the thermal conductivity falls along with the heat capacity, so a maximum appears in between.

about.h: Designing materials with high and low thermal conductivity
about.p: How readily umklapp processes occur is set by the strength of anharmonicity in the interatomic potential and by the size of phonon energies. Crystals with light atoms, strong bonds and weak anharmonicity have high room-temperature thermal conductivity; diamond, cubic boron nitride and silicon carbide are examples. Conversely, in thermoelectric materials, crystals with heavy atoms and strongly anharmonic bonds are chosen to strengthen umklapp processes, and phonons are further scattered by nanostructures and point defects to lower the lattice thermal conductivity. It is also known that isotopic enrichment, which reduces mass disorder, raises the thermal conductivity further.

faq.q: What is the difference between umklapp processes and normal processes?
faq.a: Both are collisions between phonons, but in normal processes the sum of the wave vectors is conserved, while in umklapp processes it changes by a reciprocal lattice vector. It is the umklapp process that directly impedes heat flow and causes thermal resistance.

faq.q: Why does the thermal conductivity of a pure crystal rise when it is cooled?
faq.a: Because as the temperature falls, the high-energy phonons able to cause umklapp processes decrease sharply and the phonon mean free path becomes longer. On further cooling, however, the mean free path is capped by the sample size, and the effect of the shrinking heat capacity wins, so the thermal conductivity falls.

faq.q: Do umklapp processes also affect the electrical resistance of metals?
faq.a: Yes. When electrons are scattered by phonons, there are also processes in which the sum of wave numbers changes by a reciprocal lattice vector; they can change the electron momentum greatly, so they affect the electrical resistance of metals, especially its temperature dependence at low temperature.

線膨張係数.desc: The fractional change in length when the temperature rises by 1 K. It arises from the anharmonicity of the interatomic potential and tends to be smaller in strongly bonded materials with high melting points.

about.h: Definition and relation to the volumetric coefficient
about.p: The coefficient of linear thermal expansion α expresses the fraction by which a length grows relative to its original length when the temperature rises by 1 K, and is defined as α = (1/L)(dL/dT). Its unit is K⁻¹, and 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ is sometimes written ppm/K. A temperature difference has the same size in K and in °C, so the value is the same when written in °C⁻¹. In isotropic materials, the volumetric expansion coefficient β, which expresses the fractional change of volume, is about 3α. In materials whose properties differ with direction, such as single crystals and fiber-reinforced materials, the coefficient differs with direction, and in some, such as graphite, even the sign differs.

about.h: Typical values and relation to melting point
about.p: Near room temperature, the coefficient is about 100–200×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ for polyethylene, about 23×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ for aluminum, about 17×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ for copper, about 12×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ for iron, about 4.5×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ for tungsten, about 2.6×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ for silicon and about 0.5×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ for fused silica. For metals there is an empirical rule that the product of the coefficient and the melting point (K) is roughly 0.02; for aluminum, for example, 23×10⁻⁶×933 ≈ 0.021. The numbers also show clearly the tendency for materials with strong bonds and high melting points to have small coefficients.

When expansion and contraction of a member are constrained, thermal stress arises. In a bar fixed at both ends, σ = EαΔT; for example, a steel (E = 200 GPa, α = 12×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) heated by 50 K develops a compressive stress of about 120 MPa. When materials with different coefficients are joined, a strain mismatch also arises at the interface whenever the temperature changes. In electronic components, the difference in expansion between a silicon chip (about 2.6×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) and a resin substrate (on the order of ten-odd ×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) subjects solder joints to repeated strain with each rise and fall of temperature, and they can crack by thermal fatigue. Choosing materials with matched expansion is a key to reliability.

about.h: Measurement, and cautions in using values
about.p: The coefficient is usually measured with a dilatometer, which detects the change in length of a specimen with a push rod as it is heated; there are also methods using laser interferometry and methods measuring the change of lattice parameter by X-ray diffraction. Data include instantaneous values at a given temperature and mean values from 20 °C up to a given temperature, and over a wide temperature range the two differ considerably. The coefficient changes with temperature and approaches zero at cryogenic temperatures, so applying a room-temperature value over a wide range gives large errors. There are also materials such as ZrW₂O₈ that show negative thermal expansion, shrinking as the temperature rises.

faq.q: How do I convert between the linear and volumetric coefficients?
faq.a: In isotropic materials, the volumetric coefficient is about three times the linear coefficient. If each edge grows by a factor of (1 + αΔT), the volume grows by (1 + αΔT)³ ≈ 1 + 3αΔT. In materials whose values differ with direction, it is the sum of the linear coefficients in three mutually perpendicular directions.

faq.q: Are the units K⁻¹ and °C⁻¹ different for the expansion coefficient?
faq.a: The values are the same. The coefficient is a change per temperature difference, and a difference of 1 K is the same size as a difference of 1 °C. 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ is also written ppm/K or ×10⁻⁶/°C.

faq.q: What materials have small thermal expansion?
faq.a: Examples include fused silica (about 0.5×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹), Fe-36%Ni Invar (about 1×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) and low-expansion glass-ceramics. Some glass-ceramics combine crystals with negative expansion and glass to make the expansion near room temperature almost zero, and they are used as substrates for telescope mirrors and the like.

インバー.desc: An Fe-36%Ni alloy. Its magnetovolume effect cancels ordinary thermal expansion, giving a very small linear expansion coefficient of about 1×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ near room temperature.

about.h: Discovery and origin of the name
about.p: Invar is an Fe-36%Ni (mass %) alloy found by Guillaume of Switzerland in 1896, and because its length hardly changes with temperature it was named after invariable. Guillaume received the 1920 Nobel Prize in Physics for his contribution to precision measurement through the discovery of anomalies in nickel steels. Until then, expensive platinum alloys and the like had been used for length standards and precision surveying instruments, but Invar provided an inexpensive material with small thermal expansion, and it came to be widely used in pendulum clocks, surveying tapes and similar applications.

about.h: Effects of composition, working and heat treatment
about.p: The room-temperature expansion coefficient of Fe-Ni alloys has a minimum near 36% Ni and increases when the composition deviates by only a few percent. Impurities such as carbon, manganese and silicon also increase expansion, so the composition is strictly controlled. The value also changes with working and heat treatment: quenching or cold working lowers the room-temperature coefficient further, but makes secular change, a slow change in length over time, more likely. For precision uses, therefore, a stabilizing treatment is given at a suitable temperature. Super Invar, with added Co, has an even lower room-temperature coefficient.

Magnetic expansion cancels thermal expansion only in the temperature range well below the Curie temperature, where the alloy is ferromagnetic. As the temperature rises toward the Curie temperature, the canceling effect weakens and the expansion increases sharply, so Invar is low-expansion only over a limited range roughly centered on room temperature. Its strength is also not very high, its thermal conductivity is low at around 10 W/(m·K), and its high nickel content makes it expensive. Depending on the application, Fe-Ni-Co alloys that accept slightly more expansion in exchange for a wider low-expansion temperature range are also used.

Invar is used for parts that must keep their dimensions when the temperature changes. Examples include structural members of precision measuring and optical instruments, laser resonators, the masks with fine holes used to deposit organic light-emitting diode displays and the shadow masks of former cathode-ray tubes. In membrane-type tanks of liquefied natural gas carriers, it shrinks little even when cooled to −162 °C, so the lining can be made of thin sheet. In bimetals, it is used for the low-expansion strip. Alloys such as Kovar, Fe-29%Ni-17%Co, whose expansion is matched to glass or ceramics for sealing, belong to the same family.

faq.q: Why is expansion smallest at about 36% Ni?
faq.a: Because the size of the magnetovolume effect in Fe-Ni alloys and the way the magnetization decreases with temperature change with composition, and near 36% Ni they just cancel ordinary thermal expansion around room temperature. When the composition deviates from this, the cancellation becomes incomplete and the expansion grows.

faq.q: Does Invar stay low-expansion at high temperature?
faq.a: No. It is low-expansion only in the range well below the Curie temperature, and above the Curie temperature it expands about as much as ordinary metals. It is important to check expansion coefficient data over the service temperature range.

faq.q: Is Invar attracted to a magnet?
faq.a: Yes. Invar is ferromagnetic at room temperature, and it uses its magnetovolume effect to cancel thermal expansion. When heated above the Curie temperature it is no longer attracted to a magnet, and at the same time it loses its low-expansion property.

真実接触面積.desc: The area where asperities on two surfaces actually touch. When the asperities deform plastically it equals the load divided by the hardness, and it is far smaller than the apparent contact area.

about.p: Even a flat polished metal surface has irregularities a few nm to a few µm high, and when two surfaces are placed together only the tips of their highest asperities touch. The total area of the parts actually in contact is the real area of contact Ar, usually far smaller than the apparent contact area determined by the outline. If the asperities support the load by plastic deformation, the contact pressure equals the hardness H, and Ar = W/H. For example, even when a load of 100 N is applied to a metal with a hardness of 1.0 GPa, Ar is only 0.10 mm², so even if the apparent area is several cm², only a tiny part of it is in contact.

about.h: Proportional to load even in elastic contact
about.p: When asperities support the load by elastic deformation alone, the contact area of a single asperity is proportional to the load to the 2/3 power by Hertz theory, not to the load itself. A real surface, however, has many asperities of different heights, and as the load increases new asperities come into contact one after another.
