Greenwood and Williamson showed that, considering the distribution of asperity heights, the real area of contact is nearly proportional to load even in elastic contact. Whether elastic or plastic contact dominates is judged by the plasticity index, obtained from the material's E/H and the shape of the surface roughness. This is one reason the law that friction is proportional to load holds so widely.

Electricity and heat can flow only through the real contact spots, so the electrical and thermal resistance of a contact is set by the real area of contact. When current passes through a small contact spot of radius a, the resistance due to the constriction of the current (constriction resistance) is about ρ/(2a) between materials of resistivity ρ. Raising the contact load increases the real area of contact and lowers the contact resistance, while oxide films or dirt on the surface raise it greatly. In cooling semiconductors, the air in the gap between a component and its heat sink conducts heat poorly, so thermally conductive grease or pads fill the gap to lower the thermal contact resistance.

about.h: How the real area of contact is measured
about.p: The real area of contact lies inside the interface, so it is a quantity that is hard to see directly. If one body is made of transparent glass or sapphire, the contact spots can be observed optically using total internal reflection or interference. Between metals, it is estimated indirectly from the electrical contact resistance, or from the reduction in reflection as ultrasound passes through the contact spots. Recently, it is also often found by numerical calculation from three-dimensional measurements of the surface topography. With any method, the appearance of fine irregularities changes with the scale of measurement, so note that the results include the effect of scale.

faq.q: How large is the real area of contact compared with the apparent area?
faq.a: It varies greatly with conditions, but when metals are pressed together under ordinary machine-part loads it is often less than 1% of the apparent area. Since Ar = W/H, the fraction of real contact becomes larger the higher the load and the softer the material.

faq.q: Does a larger apparent area increase the friction force?
faq.a: Hardly, in dry friction. Even if the apparent area is enlarged, at the same load the real area of contact stays at W/H, and the friction force is proportional to the real area of contact. For soft materials such as rubber, or clean surfaces with strong adhesion, however, the apparent area can have an effect.

faq.q: How are elastic and plastic contact distinguished?
faq.a: By a dimensionless number called the plasticity index, calculated from the ratio E/H of the material's elastic modulus to hardness and from the spread of asperity heights and the radius of asperity tips. Small values mean elastic contact dominates and large values plastic contact. Smooth surfaces with small E/H tend toward elastic contact, rough surfaces and soft metals toward plastic contact.

アーチャードの摩耗式.desc: The equation V = KWL/H, stating that wear volume V is proportional to the normal load W and sliding distance L and inversely proportional to hardness H. K is the wear coefficient, which varies widely with the wear mechanism.

about.p: Archard assumed that the real contact spots between two sliding surfaces produce wear debris with a certain probability during sliding. The real area of contact equals the load W divided by the hardness H, so the number of contact spots is proportional to W/H. The distance slid before a contact spot is replaced is about the size of the spot, so the number of opportunities to form wear debris over a sliding distance L is proportional to L. Putting these together, the wear volume can be written V = KWL/H. The dimensionless wear coefficient K has the meaning of the probability that a contact spot becomes wear debris.

about.h: Wear coefficient and specific wear rate
about.p: K is large, about 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻², for unlubricated adhesive wear between metals of the same kind, and falls to about 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁵ for mild wear protected by oxide films and to about 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ under good lubrication. In practice, the specific wear rate k = V/(WL), which lumps K/H together without separating out the hardness, is often used, expressed in mm³/(N·m). Because the specific wear rate can also be used for polymers, composites and coatings, whose hardness is hard to define, it is widely used to compare wear resistance. When comparing values, it is important to match the test method and conditions.

The Archard equation is useful for life estimates and material comparisons in the mild-wear regime, where wear is proportional to load and sliding distance. However, above certain loads or speeds, frictional heat can break down oxide films or adhesion can spread, causing a transition to severe wear, with wear larger by orders of magnitude. The wear rate also changes during the initial running-in period. K should therefore be determined in tests close to the actual operating conditions, and the equation should be used after confirming where the wear regime changes.

faq.q: Why do harder materials wear less?
faq.a: In a harder material, the real area of contact needed to support the same load is smaller, so there are fewer contact spots producing wear debris. In abrasive wear too, a surface harder than sand grains and the like is hard to cut. Hard but brittle materials, however, can wear by cracking.

faq.q: Does enlarging the apparent contact area reduce wear?
faq.a: In the Archard equation, the wear volume does not depend on the apparent area. Enlarging the area lowers the pressure and temperature, however, making it easier to stay in the mild-wear regime, so in practice life can be extended. For the same volume, a larger area also means a shallower wear depth.

faq.q: How is the wear coefficient measured?
faq.a: In a pin-on-disk or ball-on-disk test, the specimen is slid under a set load and sliding distance, and the wear volume is found from the mass loss or the shape of the wear track. Dividing that volume by the load and sliding distance gives the specific wear rate, and multiplying by the hardness gives the dimensionless wear coefficient.

ストライベック曲線.desc: A curve plotting the friction coefficient of a plain bearing or similar contact against the bearing characteristic number, viscosity × speed ÷ pressure. It shows the transitions among boundary, mixed and hydrodynamic lubrication.

about.h: Shape of the curve and its three regions
about.p: The Stribeck curve plots the bearing characteristic number ηN/P (η is the lubricant viscosity, N the rotational speed and P the bearing pressure) on the horizontal axis against the friction coefficient on the vertical axis. The region of small ηN/P is boundary lubrication, where asperities on the surfaces touch and the friction coefficient is about 0.1. As ηN/P increases, the bearing enters mixed lubrication, in which pressure in the oil film carries part of the load, and the friction coefficient falls sharply. Increasing it further gives hydrodynamic lubrication, in which the oil film fully separates the surfaces; the friction coefficient passes its minimum and then rises gently because of the viscous resistance of the oil.

In hydrodynamic lubrication, oil is drawn toward the direction in which the gap between the sliding surfaces narrows like a wedge, and pressure develops there to support the load. This is called the wedge effect, and the higher the speed and viscosity, the thicker the oil film. Where contact pressures are very high, as in rolling bearings and gears, elastic deformation of the contact and the rise in oil viscosity with pressure come into play, giving elastohydrodynamic lubrication in which even an oil film thinner than 1 µm can separate the surfaces. The film thickness ratio, the ratio of film thickness to surface roughness, serves as a guide to the lubrication state.

A bearing operated slightly on the hydrodynamic side of the friction minimum keeps a stable friction coefficient even when speed or load changes. On the boundary side of the minimum, a temperature rise that lowers viscosity moves the bearing still closer to boundary lubrication, increasing friction and possibly leading to seizure. Starting and stopping always pass through boundary lubrication, so materials for rubbing surfaces must resist adhesion even when the oil film breaks. Oil additives, surface treatments and solid lubricants are used mainly to reduce friction and wear in this boundary lubrication region.

faq.q: What is boundary lubrication?
faq.a: It is a state in which the oil film has become very thin, asperities touch, and friction is governed by molecules adsorbed on the surfaces and thin films formed by reaction with additives. Oil viscosity has little effect, and the friction coefficient is about 0.1. It occurs at starting and stopping, and at low speed under heavy load.

faq.q: Does a more viscous oil always lower friction?
faq.a: Not necessarily. In the boundary and mixed lubrication regions the oil film thickens and friction falls, but once the bearing is already in the hydrodynamic region, viscous resistance increases and friction loss actually grows. This is why low-viscosity oils are used to save energy.

faq.q: Why can results be organized by the bearing characteristic number?
faq.a: Pressure in a hydrodynamic oil film grows in proportion to viscosity and speed and opposes the bearing pressure. The combination viscosity × speed ÷ pressure therefore expresses whether the oil film can carry the load. Experiments under different conditions can be collapsed onto a single curve using this number.

凝着摩耗.desc: Wear in which metals bond at the real contact spots and, as sliding shears the junctions, material transfers to the counterface or detaches. It causes seizure.

about.p: When metal surfaces are pressed hard together at real contact spots, the surface oxide and adsorbed films break, fresh metals touch each other, and junctions formed by atomic bonding appear. As sliding continues these junctions are sheared, but if a junction is stronger than the base metal, it tears not at the interface but inside the weaker metal, and the fragment transfers to the counterface. The transferred fragments grow as they are rubbed again and again and eventually detach as wear particles. The wear coefficient in Archard's equation for unlubricated like metals is about 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻², orders of magnitude larger than in mild wear protected by oxide films.

In dry sliding of steel on steel, as the load or sliding speed is raised there is a transition at which the amount of wear increases by orders of magnitude. Below the transition, oxide films formed on the surface prevent metal-to-metal contact, giving gentle mild wear that produces fine oxide particles. Above it, frictional heat and high contact pressure make the oxide films impossible to maintain, adhesion between metals spreads, and severe wear producing large metallic particles results. Severely worn surfaces are rough, with metallic, shiny transferred material. Going further, the junctions spread until the parts unite with each other and stop moving: seizure.

Adhesion tends to occur readily between identical metals and between metals that dissolve well in each other, and less readily between pairs with little mutual solubility. Stainless steels, titanium alloys and aluminum alloys adhere easily, and threads can gall and lock when tightened. This is thought to be because once the thin protective surface film is rubbed through, an active metal surface appears immediately. In vacuum, oxide films do not regenerate, so clean metals can bond even at room temperature, a major problem for mechanisms used in space. Using copper alloys or tin-based alloys against steel in bearings is likewise a choice of a pair that adheres poorly.

The basic way to prevent adhesive wear is to keep metals from touching directly. Besides separating the surfaces with lubricating oil, oiliness agents that form slippery adsorbed films and extreme-pressure additives that react with the metal surface under high contact pressure to form sulfide or phosphide films are used. On the materials side, there are methods that make the surface resistant to adhesion, such as nitriding, hard coatings and diamond-like carbon (DLC). For evaluation, besides measuring wear and friction coefficient in pin-on-disk tests, tests that raise the load in steps to find the load at which seizure occurs are also used.

faq.q: Are galling and seizure the same thing?
faq.a: Both arise from adhesion, but galling usually refers to damage in which adhesion and transfer on the sliding surface roughen it as if torn, while seizure refers to the state in which adhesion spreads, friction and heating rise sharply, and the parts stick together and stop moving. Galling that progresses leads to seizure.

faq.q: Why is it bad to rub identical metals together?
faq.a: Because their crystal structures and ways of atomic bonding are the same, strong junctions form easily at the real contact spots. For sliding parts, therefore, different kinds of materials are combined, or one side is given a surface treatment or coating.

faq.q: How can adhesive and abrasive wear be told apart from the worn surface?
faq.a: In adhesive wear the surface is roughened as if torn, with traces of material transferred from the counterface. In abrasive wear, fine grooves and scratches parallel to the sliding direction line up. In practice both often occur together, so the shape and composition of the wear particles are also examined.

アブレシブ摩耗.desc: Wear in which hard particles or hard asperities on the counterface scratch and cut material from a softer surface. It drops greatly when the surface is made harder than the particles.

about.p: Abrasive wear includes two-body abrasive wear, in which hard asperities on the counterface or fixed abrasive grains scratch the surface, and three-body abrasive wear, in which hard particles trapped between two surfaces roll and slide while cutting the surface. Wear by a file or a grinding wheel is two-body; sand, dirt or wear particles mixed into lubricating oil scratching surfaces inside a bearing are examples of three-body wear. In three-body wear the particles spend more time rolling and cut less efficiently, so the wear is often about an order of magnitude less than in two-body wear. Keeping hard particles out by oil filtration and seals is the basic way to prevent three-body wear.

When a hard particle scratches a surface, material is removed in three ways: microploughing, which pushes material aside into ridges on both sides of the groove; microcutting, which removes material like a chip; and microcracking, in which brittle materials chip off by fracture. The sharper the particle's corners and the steeper the angle at which it meets the surface, the more likely cutting becomes and the more the wear increases. In ploughing, material is not lost immediately, but only once the ridges, rubbed again and again, detach by fatigue. In ductile metals ploughing and cutting dominate, and in brittle materials such as ceramics wear by cracking dominates.

The basic way to reduce abrasive wear is to make the surface harder than the particles, but hardness alone does not decide the result. In materials containing hard carbides, such as high-chromium cast irons, the size and amount of the carbides matter: if the carbides are smaller than the width of the grooves the particles make, they are cut away together with the soft surrounding matrix. Conversely, if the carbides are large and well supported by the matrix, the particles hit the carbides and stop. Also, hard but brittle materials crack and chip in wear involving large impacts, so for high-impact uses materials are chosen with the balance against toughness in mind.

Abrasive wear is evaluated with tests such as one that feeds dry sand between a rubber wheel and the specimen and measures the wear (ASTM G65), and tests that slide the specimen on abrasive paper. In construction and mining machinery that handles earth and rock, agricultural implements and pipes conveying powders, abrasive wear often determines the life of parts. On the other hand, grinding, polishing and lapping are processes that deliberately use the mechanism of abrasive wear. By choosing the size and hardness of the abrasive grains and the pressing force, they adjust the removal rate and the roughness of the finished surface.

faq.q: Is making the surface hard enough to reduce abrasive wear?
faq.a: Hardness is the most important factor, but it is sometimes not enough on its own. The size and distribution of hard phases, the strength of the matrix and toughness against impact also matter, and brittle materials chip under impact. Materials are chosen to suit the service conditions, such as the hardness and size of the particles and how they strike.

faq.q: How does erosion differ from abrasive wear?
faq.a: Erosion is wear in which particles carried by a fluid strike and cut a surface; the way force is applied differs from abrasive wear, in which particles are pressed against the surface and slide. In erosion the impact angle has a large effect: ductile materials wear most at shallow angles, and brittle materials at angles close to perpendicular.

faq.q: How is the amount of abrasive wear estimated?
faq.a: It is estimated with V = KWL/H, the same form as Archard's equation, so the wear is proportional to load and sliding distance and inversely proportional to hardness. If the particles are modeled as cones, K is set by the sharpness of the particle corners and is larger the sharper they are. Real values of K vary greatly with conditions, so they are found by testing.

浸炭.desc: A treatment in which low-carbon steel is held in a carbon-bearing atmosphere in the austenite region to raise the carbon content of the surface layer. Quenching then turns the surface into hard martensite.

about.h: The aim of different properties at the surface and in the core
about.p: In parts such as gears and shafts, the surface must resist wear, high contact stress and bending fatigue, while the core needs toughness so that it does not crack under impact, and giving the whole part the same microstructure makes both hard to achieve. Carburizing uses low-carbon steel with around 0.2% carbon, raises the carbon content of the surface layer alone to around 0.8%, and then quenches it, so the surface becomes hard martensite while the core remains a tough low-carbon structure. Compressive residual stress also remains in the surface layer, raising fatigue strength as well. Case-hardening steels with added Cr or Mo, such as SCr420 and SCM420, are commonly used.

Carbon enters by diffusion from the surface, so the depth at which a given carbon content is reached is roughly proportional to √(Dt), and doubling the depth takes about four times as long. Taking the diffusion coefficient of carbon in austenite as D = 2.3×10⁻⁵exp(−148 kJ/mol ÷ RT) m²/s gives about 8×10⁻¹² m²/s at 927 °C. When a steel with 0.2% carbon is carburized for 4 hours with its surface held at 0.9%, the error-function solution estimates the depth at which the carbon content is 0.4% at about 0.5 mm. In reality the diffusion coefficient changes with carbon content, so this is a guide. Higher temperatures are faster but tend to coarsen the grains.

In the widely used gas carburizing, the carbon potential (a guide to the surface carbon content the atmosphere gives the steel) of an atmosphere consisting mainly of CO and H₂ made from hydrocarbons is controlled to set the surface carbon content. Because this atmosphere contains slightly oxidizing components, easily oxidized elements such as Si, Mn and Cr oxidize at grain boundaries in the surface layer; this intergranular oxidation leaves regions that harden poorly and lowers fatigue strength. Vacuum carburizing, in which hydrocarbons such as acetylene flow into a furnace at reduced pressure, causes no intergranular oxidation, allows short treatment at high temperature and carburizes the inside of holes more easily.

about.h: Treatment after quenching and quality checks
about.p: After carburizing and quenching, parts are usually tempered at a low temperature of about 150–200 °C to restore toughness without lowering the hardness much. Because the surface layer is rich in carbon, some austenite tends to be retained after quenching, and when dimensional change or insufficient hardness is a problem, a subzero treatment that cools the part below 0 °C is applied. Quality is checked by measuring the hardness profile on a cross section, and the depth at which the hardness falls to 550 HV is commonly taken as the effective case depth. Quench distortion is unavoidable, so gears requiring precision are finished by grinding the tooth flanks after carburizing and quenching.

faq.q: Are carburizing and carburize hardening different things?
faq.a: Carburizing refers only to the treatment that adds carbon to the surface layer, and by itself it does not harden the steel. The whole sequence of quenching afterward to turn the surface into martensite, and then tempering, is called carburize hardening (carburizing and quenching). In practice, carburizing often refers to the whole sequence including quenching.

faq.q: How are carburizing and nitriding used differently?
faq.a: Carburizing and quenching can give a deep case of about 0.5–2 mm and suits heavily loaded gears and similar parts, but quenching causes distortion. Nitriding gives a thinner case but hardens the steel without quenching at temperatures below the transformation point, with little distortion, so it suits parts that need dimensional accuracy.

faq.q: What is done for areas that should not take up carbon?
faq.a: They are covered with copper plating or a stop-off paint so that carbon cannot enter. This is used to leave areas unhardened, such as threads or areas to be machined later. Another method is to cut those areas away after carburizing but before quenching.

窒化処理.desc: A treatment in which steel is held in a nitrogen-bearing atmosphere below the A₁ transformation temperature to form hard nitrides in the surface layer. No quenching is needed and distortion is small.

about.p: Nitriding diffuses nitrogen into steel from the surface to form hard nitrides, and it is carried out at temperatures in the ferrite region below the A₁ transformation point. It involves no phase transformation and no quenching afterward, so dimensional change and distortion are small, and parts can be treated after finish machining. In steels containing elements that readily form nitrides, such as Al, Cr, Mo and V, fine nitrides precipitate and make the surface layer very hard, and a notable feature is that the hardness drops little even at high temperature. On the other hand, the case is thinner than with carburizing, and the treatment often takes a long time.

The surface of nitrided steel consists of two layers: the compound layer at the very surface and the diffusion zone beneath it. The compound layer, a few to a few tens of µm thick, consists of the iron nitrides ε (Fe₂₋₃N) and γ′ (Fe₄N); it looks white on an etched cross section and is also called the white layer. It contributes to wear and seizure resistance, but if too thick it is brittle and causes spalling. The diffusion zone, in which nitrogen is dissolved or precipitated as fine nitrides, is effective in raising fatigue strength. In gas nitriding, the nitriding potential, set by the ratio of ammonia and hydrogen partial pressures, is controlled to tailor the type and thickness of the compound layer.

Besides gas nitriding using ammonia gas, there is plasma nitriding (ion nitriding), in which a glow discharge is created in a furnace at reduced pressure and nitrogen ions strike the parts. Plasma nitriding can treat stainless steels while removing their passive film by sputtering, and masking areas not to be treated is easy. Nitrocarburizing, which introduces carbon together with nitrogen, is a short treatment of a few hours or less at about 570 °C that mainly forms a compound layer, and it raises wear and seizure resistance even in plain carbon steels with few alloying elements. There are salt-bath and gas methods, and they are widely used for automotive parts and the like.

When austenitic stainless steel is nitrided for long at temperatures above about 450 °C, nitrogen combines with chromium to precipitate chromium nitrides, the chromium in the matrix decreases, and corrosion resistance falls. A method was therefore developed that uses plasma nitriding or similar below about 450 °C to form a hard layer called expanded austenite (S phase), in which large amounts of nitrogen are dissolved without precipitating nitrides. This hardens the surface while keeping corrosion resistance. In ordinary nitriding too, surface dirt and passive films before treatment cause uneven nitriding, so pretreatment determines quality.

faq.q: What is the difference between nitriding and nitrocarburizing?
faq.a: Nitriding diffuses nitrogen alone and gives a deep diffusion zone and high hardness in nitriding steels containing Al or Cr; it can take several tens of hours. Nitrocarburizing introduces nitrogen and carbon together and mainly forms a compound layer in a short time. The case hardness is lower, but it can be used on carbon steels and is quick and inexpensive.

faq.q: Can nitrided parts be machined to finish afterward?
faq.a: Because the case is thin, removing much material by grinding or similar would remove the hard layer. Nitriding is therefore usually done after finish machining, which its small distortion makes possible. Light polishing of the compound layer surface to adjust roughness is often done.

faq.q: Why does nitriding raise fatigue strength?
faq.a: When nitrogen dissolves or fine nitrides precipitate in the diffusion zone, the surface layer tries to expand and is constrained by the interior, so compressive residual stress develops in the surface layer. The harder surface also delays the initiation of fatigue cracks. Nitriding is therefore used for parts that carry repeated loads, such as crankshafts and gears.

無電解ニッケルめっき.desc: Plating in which nickel is deposited autocatalytically by a reducing agent without a power supply. The deposit contains phosphorus and forms a uniform thickness even on parts of complex shape.

about.p: In electroplating, current from an external power source deposits metal, so the coating is thick at corners and edges where current concentrates and thin deep in holes. In electroless nickel plating, a reducing agent in the bath supplies electrons and turns nickel ions into metal. The deposited nickel itself catalyzes the reaction, so once deposition starts, growth continues at almost the same rate over the whole surface and a uniform thickness is obtained regardless of the shape of the part. This reaction was found in 1946 by Brenner and Riddell in the course of research on electroplating. Coating the insides of holes and the bottoms of grooves is its greatest feature.

The most commonly used baths are acidic and use sodium hypophosphite as the reducing agent; they are operated at about 90 °C and a pH of about 4–5, with deposition rates of about 10–20 µm per hour as a guide. Hypophosphite ions are oxidized to phosphite ions, and some of the phosphorus is incorporated into the coating, so the coating is a Ni-P alloy. The phosphorus content changes with bath composition and pH and is classified roughly as low phosphorus at 2–5%, medium at 6–9% and high at 10–13%. The more phosphorus, the closer the coating is to amorphous. With reducing agents such as borohydride compounds, the coating becomes a Ni-B alloy.

The as-plated hardness is about 500–600 HV, and heat treatment at about 400 °C precipitates Ni₃P and hardens the coating to about 900–1000 HV, raising wear resistance. High-phosphorus coatings are amorphous with no grain boundaries, so they have excellent corrosion resistance and are used for chemical equipment parts and the like. Coatings with more than about 11% phosphorus are also almost nonmagnetic as plated, so they have been used to form a hard underlayer that does not affect magnetic recording on the aluminum substrates of hard disks. However, even high-phosphorus coatings become magnetic when heat treated above about 260–280 °C, as precipitation of Ni₃P proceeds.

Because it deposits uniformly, it is widely used for parts with many threads or holes, hydraulic components, molds and dies. If palladium, which acts as a catalyst, is applied in pretreatment, plastics and ceramics can also be plated, and on electronic circuit boards, layering electroless nickel and immersion gold over copper is used as a base for soldering. As the bath is used, nickel is depleted and phosphite accumulates, so it is used while replenishing its components, and its life is managed by how many replenishments it has had. There are also composite coatings that disperse PTFE or SiC particles in the coating to improve sliding or wear resistance.

faq.q: How are electroless and electrolytic nickel plating used differently?
faq.a: Electroless nickel plating is used for parts that need uniform thickness over complex shapes or inside holes, and for parts that need hardness or corrosion resistance. Electrolytic nickel plating deposits faster, its bath is easier to control and its cost is lower, so it suits parts of simple shape without strict thickness uniformity requirements and decorative plating.

faq.q: Why does heat treatment increase the hardness?
faq.a: An as-plated Ni-P coating consists of fine crystals supersaturated with phosphorus or is amorphous. When heated to about 400 °C, the hard compound Ni₃P precipitates finely and is dispersed in the nickel, so the hardness rises greatly. However, heating can also introduce fine cracks into the coating and lower its corrosion resistance.

faq.q: Is electroless nickel plating attracted to a magnet?
faq.a: It depends on the phosphorus content. Low- and medium-phosphorus coatings are magnetic, but high-phosphorus coatings with more than about 11% phosphorus are almost nonmagnetic as plated. However, magnetism appears when Ni₃P precipitates during heat treatment above about 260–280 °C.

網目形成酸化物.desc: An oxide such as SiO₂, B₂O₃ or P₂O₅ whose cations form oxygen polyhedra that share corners, building a glass network even on its own.

about.p: In 1932 Zachariasen proposed that an oxide forms glass readily when it can build a continuous network without long-range periodicity while keeping the same short-range bonding as the crystal. As conditions he named a small cation coordination number of 3 or 4, oxygen bonded to no more than two cations, polyhedra sharing only corners rather than edges or faces, and each polyhedron sharing at least three corners. SiO₂, B₂O₃, P₂O₅ and GeO₂ meet these conditions and form glass on their own.

Alkali and alkaline-earth oxides such as Na₂O, K₂O and CaO do not form glass by themselves; when they join the network, they break Si-O-Si bridges and create non-bridging oxygens. Their cations occupy interstices in the network, and these oxides are called network modifiers. Al₂O₃, ZnO, TiO₂ and the like are called intermediate oxides; they hardly form glass alone, but depending on composition they either join the network or modify it. For example, Al³⁺ whose charge is compensated by Na⁺ and the like enters the network as AlO₄ tetrahedra and reduces the number of non-bridging oxygens.

The more network formers and bridges a glass has, the higher its viscosity and glass transition temperature, the smaller its thermal expansion and the higher its chemical durability. Silica glass is the most fully connected glass and has excellent heat resistance, but shaping it requires very high temperatures. Soda-lime glass is a composition that lowers the forming temperature with Na₂O and restores durability with CaO. Borosilicate glass adds B₂O₃ to reduce thermal expansion and is used for laboratory ware and heat-resistant tableware. The proportions of formers and modifiers are chosen to suit the application.

faq.q: What kind of network does B₂O₃ form?
faq.a: In B₂O₃ glass, planar triangular BO₃ units, in which boron is bonded to three oxygens, share corners to form a network. Adding alkali converts some boron to fourfold-coordinated BO₄ tetrahedra, strengthening the network, so up to a certain composition property changes are not simple. This is called the boron anomaly.

faq.q: Is there a glass made only of a network former?
faq.a: Yes. Silica glass (fused silica), made of SiO₂ alone, is the classic example; its thermal expansion is very small and it transmits ultraviolet light well. Its viscosity is high, however, and melting and shaping it requires temperatures of about 2000 °C, so it is costly to make.

faq.q: Do metallic glasses have elements that play a role like network formers?
faq.a: Metallic glasses are held together by metallic bonding and have no directional network like oxide glasses. They become glass through a densely packed, disordered arrangement of atoms, and how readily they form depends on differences in atomic size and on the heat of mixing.

網目修飾酸化物.desc: An oxide such as Na₂O, K₂O or CaO that breaks bridges in a glass network to create non-bridging oxygens, with its cations occupying interstices in the network. It lowers the viscosity.

about.p: Network modifiers are oxides that do not form a glass network by themselves but enter the network of network formers and change its structure and properties. Typical examples are the alkali metal oxides Li₂O, Na₂O and K₂O and the alkaline earth oxides MgO, CaO and BaO. The oxygen brought in by a modifier breaks bridges in the network, and the cations occupy spaces in the network so as to neutralize the negative charge of nearby non-bridging oxygens. The cations are often surrounded by about five to eight oxygens and do not form strongly directional bonds like the network-forming cations. These weak, nondirectional bonds change the properties of glass greatly.

Whether an oxide forms or modifies the network is sometimes organized by the field strength Z/a², obtained from the cation charge Z and the cation–oxygen distance a (Å) (Dietzel's classification). As a rough guide, the network-forming Si⁴⁺ and B³⁺ have large values of about 1.3 to 2, the modifiers Na⁺ and K⁺ about 0.1–0.2 and Ca²⁺ about 0.3, while intermediate oxides such as Al³⁺ fall in between at about 0.5–1.0. Even among modifiers, divalent cations with stronger fields attract the surrounding oxygens strongly and hold the breaks in the network together, so they reduce chemical durability less than monovalent alkalis.

Adding modifiers weakens the connectivity of the network, lowering viscosity and the glass transition temperature so that the glass can be melted and formed at lower temperatures. In exchange, thermal expansion becomes larger and chemical durability lower. Alkali ions can also move through spaces in the network, giving glass a slight electrical conductivity. When two kinds of alkali are mixed, the mixed alkali effect is known, in which the electrical conductivity and ion diffusion coefficients fall greatly compared with a single alkali, even at the same total alkali content. The choice of type and amount of modifiers sets the balance between ease of melting, durability and electrical properties.

Soda-lime glass is a composition in which about 13% Na₂O is added to SiO₂ to make it easier to melt and about 10% CaO is added to restore durability, with a little MgO as well. K₂O acts much like Na₂O, and the two are often used together. PbO acts both as a modifier and as part of the network and raises the refractive index greatly, so it has been used in crystal glass. In chemical strengthening, the modifier cation Na⁺ in the surface layer is exchanged for the larger K⁺ to introduce compressive stress. Modifiers are the main means of adjusting the ease of melting, strength and optical properties of glass.

faq.q: How does glass change as the modifier content increases?
faq.a: Bridges in the network decrease and non-bridging oxygens increase, so viscosity and the glass transition temperature fall and the glass becomes easier to melt and form. On the other hand, thermal expansion grows and components leach more easily into water and acids, so chemical durability falls. Too much modifier makes the melt crystallize rather than form glass.

faq.q: Why is CaO added to soda-lime glass?
faq.a: Because Na₂O and SiO₂ alone give a glass that melts easily but leaches readily into water and has low durability. Adding divalent Ca²⁺, which holds the breaks in the network together strongly, raises durability. Too much CaO makes crystallization easier, however, so the amount is adjusted.

faq.q: Why does the mixed alkali effect occur?
faq.a: It is not fully understood, but it is thought that alkali ions of different sizes create differently shaped sites in the network, and ions of the other kind move into those sites less readily, so the pathways for ions become blocked. It is used in glasses where electrical insulation or chemical durability is to be improved.

非架橋酸素.desc: An oxygen in a glass network bonded to only one network-forming cation and not linked to a neighboring polyhedron. It increases when modifying oxides are added.

about.h: Difference from bridging oxygen and the Qⁿ notation
about.p: In the network of silicate glasses, an oxygen at a corner of an SiO₄ tetrahedron that is bonded to two Si atoms and links neighboring tetrahedra is a bridging oxygen (BO), and one bonded to only one Si, with its remaining negative charge neutralized by a modifier cation, is a non-bridging oxygen (NBO). If the number of bridging oxygens among the four corners of a tetrahedron is n and the tetrahedron is written Qⁿ, fused silica is all Q⁴, and as non-bridging oxygens increase it changes to Q³ and Q². Many Q³ units resemble sheet-like linkage and many Q² units chain-like linkage, so this serves as an index of network connectivity.

In binary Na₂O-SiO₂ glass, one Na₂O breaks one bridging oxygen and creates two non-bridging oxygens, so the number of non-bridging oxygens per tetrahedron, NBO/T, can be estimated as 2x/(1 − x), where x is the mole fraction of Na₂O. For example, for Na₂O·2SiO₂ (about 33 mol% Na₂O), NBO/T = 1, and on average every tetrahedron would be Q³. In real glasses, however, disproportionation occurs to some extent, with Q⁴ and Q² mixed to give an average of Q³, so the distribution of Qⁿ is not determined by composition alone. NBO/T is used as an average value.

When Al₂O₃ is added to a glass containing Na₂O, Al³⁺ has its charge compensated by Na⁺ and enters the network as AlO₄ tetrahedra, turning non-bridging oxygens back into bridges. When the molar amounts of Na₂O and Al₂O₃ are equal, non-bridging oxygens almost disappear on paper and the network becomes well connected. This makes it possible to obtain glasses that contain alkali yet have high viscosity and good chemical durability, and aluminosilicate glasses are used for cover glass for chemical strengthening and other uses. When Al₂O₃ exceeds Na₂O, there are not enough cations to compensate the charge, and the structure becomes more complex.

The amount of non-bridging oxygen and the distribution of Qⁿ are evaluated by separating the peaks with different chemical shifts for each Qⁿ in ²⁹Si solid-state NMR, or by examining the bonding states of oxygen with Raman spectroscopy or X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). Non-bridging oxygens are also the sites where leaching of glass into water and exchange of alkali ions occur. In ironmaking and smelting slags, too, NBO/T is used as a quantity expressing how broken the network of molten silicates is, and serves as a guide to viscosity, the capacity to take up sulfur and other properties. In geoscience it is also used to estimate the viscosity of magma.

faq.q: How do the properties of glass change as non-bridging oxygens increase?
faq.a: The network becomes less connected, so viscosity and the glass transition temperature fall and thermal expansion grows. Also, the modifier cations next to non-bridging oxygens readily exchange with hydrogen ions in water, so chemical durability falls. Forming becomes easier, while heat resistance and durability decline.

faq.q: How are non-bridging oxygens related to modifier cations?
faq.a: A non-bridging oxygen carries one extra negative charge, and modifier cations such as Na⁺ or Ca²⁺ nearby neutralize it. Monovalent Na⁺ compensates the charge of one non-bridging oxygen and divalent Ca²⁺ that of two. The number of non-bridging oxygens can therefore be estimated from the amount and valence of the modifier cations.

faq.q: Do non-bridging oxygens form when alkali is added to borate glass?
faq.a: With small amounts of alkali, instead of non-bridging oxygens forming, boron changes from three-coordinated BO₃ to four-coordinated BO₄, which actually strengthens the network. Beyond a certain amount of alkali, non-bridging oxygens begin to form, so the change in properties bends partway through the composition range.

強化ガラス.desc: Glass strengthened by quenching a heated sheet with air so that compressive stress remains at the surface and tensile stress inside. When it breaks, it shatters into small granules.

about.p: Fracture of glass starts when tensile stress acts on tiny flaws at the surface. Tempered glass has compressive stress left in its surface in advance, so that even when tension is applied from outside, the flaws do not open until that compression has been cancelled. As a result, its strength against bending and impact is about 3–5 times that of ordinary annealed glass. At the middle of the thickness, a tensile stress that balances the surface compression remains. The essence is not that the glass material itself has become stronger, but that residual stress keeps the surface flaws closed.

about.h: Manufacturing conditions, and glasses that are hard to temper
about.p: Sheet glass is heated to about 650 °C, above the glass transition temperature, and quenched by blowing air evenly onto both faces. The larger the temperature difference between surface and interior during cooling, the larger the stress that remains. It is therefore hard to create the temperature difference in thin sheets, and it is difficult to temper sheets thinner than about 3 mm adequately by air quenching. Also, the remaining stress is roughly proportional to the thermal expansion coefficient, so glasses with small thermal expansion, such as borosilicate glass and fused silica, can hardly be tempered by air quenching. Cutting and drilling are impossible after tempering, so all processing is finished before tempering.

When tempered glass breaks, the strain energy stored inside is released at once and the whole sheet shatters into blunt-edged granules a few mm across, so the risk of injury from large sharp fragments is small. This fracture pattern is checked by a fragmentation test that counts the number of fragments within a specified area. On the other hand, a spontaneous breakage is known in which tiny nickel sulfide particles in the glass change their crystal form and swell after some time, starting a crack from the central tensile layer. To reduce it, a heat soak treatment holds tempered glass at about 290 °C so that sheets containing such particles break in advance.

about.h: Heat-strengthened glass and where they are used
about.p: Glass cooled more gently so that the surface compressive stress is limited to about half that of tempered glass is called heat-strengthened glass. Its strength is about twice that of annealed glass, and when it breaks it forms large fragments similar to ordinary glass that tend to stay in the frame, so it is used for windows in high places and the like. Tempered glass is used for doors, partitions, furniture and the side and rear windows of cars. The windshield of a car is laminated glass with a resin interlayer so that it keeps visibility and shape even when cracked. In this way, the types are chosen with the difference in fracture pattern in mind, not strength alone.

faq.q: How much compressive stress is there in the surface of tempered glass?
faq.a: In tempered glass for buildings, the surface compressive stress is roughly 70–150 MPa, often around 100 MPa. Standards set a lower limit; ASTM C1048, for example, requires at least 69 MPa. Heat-strengthened glass has about half of that. The stress is measured without breaking the glass by photoelastic methods using polarized light.

faq.q: How does tempered glass differ from chemically strengthened glass?
faq.a: Tempered glass creates surface compression through the temperature difference produced by quenching, and chemically strengthened glass through ion exchange. In tempered glass the compressive layer is thick, about one fifth of the thickness, but it is unsuitable for thin sheets. Chemically strengthened glass has a thin compressive layer of a few tens of µm but a high stress, and can be used for sheets of 1 mm or less.

faq.q: Why does tempered glass break into small granules?
faq.a: Because a large tensile stress is stored at the middle of the thickness, and once a crack enters that layer, the released strain energy drives the crack forward while it branches again and again. The larger the central tensile stress, the finer the fragments.

化学強化ガラス.desc: Glass strengthened by exchanging Na⁺ in its surface layer for larger K⁺ in a molten salt, introducing large compressive stress in the surface layer. It can be used even for thin sheets.

about.p: In chemical strengthening, glass is immersed in molten potassium nitrate at a temperature below the strain point, and Na⁺ in the surface layer is exchanged for K⁺, which has a larger ionic radius. At this temperature the network hardly flows, so the state in which large ions have been forced into sites meant for small ions remains; the surface layer tries to expand, is constrained by the interior, and a large compressive stress develops in it. Whereas thermal tempering uses a temperature difference, chemical strengthening uses a difference in composition, so thin sheets and complex shapes can be strengthened and a large stress can be left. The technique was developed and put into practical use in the 1960s.

about.h: Compressive stress and depth of layer
about.p: The performance of chemically strengthened glass is expressed by the surface compressive stress (CS) and the depth of the compressive layer (DOL). In soda-lime glass K⁺ diffuses slowly and DOL is limited to about 10 µm, but in aluminosilicate glasses diffusion is fast, and a few hours of treatment can create a layer with CS of several hundred to about 1000 MPa and DOL of a few tens of µm. Because DOL is set by diffusion, it deepens roughly in proportion to the square root of the treatment time. However, raising the temperature or extending the time too much lowers CS through stress relaxation, so the conditions are chosen by balancing the two.

about.h: Internal tensile stress and sheet thickness
about.p: A tensile stress (CT) develops inside to balance the compression of the surface layers. Assuming a triangular profile in which the compressive stress falls linearly with depth, force balance gives CT ≈ CS × DOL/(t − 2DOL), where t is the sheet thickness. For example, with CS = 800 MPa, DOL = 40 µm and t = 0.70 mm, CT is about 52 MPa. The thinner the sheet and the deeper the DOL, the larger CT becomes, and if it is too large the glass shatters into fine pieces when broken. In glasses containing lithium, two-step exchanges of Li⁺ for Na⁺ and Na⁺ for K⁺ combine a deep layer with a high surface stress.

about.h: Where it is used and cautions
about.p: Chemically strengthened glass is used for the cover glass of smartphones and tablets, watch covers, and windows of aircraft and railway vehicles. Because the compressive layer is thin, a flaw deeper than the DOL has its tip in the internal tensile layer, and the strengthening effect is lost. To make the glass resist flaws from sharp, hard particles, deepening the DOL is therefore effective. Also, if the glass is cut after strengthening, the cut edge has no compressive layer, so normally the shape is finished before strengthening. The surface stress is measured without breaking the glass, for example with surface stress meters based on optical waveguiding.

faq.q: Which is stronger, chemically strengthened glass or thermally tempered glass?
faq.a: The surface compressive stress is much larger in chemically strengthened glass, several hundred MPa or more. However, its compressive layer is thin, a few tens of µm, so it is vulnerable to deep flaws. Thermally tempered glass has a smaller stress of around 100 MPa, but its compressive layer is thick, about one fifth of the thickness, so it resists deep flaws better.

faq.q: Why are aluminosilicate glasses used?
faq.a: Because Na⁺, compensating the charge of AlO₄ tetrahedra, is only weakly bound to the network and moves easily, ion exchange proceeds quickly and a deep layer can be formed. Also, the well-connected network makes stress relaxation slow, so a high compressive stress can remain. Soda-lime glass can also be chemically strengthened, but the layer is shallow.

faq.q: Is chemically strengthened glass resistant to heat?
faq.a: If it is held for long at a high temperature close to the treatment temperature, the strengthening stress is gradually lost by ion diffusion and network relaxation. It does not change at ordinary service temperatures, but it is unsuitable for use at temperatures of several hundred °C. Where resistance to sudden temperature changes is needed, a glass with small thermal expansion is chosen.

金属ガラス.desc: An amorphous alloy solidified from a metallic melt without crystallizing. With no dislocations, it has high strength and a large elastic strain limit. Thick pieces are called bulk metallic glasses.

about.p: Metallic melts have low viscosity and their atoms rearrange quickly, so they normally crystallize as soon as they are cooled. Since an amorphous alloy was first made in 1960 by quenching an Au-Si alloy at about 10⁶ K/s, early metallic glasses were ribbons a few tens of µm thick made by melt spinning, in which the melt is jetted onto a rotating copper wheel, and similar methods. From around 1990, multicomponent alloys based on Zr, Pd, Mg, Fe and others brought critical cooling rates down to about 1–100 K/s, and bulk metallic glasses from several mm to centimeter scale could be made simply by casting into a copper mold.

Metallic glasses have no dislocations or grain boundaries, so their yield strength is much higher than that of crystalline alloys of the same elements: about 1.8 GPa for Zr-based glasses, and over 5 GPa for some Co-based ones. Their Young's modulus is about 30% lower than that of crystals, and their elastic strain limit of about 2% is several times that of most crystalline metals. At room temperature, however, deformation concentrates in thin shear bands and there is no work hardening, so in tension they fracture with almost no elongation. To offset this brittleness, composites with dispersed crystalline phases and similar approaches are being studied.

about.h: Forming in the supercooled-liquid range, and uses
about.p: When a metallic glass is heated, it becomes a supercooled liquid of reduced viscosity above the glass transition temperature Tg and crystallizes at the higher crystallization temperature Tx. In the range between Tg and Tx it can deform greatly under small forces like a plastic, allowing precision forming that replicates fine mold features. Uses include springs, sporting goods and precision parts that exploit the large elastic energy, and Fe-based ribbons, which have no magnetocrystalline anisotropy and small coercivity, are used for low-loss transformer cores.

faq.q: Do metallic glasses crystallize over time?
faq.a: They are thermodynamically less stable than crystals, but at room temperature atoms barely move, so for practical purposes they do not crystallize. Held long near Tg, however, they can become brittle through structural relaxation or crystallize, so the service temperature is kept well below Tg.

faq.q: Are metallic glasses and amorphous alloys the same thing?
faq.a: Both refer to alloys without crystalline periodicity and are used almost interchangeably. Those that show a clear glass transition on heating and have a supercooled-liquid range are sometimes distinguished specifically as metallic glasses.

faq.q: Why do multicomponent alloys form glass more readily?
faq.a: When atoms of different sizes mix while attracting each other, the liquid takes a dense, disordered arrangement in which atoms move slowly, and forming crystals requires extensive rearrangement of atoms. A lower liquidus temperature, which raises the reduced glass transition temperature, also helps.

換算ガラス転移温度.desc: The glass transition temperature Tg divided by the liquidus temperature Tl, Trg = Tg/Tl. The larger it is, the more readily a melt forms glass, with about 2/3 or more taken as a guideline.

about.h: Definition and ease of glass formation
about.p: The reduced glass transition temperature Trg is the glass transition temperature Tg divided by the liquidus temperature Tl, both expressed in absolute temperature. When a melt is cooled, crystals can form below Tl, but once it has cooled to Tg the atoms can hardly move and crystals can no longer form. In other words, the temperature span of the supercooled liquid in which crystallization is a risk runs from Tl to Tg, and a larger Trg means that this span is narrower and that the liquid is more viscous within it. For this reason Trg has been used as a simple index of how easily a liquid forms a glass (glass-forming ability).

In 1969 Turnbull used the theory of homogeneous nucleation to estimate what values of Trg make glass formation easy. Assuming that the viscosity of the liquid reaches about 10¹² Pa·s at Tg and varies with temperature in a certain way, the result is that in liquids with Trg greater than about 2/3 the rate of crystal nucleation during cooling is very small, and they form glasses easily even when cooled slowly. Liquids with Trg of about 1/2 need very fast quenching to form a glass. Pure metals are thought to have very small Trg and do not form glasses with ordinary rapid quenching.

In metallic glass alloys, moving the composition close to a deep eutectic lowers Tl greatly while Tg changes little, so Trg increases. For example, an alloy with Tg of 650 K and Tl of 1000 K has Trg of 0.65. If the composition can be changed to lower Tl to 900 K, Trg becomes about 0.72, and glass formation can be expected to become easier. In fact, most bulk metallic glasses have Trg of about 0.6 or more, and a trend has been reported for alloys with smaller critical cooling rates to have larger Trg. Lowering the liquidus temperature by using many components is an idea consistent with Inoue's empirical rules.

about.h: Limits of the index and other indices
about.p: Trg is simple and convenient, but it does not always rank glass-forming ability correctly. Not only nucleation but also the rate of crystal growth matters, and Tg varies by several K to more than ten K with heating rate, while Tl also depends on measurement conditions. For metallic glasses, therefore, other indices are used alongside it, such as ΔTx (the width of the supercooled liquid region), the difference between Tg and the temperature Tx at which crystallization starts on heating, and γ, expressed as Tx/(Tg + Tl). The usual approach is to compare several indices and finally confirm by actually casting the alloy and finding the maximum thickness that becomes glass.

faq.q: Is the melting point Tm ever used instead of Tl?
faq.a: Yes. For pure substances and compounds the melting point Tm is used, and the ratio is sometimes written Tg/Tm. In alloys the temperature at which solid starts to melt differs from the temperature at which it is fully molten, so the liquidus temperature Tl, at which it becomes fully liquid, is generally used as the upper limit of the range where crystallization must be avoided.

faq.q: Does a Trg of 2/3 or more guarantee glass formation?
faq.a: No. 2/3 is a guide from nucleation theory, and actual glass-forming ability also depends on the rate of crystal growth, heterogeneous nucleation on impurities and the cooling rate. Some alloys with large Trg form glasses poorly, and some show the opposite.

faq.q: Is there a similar relation for polymers?
faq.a: Yes. For many crystalline polymers there is an empirical rule that Tg is about 1/2 to 2/3 of the melting point Tm (in absolute temperature). For poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET), for example, Tg is about 350 K and Tm about 530 K, a ratio of about 0.66.

アモルファスシリコン.desc: Silicon without long-range periodicity. a-Si:H, with its dangling bonds terminated by hydrogen, is used in thin-film transistors and thin-film solar cells.

about.p: In amorphous silicon, almost every Si atom is covalently bonded to four Si atoms, just as in the crystal. However, the bond angles deviate from the crystalline 109.5° by about 10° on average and the bond lengths also vary slightly, so long-range periodicity is lost. Such a structure is represented by a continuous random network of tetrahedra linked with disorder. Because of strain in the network, some atoms cannot complete four bonds and dangling bonds remain. This disorder and these dangling bonds, absent in the crystal, are major factors that determine the electrical properties.

about.h: Density of states and electrical properties
about.p: In a crystal, the edges of the valence and conduction bands are sharp and there are no electronic states between them. In a-Si:H, network disorder creates tail states that extend exponentially from the band edges into the gap. Electrons in tail states are localized and hard to move, and the energy span between the boundaries with mobile states is called the mobility gap. The optical band gap is about 1.7–1.8 eV. Dangling bonds create levels near the middle of the gap. In 1975 Spear and LeComber showed that the conduction type of films in which defects had been reduced by hydrogen could be controlled by adding phosphorus or boron, opening the way to electronic devices.

about.h: Light-induced degradation and solar cell structure
about.p: a-Si:H absorbs visible light strongly, but its carriers can diffuse only a short distance, so solar cells use a pin structure in which an undoped i-layer a few hundred nm thick lies between the p- and n-layers, and the internal field extracts the carriers. Under continued illumination there is the Staebler–Wronski effect, in which dangling bonds increase and efficiency falls; efficiency drops early in use and then becomes nearly constant. The degradation recovers on heating to about 150 °C. The stabilized efficiency of single-junction cells is only about 10% even for the best laboratory cells, and improvements were sought with tandem cells stacked with microcrystalline silicon and other designs.

about.h: Roles in displays and crystalline silicon solar cells
about.p: Because a-Si:H can be deposited uniformly on large glass substrates by plasma CVD at about 300 °C or below, it has been used in the thin-film transistors (TFTs) that switch the pixels of liquid crystal displays. However, the field-effect mobility of its TFTs is small, about 0.5–1 cm²/(V·s), so for high resolution and for driving organic light-emitting diodes, oxide semiconductors (IGZO) at about 10 cm²/(V·s) and low-temperature polysilicon at around 100 cm²/(V·s) have come into use. In crystalline silicon solar cells, on the other hand, heterojunction cells in which thin a-Si:H layers passivate surface defects support high efficiencies.

faq.q: What is the difference between amorphous silicon and polycrystalline silicon?
faq.a: Polycrystalline silicon is an aggregate of crystal grains, and within each grain the atoms are arranged periodically. Amorphous silicon has no crystal grains and lacks long-range periodicity throughout. Polycrystalline silicon has far higher mobility, while amorphous silicon has the advantage of being easy to deposit uniformly over large areas at low temperature.

faq.q: What happens when amorphous silicon is heated?
faq.a: Heating above a few hundred °C drives out hydrogen and increases defects, and holding it for long above about 600 °C, or melting it momentarily with a laser, crystallizes it into polycrystalline silicon. Low-temperature polysilicon TFTs are made by crystallizing an a-Si film on a glass substrate with an excimer laser.

faq.q: Where have amorphous silicon solar cells been used?
faq.a: Because they generate power well even in weak light such as indoor fluorescent lighting, and can be made thin, cheaply and over large areas, they have been widely used to power small devices such as calculators and watches. For outdoor power generation, higher-efficiency crystalline silicon solar cells dominate.

べき乗則クリープ.desc: Creep in which the steady-state creep rate is proportional to the stress raised to the power n (n is about 3 to 8). It arises from dislocation glide combined with recovery by climb, and dominates at high stresses.

about.p: The steady-state creep rate in power-law creep is written ε̇ = Aσⁿexp(−Q/RT). Dividing the stress by the shear modulus G and using the self-diffusion coefficient D to write ε̇ ∝ D(σ/G)ⁿ makes different materials easier to compare. n is the stress exponent; for pure metals and many single-phase alloys it is about 4 to 7, and values close to 5 are especially common. Because n is large, with n = 5, for example, lowering the stress by only 10% changes the rate by a factor of 0.9⁵ ≈ 0.59. That the activation energy Q is close to that of self-diffusion shows that atomic diffusion sets the rate of deformation.

Dislocations move on their slip planes, but they stop when they catch on precipitates or become tangled with other dislocations. At high temperature, vacancies gather at or leave a dislocation, so it climbs out of its slip plane; this lets it get past obstacles or annihilate with a dislocation of opposite sign. Because the rate of this recovery is set by vacancy diffusion, power-law creep, although carried by dislocations, shows the same temperature dependence as diffusion. As deformation proceeds, dislocations line up into low-angle grain boundaries, and subgrains form inside the grains. The higher the stress, the smaller the subgrains.

The stress exponent is not a fixed constant for each material. In alloys such as Al-Mg, where solute atoms drag on moving dislocations, glide itself becomes the slow step and n ≈ 3, distinguished from the value of about 5 for pure-metal behavior. At still higher stresses the rate rises faster than a power of stress and the equation no longer holds (power-law breakdown). In alloys strengthened by dispersed oxide particles and similar materials, the apparent stress exponent can far exceed 10, and the apparent activation energy can exceed that of self-diffusion. This is due to a threshold stress σ_th at which particles stop dislocations; using σ − σ_th in place of σ brings n back toward ordinary values.

about.h: Finding n and Q from tests
about.p: n and Q are determined by creep tests. Measuring the steady-state creep rate at several stresses at constant temperature and plotting it on log-log axes gives n as the slope. Stress-change tests, in which the stress on a single specimen is changed in steps, reduce the effect of microstructural differences between specimens. Similarly, holding the stress constant, varying the temperature and plotting ln ε̇ against 1/T gives Q from the slope −Q/R. In design, the equation found this way is used to find, for example, the stress that produces the allowable strain (such as 1%) in 100,000 hours. Extrapolating to stresses below those tested, however, may cross into another mechanism such as diffusion creep.

faq.q: Are power-law creep and dislocation creep the same thing?
faq.a: They are used with almost the same meaning. Power-law creep is the name that focuses on the form of the equation, with the rate proportional to a power of stress; dislocation creep focuses on dislocations carrying the deformation. When contrasting it with diffusion creep, it is more often called dislocation creep.

faq.q: Can the rupture time be estimated from the minimum creep rate?
faq.a: For many metals, the Monkman–Grant relation is known, in which the product of the minimum creep rate and the rupture time is nearly constant. Measuring the minimum creep rate in a short test gives a rough idea of the rupture time, but the constant must be determined by measurement for each material.

faq.q: What care is needed in design when the stress exponent n is large?
faq.a: The larger n, the more a small difference in stress changes the rate. With n = 5, doubling the stress raises the rate 32 times. Stress concentrations, residual stresses and errors in estimating loads strongly affect life, so the actual stress distribution is checked with the finite element method or similar tools, and a margin is built into the design.

拡散クリープ.desc: Creep that proceeds as grains elongate by atomic diffusion, with a rate proportional to stress. It includes Nabarro–Herring creep by lattice diffusion and Coble creep by grain boundary diffusion.

about.p: At a grain boundary under tensile stress σ, the energy needed to create a vacancy falls by σΩ, where Ω is the volume of one atom; at a boundary under compression it rises. Boundaries under tension therefore have more vacancies nearby and those under compression fewer, so vacancies diffuse from the tensile to the compressive boundaries and atoms diffuse the opposite way. As atoms pile onto the boundaries under tension, the grains lengthen in the direction of the stress. σΩ is small compared with the thermal energy kT: with σ = 10 MPa, Ω ≈ 1.1×10⁻²⁹ m³ (close to the value for Ni) and 1000 K, σΩ/kT ≈ 0.008. The difference in vacancy concentration is therefore proportional to stress.

about.h: Grain size and the two paths
about.p: The rate of diffusion creep depends strongly on the grain size d: it is proportional to 1/d² for Nabarro–Herring creep, with diffusion through the grain interiors, and to 1/d³ for Coble creep, with diffusion along grain boundaries. Increasing the grain size tenfold, from 10 µm to 100 µm, lowers the rates to 1/100 and 1/1000 respectively. Grain boundary diffusion has a lower activation energy than lattice diffusion, so the share of Coble creep grows at lower temperatures and finer grain sizes. In ionic crystals, matter is transported only if both cations and anions move, so the slower ion, moving along its fastest path, controls the overall rate. In fine-grained ceramics, diffusion creep is prominent at high temperature.

about.h: Differences from grain boundary sliding and superplasticity
about.p: If grains lengthened by atomic diffusion alone, gaps or overlaps would form between neighboring grains, so diffusion creep is always accompanied by grain boundary sliding. Conversely, in superplasticity grain boundary sliding is the main deformation and is accommodated by dislocation motion and other processes; slowly pulling a material with fine grains of a few µm at more than half its melting point gives elongations of several hundred percent or more. The stress exponent of superplasticity is about 2, distinguishing it from the value of 1 for diffusion creep. Harper–Dorn creep, with n ≈ 1 but no grain size dependence, has been reported in coarse-grained materials at very low stresses, but its existence and mechanism are debated.

about.h: Where it matters and what to do
about.p: Diffusion creep does not stop even at low stress, so it is a problem for parts exposed to high temperature under low stress for long times. The basic remedy is coarser grains, which is why coarse-grained, columnar-grained and single-crystal materials are used for high-temperature parts. In tungsten filaments for incandescent lamps, a trace of potassium is added to create long interlocking grains that suppress sagging under their own weight by grain boundary sliding. On the other hand, diffusion creep is the main deformation in part of the flow of rock in the Earth's mantle and in the high-temperature deformation of fine-grained ceramics. Its characteristic behavior, with the rate proportional to stress, is close to viscous flow.

faq.q: How can Nabarro–Herring creep and Coble creep be distinguished?
faq.a: By the grain size dependence of the rate and the activation energy. If, in specimens of different grain sizes, the rate is proportional to 1/d² and the activation energy is close to that of lattice diffusion, it is Nabarro–Herring creep; if it is proportional to 1/d³ and close to that of grain boundary diffusion, it is Coble creep. In practice both act in parallel and their rates add.

faq.q: Why is the stress exponent of diffusion creep 1?
faq.a: Because the difference in vacancy concentration between grain boundaries is proportional to the ratio of the work done by the stress, σΩ, to the thermal energy kT. Since σΩ is far smaller than kT, the concentration difference is proportional to stress, and so are the resulting vacancy flow and therefore the creep rate.

faq.q: Is diffusion creep the same as viscous flow?
faq.a: They share a rate proportional to stress, and diffusion creep behaves much like Newtonian viscous flow. However, viscous flow of glasses and liquids occurs by cooperative rearrangement of atoms, whereas diffusion creep is a change in grain shape by atoms diffusing between grain boundaries, and its rate depends strongly on grain size.

変形機構図.desc: A map with normalized stress and homologous temperature as axes, showing the fields of the mechanism that deforms fastest, such as dislocation glide, power-law creep and diffusion creep.

about.p: The deformation mechanism map was proposed by Ashby in 1972, and maps for many metals and ceramics were collected in his 1982 book with Frost. Values such as diffusion coefficients, shear modulus, atomic volume and grain size are inserted into the rate equation of each mechanism, such as dislocation glide, power-law creep and diffusion creep, and the rate is calculated for each combination of stress and temperature. Rates of mechanisms that act independently are added, while for mechanisms that act as alternatives the faster one is chosen, and the field of the mechanism with the largest contribution is shaded. A boundary line is the condition at which the rates of two neighboring mechanisms are equal.

Using the homologous temperature T/Tm, the absolute temperature divided by the melting point Tm, on the horizontal axis lets the high-temperature behavior of materials with different melting points be compared on the same scale. As a guide, creep becomes noticeable once T/Tm exceeds about 0.4. Room temperature, 20 °C, is only T/Tm ≈ 0.08 for tungsten (Tm ≈ 3695 K) but as much as about 0.49 for lead (Tm ≈ 601 K). Old lead pipes and roofing sag slowly under their own weight because they are in the creep regime even at room temperature. Conversely, T/Tm = 0.6 for pure Ni corresponds to about 1040 K, or around 760 °C.

A deformation mechanism map is calculated from model rate equations and literature constants for a fixed grain size and purity. Just as refining the grains enlarges the diffusion creep field, the boundaries move considerably when the microstructure changes, and maps for pure metals cannot be applied directly to alloys containing precipitates. The constants in the rate equations carry errors, so the positions of the boundaries need to be checked by experiment. The map also shows the rate of steady-state deformation and does not tell when fracture occurs. For fracture, separate fracture mechanism maps have been made, showing fields such as cleavage, intergranular fracture and ductile fracture in the same way.

about.h: Use in design and materials selection
about.p: Placing the service stress and temperature on the map shows which mechanism dominates, and the contours of constant strain rate drawn on the map give a rough idea of the deformation rate. If the point lies in the diffusion creep field, coarser grains help; if it lies in the power-law creep field, precipitates or solute elements that hinder dislocation motion help, so the effective remedy differs. If the point is near a boundary, a slight change in conditions can switch the mechanism, and extrapolation from short tests is likely to fail. In the Earth sciences, maps for rocks and ice are also used to consider the mechanisms of flow in the mantle and in glaciers.

faq.q: What is homologous temperature?
faq.a: It is the absolute temperature T divided by the melting point Tm (also absolute), T/Tm. The ease of atomic diffusion becomes similar across materials when referred to the melting point, so it is used as a guide to high-temperature deformation. Dividing Celsius temperatures gives a meaningless value, so it must always be calculated with absolute temperatures.

faq.q: Why is the stress on the vertical axis divided by the shear modulus?
faq.a: Because the rates of dislocation motion and creep depend not on the stress itself but on how large the stress is relative to the strength of interatomic bonding. Using σ/G, divided by the shear modulus G, lets materials of different strength be compared on the same scale. Maps often also carry a scale of actual stress (MPa) alongside.

faq.q: What does a boundary line on a deformation mechanism map represent?
faq.a: It is the combination of stress and temperature at which two neighboring mechanisms produce deformation at the same rate. On the line their contributions are equal, and farther from it one of them dominates. A boundary is not a line where the mechanism switches abruptly; near it, both mechanisms are at work.

ラーソン・ミラー・パラメータ.desc: The value P = T(C + log₁₀t_r) that combines the temperature and time of creep rupture. Taken as constant at a given stress, it is used to estimate long lives from short tests.

about.p: The time to creep rupture, t_r, shortens rapidly with rising temperature in an Arrhenius manner. Larson and Miller showed that when rupture time and temperature are combined into a single value, P = T(C + log₁₀t_r), P is nearly constant at a given stress. T is the absolute temperature, t_r is in hours (h), and C = 20 is commonly used for many steels and heat-resistant alloys. When data are plotted with P on the horizontal axis and stress on the vertical axis, results from tests at different temperatures collapse onto a single curve, and reading P from the stress lets you calculate the rupture time at any temperature.

High-temperature components may be used for 100,000 hours (about 11 years) or more, and tests of that length cannot all be performed. Instead, tests of several hundred to several thousand hours are run at temperatures above the service temperature, and the life at the service temperature is estimated from the value of P. For example, with C = 20, rupture in 1000 h at 1000 K corresponds to P = 23000, which at the same stress corresponds to a life of 10⁵ h at 920 K. That lowering the temperature by only 80 K extends the life a hundredfold also shows how important temperature control is in high-temperature components.

The method assumes that the same creep mechanism operates at the test and service temperatures and that the microstructure changes in the same way. If precipitates coarsen, other phases precipitate, or the deformation mechanism shifts from dislocation creep to diffusion creep over long times, extrapolation from short tests can overestimate the life. The value of C also varies between materials, so it is preferably determined from measured data, and it is important not to stretch the extrapolation range needlessly. Other parameters, such as the Orr–Sherby–Dorn parameter, are used for the same purpose.

faq.q: Why is the constant C equal to 20?
faq.a: Fitting data for many steels and heat-resistant alloys gives C in the range of roughly 15 to 25, and 20 is commonly used as a representative value. It is not fixed by theory, so when accuracy is needed, C is determined from test data at several temperatures for the material in question.

faq.q: What does a large P mean?
faq.a: P expresses the severity of the combination of temperature and time; a larger P corresponds to a higher temperature or longer time. On a curve of P against rupture stress, the rupture stress falls as P increases. A material with a higher rupture stress at the same P is more resistant to creep rupture.

faq.q: Can the rupture time be expressed in seconds?
faq.a: The form of the equation is the same, but the value of log₁₀t_r changes, so the value of C that fits also changes. C = 20 is the value for rupture time expressed in hours (h), so units must match when comparing with other data.

Ni基超合金.desc: A heat-resistant alloy with a large amount of the L1₂ ordered phase γ' (Ni₃Al) coherently precipitated in an FCC Ni matrix. Used for turbine blades, it retains strength up to temperatures close to its melting point.

about.p: A nickel-based superalloy is an alloy in which the L1₂ ordered phase γ' (Ni₃(Al,Ti)) precipitates as cuboids in the matrix γ, an FCC Ni solid solution. Because γ and γ' have nearly the same lattice parameter and coherent interfaces, γ' resists coarsening even at high temperature, and in alloys for single-crystal blades it occupies 60 to 70% of the volume. When a dislocation in γ enters γ', it disturbs the ordered arrangement and creates an antiphase boundary, so dislocations must travel in pairs and meet a large resistance. In addition, Cr, Mo, W, Re and other elements provide solid-solution strengthening of the matrix.

In turbine blades pulled for long times at high temperature, grain boundaries perpendicular to the stress become the starting points of creep damage. Blades with columnar grains, made by solidifying in one direction from the bottom of the mold so that the boundaries are aligned with the stress, were therefore produced, followed by single-crystal blades grown by selecting just one crystal. A single crystal can do with fewer grain-boundary-strengthening elements, so solution treatment can be done at high temperature to make γ' uniform and fine. The blade length is aligned with the low-modulus 〈001〉 orientation to reduce thermal stress.

On the surface of a blade exposed to hot gas, Al and Cr in the alloy oxidize to form protective Al₂O₃ or Cr₂O₃ scales. Adding many strengthening elements may force Al or Cr to be reduced, so coatings rich in Al (aluminide coatings or MCrAlY coatings) are applied to the surface to make up the oxidation resistance. A zirconia thermal barrier coating is then layered on top to lower the metal temperature, and air flows through internal cooling holes to cool the blade, so that it can be used in gas at temperatures that can exceed the melting point of the alloy.

faq.q: Why are they called superalloys?
faq.a: They came to be called by this name as alloys that keep high strength and oxidation resistance even at high temperatures at which the strength of ordinary steels and similar alloys drops sharply. Besides Ni-based superalloys, there are also Co-based and Fe-Ni-based superalloys.

faq.q: Does γ' become weaker as the temperature rises?
faq.a: The Ni₃Al of γ' shows an anomalous temperature dependence in which the yield stress rises with temperature, being strongest at about 700 to 800 °C. This is because heat promotes cross slip that converts dislocations into a configuration that moves with difficulty.
