At still higher temperatures, however, γ' coarsens or dissolves and the strength falls.

faq.q: What happens if too much Re is added?
faq.a: Re slows diffusion and raises creep strength, but too much makes brittle TCP phases such as the σ phase likely to precipitate as needles or plates, lowering strength and ductility. Re is also expensive and dense, so the amount added is set by balancing these factors.

遮熱コーティング.desc: A ceramic coating of low thermal conductivity applied to the surface of high-temperature components. It consists of a zirconia top coat and a bond coat, and greatly lowers the metal temperature.

about.p: In a gas turbine, the higher the temperature of the gas entering the turbine, the higher the thermal efficiency and output. That gas temperature, however, can be close to or even above the melting point of the nickel-based superalloys used for the blades, which cannot withstand it on their own. Cooling air is therefore passed through the blades while a ceramic layer of low thermal conductivity on the surface lowers the metal temperature. The key point is that this temperature difference arises from heat flowing through the layer: the heat flux q in ΔT = qL/k is created by the internal cooling. Without cooling, the metal would in time reach the gas temperature, and no insulating effect would remain.

The top coat is zirconia partially stabilized by adding about 6 to 8 wt% Y₂O₃ (YSZ). Adding Y creates oxygen vacancies, and these vacancies and the substituted Y atoms scatter phonons strongly, so even dense material has a thermal conductivity of about 2.3 W/(m·K) at 1000 °C, low for a ceramic. Its thermal expansion coefficient of about 11×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ is also large for a ceramic, keeping the mismatch with the metal relatively small. The addition is kept in the partially stabilized range to prevent the tetragonal-to-monoclinic transformation on cooling, with its volume expansion of about 4%, while obtaining high toughness from the metastable tetragonal phase (t').

about.h: How the coatings are made and their structure
about.p: There are two main processes. In atmospheric plasma spraying (APS), molten particles pile up as flattened splats, and fine cracks and pores parallel to the surface block the heat flow, lowering the thermal conductivity to about 1 W/(m·K). Electron beam physical vapor deposition (EB-PVD) gives a coating of aligned columnar crystals, and the gaps between the columns open and close to relieve strain from the thermal expansion mismatch. Although its thermal conductivity, about 1.5 to 1.9 W/(m·K), is higher than that of sprayed coatings, it resists thermal cycling well and has a smooth surface, so it is often used on the rotating blades of aircraft engines. Sprayed coatings, cheaper and easy to apply thickly, are used on combustors and similar parts.

Several kinds of degradation proceed together in service. The thermally grown oxide at the interface with the bond coat thickens roughly according to the parabolic law, and on each cooling, stress from the thermal expansion mismatch concentrates there and leads to spallation of the top coat. Long use well above about 1200 °C decomposes the metastable t' phase and reduces porosity by sintering, so the coating loses its ability to relieve strain. Another problem is damage from ingested sand or volcanic ash that melts as calcium-magnesium-aluminum silicate (CMAS), soaks into the pores and solidifies. New top coats with lower thermal conductivity, such as gadolinium zirconate (Gd₂Zr₂O₇), are therefore being studied.

faq.q: How much does a thermal barrier coating lower the metal temperature?
faq.a: It depends on the coating thickness L, the thermal conductivity k and the heat flux q through the coating, and can be estimated as ΔT = qL/k. For the same thickness and heat flux, a coating with half the thermal conductivity gives twice the temperature difference. Since it assumes heat keeps flowing through internal cooling, the difference varies greatly with operating conditions.

faq.q: What is the difference between a thermal barrier coating and an environmental barrier coating (EBC)?
faq.a: A thermal barrier coating mainly lowers the temperature of metal parts. An environmental barrier coating protects ceramic parts, such as SiC fiber-reinforced SiC composites, from losing their surface SiO₂ to hot water vapor and receding; ytterbium silicates and similar materials are used.

faq.q: What does "partially stabilized" mean?
faq.a: ZrO₂ changes among monoclinic, tetragonal and cubic forms with temperature. Adding a large amount of Y₂O₃ gives fully stabilized zirconia that is entirely cubic, but in thermal barrier coatings less is added, keeping the material mainly tetragonal. This suppresses the volume change from phase transformation while giving a tough coating.

ピリング・ベドワース比.desc: The ratio of the volume of an oxide to the volume of metal used to form it. A guide by which values below 1 tend to give cracked scales and values of about 1 to 2 tend to give protective ones.

about.p: In 1923, Pilling and Bedworth organized how metals oxidize by the ratio of the volume of oxide formed to the volume of metal consumed. The key is to compare equal numbers of metal atoms: the volume of 1 mol of the oxide M_aO_b is divided by the volume of the a mol of metal it contains. If the ratio is less than 1, the oxide cannot fully cover the metal surface; if it is greater than 1, the scale grows in a compressed state, squeezed sideways. Because it can be calculated from densities and molar masses alone, it has been used as a first guide for judging whether a scale will be protective.

Calculated from room-temperature densities (the values shift by 0.1 to 0.2 depending on the densities used), the PBR is about 0.57 for Na and about 0.65 for Ca, below 1, which agrees with the fact that oxidation of these metals does not easily stop. Al is about 1.3, and Ni and Cu (Cu₂O) are about 1.7, in the range that tends to give protective scales. Ti (rutile TiO₂) is about 1.8 and Cr (Cr₂O₃) about 2.0. In contrast, Nb (Nb₂O₅) is about 2.7 and W (WO₃) about 3.4, so large compressive stresses build up in the scale and cracking and spallation occur easily. W, whose oxide also volatilizes at high temperature, is hard to use in hot air as it is.

There are many cases where the PBR alone cannot judge protectiveness. Iron forms FeO with a ratio of about 1.8, but FeO formed at high temperature contains a very large number of defects through which ions diffuse rapidly, so the scale grows thick and fast. Si and Cr have rather large values of around 2, yet dense SiO₂ and Cr₂O₃ make excellent protective scales. The PBR assumes that the scale grows at its interface with the metal; when metal ions diffuse outward and oxide forms at the scale surface, stress from the volume difference does not build up much. Protectiveness is judged together with diffusion rates in the scale, adhesion and the thermal expansion mismatch on cooling.

about.h: Use in the thermal oxidation of Si
about.p: The idea of the PBR is also useful for relating the thickness of a scale to the thickness of metal consumed. When Si is thermally oxidized to amorphous SiO₂ in semiconductor manufacturing, taking densities of 2.33 g/cm³ for Si and 2.20 g/cm³ for SiO₂ gives a ratio of about 2.27. Assuming the area stays the same and only the thickness increases, forming SiO₂ of thickness x consumes about 0.44x of Si, so about 44% of the oxide grows below the original Si surface and the rest above it. A 100 nm oxide consumes about 44 nm of Si, and this is allowed for in designing device dimensions and steps.

faq.q: How is the Pilling–Bedworth ratio calculated?
faq.a: It is found from PBR = (M_ox ρ_M)/(n M_M ρ_ox). M_ox and ρ_ox are the molar mass and density of the oxide, M_M and ρ_M those of the metal, and n is the number of metal atoms in one formula unit of the oxide. It is a dimensionless ratio, so it can be calculated as long as the units of density and molar mass are consistent.

faq.q: Why does a scale spall easily when the PBR exceeds 2?
faq.a: Because the oxide tries to swell to more than twice the volume of the original metal while being restrained sideways by the metal, so large compressive stresses build up in the scale. The stored energy grows as the scale thickens, and beyond a certain thickness the scale lifts off or cracks and spalls.

faq.q: Does the PBR change with temperature?
faq.a: It changes slightly because the thermal expansion of the metal and oxide differs a little, but values calculated from room-temperature densities are used as a guide. What matters much more is which oxide forms; if the oxide that forms changes with temperature or oxygen partial pressure, the value for that oxide must be used.

酸化の放物線則.desc: The relation x² = k_p t, in which the square of the oxide scale thickness increases in proportion to time. It holds when diffusion of ions through a dense scale controls the growth rate.

about.h: Origin of the law and Wagner's theory
about.p: When diffusion through the scale controls growth, the flow of matter through the scale is inversely proportional to its thickness x, so the growth rate is dx/dt ∝ 1/x, which integrates to x² = k_p t. In 1933, Wagner related k_p, through the rate at which ions and electrons move via point defects in the scale, to the defect concentration and diffusion coefficients of the oxide and to the difference in oxygen partial pressure across the scale. This theory also explains why small additions of elements that change the defect concentration of the oxide alter k_p. k_p increases with temperature in the Arrhenius form k_p = k₀exp(−Q/RT).

In actual tests the mass gain of a specimen is often measured continuously with a thermobalance, and with the mass gain per unit area Δm/A the law is written (Δm/A)² = k_p t. The unit of k_p is then g²/(cm⁴·s) or similar, and its value differs from a k_p in m²/s written with thickness, so the definition must be checked when comparing literature values. The mass gained is that of the oxygen taken into the scale. For Al₂O₃, for example, oxygen makes up about 47% of the mass, so with a density of 3.95 g/cm³, a gain of 0.1 mg/cm² corresponds to a scale about 0.54 µm thick.

The parabolic law is a sign that a dense, adherent scale controls growth. If the scale is cracked or porous, a linear law results, proceeding at a constant rate regardless of thickness, and thin films near room temperature show a logarithmic law in which growth almost stops at a few nm. If the scale volatilizes at high temperature, growth by diffusion and loss by volatilization combine in a paralinear law; the thickness approaches a constant value, but metal continues to be lost at a constant rate. Volatilization of Cr₂O₃ as CrO₃ is a typical example. Breakaway oxidation, in which the scale cracks partway through and the rate suddenly increases, also needs attention.

about.h: Application to the thermal oxidation of Si
about.p: For the thermal oxidation of Si in semiconductors, Deal and Grove in 1965 expressed the relation between oxide thickness x and time t as x² + Ax = B(t + τ). It is a model in which diffusion of oxygen through the SiO₂ film and reaction at the interface with Si act in series. While the film is thin, the interface reaction is the slow step and the thickness grows nearly in proportion to time; as it thickens, diffusion takes control and growth approaches the parabolic law x² ≈ Bt. The parabolic rate constant B is larger in water vapor than in dry oxygen, so thick films are grown quickly in steam. Very thin films grown in dry oxygen, however, are known to grow faster than this model predicts.

faq.q: What are the units of the parabolic rate constant k_p?
faq.a: Written with thickness, x² = k_p t, it is in m²/s or cm²/s; written with mass gain, (Δm/A)² = k_p t, it is in g²/(cm⁴·s), mg²/(cm⁴·h) or similar. Some definitions include a factor of 2, as in x² = 2k_p t, so the form of the equation and the units should be checked when using literature values.

faq.q: How can one check whether oxidation follows the parabolic law?
faq.a: Plot the square of the thickness or mass gain against time and see whether it is a straight line, or see whether the slope on log-log axes is 0.5. Other processes often mix in at short times, so that part is excluded when judging. A slope near 1 suggests a linear law, and about 0.33 a cubic law.

faq.q: How is the parabolic law related to the diffusion distance √(Dt)?
faq.a: Both reflect the same property: the distance of a process driven by diffusion is proportional to the square root of time. Because diffusion through the scale controls growth, k_p is related to the diffusion coefficients in the scale and the difference in oxygen partial pressure, and like a diffusion coefficient it increases with temperature in Arrhenius form.

密度汎関数理論.desc: A theory that uses the fact that the ground-state energy is determined by the electron density, solving the Kohn–Sham equations to obtain the electronic states and energy of a material. The core of first-principles calculation.

about.p: The properties of materials are determined by the states of their electrons, but the wave function of many mutually interacting electrons has too many variables to be solved as it is. Hohenberg and Kohn showed that the ground-state energy is determined by the electron density alone, a function of only three dimensions. Kohn and Sham replaced this with a problem in which fictitious non-interacting electrons move in an effective potential, arranged so that their electron density is the same as that of the real system. The complicated interactions between electrons are gathered into a term called the exchange-correlation energy.

DFT takes the kinds and arrangement of atoms as input and gives the total energy, the forces on the atoms, the electronic band structure and so on. Moving the atoms until the forces are zero gives the stable structure and lattice parameter; comparing energies of different structures gives phase stability; supercell calculations give the formation energies of defects such as vacancies; and calculations with applied strain give elastic constants. Because it uses no experimental data, it is also called first-principles calculation, and it is used to predict materials not yet made and to generate data for the CALPHAD method and for interatomic potentials.

The exact form of the exchange-correlation energy is unknown, so approximations such as the local density approximation (LDA) and generalized gradient approximation (GGA) are used. These have limits: band gaps come out smaller than experiment, van der Waals forces are described poorly, and the properties of oxides with localized d or f electrons are sometimes wrong; hybrid functionals and correction methods are used to address them. Ordinary calculations are also of the ground state at 0 K and handle a few hundred atoms. For finite-temperature properties, phonon calculations or molecular dynamics are combined.

faq.q: Are first-principles calculation and DFT the same thing?
faq.a: First-principles calculation is a general term for methods that calculate from the basic laws of quantum mechanics without empirical parameters, and in materials science calculations by DFT are by far the most widely used. The two are therefore often used almost interchangeably, but more rigorous methods of quantum chemistry are also included in first-principles calculation.

faq.q: Why do band gaps come out too small?
faq.a: Because the LDA and GGA exchange-correlation energies retain an error in which an electron interacts with itself, and they do not correctly describe how the energy changes with the number of electrons. Another reason is that the eigenvalues of the Kohn–Sham equations do not, in principle, represent excitation energies. The GW approximation and hybrid functionals improve this.

faq.q: How large a system can be calculated?
faq.a: Ordinary calculations handle tens to hundreds of atoms, and the cost grows roughly as the cube of the number of atoms. Because periodic boundary conditions are used, a crystal can be represented by its unit cell or a supercell of a few hundred atoms, but problems needing large regions, such as dislocations and grain boundaries, are handled by combining DFT with molecular dynamics using interatomic potentials and similar methods.

分子動力学法.desc: A method that numerically integrates Newton's equations of motion for many atoms, using forces obtained from interatomic potentials, to calculate atomic motion over time.

about.p: In molecular dynamics, the initial positions of the atoms and velocities following the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution at the target temperature are given first. Next, the force on each atom is found from an interatomic potential, and the equations of motion are integrated step by step with the Verlet method or similar to update positions and velocities. Repeating this hundreds of thousands to millions of times gives the trajectories of the atoms. To represent the interior of a crystal or liquid, periodic boundary conditions that join opposite faces of the simulation box are used to remove surface effects. The method was begun by Alder and Wainwright in 1957 with a system of hard spheres and is now widely used in materials, chemistry and biomolecules.

Averaging the atomic trajectories over time gives a wide range of properties. The diffusion coefficient, for example, is found from the fact that the mean of the squared distance moved by atoms (the mean square displacement) grows as 6Dt in three dimensions. If it grows by 0.6 nm² in 100 ps, D = 1×10⁻⁹ m²/s, of the same order as in liquid metals. The radial distribution function, which describes the distribution of distances between atoms, reveals the structure of liquids and amorphous materials and can be compared with X-ray and neutron diffraction results. Thermal expansion, elastic constants, melting points, thermal conductivity and the energies of grain boundaries and dislocations can also be calculated.

Solving the equations of motion as they are calculates a state in which the number of atoms, volume and total energy are constant (the NVE ensemble). To hold temperature or pressure constant as in experiments, a thermostat representing energy exchange with a heat bath, or a barostat that changes the size of the box, is added to calculate the NVT or NPT ensemble. Nosé's method, the basis of the widely used Nosé–Hoover method, was proposed in 1984. At first the system is not in equilibrium, so the part before temperature and energy settle is excluded from averages, and averages are taken over a sufficiently long time afterward.

The times that molecular dynamics can follow are usually nanoseconds to microseconds. A simulated tensile test therefore runs at a strain rate of about 10⁸ s⁻¹ (10% strain in 1 ns), more than ten orders of magnitude faster than the roughly 10⁻³ s⁻¹ of experiments. Dislocations have no time to overcome obstacles with the help of thermal activation, so strengths tend to come out higher than in experiments. Rarely occurring events, such as diffusion in solids, are also hard to follow directly, and kinetic Monte Carlo and similar methods are combined. Because the calculation is classical, quantum effects also cause deviations in heat capacity and other properties well below the Debye temperature.

faq.q: What is the difference between molecular dynamics and the Monte Carlo method?
faq.a: Molecular dynamics solves the equations of motion, so it follows atomic motion along real time and also gives dynamic properties such as diffusion and vibrations. Monte Carlo methods such as the Metropolis method choose states according to probabilities to find equilibrium averages; they carry no information about time but can also handle slow changes such as the exchange of atoms.

faq.q: What is first-principles molecular dynamics?
faq.a: It is molecular dynamics in which the forces on the atoms are obtained at each step not from an interatomic potential but from electronic structure calculations such as density functional theory. It can also handle the breaking and forming of chemical bonds, but the computational cost is high, and it handles only a few hundred atoms over times of a few tens of picoseconds.

faq.q: What determines the accuracy of molecular dynamics results?
faq.a: The biggest factor is the accuracy of the interatomic potential: properties the potential cannot describe will not come out correctly. Size effects from too small a simulation box, statistical scatter from short averaging times and integration errors from the time step also matter, so one checks that results do not change when these conditions are varied.

原子間ポテンシャル.desc: A function that gives the energy and forces from the arrangement of atoms. Types include the Lennard-Jones form, the embedded atom method for metals, potentials for covalent bonds and machine-learning potentials.

about.p: An interatomic potential is a function that returns the energy for a set of atomic positions, and the forces are found by differentiating that energy with respect to the atomic positions. Instead of solving for the electronic states, it approximates their result with a convenient formula, so it is far faster than calculations that treat electrons directly and can handle many atoms over long times. The parameters in the formula are fitted to experimental values such as lattice parameter, cohesive energy, elastic constants, vacancy formation energy and stacking fault energy, or to energies and forces from first-principles calculations. What a potential was fitted to determines what it does well and badly.

The simplest form is a pair potential determined only by the distance between two atoms, such as the Lennard-Jones and Morse forms. For ionic crystals, a Coulomb term is added to a short-range repulsive term, and the long-range Coulomb interaction is summed with the Ewald method or similar. To speed up calculations, interactions with atoms beyond a certain distance (the cutoff) are usually neglected. Cutting the Lennard-Jones form at 2.5σ leaves an energy there only about 1.6% of the well depth in magnitude. Each atom then interacts with a limited number of partners, and the computational cost becomes roughly proportional to the number of atoms.

about.h: Forms matched to the type of bonding
about.p: For metals, the embedded atom method (EAM) proposed by Daw and Baskes in the 1980s is widely used, and the modified embedded atom method (MEAM) adds the directionality of bonding. For covalent bonds as in Si and C, bond-order potentials, in which bond strength changes with the number and angles of surrounding bonds, are used, and reactive potentials extend these to handle bond breaking and formation. Even for the same element there are many potentials made for different purposes, and they often give different values for the same property. Properties not included in the fitting are often poorly reproduced, so one checks before use that the potential reproduces the property of interest.

In recent years, machine-learning potentials trained on the energies and forces of many atomic configurations from first-principles calculations have come into wide use. The environment around each atom is turned into numbers by descriptors representing the distributions of distances and angles, and the relation to energy is learned with neural networks or Gaussian process regression. They keep accuracy close to first-principles calculations while being many orders of magnitude faster, though heavier than EAM and similar potentials. When they meet configurations not included in training, they can return plausible but wrong values. Active learning, which finds configurations with large uncertainty during a calculation and adds them to the training, is used as a remedy.

faq.q: What is the difference between an interatomic potential and a force field?
faq.a: They often refer to the same thing; materials science tends to say interatomic potential, while chemistry and biomolecular science tend to say force field. A force field often means a set of functions and parameters for molecules that combines terms for bond lengths, angles, torsions, charges and so on.

faq.q: What do ε and σ in the Lennard-Jones potential represent?
faq.a: ε is the depth of the energy well and represents bond strength, and σ is the distance at which the energy is zero and represents atomic size. For argon, ε divided by the Boltzmann constant is about 120 K (ε ≈ 0.010 eV) and σ is about 0.34 nm, which describe the properties of noble-gas solids and liquids well.

faq.q: How should a potential be chosen?
faq.a: Choose one made by fitting quantities close to the property you want to calculate and validated for it. For dislocations, check whether it reproduces stacking fault energy and elastic constants; for melting, the melting point, using the literature or your own calculations. Databases collecting published potentials and their validation results are also available.

モンテカルロ法.desc: A method that finds answers by repeating probabilistic trials using random numbers. In materials it includes equilibrium calculations by the Metropolis method and kinetic Monte Carlo for following diffusion.

about.p: The Monte Carlo method is a general name for methods that repeat many trials using random numbers and estimate an answer from their average; the name comes from Monte Carlo in Monaco, known for its casino. For example, scattering points uniformly in a square and counting the fraction that fall inside the inscribed circle gives an estimate of π. The error is inversely proportional to the square root of the number of trials N, so making the result ten times more precise takes 100 times as many trials. This rate of error reduction does not depend on the number of variables, so the method is especially powerful for integrals in statistical mechanics, which have a huge number of variables, such as atomic positions.

about.h: Finding equilibrium with the Metropolis method
about.p: The method most often used in materials calculations is the one presented by Metropolis and colleagues in 1953. When trials that change the state slightly are accepted or rejected with probabilities based on the Boltzmann factor, the frequency of the states visited follows the equilibrium distribution at that temperature. In alloys, repeated trials that swap atoms on lattice sites give order-disorder transition temperatures, short-range order, solubility limits and so on. The energy change from a swap is often given by a cluster expansion based on first-principles calculations. Another use is the Potts model, in which numbers distinguishing grains are placed on lattice sites to calculate grain growth.

about.h: The number of trials is not time
about.p: The number of trials in the Metropolis method (Monte Carlo steps) is not real time. The sequence of states is a route for sampling the equilibrium distribution and does not represent the order of physical changes, so it normally cannot be used to discuss rates of change. Even when steps are used in place of time, as in Potts-model grain growth, their correspondence to real time is set by comparison with experiment. The part still influenced by the initial state is excluded from averages, and errors are estimated with the similarity between successive states (correlation) taken into account. When time is needed, the kinetic Monte Carlo method, which advances time by giving a rate for each event, is used.

about.h: Why kinetic Monte Carlo is useful
about.p: The frequency with which an atom in a solid jumps to a neighboring site is ν exp(−E_a/kT); with a vibration frequency ν ≈ 10¹³ s⁻¹, E_a = 1.0 eV and 600 K, it is about 4×10⁴ times per second. An atom vibrates about 2.5×10⁸ times before making one jump, so molecular dynamics, which follows every vibration, can hardly follow diffusion. Kinetic Monte Carlo skips the vibrations and chooses the next event from a list of events and their rates, so it can follow precipitation and the evolution of irradiation defects on scales of seconds or hours. Events not on the list, however, never occur, so the choice of events prepared determines the result.

faq.q: How does the accuracy of the Monte Carlo method change with the number of trials?
faq.a: The statistical error falls as 1/√N with the number of independent trials N. Halving the error takes four times as many trials. If successive states are correlated, the actual number of independent samples is smaller, so errors are estimated by methods such as averaging over blocks.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Metropolis method and kinetic Monte Carlo?
faq.a: The Metropolis method decides whether to accept a trial from the energy difference alone and finds equilibrium averages. Kinetic Monte Carlo uses event rates obtained from activation energies and advances time each time an event is chosen, following changes on the way to equilibrium in real time.

faq.q: Does the quality of the random numbers affect the results?
faq.a: Yes. If the random numbers have periodicity or correlations, averages can be biased or only some states may be visited. Today it is usual to use pseudo-random number generators with long periods that pass statistical tests, such as the Mersenne Twister. In parallel calculations it is also important to use an independent random-number stream for each calculation.

CALPHAD法.desc: A method that models the Gibbs energy of each phase as a function of temperature and composition and calculates multicomponent phase diagrams and phase fractions from a database fitted to experimental and other data.

about.p: In the CALPHAD method, the Gibbs energy of each phase, such as liquid, solid solutions and compounds, is written as a formula in temperature and composition. For a solid solution it is the sum of pure-substance terms, an ideal mixing entropy term and an excess term representing interactions between components, the excess term being expressed as a polynomial in composition (the Redlich–Kister expression). For phases in which atoms occupy fixed sites, such as compounds, sublattice models are used. For the pure-substance terms, common values for each element are defined as a database.

The parameters in the formulas are fitted to experimental data such as phase boundaries, heat capacities, heats of mixing and activities, and to formation energies obtained by first-principles calculations. This work is called thermodynamic assessment, and multicomponent thermodynamic databases are built up by accumulating assessments of binary and ternary systems. Interactions of quaternary and higher order are often neglected as small, which allows extrapolation to multicomponent compositions without experiments. Databases have been developed for practical alloy systems such as steels, nickel-based superalloys, aluminum alloys and solders.

about.h: Uses and limits of the calculations
about.p: Finding the combination of phases and the composition of each phase that minimize the Gibbs energy of the whole system at a given temperature, pressure and composition gives phase diagrams, phase fractions, liquidus temperatures and more. This can be used to narrow down the composition range in which harmful phases do not appear in multicomponent alloys. Combined with data on diffusion mobilities it can also calculate the rates of diffusion and precipitation, and combined with the phase-field method, microstructural change. What is obtained, however, is the equilibrium state, and the accuracy depends on the quality and range of the database assessment.

faq.q: What does CALPHAD stand for?
faq.a: It stands for CALculation of PHAse Diagrams. It was originally the name of a method for calculating phase diagrams, but it now refers to the whole approach of building thermodynamic databases and using them to calculate phase equilibria and thermodynamic quantities.

faq.q: How does it differ from first-principles calculation?
faq.a: First-principles calculation starts from the electronic states and gives quantities such as the energies of compounds at 0 K. The CALPHAD method uses those results and experimental data to determine Gibbs energy formulas and calculates phase equilibria of multicomponent systems at finite temperature. The two do not compete; rather, first-principles calculation supplies part of the data for CALPHAD.

faq.q: Can metastable phases also be calculated?
faq.a: For phases whose Gibbs energy models are in the database, metastable phase diagrams can be calculated by excluding stable phases from the calculation. An example is calculating equilibrium with cementite in steel by excluding graphite. Phases without models, however, cannot be calculated.

フェーズフィールド法.desc: A method that calculates the time evolution of microstructure in the direction that lowers the free energy, treating an order parameter for the phase or crystal orientation as varying smoothly across interfaces. Used for solidification and precipitation.

about.h: Why the interface is given a width
about.p: When calculating microstructural change in solidification or precipitation, treating the interface as a surface of zero thickness requires tracking its position at every moment and imposing temperature or concentration conditions there (such as the Gibbs–Thomson effect). When shapes change in complex ways, as when dendrite arms branch or precipitates join, this tracking becomes very difficult. The phase-field method treats the interface as a region of finite width over which an order parameter changes smoothly and solves the same equations throughout space, so the interface position need not be tracked. The idea rests on Cahn and Hilliard's 1958 theory of the free energy of nonuniform systems.

about.h: What sets interfacial energy and width
about.p: The free energy is written as the sum of a function with two valleys corresponding to the two phases (a double well) and a term in the square of the gradient of the order parameter multiplied by a coefficient κ. With W the height of the barrier of the double well, the interfacial energy is proportional to √(κW) and the interface width to √(κ/W). A steep interface pays in the gradient term, while a gradual one pays by spreading the region sitting on the barrier, so the width is set by the balance between them. Real interfaces are on the order of nanometers wide, but calculations use much wider interfaces, with "thin-interface limit" formulations devised so that results do not depend on the width.

The reliability of phase-field results depends on the property values put in. For the chemical free energy of each phase, thermodynamic databases of the CALPHAD method are often used. Interfacial energy and its anisotropy, interface mobility and diffusion coefficients are obtained from experiments and from molecular dynamics or first-principles calculations. When a precipitate and the matrix have different lattice parameters, elastic strain energy is also added. The arrangement of cuboidal γ' in nickel-based superalloys, and its joining into plates under stress, can be reproduced only when this elastic term is included. When property values are uncertain, it is safer to use the results to read trends with conditions rather than absolute values.

about.h: Fields of use and scale of calculation
about.p: Typical uses are solidification structures and segregation in welding and additive manufacturing, grain growth and coarsening of precipitates in heat treatment, spinodal decomposition and martensitic transformation. Recently it has also been used for fracture analysis, in which a crack is represented by an order parameter to calculate its path, and for phase separation as lithium enters and leaves battery electrodes. Because the interface width must be represented by several grid points, the grid spacing is set by the interface width, and the method mainly handles microstructures on scales from nanometers to micrometers. Three-dimensional calculations need very many grid points, so parallel computing with GPUs is widely used.

faq.q: What is an order parameter?
faq.a: It is a continuous variable that indicates, at each location, which phase or grain the point belongs to. For example, it is 1 in the solid and 0 in the liquid and takes intermediate values at the interface. Sometimes a measurable quantity such as concentration is used, and sometimes a quantity introduced for the calculation, such as one distinguishing grains.

faq.q: Is the interface width used in calculations the same as that of real interfaces?
faq.a: Usually not. Calculating with the real width would need too many grid points, so a much wider interface is used. It is therefore important to check that results do not change when the interface width is varied, or to use formulations devised to cancel the effect of the width.

faq.q: What is the difference between the phase-field method and the cellular automaton method?
faq.a: The phase-field method solves partial differential equations based on free energy to calculate interface shapes in detail. The cellular automaton method updates the states of grid cells by simple rules; it is less accurate but computationally light, and suits large regions such as the grain structure of castings.

有限要素法.desc: A numerical method that divides a body into small elements and solves simultaneous equations with nodal displacements or similar as unknowns to find approximate distributions of stress or temperature.

about.p: The finite element method divides a body of complex shape into a collection of simple elements such as triangles, tetrahedra and hexahedra, and solves the whole by assembling equations approximated element by element. The original differential equations are recast in the form of the principle of minimum energy or virtual work (the weak form), so boundary shapes and differences in material are handled naturally. It grew out of aircraft structural analysis in the 1950s, and the name finite element method is generally traced to its use by Clough in 1960. Today it is used not only for stress but also for heat conduction, electromagnetic fields, fluids and coupled problems in which these interact.

Linear elements, which interpolate the displacement within an element linearly from nodal values, are cheap, but in regions under bending they cannot represent the strain correctly and can come out stiffer than reality (shear locking). Materials whose volume hardly changes, such as rubber or plastically deforming metal, likewise come out too stiff through volumetric locking. Quadratic elements and reduced-integration elements with fewer integration points ease this, but reduced integration can produce zero-energy hourglass-shaped deformation (hourglass modes), which must also be suppressed. Because results depend on the element used, it is important to choose elements suited to the problem.

about.h: What to check before trusting results
about.p: The finite element method only solves the equations under the conditions given; it does not guarantee that those conditions match reality. Large errors often come not so much from the mesh as from the boundary conditions (where and how the body is fixed, and where and how loads are applied) and from the material data. For example, applying a concentrated load at a single point, or using a shape with sharp corners as it is, makes the stress at that point grow as the mesh is refined, so it does not converge to a meaningful value. Results are checked against theoretical solutions for simple shapes and against measurements such as strain gauges.

In materials work it is used heavily for nonlinear problems such as plasticity, creep and thermal stress, not just elasticity. Typical applications are process simulations: material flow and springback in forging and press forming, temperatures and residual stresses in welding and heat treatment, and the solidification of castings. In the crystal plasticity finite element method, each grain is represented by elements and deformation on each slip system is calculated, allowing the development of texture and the uneven distribution of strain among grains to be studied. In composites, it is also used for homogenization, calculating a representative volume element that resolves the fibers and matrix to find the average properties of the whole.

faq.q: What is the difference between the finite element method and the finite difference method?
faq.a: The finite difference method replaces derivatives with differences at the points of a regular grid; it is easy to set up and fast for regions of simple shape. The finite element method allows the shape and size of elements to be chosen freely, so it suits parts of complex shape and problems where the fineness should vary from place to place.

faq.q: How are explicit and implicit methods used?
faq.a: An explicit method finds the next state directly from the current one, so each step is light, but the time step must be very small for stability. An implicit method solves simultaneous equations, so each step is heavy, but large steps can be used. Explicit methods are often used for impact and high-speed forming, and implicit methods for static problems.

faq.q: What material data does the finite element method need?
faq.a: Elastic calculations need Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio; thermal calculations need thermal conductivity, specific heat and density; thermal stress also needs the coefficient of linear expansion. Plasticity needs the stress-strain curve, and creep the constants of the rate equation, entered including their variation with temperature and strain rate.

マテリアルズ・インフォマティクス.desc: An approach that analyzes materials data with machine learning and other methods to help predict properties and choose which materials to try next. Combined with computation and experiment, it speeds up materials development.

about.p: Materials informatics (MI) is a field that speeds up materials research and development with the methods of data science. Counting combinations of elements, compositions, structures and processing conditions, the candidate materials are enormous in number, and they cannot all be tried. So relationships between composition or structure and properties are learned from past experimental and computational data, and promising candidates are narrowed down. Spurred by the Materials Genome Initiative launched in the United States in 2011, the field spread worldwide, and research is advancing in universities and companies in Japan as well. Databases built by automatically running first-principles calculations on large numbers of materials also support this trend.

A typical flow is to collect data, build descriptors, train and evaluate a model, and use its predictions to choose the next experiments or calculations. Descriptors include the means and differences of the electronegativities and atomic radii of the constituent elements, the number of valence electrons and features of the crystal structure; choosing physically meaningful descriptors tends to give good models even with little data. Models include linear regression, random forests, Gaussian process regression and neural networks, and graph neural networks that treat crystal structures directly as graphs are also used. Examining which descriptors are effective can also give clues to the factors that govern a property.

about.h: Data bias and pitfalls in evaluation
about.p: Materials data are biased in that successful results tend to be published while failed ones are rarely recorded. Measurement conditions and specimen preparation also vary between papers, so values for the same material often scatter. In addition, if materials of very similar composition are in both the training and validation sets, the validation error comes out small and the model's ability on new families of materials is overestimated (data leakage). To avoid this, data are split and validated in groups by compositional family or type of compound. When predictions miss, it is also important to suspect the quality of the data rather than the model.

In inverse design, which searches for materials from properties, generative models and optimization methods are used to propose compositions and structures with the desired properties. Research is also advancing on autonomous experiments, in which active learning, alternating prediction and experiment, is combined with robotic synthesis and measurement and run with almost no human intervention. Also in use are process informatics, which learns relationships among processing conditions such as temperature and time, microstructure and properties, and surrogate models, which replace time-consuming simulations with machine-learning models to speed them up. Combining computation, experiment and data is the hallmark of this field.

faq.q: What is the difference between materials informatics and computational materials science?
faq.a: Computational materials science finds properties by solving equations based on physical laws. Materials informatics learns relationships statistically from data obtained by computation and experiment. The two are not opposed; they are combined, for example by generating data with first-principles calculations and searching widely with machine learning.

faq.q: What can be done when data are scarce?
faq.a: Approaches include using a small number of physically meaningful descriptors, using transfer learning to repurpose a model trained on a large dataset for a similar property, and adding computed values as auxiliary data. With little data, Gaussian process regression, which can also show the uncertainty of predictions, is often used.

faq.q: What is a descriptor?
faq.a: It is a representation of the features of a material's composition or structure as a sequence of numbers, so that the material can be input to a machine-learning model; it is also called a feature. Means of elemental properties, crystal symmetry and the like are used, and choosing descriptors physically related to the property to be predicted improves both the accuracy and the interpretability of the model.
